16139-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
This July 1897 number of The Great Round World, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls, leads with England's planned expedition into the Sudan to retake the province of Dongola. Publisher William Beverley Harison sold the paper from West Eighteenth Street in New York, and offered subscribers fine cloth books, from Andersen's fairy tales to Treasure Island, for bringing in new readers.

Inside, short reports turned empire, war, and discovery into news a schoolchild could follow. The paper's mix of current events and book premiums shows how editors tried to hook young readers on the wider world. This issue preserves a child's-eye view of Britain's Sudan campaign and of Victorian children's publishing.
5941-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
An enchanted head alone fills this Don Quixote installment, chapter sixty-two, with other trivial matters that cannot be left untold. Quixote's host in Barcelona is Don Antonio Moreno, a gentleman of wealth and intelligence, very fond of diverting himself in any fair and good-natured way. The head, which seems to answer questions, becomes the center of a polite trick played on knight and squire.

Readers watch Barcelona society amuse itself with Quixote, kindly and cruelly at once, as a mechanical wonder tests his faith in marvels. The single chapter favors drawing-room comedy over road adventure, letting a host's ingenuity mirror Cervantes's own. It suits readers nearing volume two's end, since the head episode shows fame turning Quixote into a spectacle.
8957-the-life-of-samuel-taylor-coleridge:
James Gillman, a surgeon and close friend of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, wrote this life of the poet in 1838, four years after Coleridge's death. Gillman knew the poet in his last years at Highgate and dedicates the work to Joseph Henry Green, Coleridge's faithful friend. The preface praises Izaak Walton's gentle lives as its model.

The book traces Coleridge's youth, his gift, and his troubled later life, with a friend's warmth rather than a critic's cool eye. Its value lies in that closeness: Gillman saw the man, not just the poems. For readers of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner and Kubla Khan, it is a moving first portrait by one who lived beside him.
an-examination-of-phrenology-in-two-lect:
An Examination of Phrenology, published in 1838 by Thomas Sewall, prints two lectures delivered to the students of Columbian College in the District of Columbia in February 1837. The lectures were published by request, and the book runs to some seventy pages with seven pages of plates. Sewall takes the fashionable science of phrenology as his subject and subjects its claims to formal examination before a medical audience.

Lecture courses like these were where phrenology met organized medicine, and the printed form carried the encounter to a wider public. The plates gave readers the anatomical evidence to judge by. The book preserves an early American academic hearing for the head-reading doctrine, taken seriously enough to test in a college hall.
anderson-constitutions-1738:
James Anderson, a Scottish minister in London, rewrote his Constitutions of the Free-Masons for this second edition of 1738. The first edition of 1723 had founded modern Freemasonry on paper. The New Book of Constitutions recasts that work substantially, with a fuller legendary history and revised charges and regulations for the Grand Lodge.

Anderson's history carries Masonry from Adam through the builders of Scripture and the kings of Britain. His charges set the Craft's famous rules on God, government, and conduct. The library holds the 1723 first edition; this 1738 text shows the founding document growing. Every later Masonic constitution descends from Anderson's pages in one of their two forms.
arxiv-2509-00338:
Mikael Henaff, Scott Fujimoto, Michael Matthews, and Michael Rabbat present Scalable Option Learning in 2025, a hierarchical reinforcement learning method built for high-throughput training. Hierarchical methods learn options, which are multi-step skills, to decide over long timescales. Prior approaches had yet to gain from large-scale training.

Their method, SOL, fixes several scaling blocks and reaches about thirty-five times the throughput of prior hierarchical methods. Agents train on thirty billion frames of the complex game NetHack, far past flat agents, with positive scaling trends. Tests on MiniHack and MuJoCo control tasks show the method travels well. Open code accompanies the work for reuse.
arxiv-2509-00538:
Katerina Hlavackova-Schindler and one co-author, Suzana Marsela, tackle telling cause from effect for two continuous variables, with no hidden confounders assumed. Without extra assumptions, direction cannot be settled, so they base a score on Minimum Description Length, the idea that the best model compresses the data most.

Hlavackova-Schindler and Marsela use functions with the density property, meaning they can approximate many shapes on a bounded interval, and prove when their score identifies direction. Noise need not be Gaussian, only low. Their LCUBE method uses cubic splines, smooth piecewise curves, has one tuning choice, and is fast and interpretable. On the Tuebingen cause-effect pairs and other benchmarks, it scores high precision.
arxiv-2509-00638:
Hongyuan Rui and one co-author, Ce Xu, study parity results for cyclotomic Euler sums and multiple polylogarithm functions. Euler sums are infinite series built from harmonic numbers and powers, cyclotomic versions add roots of unity, and parity asks when such sums reduce to simpler known constants.

Rui and Xu define extended trigonometric functions by series and use contour integration, integrating a function around a closed path in the complex plane, to attack the problem. They state parity results for cyclotomic Euler sums of arbitrary order, give explicit formulas for linear and quadratic cases, and add formulas for some cubic sums and multiple polylogarithms. Known results for classical and alternating Euler sums follow as direct corollaries.
arxiv-2509-00938:
Srushti Thakar and Amit A Nanavati explore Fortunato's performance measure for finding communities in networks. The measure counts correctly interpreted pairs of vertices. A pair counts if both vertices share a group and an edge. It also counts if they sit in different groups with no edge. The setting is unweighted, undirected networks.

They give a greedy algorithm, fpGreed, that optimizes the measure at two levels. At vertex level, a vertex joins a group only if the value improves. At group level, two groups merge only on improvement. The algorithm alternates levels until no changes remain. A faster heuristic, fastFp, suits large datasets better. On datasets like YouTube and LiveJournal, fastFp performs well in time and quality.
arxiv-2509-01038:
Mihir Bafna, with two co-authors, presents DynaProt for learning protein dynamics at residue level. Many methods predict static protein structures well. Dynamics, though, are essential for biological function. Simulations are the gold standard in silico for dynamics. Their high cost limits scale for large studies.

DynaProt is a lightweight framework, invariant to rotations and shifts. It predicts rich dynamics descriptors from static structures directly. The problem is cast through multivariate Gaussians, as the title states. Per-residue anisotropy is estimated as a 3 by 3 matrix for local flexibility. Joint scalar values encode pairwise coupling across residues. From these, flexibility is predicted with high accuracy. Full matrix rebuilds enable fast ensemble generation. It uses far fewer parameters than prior methods.
arxiv-2509-01338:
Systems that move through the world in several distinct modes, such as a drone that may hover or dash, are hard to monitor with one prediction range. Francesca Cairoli, with four co-authors, studies runtime forecasting of whether a system will meet a stated temporal logic property, a formal rule about its behavior over time. Fast learned stand-ins give prediction ranges with statistical guarantees, but ignoring modes makes those ranges too wide.

Their method, GenQPM, uses score-based diffusion models, a class of generative models, to capture the system's multi-modal dynamics faithfully. Separate ranges can then reflect each mode's likely satisfaction level, instead of one blurred average. Cairoli and the team aim for timely warnings against predicted rule violations, with ranges sharp enough to guide real intervention rather than blanket caution.
arxiv-2509-01638: Mohammad Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh introduce uniformly S-essential submodules, a new notion in module theory. The short name is u-S-essential. A submodule is u-S-essential when its meet with any other part is u-S-torsion only if that part is u-S-torsion too. The set S is a multiplicative subset of a commutative ring. The pair studies several traits of the notion. They then define u-S-uniform modules and u-S-injective envelopes. Both are characterized through the new u-S-essential submodules.
arxiv-2509-01738:
Andreas Fring works out a concrete case of an extended particle model with endless symmetry. The base Calogero model tracks many particles that pull and push on each other. New versions carry symmetry groups of affine and hyperbolic type, which are endless in size. Fring builds on a hyperbolic extension of a known algebra to make the model explicit with endless root systems.

Summing over endless roots is the main snag, since no sum can run forever in a formula. His fix picks short string stand-ins that span the root space yet keep the symmetry intact. The potentials then come out in closed form, meaning short exact formulas. In a set limit, the model shrinks back to the classic four particle case.
arxiv-2509-02338:
Srinivasan Arunachalam, Davi Castro-Silva, Arkopal Dutt, and Tom Gur wrote a 2025 theoretical computer science paper giving algorithmic versions of a recent breakthrough in additive combinatorics. The underlying theorem describes the structure of sets whose pairwise sums stay small.

For a set inside a binary vector space with a bounded doubling constant, their classical and quantum algorithms run in polynomial time. Each algorithm outputs an explicit subspace, no larger than the set itself. The set can then be covered by a bounded number of shifted copies of that subspace. Turning a pure existence theorem into a working algorithm matters because the structure can now be found, not just promised, which opens doors for coding and learning applications.
arxiv-2509-02838: Felipe Estrada, Alf Onshuus, and David Rincon wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on numerical semigroups that use only two generators. A numerical semigroup is a set of whole numbers closed under addition, built by combining multiples of its generators. The authors study the limit theory of such sets, meaning the first-order logical view of their behavior as the generators vary. In some cases they give a complete axiomatization, a full list of basic truths that settle every statement in that view.
arxiv-2509-02938:
J. D. Norris and D. Blume presented a 2025 method for computing the states of tiny groups of trapped atoms. Systems of three or four atoms sit at the border between few-body and many-body physics. Studying them helps explain how bulk quantum behavior grows out of simple parts.

Their atoms sit in a harmonic trap, a bowl-like potential that holds them in place. Bosons and fermions, the two great families of particles, get different contact interactions in their setup. Fermions need a special form that includes derivative operators, meaning terms based on rates of change. The paper lays out the derivation in detail and checks the numerical scheme against known cases. The authors also discuss how the approach could extend to other small systems.
arxiv-2509-03138:
Bikai Gao and Michał Marczenko asked in 2025 when quarks start to matter inside dense nuclear matter. Deep inside neutron stars, ordinary particles may give way to free quarks, their smaller building blocks. Two pictures compete: quarks filling states above the nucleon surface level, or quarks settling inside that sea instead.

Working in a parity doublet model that tracks a key symmetry of strong interactions, the authors compare the free energy of each picture. The second picture usually wins between the two, yet purely hadronic matter, matter made only of composite particles, stays cheapest well past normal nuclear density. Their self-consistent treatment of a momentum-space shell drives that outcome. One upshot is that quark onset and symmetry restoration need not happen together.
arxiv-2509-03238:
Martin Goubej and 3 co-authors refurbished a kinetic art installation in a 2025 engineering paper. The work, by artist Rafael Lozano-Hemmer, hangs many belts from a ceiling and turns them to follow visitors below. The original system swung and twisted too much, which limited turning speed and weakened the interaction with the audience.

The team upgraded both hardware and motion control. A detailed mathematical model of each flying belt captured its pendulum and torsional behavior. On that model they built input shaping, a method that pre-distorts commands so vibrations cancel themselves out, posed as a convex optimization problem. Tests showed smoother, faster belt motion and better audience response. The project shows how robotics and control engineering can serve large interactive artworks.
arxiv-2509-03438:
Benjamin Heymann and Otmane Sakhi studied a 2025 optimization problem where the goal is a nonlinear function of a total built from many small parts. Because of the nonlinearity, maximizing the average of individual outcomes is not the same problem. A business example is aiming to maximize the chance that an A/B test clears a target uplift, rather than chasing the highest expected payoff.

Sums of many contributions concentrate tightly around their mean, a statistical fact the authors exploit. From it they derive a scalable descent algorithm that targets the true objective directly. The method works at the level of the aggregate outcome, the counterfactual total under a candidate policy. That makes it usable where decision makers care about thresholds and probabilities of success. Such criteria appear in experimentation, marketing, and policy design.
arxiv-2509-03538:
A 2025 research paper by Jiayao Shao and two co-authors surveys rare escapes driven by random noise in dynamical systems. Their setting is a system resting at a stable point that noise occasionally pushes across a saddle, a mountain-pass-like threshold. Realistic forcing is often coloured, meaning correlated over time, rather than pure white noise.

Standard large-deviation theory covers the small-noise limit, but computation struggles with coloured or degenerate forcing and with open-ended time spans. The authors extend the framework using filters that colour white noise, plus a Hamiltonian control method for degenerate cases. Their new Method of Division approximates rare transition paths and the rates at which escapes happen. Two demonstrations follow: a double-well system turned upside down, and a simplified roll model for a capsizing ship.
arxiv-2509-03638:
David Alvear and two co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to two robots cooperatively grasping and carrying one object through tight spaces. Deciding where each robot should grip is hard when walls and obstacles restrict how the pair can move. A grasp that works in open space may fail completely in a cramped room.

Their framework centres on a Conditional Embedding model made of two neural networks. Grip configurations are mapped into an embedding space, a learned coordinate system where vectors summarise each option. Those vectors are then used to pick grips that let both robots transport the object together. Training covers many environment maps and object shapes, with negative sampling teaching the model to reject unworkable grips. Simulations across varied settings show reliable selection, and tests on a physical robot platform confirm the approach works in practice.
arxiv-2509-03738:
Bahareh Tolooshams and two co-authors consider sparse autoencoder neural operators, a new tool for mechanistic interpretability of neural networks, in a 2025 research paper. Sparse autoencoders unpack a network's internal activations into a small set of concepts, helping researchers see what a model has learned. Standard versions treat each concept as one number inside a fixed-size vector.

Their version works in function spaces instead of fixed vectors, and each concept becomes a function with a shape. Two kinds of sparsity act together: concept sparsity picks active concepts, and domain sparsity controls where each is expressed. A Fourier neural operator version writes concepts as operators acting in the frequency domain, suiting spatially structured data. On vision data, the method learns localised patterns and uses concepts more efficiently than standard autoencoders. It also adapts to changed domain sizes and resolutions beyond training, where standard versions fail. A lifting step speeds optimisation.
arxiv-2509-03838:
A new family of charged black holes in five-dimensional Gauss-Bonnet gravity is examined in a 2025 physics paper by Moisés Bravo-Gaete and three co-authors. Gauss-Bonnet gravity extends Einstein's theory with a curvature term that matters in higher dimensions. Their solutions add a nonlinear electric charge to known configurations whose horizons can take any Thurston geometry, the eight standard shapes for three-dimensional spaces.

Constraints on the parameter space mark which black holes are physically viable, checked against the energy conditions that reasonable matter should obey. The first law of black hole thermodynamics is proved for this setting, linking mass change to temperature, entropy, and charge. Holographic techniques then characterise the direct-current conductivities of the dual theory for each horizon geometry. A critical temperature appears, signalling phase transitions in the holographic system. Limiting cases are explored to connect the new family with known black holes.
arxiv-2509-04338:
JiYuan Wang and seven co-authors turn an image editor into a geometry estimator in a 2025 research paper. Dense geometry estimation assigns every pixel a depth and a surface direction. Earlier work borrowed priors from text-to-image generators, but editing models work image-to-image, a closer match for the task. A systematic comparison shows editors carry built-in structural priors, refine them stably during fine-tuning, and finish ahead of generators.

Their framework, FE2E, adapts a Diffusion Transformer editor with a steadier training objective and a number encoding that preserves precision. Depth and surface normals come out together in one pass, each supervising the other. Without extra training data, zero-shot results jumped sharply, beating a leading rival trained on far more data.
arxiv-2509-04538:
Ao Liu and seven co-authors train a deep learning detector for dark matter marks inside gravitational waves in a 2025 research paper. Compact dark matter objects can lens passing waves, stamping wave-optics diffraction patterns when the lens is small. Standard detection is slow and prone to waveform errors. Their Wavelet Convolution Detector mixes multi-scale wavelet analysis, which reads time-frequency structure, inside residual blocks tuned for interference patterns. Training data mimicked dark matter masses and lensing probabilities with care.

On fake binary black hole events the detector scored high accuracy, rising further at strong signal levels. One trained model handled wide lens mass ranges without retraining. Compared with Bayesian inference it runs vastly faster, suiting third-generation detectors.
arxiv-2509-04638:
Timing a particle to tens of picoseconds is the goal behind detectors tested by Tao Yang, lead author with eleven co-authors, in a 2025 instrumentation paper. They characterise 4H silicon carbide low gain avalanche detectors, using beta particles from a strontium-90 source. Such detectors give fast signals for precision tracking.

The devices reached a time resolution comparable to standard silicon versions. The authors find limited charge generation is the main current limit. Because the material tolerates higher voltage and carriers drift faster, they argue better charge collection could let these detectors match or surpass silicon timing.
arxiv-2509-04738:
In an ultracold Fermi gas, how strongly atoms interact in a p-wave channel changes with temperature. Kenta Nagase, lead author with three co-authors, measure that dependence in a 2025 atomic physics paper. They work with lithium-6 atoms in a harmonic trap near a p-wave Feshbach resonance, a tuning point for interactions.

From the anisotropic pattern of dissociated molecules, they separate three magnetic components of the resonance and determine a contact for each. Peak contacts grow as the gas gets colder relative to its Fermi temperature. Their trends match estimates from a virial expansion, informing the thermodynamics of such gases.
arxiv-2509-05038:
Four small planets around cool M dwarf stars are discovered and validated in a 2025 astronomy paper by S. Yalçınkaya, lead author with sixty-four co-authors. The TESS space mission found the transiting planets, which range from super-Earth size to slightly larger than Neptune. Ground-based multi-colour observations support the validation.

Combined data constrain each planet's size, orbit, and equilibrium temperature. One planet sits on a short orbit hotter than the others, while an outer companion lies near the inner edge of its star's habitable zone. The authors use statistical validation and a dedicated search pipeline to confirm the four worlds.
arxiv-2509-05138:
Surface states in a non-Hermitian Weyl semimetal behave in a way that breaks the usual bound-versus-free distinction. Shuxin Lin, lead author with five co-authors, identify the mediating states in a 2025 condensed matter paper. A non-Hermitian chiral anomaly was known to affect those surface states, generalising the ordinary quantum anomaly.

The authors show anomaly inflow is carried by continuum Landau modes, eigenstates that are spatially localised yet have a continuous spectrum. The number of surface modes scales with sample volume rather than area, tied to the modes' unusual multiplicity. Their other properties match field theory predictions, and metamaterials may allow experimental tests.
arxiv-2509-05238:
Numerical noise from training a brain scan model becomes a resource in a 2025 paper by Inés Gonzalez-Pepe and three co-authors. Deep learning tools now segment brain images fast, but small random changes during training can shift the results in ways users rarely measure.

Working with the FastSurfer model, the team shows its training uncertainty exceeds that of the older FreeSurfer tool in outer brain regions. Changing the random seed mimics that noise closely. They then use many seed variants together as extra training data, which improves brain age prediction. Uncertainty, usually treated as a flaw, here becomes a measurable risk and a useful source of variation.
arxiv-2509-05338:
A living plant wired to a small robot becomes a single agent in Plantbot, a 2025 system paper by Atsushi Masumori and five co-authors. Language model modules handle sensing, vision, dialogue, and action separately, each running on its own schedule and passing natural language messages to the others.

Soil moisture, temperature, and camera context are translated into words that coordinate the whole system. Plant states thereby turn into robot movements, closing a loop between sensing and action that gives the hybrid a basic form of agency. The design points toward a new model of artificial life built from loose, language-linked parts. Biological and artificial components each keep their own character while acting together.
arxiv-2509-05538:
Precise masses of krypton isotopes push the edge of a deformed nuclear region, in a 2025 nuclear physics paper by D. Lunney and nineteen co-authors. Around mass one hundred and neutron number sixty, nuclei abruptly become collective and deformed, and where that region ends at low proton number was unclear.

Masses of three krypton isotopes were measured with the ISOLTRAP spectrometer at CERN, one of them for the first time and another far more precisely than before. Compared with advanced theory, the new mass surface suggests collective behaviour persists for the krypton chain. The supposed low-proton-number boundary of the deformed region therefore looks blurred rather than sharp.
arxiv-2509-05838:
Whether TikTok actually shields young accounts from harmful videos is tested in a 2025 paper led by Linda Xue with five co-authors. The platform claims age-based moderation limits what youth accounts see. The authors set out to audit that claim from the outside, as ordinary users would experience it.

They gathered thousands of videos, labeled them harmful or not, and browsed through age-specific test accounts using both passive watching and active engagement. Adult and youth accounts ended up seeing nearly the same mix, a result the authors read as weak age-based enforcement. They also graded large language and vision-language models at spotting harmful clips, finding precision and scale still hard. Stronger youth safeguards and clearer moderation reporting are their closing call.
arxiv-2509-06038:
Spin waves in magnetic materials can be retuned by the material's own inertia, show Subhadip Ghosh and two co-authors in a 2025 paper. Magnetic inertia, the lag of magnetization behind a driving field, was recently confirmed in two-sublattice ferromagnets like CoFeB and permalloy. The authors include the full inertia tensor, split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts, inside linear spin-wave theory.

The spectrum then holds two precessional and two inertial magnon bands, and the upper precessional band crosses the lower inertial one inside the Brillouin zone. Cross-sublattice and chiral parts of the tensor act as knobs for the band structure. Propagation also turns nonreciprocal, different forward and backward, where a known interaction acts, and chiral inertia alone can create that asymmetry. The findings open a route to engineered magnon transport.
arxiv-2509-06538:
Spin waves that travel one way more easily than the other are reported for layered magnets by Quanchao Du and four co-authors in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Such nonreciprocal magnons matter for spintronics, which uses spin rather than charge in devices. Finding them in layered antiferromagnets, materials whose neighboring layers have spins pointing against each other, had remained out of reach.

The study covers a family of honeycomb compounds with vanadium, phosphorus, and sulfur, selenium, or tellurium. Alongside an internal coupling that favors twisting magnetic order, the authors show that layer count, coupling between layers, and coupling among the waves themselves all shape the one-way behavior. Most strikingly, the effect varies in an asymmetric repeating pattern as the overall magnetic direction turns. That pattern offers a new experimental way to read off hidden antiferromagnetic order in very thin samples.
arxiv-2509-06638:
One reusable stand-in model for distillation columns, across many chemicals and designs, is built by Martin Bubel and two co-authors in a 2025 chemical engineering paper. Surrogate models speed up process optimization when full simulators are too slow. Most, however, are trained for one fixed chemical system and a narrow range of conditions.

The key is a new model-fluid representation powered by machine learning, which lets the team generate more than a million training samples. The single surrogate then generalizes over column specifications and over the whole space of uniform three-component vapor-liquid mixtures. A case study on entrainer distillation, a separation that adds a helper substance, shows the model screening and ranking candidate entrainers with far less computing than rigorous optimization. Accuracy checks support its practical use.
arxiv-2509-06938:
Why transformer models hallucinate is traced to their internal concept patterns by Praneet Suresh and four co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Hallucinated output undermines trust in high-stakes uses. The authors probe pretrained transformers with sparse autoencoders, tools that extract readable concepts from internal activations, while controlling how unstructured the input is.

As input information grows less structured, the number of semantic concepts the model uses grows too. Under rising uncertainty, the model starts activating coherent but input-insensitive concepts, and hallucinated output follows. With pure noise as input, a wide variety of meaningful concepts still trigger robustly, and steering experiments confirm those activations do real work. Hallucinations in the output can be predicted reliably from concept patterns in intermediate layers. The findings inform safety work, attack surfaces, and automatic measurement of hallucination risk.
arxiv-2509-07038:
Singing voices whose loudness a user can sculpt over time are synthesized by Yerin Ryu and two co-authors in a 2025 audio technology paper. Singing voice synthesis has reached high audio quality, but most systems model sound probabilistically, leaving attributes like dynamics imprecise. Dynamics, the moment-to-moment loudness variation, carry much of a performance's expression.

The model is conditioned explicitly on energy sequences taken from ground-truth spectrograms, which cuts annotation costs while improving control. A phoneme-level version of the energy sequence makes the control user-friendly: loudness can be set sound by sound. The authors describe this as the first attempt at user-driven dynamics control in singing synthesis. Experiments cut the error of the produced energy sequences by over half compared with baselines and energy-predictor models, with no loss in synthesis quality.
arxiv-2509-07138:
On-sky tests of the Keck telescope's NIRC2 camera are reported by Rachel Bowens-Rubin and 4 co-authors in 2025. NIRC2 is a near-infrared imager used to photograph planets and brown dwarfs next to bright stars, a task called high-contrast imaging. Three effects that may limit its performance at wavelengths of 3 to 5 micrometers are put under the microscope.

First, the team measures how much light a vortex coronagraph, a device that blocks starlight, lets through in two filters. Second, using a recent electronics upgrade, they find the sky background changes in under 30 seconds, which could improve background removal. Third, they track how the image derotator makes the background uneven across the frame. Practical advice for future surveys ends the report, so observers can plan around each effect.
arxiv-2509-07238:
Pranav Pawar and 5 co-authors report a tuning study in 2025 for open-source language models on math reasoning tasks. Getting the best from such models depends on settings like temperature, which controls randomness, and how many reasoning steps the model may take. The team searched these settings in a systematic way for five large models, including Qwen, Llama, DeepSeek, Mixtral, and Yi variants.

Their optimized setups cut computing cost by about 29 percent on average and sped up replies by about 24 percent, while keeping answers correct. Lower temperatures and fewer reasoning steps, four to six, helped most. DeepSeek-V3 reached the highest accuracy in their tests, while one Mixtral model gave the cheapest correct answers. One caution: every claim rests on their own benchmark runs, so other tasks may favor different settings.
arxiv-2509-07438:
Ya-Chuan Hsu and 3 co-authors study when a spoken assistant should talk in time-critical help settings in a 2025 paper. Alerts and vibrations grab attention fast but leave the person to interpret the scene alone, which can delay action. Spoken instructions carry context, yet speaking takes time, listening takes time, and acting takes still more, so a helpful message can arrive too late.

The team frames the timing-versus-detail trade-off as a sequential decision problem using an augmented-state Markov Decision Process, a model that tracks an enlarged state. Their framework pairs reinforcement learning with an automatically generated taxonomy dataset, a labeled catalogue of message types. In tests with synthetic humans, success rates rose by over 40 percent against methods that ignore timing delays. The lesson applies to assistive driving and other settings where seconds decide outcomes.
arxiv-2509-07538:
Asking a question out loud about a scanned document is natural, but no system had handled speech queries over document images end to end. Peijin Xie and 5 co-authors built TextlessRAG to fill that gap, in a 2025 research paper. Their system takes spoken questions, searches a large collection of document images, and generates answers. It skips speech recognition, text synthesis, and optical character recognition entirely.

A layout-aware reranking step refines which documents get retrieved. Experiments show gains in both speed and accuracy over text-based pipelines. The team also released the first bilingual speech-document dataset, pairing Chinese and English voice queries with multimodal document content. Removing the text middlemen cuts error build-up between stages. The work opens document question answering to hands-free and low-literacy settings.
arxiv-2509-07638:
Milton C. Lopes Filho and 1 co-author survey the singularity problem for the Navier-Stokes and Euler equations in a 2025 note written in Portuguese. The Navier-Stokes equations govern fluid motion, and whether their solutions can develop singularities, points where values blow up in finite time, is a Millennium Prize problem. The note gives a bird's-eye view of the history and current state of that research.

The text presents the content of a plenary talk delivered by Helena Nussenzveig Lopes at the 2024 biannual meeting of the Brazilian Mathematical Society. It covers the general problem of singularities in fluid dynamics alongside the corresponding question for the Euler equations, the frictionless special case. As a survey talk in written form, it aims to orient mathematicians across fields on what is known, what is conjectured, and why the problem resists solution.
arxiv-2509-07738:
V. Patkóš and 1 co-author compute energy levels of antiprotonic atoms with high precision in a 2025 paper. An antiprotonic atom replaces an electron with an antiproton that orbits a nucleus. Such atoms probe strong charge and nuclear structure. The framework is nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics. It works even for large nuclear charge here. For rotational states, the expansion parameter stays small.

Finite nuclear mass is included exactly, up to a stated order. Electron vacuum polarization potentials enter in a nonperturbative way, at one and two loops. They enter both the main Hamiltonian and the leading relativistic correction. The results for the stated states are described as the most accurate to date. A user-friendly Mathematica code, PbarSpectr, is released with the work. It can be improved by adding further effects. Rotational states of such atoms can even help pin down nuclear charge radii.
arxiv-2509-07938:
GJ 436 b, a warm Neptune on a tilted, eccentric orbit, is modelled across deep time by M. Attia and 7 co-authors in a 2025 exoplanet paper. The planet's strange architecture hints at a violent past and a possible unseen companion. Their code, JADE, follows atmosphere and orbit together over secular timescales, starting from present-day observations.

Inside the model, starlight slowly evaporates the atmosphere while gravitational cycles driven by an outer perturber pump the orbit's shape and tilt, so each process feeds back on the other. Matching today's planet constrains how it migrated and what companion could have driven it. Coupled modelling of this kind separates plausible histories from stories the surviving planet rules out.
arxiv-2509-08338:
Jihyun Moon and Charmgil Hong improve skin cancer checks by letting a model consult like cases in a 2025 medical AI paper. Early, correct calls on melanoma save lives. Image networks read skin photos well, but they skip the patient's clinical facts. Broad vision-language models use both, yet lack medical sharpness.

Their fix is retrieval. For each new case, the system finds past cases that look and read alike. Those cases go into the prompt that guides the call. No retraining is needed. Scores rose sharply in their tests. Doctors build trust in a diagnosis the same way, by match to cases they have seen. A tool that shows its matches earns trust faster.
arxiv-2509-08538:
Garry Yang and 7 co-authors present MESH, a benchmark for hallucinations in large video models, in a 2025 paper. Video models can describe objects or actions that are not really there. Existing tests rely heavily on manual sorting and miss how people naturally watch video.

MESH uses question answering with binary and multiple choice items, including traps. It moves from basic objects to finer features and then to subject and action pairs. That bottom-up order mirrors human viewing. Tests show models handle basic objects well but fail more on fine detail and long videos. The benchmark gives a systematic way to find these errors.
arxiv-2509-08638:
A specialized AI model may pass its tests yet fail in some corner of its operating world that nobody probed. Rebecca Martin, Jay Patrikar, and Sebastian Scherer present AutoODD in a 2025 research paper. AutoODD uses language-model agents to audit black-box models automatically. Its job is mapping the operational design domain, the conditions a model can handle safely.

The agents generate semantically meaningful test cases and record the model's responses. Their search happens on a low-dimensional map built from text embeddings. A Bayesian, uncertainty-aware model of the failure landscape guides where to probe next. Demonstrations cover a digit-recognition setup with missing digits and a real vision system watching for aerial intruders. Automated red teaming like this could make safety audits for high-risk AI far cheaper and more thorough.
arxiv-2509-08938:
Emile Avérous and 1 co-author study FK-percolation with random edge weights near the critical point in a 2025 paper. In percolation, edges open by chance and form clusters. Here each edge weight is itself drawn at random, centered close to the threshold.

If the fixed weight model looks critical in a small window, the random one tends to look critical in a wider window, up to log scale fixes. That claim rests on a conjectured law about critical exponents. A plain Bernoulli case is also solved: with weights centered at one half, the random model looks critical at large scales with near certainty. Fixed random settings are the focus.
arxiv-2509-09138:
Akira Matsui and 3 co-authors study exploration and exploitation behavior in live streaming in a 2025 paper. Users both explore new creators and exploit favorites by returning to them. Real time interaction sets live platforms apart from on-demand services, but its effect was unclear.

Two years of data from a large live streaming platform are analyzed. Users do show exploration and exploitation behavior, but with a longer exploration period than on-demand users. Daily rhythms and other external factors shape the dynamics and user loyalty. The authors argue platform design must balance the two behaviors carefully. Timely engagement and retention strategies for creators and developers follow.
arxiv-2509-09438:
Zhaohan Zhang and 2 co-authors present GrACE in 2025, a method that lets a large language model state how confident it is while it writes. Trustworthy confidence matters where errors are costly, such as medicine and finance. Older approaches either demand heavy extra computing or give scores that track real accuracy poorly.

GrACE reads confidence from how close the model's final hidden state sits to a special token added to its vocabulary, then fine-tunes that signal toward correctness. Tests on open-ended generation found the strongest separation and calibration without extra sampling or helper models. Two test-time strategies using the score also raised final accuracy while needing fewer samples.
arxiv-2509-10238:
Xijin Chen and three co-authors rethink early cancer drug trials in this 2025 statistics paper. In phase I dose-finding studies, the goal is to learn which dose is safe, using only small groups of patients. Targeted and immune therapies make predictive biomarkers valuable, since a marker measured repeatedly might warn of toxicity early.

The authors build a joint model that ties repeated biomarker values to the binary toxicity outcome and uses both to guide dose choices. Simulations against the standard continual reassessment method show the joint model eases estimation troubles that small samples cause and raises the share of trials picking the right dose. Still, they warn that the sheer scarcity of early-phase data sets a hard limit that no frequentist method fully escapes.
arxiv-2509-10338:
Arup Kumar Marik, Basabdatta Palit, and Sadananda Behera address a trust problem in quantum key distribution networks in this 2025 paper. QKD promises security guaranteed by physics. Its signals fade with distance, though. Optical networks therefore need trusted repeater nodes to stretch coverage. Most designs simply assume each repeater and its key server is fully trustworthy. That ignores software exploits and insider threats.

Their placement method gives each candidate node a trust score. It folds that score into a shortest-path search through link weights. Nodes are then ranked by a blend of two centrality measures. On a reference metro topology, the method covered notably more shortest paths than degree-based selection. It used about the same number of repeaters, roughly eight. The work points to a safer way to choose where quantum trust anchors belong.
arxiv-2509-10438:
André Grossi Fonseca and five co-authors turn phase hunting into an optimization problem in this 2025 paper. New quantum phases have changed physics and technology again and again. Finding them usually depends on slow theory or lucky accidents. Their framework defines a target-phase loss function. The function is differentiable. It encodes the fingerprints of a desired quantum state as a score. Searching Hamiltonian space then becomes gradient descent.

The method works with most many-body solvers. It covers symmetry-broken and topological orders alike. The team demonstrates it on spinless fermions on a kagome lattice. Guided by the loss, exact diagonalization uncovers two fractional Chern insulators. One is an unusual Abelian case. Its band geometry breaks the usual Landau-level mold. The other is non-Abelian. Pure finite-range interactions hold it together. Both are first explicit examples of their kind.
arxiv-2509-10538:
Rumeng Li and 2 co-authors present DualAlign, a method for making synthetic clinical data, in this 2025 paper. Real health records are locked down by privacy rules, rare conditions have little labeled data, and observed data carry biases. Language models can write fluent clinical text, but fluent is not the same as clinically believable.

DualAlign aligns generation on two sides: statistics, by conditioning on patient demographics and risk factors, and meaning, by guiding text with real symptom paths over time. Using Alzheimer's disease as the test case, models fine-tuned on a mix of DualAlign output and human-labeled data beat models trained on either alone. The authors note the method still misses long-range complexity.
arxiv-2509-10638:
Black holes eating faster than the classic Eddington limit are simulated by Lizhong Zhang and five co-authors in this 2025 paper. It is the second in a series on radiation and magnetohydrodynamics around stellar-mass black holes. The simulations couple relativistic fluid equations to radiation transport, tracked angle by angle. Runs span several accretion rates, two spins, and two magnetic field layouts.

Super-Eddington flows always puff into thick disks held up by radiation pressure. Light from the inner disk blasts outflows into cone-shaped funnels. Photons get trapped, and efficiency stays low. Angular momentum rides outward mainly on magnetic stress. Jets split into two families. Strong ones clear the funnel and beam radiation out. Weak ones leave it clogged, giving observers a different face. The models speak to ultraluminous X-ray sources and other extreme feeders.
arxiv-2509-10738:
N. Joshi and O. Meusel characterize a small electric space thruster in this 2025 paper. The RIT-2.5 is a radiofrequency ion thruster, the kind of low-power engine considered for steering nanosatellites. The team ran it in a vacuum facility and measured it with light spectroscopy, a Faraday cup, and an energy analyzer, avoiding probes inside the plasma itself.

Computer simulations of the discharge ran alongside the tests. Matching simulated and measured ion energy spectra let the authors infer the plasma density, a value their instruments could not reach directly. Beam energy spread depended strongly on that density and on electron temperature. The paired approach offers a non-intrusive route to tuning such thrusters and a test case for plasma codes.
arxiv-2509-10938:
Artem Stoyan is the sole author of this 2025 mathematical physics paper. It studies blowup relations. These are equations obeyed by the partition functions of certain five-dimensional gauge theories. The theories are supersymmetric and carry four flavors of matter.

Stoyan studies how a symmetry group acts on the full set of relations. He shows that each relation's whole-number parameters match the weights of a Lie algebra. He also traces that action to a symmetry of the partition function itself. The relations then yield two-term identities. Those identities govern the tau functions of the q-Painlevé VI equation. That discrete equation sees wide use in mathematical physics.
arxiv-2509-11138:
Kazem Rezazadeh and 2 co-authors give dark matter a new equation of state in this 2025 paper. In the standard picture, dark matter barely presses on its surroundings. Their model lets its pressure grow with the square of its density, an effect that only matters in the dense early universe. That change alters how the young cosmos expanded.

The authors rewrite the background expansion equations for the model, then track how matter clumps grew under it. They compare both the expansion history and the growth of structure against current observations out to high redshift. The model stays consistent with the background data while leaving a distinct mark on structure growth, which the authors offer as a fresh angle on standing cosmological tensions.
arxiv-2509-11238:
Dongming Jin and 7 co-authors present UserTrace, a system that writes user-level requirements from code, in this 2025 paper. Software stays maintainable when its requirements are clear and linked to the code that implements them. Existing tools mostly summarize code for developers, unit by unit, and ignore how projects evolve. What end users need — plain statements of what the software does for them — is rarely generated.

UserTrace runs four cooperating agents, reviewing, searching, writing, and verifying, through a three-stage process over a repository. In comparative tests it produced requirements judged more complete, correct, and helpful than a known baseline, and it recovered links between requirements and code more precisely than five rival methods. A user study backed the approach.
arxiv-2509-11338:
Rok Cestnik and Erik A. Martens present a lean way to learn the behavior of dynamical systems from data in this 2025 paper on next-generation reservoir computing. Their implementation projects delayed measurements through a pseudorandom nonlinear map, so the feature size can be chosen freely instead of being tied to the size of the observations.

The models were tested on rebuilding attractors and estimating bifurcation diagrams from partial, noisy measurements. A small amount of noise during training acted like a regularizer, keeping long autonomous runs stable where plain regression drifted. Across the tests the models stayed reliable over long rollouts and generalized beyond their training data. Because the method gives explicit control of the state during prediction, the authors see it as a natural fit for surrogate models and digital twins.
arxiv-2509-11538:
In this 2025 paper on economic theory, Jiyuan Lyu works alone. He revisits a famous claim about profit rates. The Okishio theorem says cost-cutting progress must lift the profit rate. Lyu asks if this survives careful costing of fixed capital. Fixed capital means plant and machines that last many rounds.

Lyu argues that past fixed-capital versions mixed two things. Depreciation was folded into profit. Cost checks then used capitalized cost, not operating cost. The annuity method pulls the two apart. Two thresholds appear once they are split. One governs whether firms adopt a new technique. The other governs which way the profit rate moves. When capital lasts past one period, a gap opens between them. Inside the gap, firms adopt the cheaper technique yet the profit rate falls.
arxiv-2509-11638:
Yongzhe Lyu and 3 co-authors improve diffusion-based image inpainting by fixing its starting noise, in a 2025 computer vision paper. Inpainting fills masked regions of an image. Random initial noise can inject mismatched semantic content into those regions, biasing results away from the unmasked surroundings.

Their method, IS-Diff, needs no training. It samples initial seeds from unmasked areas so the noise imitates the masked region's distribution, setting a harmonious direction for generation. A dynamic mechanism then detects badly unharmonious inpainting in intermediate stages and adjusts the initialization strength accordingly. Tests on standard and large-mask tasks across three datasets, covering faces, objects, and scenes, showed effectiveness on all metrics against leading methods.
arxiv-2509-11838:
Navid Hashemi and six co-authors make safety guarantees for segmentation networks less timid. This 2025 machine learning paper treats networks that label every pixel of an image. They drive medical imaging and self-driving perception. Robustness under uncertainty is essential. Probabilistic checks scale badly to high-dimensional tasks. Their guarantees come out so cautious they are nearly useless.

Their framework is architecture-agnostic. Conformal inference supplies the base. A novel clipping block trims the excess caution of past methods. The guarantees stay provable. Large segmentation models were tested on street scenes, retinal scans, and lung scans. Reliable safety guarantees came with far less conservatism than the state of the art. The code is public.
arxiv-2509-11938:
Chemical makeup in two nearby star clusters is the subject of a 2025 paper by Deusalete Vilar and 10 co-authors. They study fourteen cool M dwarf stars and six warmer G dwarfs in the Hyades and Coma Berenices clusters. Open clusters like these are useful test sites because their stars formed together from the same cloud.

The team used high-resolution near-infrared spectra from the APOGEE survey, along with model atmospheres and a radiation code, to measure each star. They derived amounts for thirteen elements, from carbon and oxygen to iron. Cool and warm stars in each cluster gave nearly the same mix, which supports using faint M dwarfs to trace cluster chemistry. Their overall metal levels also matched earlier published values.
arxiv-2509-12338:
A sensor network can measure a shared quantity without any node revealing its own reading. A. de Oliveira Junior and seven co-authors prove that feat possible in 2025 for continuous-variable quantum sensors, where each node stamps a local phase onto a shared entangled light state.

Only the average phase comes out, and it can be read with precision that improves at the Heisenberg limit as photon numbers grow, while every individual phase stays hidden. A no-go result shows complete privacy is impossible for three or more parties with finite-energy Gaussian light, making the two-party case special. Losses and displacements trade accuracy against privacy.
arxiv-2509-12438:
Neutron stars ring like bells after a disturbance, and their fundamental tone depends on whether the pressure inside pushes equally in all directions. José D. V. Arbañil and five co-authors compute that tone in 2025 inside full general relativity, letting the stellar fluid be anisotropic with a profile that fades at the center and the surface.

The star's matter follows an equation of state stitched from nuclear calculations and quantum chromodynamics. Both the oscillation frequency and the tidal deformability, the star's stretch under a companion's pull, shift noticeably as anisotropy grows. The authors then test how those shifts line up with the famous gravitational wave event GW170817.
arxiv-2509-12538:
Instrumental variable studies rest on a quiet assumption. One person's treatment does not leak onto another's outcome. Classrooms and villages break that assumption daily. Didier Nibbering and one co-author rebuild the method for that reality in 2025. They define direct and spillover effects. A policymaker can read both.

Their framework allows two kinds of spillover. The instrument can spill onto treatment. Treatment can spill onto outcomes. Several peers per person are allowed. The classic monotonicity assumptions on response and selection are widened. That yields informative bounds on the policy-relevant effects. No shape or direction for the interference is imposed. The results extend program evaluation to the social settings where programs run.
arxiv-2509-12738:
Toke Meier Carlsen and Eun Ji Kang give in 2025 an exact formula for a key invariant of algebras built from Boolean systems with extra relative rules. These algebras encode moves on sets with labels, and their invariants sort them into types.

They also name clear makers for the second invariant group. Next they show each fixed ideal is close, in a set sense, to an algebra of the same kind. When the base system meets a known split rule, the algebra can be lifted in a clean way. For split, endless algebras they prove a rank trait holds. The work firms up how these algebras are classed.
arxiv-2509-13038:
Philippe Balbiani adds a diamond step in 2025 to intuitionistic logics of belief and knowledge with shared knowledge. The base tongues came from Artemov and Protopopescu and used box steps alone. Shared knowledge means what a whole group can pool.

Main results prove completeness for both enriched logics. Each logic is matched to its right relational meaning. The belief form and the knowledge form are both covered with the new diamond present. The work rounds out how hunch-based reasoning can treat group knowledge without classic shortcuts. Formal readers gain exact semantics for these systems.
arxiv-2509-13138:
Paul Garnier, Vincent Lannelongue and Elie Hachem train flow nets from coarse meshes upward in 2025. Graph nets can stand in for fluid models, but fine meshes with vast node counts cost too much to train on at once.

Only the training data grade changes over time; the model stays fixed. Steps move from very coarse to mid and then fine meshes. Final skill matches direct fine training. Total clock time falls by up to half. On sets where the model lacks room to learn the physics, the staged path breaks past flat spots that block direct training.
arxiv-2509-13238:
C. Ramya and Pratik Shastri prove in 2025 that near-best ordering for read-once branching programs is hard to approximate. Program width hinges on variable order. Past hardness leaned on a strong set-expansion guess.

Any constant-factor approximation now proves NP-hard for circuit inputs, with no extra guess. Testing orbit membership for sparse inputs against width-bounded programs is also NP-hard. Over zero-characteristic fields the result holds for homogeneous inputs too. Hardness persists even for quadratic forms, the lowest non-trivial degree. Dense program classes gain their first membership hardness marks.
arxiv-2509-13338:
Hassan Gharoun, Mohammad Khorshidi and three co-authors retrieve nearby proof cases in 2025 for doubt-aware decisions without a global cutoff. Fixed entropy cutoffs tag too many sound calls as doubtful, or miss bold errors. Per-case proof offers a calmer rule.

Near cases in embedding space supply predictive spreads. Dempster-Shafer fusion joins them into a belief that sets the per-case bar. Decisions stay transparent since proof cases are explicit. Image sets with strong backbones show fewer bold errors at a fair review load. Few proof cases suffice; more add little.
arxiv-2509-13638:
Meesum Qazalbash, Muhammad Zeeshan, and Richard O'Shaughnessy present GWKokab in a 2025 gravitational wave paper. GWKokab is a software framework for learning the population patterns of merging black holes and neutron stars. Detectors keep getting sharper. But older inference tools are costly and scale poorly as catalogs grow.

Built on the JAX library, GWKokab lets users assemble models from separate subpopulations. Examples include black hole pairs, neutron star pairs, and mixed binaries, each with its own rate. A normalizing-flow sampler speeds the inference. The team checks it on simulated spinning, eccentric binaries. It recovers even how stretched their orbits are. It also reproduces published results on black hole masses from the fourth gravitational wave catalog.
arxiv-2509-13938:
Yifan Mo, Youcheng Cai, and Ligang Liu stabilize 3D Gaussian Splatting in a 2025 computer graphics paper. The technique renders scenes from clouds of three-dimensional Gaussians at high speed. Complex scenes develop blur and floating artifacts. Redundant Gaussians settle into unstable, ambiguous arrangements during optimization. That settling is the root cause.

The authors derive that the splatting optimization itself follows a partial differential equation. They add a viscosity term to keep it stable. They solve it with the material point method, a simulation technique that enforces global and local constraints. A smarter densification strategy and particle constraints preserve fine detail. The method plugs into existing pipelines without redesign. It reached the best reported rendering and surface reconstruction quality across their experiments.
arxiv-2509-14038:
David Martínez-Delgado and nine co-authors dissect a galactic merger fossil in a 2025 astronomy paper. Around the spiral galaxy NGC 7531 lies shell-shaped tidal debris. One compact stellar system sits embedded in it. Such leftovers record how the galaxy assembled. The team set out to learn what the compact object is and how the shell formed.

Survey imaging, deep amateur telescope photographs, and Keck spectroscopy confirm the object belongs to NGC 7531. They identify it as an ultra-compact dwarf. Most likely it is a nuclear star cluster torn out of a smaller galaxy and stripped down, tidal tails and all. The shell's mass implies a very unequal merger. Simulations reproduce the debris with a near-radial infall and two close passages. The first passage matches a burst of star formation about a billion years ago.
arxiv-2509-14138:
Ran Yang and three co-authors teach robot policies to notice when a step is done in a 2025 robotics paper. Long manipulation jobs chain interdependent subtasks in strict order, and missing the moment one subtask finishes cascades into failure downstream. Strong vision-language-action models such as pi-zero steer arms smoothly but carry no internal signal for subtask completion.

SeqVLA adds a light detection head to that base model, so one network both acts and judges whether the current subtask is complete, triggering transitions on its own. The team compared four fine-tuning strategies varying how the two heads train and whether the backbone stays frozen. On salad packing with seven subtasks and candy packing with four, joint fine-tuning with an unfrozen backbone won decisively, removing sequence-related failures.
arxiv-2509-14438:
Kiana Kiashemshaki and three co-authors review bias in large language models in 2025 and test fixes in a controlled simulation. Bias threatens fairness and trust in systems now used widely. It can enter through training data, model design or deployment context.

The review sorts biases into implicit and explicit kinds and traces their expression across language tasks. A simulation framework then compares mitigation routes head to head. Routes include curating data, debiasing during training and calibrating outputs after generation. Controlled trials measure how much each route cuts biased output. The authors argue reviews alone are not enough. Practitioners need tested numbers for which intervention helps, at what cost, before choosing a mitigation plan.
arxiv-2509-15038:
Ayan Sengupta, Siddhant Chaudhary, and Tanmoy Chakraborty compress the memory cache of language models by valuing value vectors in a 2025 machine learning paper. During generation, models store key-value pairs for past tokens, and that cache grows costly. Most compression methods rank tokens by attention scores and evict the lowest, assuming attention strength equals importance.

The authors argue that value vectors, which directly shape the output, deserve the deciding role. Their CurDKV method scores tokens by leverage computed from a CUR matrix decomposition of the attention output. Theory shows attention-score ranking cannot guarantee the output is preserved, while CUR-based selection directly minimizes reconstruction loss for the full attention computation. Experiments confirm the value-guided cache keeps model behavior closer to the uncompressed original at equal memory.
arxiv-2509-15238:
Dylan Léveillé generates action plans for belief-desire-intention agents automatically in a solo 2025 multi-agent systems paper. In the BDI framework, software agents act from beliefs about the world, desires they pursue, and intentions they commit to. Plans, the action sequences that serve a goal, usually demand heavy manual design and target single agents.

Léveillé's tool generates plans with Alternating-Time Temporal Logic, a formalism that reasons about what groups of agents can force to happen. Because the logic handles cooperation and competition natively, generated plans anticipate partners and rivals instead of assuming a passive world. A demonstration game requiring collaboration shows agents reaching their shared goal on generated plans. The work aims to cut the hand-crafting bottleneck in multi-agent system design.
arxiv-2509-15338:
Noah Silva de Leonardi and Benjamin Dalziel show how linked superspreading can fire epidemics that mean rates say should die out, in a 2025 paper. Some sick people pass a germ on far more than most. Spread power also runs in contact groups: those who infect and those they infect tend to match, since risk traits bunch among close contacts.

Their frame tracks how each person's spread count links along chains of spread. When strong spreaders tend to infect future strong spreaders, chains of high spread can keep an epidemic alive. That holds even while the mean spread rate for the whole group sits below the classic cut point of one. A math cut point marks where the link grows strong enough for this boost. Plans based on means alone can badly low-ball the risk.
arxiv-2509-15938:
Maximilian Pierer von Esch, Andreas Völz, and Knut Graichen fix a distributed solver for coupled problems. Their base method splits a large nonlinear program across a network of subsystems. Each part uses sensitivity facts and talks to neighbors. Whether the base method converges hinges on how strongly the parts couple, a real limit in practice.

Their upgrade, SBDP+, reshapes the joint update of the core variables and their dual partners. Local subproblems stay small and run in parallel. They prove the method settles at a linear rate near a solution, for general coupling shapes and for non convex problems that meet standard conditions. Tests in statistical learning and beyond show stronger robustness than the base method and peer solvers. The design keeps communication neighbor to neighbor.
arxiv-2509-16038:
Tools that spot intrusions on a network are hard to test, since real traffic data that is both safe and well labeled is scarce. Miel Verkerken and four co-authors present ConCap, a tool that builds a small, isolated network and records its traffic with labels added for free. One settings file captures the whole setup, so other teams can repeat the same test.

Trials cover ten network activities, plus deep checks on variants and repeats. The traffic looks like that of a real network, and its flow records match those from benchmark sets and a smart home. Teams can also replay complex attack chains in safety.
arxiv-2509-16138:
Galaxies like our own seem to form in two acts, and their dark matter halos may set the tempo. Qinglin Ma, Yangyao Chen, and Houjun Mo use detailed zoom-in simulations to track Milky Way-sized galaxies and their halos together. Early on, stars form in bursts, motion is hot, and the shape is a bulge; later, a calm disk forms stars at a steady pace.

The switch lines up with the halo's shift from fast to slow growth. Two star birth modes leave distinct marks on young galaxies. Those marks give telescope tests a clear target for checking how galaxies and halos grow up together.
arxiv-2509-16338:
Most models of Earth-like planets treat them as uniform balls, yet real worlds have patchy clouds and continents that shift with time. Kenneth E. Goodis Gordon and six co-authors model how polarized light, which tracks light's direction of vibration, would reveal that patchiness. They compute signals for varied Earth scenes and for an early, wet Mars, across colors and viewing angles.

The polarized signal reacts more sharply than plain brightness to clouds and land turning in and out of view. Curves grow lopsided and spectra vary with phase. These forecasts can guide the design of future telescopes built to judge whether distant worlds could host life.
arxiv-2509-16738:
Kai Jiang and co-authors teach models new classes without forgetting old ones in a 2025 paper. A pre-trained model can learn step by step as new types arrive. The risk is drift that erases past skill. The team add noise in a planned way, mixing it into the learning process.

Their results show that the right noise helps rather than hurts. The model keeps old classes while picking up new ones. Code is shared in public for others to test. Helpful noise is a cheap trick if it holds up. It could keep photo and product tools current without full retraining each time a class is added.
arxiv-2509-16838:
Zhong-Wu Xia, Huajie Gong, Qiyuan Pan, and Jiliang Jing probe a symmetry-breaking field with future space detectors in a 2025 paper. Some gravity models add a Kalb-Ramond field that breaks Lorentz symmetry. A small body spiraling into a huge black hole sends out waves that carry fine clues. The team model how that field would change those waves.

They find the space detector LISA could spot the effect at tiny field values after a year of watching. A standard estimation method pins down the measurement error. The error stays small at a fair signal strength. Space wave detectors could thus test deep symmetry claims that lab tests cannot reach.
arxiv-2509-16938:
Dat Thanh Tran and co-authors blend ant colony search with neural guidance for the traveling salesman problem in a 2025 paper. The classic problem asks for the shortest tour through a set of cities. Ant colony methods build tours step by step with learned scent trails. Their system trains a graph network to guide those ants for each specific instance.

Training uses a policy method with an entropy bonus for exploration. Candidate lists and local search then refine the tours. The hybrid aims for strong tours without generating them token by token. Better tour solvers feed into routing for deliveries, circuits, and scheduling at many scales.
arxiv-2509-17038:
Hong-Ming Cui and Zhong-Ying Fan study supercritical fluids through an Ising lens in a 2025 physics paper. Fluids above their critical point cross over between liquid-like and gas-like behavior. The Ising model, a grid of interacting spins, sets the classic picture of critical change. Its symmetry seemed to clash with a single crossover story for fluids.

The pair derive two analytic crossover lines for a class of fluids. Their results partly resolve the symmetry puzzle. The work also suggests the Ising model's reach in critical phenomena goes well beyond magnetic transitions. Supercritical fluids serve in power cycles and extraction, so their crossovers matter in practice too.
arxiv-2509-17138:
Zhaoyang Cao, Lael Schooler, and Reza Zafarani study memory-like behavior in language models through psychology in a 2025 paper. Human memory is adaptive but fallible, with classic sins cataloged by Schacter. The team borrow paradigms from human memory research to test top language models. They ask how far model recall mirrors human recall, in both success and error.

Results show alignments and divergences side by side. Models reconstruct memory in ways that echo core human features. Their errors also follow distinct patterns tied to their architecture. The lens of cognitive psychology gives researchers a richer vocabulary for model behavior than raw accuracy alone.
arxiv-2509-17238:
Soheil Zibakhsh and five co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on squeezing more skill out of mixture-of-experts language models. These models route each token to a few expert sub-networks. Most gains so far come from longer chains of thought at the sequence level. The team instead scales effort at the level of a single token.

Their method, called RoE, needs no retraining. It adds controlled randomness to the routing step, samples several experts for each token, and blends their outputs into one stronger guess. Batching tricks and a special cache keep the extra cost and memory low. In their example, a mid-size model with RoE matched a much larger model while using notably less compute. The work suggests that expert models hold spare capacity that smarter inference can unlock.
arxiv-2509-17538:
Mykhailo V. Klymenko and eight co-authors built a unit testing framework for quantum subroutines. Their 2025 arXiv paper brings a bread-and-butter software habit, small tests for small pieces, into quantum code. Quantum subroutines are hard to test because their data can be measurement outcomes, density matrices, or process matrices, each with its own statistics.

The framework, QUT, is built for ease of use and plain design. Its core is a family of probabilistic assertions that adapt their checking method to the type of data they receive. Each type pairs with a fitting protocol, from tomography to a chi-squared test, and new protocols can be added later. QUT runs on the Qiskit stack, so it fits many hardware backends and simulators. The authors present a working prototype alongside the architecture.
arxiv-2509-17738:
Ting Han, Linara Adilova, Henning Petzka, Jens Kleesiek, and Michael Kamp pull apart two darlings of deep learning theory. Their 2025 arXiv paper concerns neural collapse, where class representations settle into a neat symmetric pattern, and flatness of the loss landscape. Both often appear near good generalization, and both have been cast as its cause.

The team uses grokking, the regime where a model memorizes first and generalizes much later, to separate cause from coincidence in time. Both collapse and flatness show up as generalization begins. Only flatness, though, predicts it across their tests. Models pushed toward or away from collapse generalize alike, while models steered away from flat solutions stall, even where grokking never normally occurs. A theory result ties collapse to flatness under classic assumptions. The verdict: flatness is necessary, collapse is not.
arxiv-2509-17838:
Raghavendra N Bhat and 4 co-authors study a group built from sign-flip matrices with a twist. Their 2025 paper defines a subgroup of matrices over the whole numbers. Each key matrix matches the plain identity, save for one line where minus one and plus one take turns.

The team works out the traits of that group in depth. They then track what comes from using a fixed string of such flips again and again on a grid point. Paths from that loop show several clear traits. The work ties a simple flip rule to rich group behaviour.
arxiv-2509-17938:
Satyapriya Krishna and 8 co-authors build a bench to catch language models that reason badly but answer sweetly. Their 2025 set, D-REX, targets a sneaky fail mode: a model may output a mild reply while its inner steps aim at harm. Trick system prompts can set off that split, and plain output checks miss it.

The set grew from a red-team contest where folk wrote prompts to bait such splits. Each case keeps the bait prompt, a user query, the mild reply, and the inner chain of thought. Tests show the set is a hard challenge for current models and safety tools.
arxiv-2509-18038:
Sromona Nandi and 7 co-authors tune a double perovskite by swapping one metal for a non-magnetic one. Their 2025 study tracks how magnet and electron traits shift as titanium takes the place of iridium in the compound. The base stuff shows a magnet-like state at a set heat point.

As swap share grows, the cell shrinks while its shape class stays the same. The magnet-like state fades into an opposed-order state at full swap. Squeeze from outside boosts the base compound's pull, which hints at a piezo-magnet trait. Heat growth tests also show spin and lattice move as one.
arxiv-2509-18138:
Tiantian Zhang presents a new learning rule for advice from experts who wake and sleep. Her 2025 paper deals with the sleeping experts task, where just some advisors are live each round. A learner must pick whom to trust while the live set shifts over time.

Her rule, RIPLM, works in a rank-based form drawn from the Plackett-Luce model. Past rules worked on expert names, not ranks. By staying in the rank form at each round, the rule keeps a known match with a rank bench mark. Zhang claims it is the first such rule that is both rank-true and adapts to variance.
arxiv-2509-18338:
Restaking lets blockchain validators take on extra duties beyond keeping the chain running. Tarun Chitra, Paolo Penna, and Manvir Schneider study a key risk: Sybil attacks, where one actor fakes many identities. Their 2025 paper builds a formal frame for what it means for a restaking network to resist such attacks. They split attacks into two types.

In one type, the fake identities stay out of the main attack; in the other, they join in. The team studies two penalty styles, one based on edge effects and one that multiplies losses. They find the conditions under which each style deters fakes. Then they prove a hard limit: no penalty rule can block both attack types at once. Network shape matters too. Even mild clumping in who links to whom can make Sybil attacks pay off.
arxiv-2509-18438:
Twisted layers of certain crystals host flat electron bands with opposite twists in each valley. Guopeng Xu, Nemin Wei, Inti Sodemann Villadiego, and Chunli Huang study how those bands mix in this 2025 paper. Strong spin-orbit coupling points spins in opposite directions in the two valleys. That split sorts electron interactions into like-spin and unlike-spin kinds.

Using a step-by-step approximation method, the team computes how band mixing corrects each interaction kind at varied fillings. In the lowest band, screening shows an even-odd pattern across angular momentum channels. In the next band, the strongest spin contrast appears in one specific channel. A rare feature also appears: spin-flip excitations form localized particles, unlike in classic quantum Hall systems. The team computes their spectrum. The results bear on candidate fractional quantum spin Hall states and on magnetism in a real material, MoTe2.
arxiv-2509-18838:
Light sensors made of silicon can count single photons, but radiation in busy accelerators damages them. Jesús Peña-Rodríguez, Jörg Förtsch, Christian Pauly, and Karl-Heinz Kampert test that damage for a planned detector in this 2025 paper. The sensors are candidates for the CBM experiment's ring imaging camera. Neutron hits scar the silicon lattice and spoil the sensors' quiet behavior.

Three commercial sensor models were exposed to neutron doses spanning a wide range. Dark current rose up to a thousandfold at the top doses. Dark counts rose up to a hundredfold, and false after-pulses grew as well. Gain and photon resolution fell. A bake-out step, heating the sensors electrically, partly reversed the harm. It restored photon resolution and cut dark current and counts. The results set the operating envelope for these sensors at CBM.
arxiv-2509-18938:
Sorting images into classes usually needs many labeled examples, which are costly to make. Matheus Vinícius Todescato and Joel Luís Carbonera present a way to sort images with no labeled training data at all. Their method needs only the list of class names. It pairs a vision-language model with a pre-trained visual model in a self-learning loop.

The vision-language model first picks test images it judges with high confidence. The visual model then sharpens the features of those images, and the improved features train a small classifier right on the test data. Step by step, the system adapts to the task at hand. Tests on ten varied datasets show the method beats the standard zero-shot baseline, without fine-tuning the large model or using a language model.
arxiv-2509-19038:
The ATLAS Collaboration reports a hunt for a rare process at the Large Hadron Collider. The target is a top quark pair made together with a W boson and an extra jet, through the electroweak force. Buried in that process is a vertex where a top quark and a W boson scatter, probed directly here for the first time. The data come from the collider's second run, at an energy of 13 TeV, recorded with the ATLAS detector.

The search picks events with two same-charge leptons and several jets, at least one tagged as coming from a bottom quark. The most forward jet's traits separate the rare signal from its far commoner strong-force twin. No excess appeared, so the team sets an upper limit on the rate, well above the standard model's small prediction. They also bound two effective-theory operators that could alter top quark couplings.
arxiv-2509-19238:
Raphaël Clouâtre, writing alone, finds a new obstruction to a famous open conjecture in operator algebra. Arveson's hyperrigidity conjecture concerns when a small operator system inside a larger algebra forces its representations to extend in exactly one nice way. Clouâtre enlarges the system by pairing it with an ideal of the algebra inside a two-by-two matrix algebra. He shows the enlarged system can be hyperrigid only if extra uniqueness holds for representations that kill the ideal's overlap.

That hidden rigidity is strong enough to build counterexamples to the conjecture. The key condition is that two projections, one from the system's envelope and one supporting the ideal, sit perpendicular to each other. For the ideal of compact operators, the construction recovers a recent counterexample by Bilich and Dor-On.
