In purely finite-dimensional settings the pathology cannot arise, marking the obstruction as genuinely noncommutative.
arxiv-2509-19438:
Carbon lines in the light of exploded stars can weigh the carbon a star ejected, and Stan Barmentloo and Anders Jerkstrand map how. Their subject is stripped-envelope supernovae, whose outer layers were lost before the explosion. The team built a grid of model spectra with a radiation code, fed by stellar evolution and explosion models. Only two carbon features matter in the optical range, fed by the oxygen-carbon and helium-carbon zones.

One line blends with a calcium feature, so they built a Monte Carlo code to disentangle it. In real supernovae, the cleaner carbon lines brighten over time, as models predict, but both lines are weaker than the models produce. Possible fixes include lower carbon in the star models and stronger cooling through molecules. Where both lines are clear, ejected carbon masses run from about a fifth to two solar masses.
arxiv-2509-19538:
Learning control policies from logged data is hard when fresh trial and error is banned. Zongyue Li and four co-authors build DAWM, a world model that dreams up new experience for such offline learning. A diffusion model paints future states and rewards from a start state, an action, and a target return. A second model then infers which actions link those states, step by step.

That split keeps training simple while still yielding full step records. Standard offline methods can learn from those records with ordinary one-step updates. Two known algorithms gained clearly when trained on the dreamed data. They beat earlier diffusion-based rivals across the tests. The design shows that careful structure, not just a bigger model, can make synthetic experience useful.
arxiv-2509-19638:
Fake time series can stand in for real data when records are scarce, private, or costly. MohammadReza EskandariNasab, Shah Muhammad Hamdi, and Soukaina Filali Boubrahimi build TIMED, a generator that blends three engines. A diffusion model learns the global shape of the data. A supervisor network learns step-by-step dependence by predicting each next value. A critic in the Wasserstein style grades realism and pushes for smooth, faithful series.

An extra loss term aligns the real and fake data in feature space, guarding both variety and quality. Making series is harder than making static rows, since order itself carries meaning. The authors aim the tool at forecasting and anomaly detection. Trustworthy synthetic series could let teams train and test models without exposing sensitive records.
arxiv-2509-19738:
José F. Nieves and Sarira Sahu compute how waves lose energy in a model of a charged Bose-Einstein condensate. Two wave families in the model mix light with the condensate's own massive field. Earlier work by the authors found the real parts of those waves' dispersion relations, which set their speeds. This paper adds the imaginary parts, which set damping.

Damping also enters the photon's polarization response and the material's dielectric constant along the wave direction. The mixed modes show features with no plain-plasma counterpart. Condensates of charged bosons appear in models of dense astrophysical matter and exotic superconductors. Knowing both speed and damping is required to predict what such matter does to passing light. The authors work through the appropriate limits to check their formulas.
arxiv-2509-19838:
Continuous gravitational waves from spinning neutron stars are faint, steady hums buried in detector noise. Damon H. T. Cheung trains an attention U-Net, a convolutional network, to spot them across the whole sky. Template searches for such signals are notoriously costly. The network learned from about eleven days of simulated noisy data across a wide frequency band.

The best model, trained at low frequency, reached strong detection sensitivity at a one percent false alarm rate. A single model covering the full band did worse, a useful lesson in specialization. Training took under half the time and data of comparable deep learning searches. Machine listening could make all-sky hum searches routine. A detection would open a new window on neutron star interiors.
arxiv-2509-20138:
Wieger Wesselink, Kees Huizing, and Huub van de Wetering wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on game-playing software. Minimax search with alpha-beta pruning sits at the heart of classical game engines. These routines are heavily optimized and notoriously subtle. Small errors can hide from ordinary testing for years.

Using the Dafny verification system, the authors formally verified a family of minimax algorithms. The set includes versions with pruning and with transposition tables that cache past positions. For depth-limited search, they propose a witness-based rule for when a returned value is justified. One practical variant passed a complete machine-checked proof. For another, they built a concrete counterexample that breaks the proposed rule. All proofs and runnable Python versions are public.
arxiv-2509-20238:
Xiao Ma and Tariq Alkhalifah wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on seismic imaging. Geophysicists build velocity models that describe how sound waves speed through the earth. Sharp, accurate models are hard to get from field data with learning methods, since such methods often fail to generalize. The authors propose an inversion framework built around a convolutional neural operator.

First, the operator learns to map a velocity model to a seismic image, training on synthetic data rich in fine structure. Crucially, training pairs each image with both a starting and a true velocity model. The trained operator then sits inside an optimization loop. Its smooth derivatives let the loop push fine detail from the image into the starting model. Tests on synthetic and real field data showed accurate results at much lower computing cost than classical solvers.
arxiv-2509-20438:
A radio source pulses every twenty-one minutes, far slower than ordinary pulsars, and Ingrid Pelisoli and sixteen co-authors hunt for its visible partner in a 2025 arXiv letter. Such long-period transients may be neutron stars or white dwarfs. A white dwarf would likely shine in optical light, especially with a companion feeding it charged particles. No optical counterpart for this source, GPM J1839-10, was confirmed.

The team used HiPERCAM, a fast camera that images in five colors at once. They found no direct white dwarf detection. Distance and dust uncertainties mean a white dwarf cannot be ruled out either. Their data did show periodic behavior at harmonics of the radio period, as the white dwarf picture predicts. The result keeps both explanations alive while tightening what future observations must explain.
arxiv-2509-20638:
Gum disease measured in national surveys needs statistics that respect messy data. Qingyang Liu, Debdeep Pati, and Dipankar Bandyopadhyay build such a model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their single-index mixed-effects design targets periodontal disease, combining two clinical markers, attachment level and pocket depth, in one framework. The fixed effect runs through a monotone single-index function, keeping the direction of risk interpretable.

Skewed random effects and heavy-tailed residuals handle the non-normal distributions honestly. A grouped horseshoe prior selects among the many candidate risk factors. Survey weights, standard in national samples, enter the inference so estimates represent the population. The method ships as a public software package. The authors present it as a more precise and nuanced way to quantify disease progression and its drivers.
arxiv-2509-20738:
J Huang and Z Xiao study how complex a dynamical system looks when another system is watching, in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their setting involves actions of amenable groups, a class of groups with well-behaved averaging. Two systems evolve under the same group.

The authors define conditional local intricacy and average sample complexity, in both topological and measure-based versions. These quantities gauge how many samples are needed to resolve one system given knowledge of the other. They prove links between the different versions, using averaging sequences called Folner sequences. The results extend entropy-style ideas that measure information and complexity in dynamics. The paper is technical work aimed at specialists in ergodic theory and topological dynamics.
arxiv-2509-21038:
Measuring a plant's shape in 3D helps breeders select better crops, but organ segmentation tools are usually built for one species or one sensor. Andreas Gilson and three co-authors present OmniPlantSeg in a 2025 paper on plant phenotyping. Their pipeline aims to be species-agnostic across sensing modalities.

The core is KDSS, a subsampling algorithm for biological point clouds that ignores species and sensor type. Smart subsampling avoids the usual downsampling that throws away detail. Full-resolution point clouds can therefore be segmented, preserving fine organs such as leaves and stems. Paired with leading segmentation models, the authors report satisfying results. The approach targets high-resolution phenotyping, where small structures carry the traits breeders care about.
arxiv-2509-21138:
Classifying text by intent is routine work that still demands hand-tuned models for each new product. Ilya Alekseev and three co-authors present AutoIntent, an automated machine learning tool for text classification, in a 2025 system demonstration paper for EMNLP 2025. It wraps the whole pipeline in a modular, sklearn-like interface.

AutoIntent automates three choices that practitioners usually make by trial and error. It selects the embedding model, optimizes the classifier, and tunes the decision threshold. Multi-label classification and out-of-scope detection, flagging inputs that fit no known intent, are supported natively. On standard intent datasets, the authors report better performance than existing AutoML tools. Users can trade accuracy against resource use, suiting the tool to production chatbots and support systems.
arxiv-2509-21238:
Rahul Bandyopadhyay and Simon Casassus wrote an astronomy paper in 2025 on the disk around the star T Cha. T Cha is a young T Tauri star with a protoplanetary disk. A dust gap splits the disk into inner and outer parts. JWST spectra show strong aromatic bands, which are light features from carbon based molecules called PAHs.

The authors fit the observed bands to find which PAH types produce them. They pass starlight through a model disk to match spectra and flux data. PAH grains in the model are heated by chance photon hits, as in real disks. From the fits, they estimate PAH sizes, the charged fraction, and total mass. Results describe the carbon material present during planet formation.
arxiv-2509-21338:
Waves in a one dimensional lattice can localize, spread, and localize again as conditions change. The work is by Pei-Jie Chang and 2 co-authors. Localization means waves stay trapped instead of spreading. Recent work found reentrant cases, where states localize, spread, then localize again. Dimerized hopping and staggered disorder drive that effect. The paper tests how general the effect is under added potentials.

The lattice adds a periodic potential plus a quasi periodic modulation. The authors use eigenstate measures and dynamic observables that experiments can access. They find robust multiple reentrant transitions. The dimer structure of the unit cell stabilizes the effect. The contest between the onsite periodic potential and the modulation peaks there. The study maps how the transitions shift as periodicity varies.
arxiv-2509-21438:
Holographic quantum codes link bulk space physics to boundary error correction. Xi Dong and 2 co-authors study how those codes change under coarse graining in a 2025 paper. Their notion of bulk renormalization group flow is generalized. Renormalization tracks how a system looks at larger, coarser scales. The focus is a famous entropy term in the Faulkner Lewkowycz Maldacena formula.

The authors follow that term and its Renyi generalization under the flow. Their analysis gives a quantum code perspective on arguments by Susskind and Uglum. Starting from an ultraviolet code with two sided recovery and a flat entanglement spectrum, they build an infrared code. The new code contains chosen seed states and has minimal size in a defined sense.
arxiv-2509-21738:
Tiny retinal vessels signal early disease, but segmenting them with small models is hard. Mehwish Mehmood and 2 co-authors propose a lightweight network in a 2025 paper. LFA-Net targets real clinical settings with limited compute. Its LiteFusion attention module mixes residual connections, Vision Mamba inspired dynamics, and modulation based attention. Local and global context are captured fast in that design.

The network has very few settings and a tiny memory footprint by their report. Computational cost is low in floating point steps as well. Small vessel segmentation and high cost are the twin challenges addressed. Early diagnosis of vision threatening and systemic diseases motivates retinal vessel work. Resource constrained environments are the meant deployment setting for the model.
arxiv-2509-21938:
Guided image generation works well when the guide, like a pose or an edge map, lines up exactly with the prompt. Woosung Joung, Daewon Chae, and Jinkyu Kim address the common case where it does not, in this 2025 paper, presented at BMVC. A prompt may ask for a cat cooking in a certain pose, while the only pose guides available show humans cooking.

Their method, SemanticControl, needs no extra training. It first runs a side pass with a stand-in prompt that matches the guide, such as a human playing guitar. From that pass it extracts attention masks that mark where the guide disagrees with the real prompt. During the main generation, the masks mute the guide where it conflicts and strengthen the text where it matters. Across depth maps, edge maps, and human skeletons, the method beat existing baselines under loose alignment.
arxiv-2509-22338:
Felix Vossel, Till Mossakowski, and Björn Gehrke test how well fine-tuned language models translate plain sentences into first-order logic. That translation underpins knowledge representation and formal methods, where machines must reason over exact statements. Their 2025 study, accepted at a learning and reasoning conference, compares model architectures and training strategies on two known data sets. It introduces scoring measures for exact match, logical equivalence, and how well the predicates, the relation words of logic, line up.

A fine-tuned model from the T5 family, given a list of predicates to use, reached the best accuracy. It beat a leading general model and a strong reasoning model. It also beat a classic symbolic translator. Supplying the predicate list lifted performance by a wide margin. Encoder-decoder models beat larger decoder-only ones at this structured task. And the models generalized to logical arguments they were never trained on.
arxiv-2509-22438:
Nicholas Hunter-Jones and Marius Lemm prove that two kinds of quantum spin systems always have a gap. A gap means the lowest excited state sits a fixed amount above the ground state. Their systems live on any graph where each site has a bounded number of links. The interactions do not commute, which makes the analysis hard.

One class uses a random rank-one projection; the other uses Haar projectors. For both, the gap holds once the local dimension is large enough. The proof checks finite-size criteria of Knabe type, adapted to general graphs. The result extends a known one-dimensional qubit result to far wider networks.
arxiv-2509-22738:
Parikshit Bansal and Sujay Sanghavi close the gap between how diffusion language models generate text and true joint sampling. Autoregressive models sample each token from the full history, so the whole string follows the model's joint distribution. Masked diffusion models unmask tokens out of order, often several at once. Each parallel step drifts further from the true joint, trading accuracy for speed. Exact joint sampling would need one token per costly full-model pass.

Their fix adds a light single-layer sampler on top of a frozen diffusion model. One full pass can now be followed by several cheap sampler passes that unmask multiple tokens near-jointly. On pretrained and tuned models, quality versus the true joint rose sharply over the marginal baseline.
arxiv-2509-22938:
Yanqing Lu, Letao Wang, and Jinbo Liu compare three training optimizers through the lens of gradient whitening. The three are Adam, Shampoo, and SOAP, a newer method that mixes the other two. Each method rescales gradients with a matrix that mimics second-order curve data. The authors read all three as rough whitening tools.

In ideal form, SOAP and Shampoo turn out to be the same method under a standard assumption. The team reran language model tests with nanoGPT and an image color task. SOAP matched Shampoo on speed and showed no clear edge in final loss. That outcome fits their theory of equivalence.
arxiv-2509-23038:
Fast camera pose regression is quick but can bend geometry in subtle ways. Jingxing Li, Yongjae Lee, and Deliang Fan add geometric consistency training to fix that. Their method, GeLoc3r, builds on the fast ReLoc3R system. During training, true depth data yield dense 3D-2D matches. A transformer weighs which matches matter most.

A weighted RANSAC step turns those matches into consistent poses. The gap to those poses becomes a loss that teaches the network. At test time, only the regression head runs, so speed stays high. Scores beat ReLoc3R on three benchmarks, closing much of the gap to slower correspondence methods.
arxiv-2509-23138:
Blowing up points and rational curves reshapes a variety step by step, and its Chow ring tracks the geometry. Daniel Camazón Portela studies a chain of such blow-ups that starts from projective 3-space. Each variety in the chain is smooth and three-dimensional. He gives an explicit presentation of the Chow ring of the final sky. One result cuts against the point-only case.

Two chains with the same length and same proximity relations can have non-isomorphic Chow rings. He also explores conditions that an isomorphism would need. The results pin down which proximity types can occur between two exceptional components. Both components are assumed regularly and projectively contractable.
arxiv-2509-23238:
Spectrograms cost time and throw away phase data, so raw-waveform audio models have clear appeal. Goksenin Yuksel and 4 co-authors built WavJEPA for general audio, not just speech. Speech-unit level learning had limited past waveform models. Their design uses joint-embedding prediction at a semantic level. It learns high-level codes straight from the waveform.

Across many downstream benchmarks, WavJEPA beat top time-domain foundation models. It also used far less compute. A multi-channel variant, WavJEPA-Nat, trains on simulated natural scenes. That variant stayed robust under noise and reverberation. The results support low-latency waveform models for real-world audio.
arxiv-2509-23338:
Translating SQL between database systems sounds mechanical, but dialects hide custom functions and syntax traps. Wei Zhou and 6 co-authors built PARROT, a benchmark for cross-system SQL translation. It holds five hundred ninety-eight translation pairs from thirty-eight sources. Real business services contribute cases alongside open benchmarks. Models average under thirty-nine percent accuracy on it, which shows the difficulty.

Two variants widen the net. A diverse set holds about twenty-eight thousand translations for syntax breadth. A simple set holds about five thousand focused stress cases. Coverage spans twenty-two production-grade systems. A public leaderboard and code support future work.
arxiv-2509-23538:
Gas flow with friction and an outside force field can settle down or blow up, depending on the balance. Young-Pil Choi and 2 co-authors study the three-dimensional isothermal Euler equations with linear damping and an exterior potential. With strong enough damping, they prove global well-posedness even for very large starting data. A comparison principle and scaled energy estimates keep the density bounded.

With small starting data, any damping level yields global smooth solutions, and the team derives sharp decay rates that they prove best possible under a mild condition. For the pressureless case, a weighted functional shows solutions can blow up in finite time when damping is too weak, a sharp contrast with the pressured case.
arxiv-2509-23938:
Knowing when to speak is the hidden skill of a natural voice assistant. Guojian Li and 10 co-authors release Easy Turn, an open-source model that detects dialogue turn states in full-duplex spoken systems. It fuses acoustic and linguistic cues to call four states: complete, incomplete, backchannel, and wait. Existing tools are often closed, huge, or single-modality, and full-duplex training data are scarce.

Alongside the model comes a training set of more than a thousand hours of speech built for this task. On their open test set, Easy Turn beat existing open models such as TEN Turn Detection and Smart Turn V2. Data and model are promised on GitHub.
arxiv-2509-24138:
Rating faces for beauty sounds like a soft task, yet models that do it can bake in ethnic bias. Chandon Hamel and Mike Busch compare two beauty-prediction models trained on large face data sets. Even on a balanced test set, both models scored ethnic groups unevenly, with gaps that passed strict statistical checks.

Cross-data-set tests showed the models amplify social beauty bias rather than soften it. Only a small share of group comparisons met a parity standard. The pair warn that such tools can shape beauty norms at scale. They set out mitigation steps in detail and argue that current approaches fall short of fair use.
arxiv-2509-24238:
Easy questions waste deep thought, and hard ones may get too little. Yixin He and Lumingyuan Tang built FR-Ponder, a frame that lets a model vary its reasoning depth per input, without retraining the backbone. A tiny controller watches hidden states and decides whether to stop or take a small extra ponder step.

That step adds a precomputed steering vector drawn from deeper reasoning traces. A policy method tunes the controller to balance accuracy against cost, with curriculum learning and careful rewards. On two math benchmarks, FR-Ponder used less compute at matched accuracy and beat early-exit rivals. Its learned effort also tracked problem difficulty in an interpretable way.
arxiv-2509-24338:
Models that speak many languages still favor the dominant ones, and fine-tuning on bigger mixed corpora aligns them only loosely. Mengyu Bu and 4 co-authors propose AlignX, a two-stage framework that works at the representation level. Stage one aligns representations across languages by joining semantic alignment with language feature integration.

Stage two then fine-tunes on multilingual instructions to wake up cross-language skill. On several pre-trained models, AlignX improved both general multilingual performance and cross-lingual generation. Analysis shows the representations of different languages moved closer together. The gap for non-dominant languages narrowed without the cost of training on a huge balanced corpus.
arxiv-2509-24538:
A random orthogonal matrix, drawn evenly, has small blocks that look like plain Gaussian noise when scaled. Philipp Tuchel characterizes that convergence on the large deviation scale, where rare events are weighed rather than typical ones. He studies the upper-left block of such a matrix as its size grows.

The empirical distribution of the block's entries obeys a large deviation principle, with relative entropy to the normal law as its rate. Tuchel also adds a moderate deviation principle for the whole matrix sequence, complementing an earlier large deviation result. At that middle scale the rate keeps a Gaussian flavor, unlike the full large deviation case. The setting includes the Stiefel manifold of frames.
arxiv-2510-00138:
Gabriel-Dominique Marleau wrote this 2025 astronomy paper asking why forming planets look so faint. Surveys hunt young planets by the glow of hydrogen gas falling onto them. Far fewer have turned up than early estimates led observers to expect. Past estimates borrowed scaling rules from stars, which may overstate a planet's glow. Marleau instead follows the gas flow with a simplified physical model.

The model tracks how infalling gas conserves spin as it approaches a giant planet. Only a tiny share of the gas entering the planet's domain actually lands and shines. Most forming planets end up fainter than the few bright examples already known. Their hydrogen glow stays near a low cap almost regardless of planet mass. The paper argues that past non-detections were less damning than thought, and deeper searches close to stars could find many more.
arxiv-2510-00238:
Armin Gerami and Ramani Duraiswami at the University of Maryland published this 2025 paper on rendering room acoustics in real time. Virtual and augmented reality need sound that matches the room a listener seems to occupy. Classic convolution with long room filters is too slow and too rigid for moving listeners. The authors instead synthesize the room response with a feedback delay network they can tune directly.

Their network's parameters are optimized through differentiable programming against the target room's response. The match covers both raw acoustics and perceptual measures such as clarity and definition. Because the network runs live, the room sound can shift as sources or listeners move. Rendering quality rivaled convolution with long binaural filters in their tests. The computational cost fell by a factor of about fifty against convolution. Edge devices could thus carry convincing spatial audio without heavy hardware.
arxiv-2510-00938:
Peng and nine co-authors, across Meta, Georgia Tech, and IBM Research, teach reasoning models to recover from flawed thinking in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI safety. Large reasoning models write a chain of thought before answering, but a premise slipped into that chain can steer them past their training. Their method, RECAP, trains on counter-aligned chains of thought that start wrong, alongside standard prompts. The model learns to notice the bad trajectory, override it, and reroute to a safe answer.

The training needs no extra cost or changes beyond reinforcement learning from human feedback. RECAP improved safety and jailbreak robustness while reducing overrefusal of harmless requests. Core reasoning ability and the inference token budget were preserved. Under adaptive attacks the models stayed robust and self-reflected more often. The paper shares an example where the method's symmetry-aware reasoning beat a baseline's inflated count.
arxiv-2510-01038:
Chanchal, Kelly, and Chockler propose a new way to explain image classifiers in this 2025 arXiv paper on explainable AI. Popular black-box explainers hide parts of an image and watch the prediction change, but those occluded images look unnatural, so the model's behaviour on them may mislead. Picking the fill value for hidden regions also needs domain knowledge. Their Activation-Deactivation paradigm instead switches off the internal parts of the network that correspond to the hidden features.

Their mechanism, ConvAD, drops into any trained convolutional network with no extra training or fine-tuning. They prove it leaves the network's ordinary decision process unchanged when nothing is masked. Across datasets and architectures, explanations grew more robust by up to about sixty percent against occlusion-based rivals, by their measures. The explanations also stayed smaller and tracked the model's confidence more faithfully.
arxiv-2510-01238:
Himelstein and co-authors show that the filler tokens used to pad batched prompts are not as harmless as everyone assumes. Padding should be fully masked, yet common toolkits let it leak into computation quietly. The team inserted controlled amounts of padding into three open model families and measured the damage.

Even small padding shifted internal activations and degraded output quality in smaller models. Bias measures moved in unpredictable directions under padding. Safety guardrails weakened as well, an especially unwelcome surprise. The authors argue padding deserves first-class attention in evaluation and deployment checklists. Three model families, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen, showed the same vulnerability. A single stray token destabilizing behavior contrasts sharply with human robustness. Missing attention masks in popular libraries are a documented trap. Strict input handling is the paper's first commandment. Silent inputs deserve loud scrutiny.
arxiv-2510-01338:
Gandhi and co-authors catch a famous black hole binary glowing in the mid-infrared during its quiet, disk-dominated mood. The source, GX 339-4, usually shows its jet loudly in bright hard states, leaving the soft state unexplored at these wavelengths. A coordinated campaign built around a space telescope's mid-infrared instrument changed that during the recent outburst.

Infrared synchrotron emission persists even when the disk rules the X-rays. Placing this system on the luminosity plane shared with other black hole binaries clarifies which component shines when. Simultaneous X-ray coverage within a day anchors the comparison. Soft states, long assumed jet-free, prove more complicated. The JWST timing consortium coordinated the multiwavelength chase. Quiescent and hard states already populate the comparison plane from archives. Jet emission was the default suspect for infrared light in these systems. Simultaneity disciplines every cross-band claim.
arxiv-2510-01438:
Wei and co-authors teach laboratory robots to carry powder without spilling it, by optimizing trajectories inside a differentiable physics simulator. Granular material shifts unpredictably under contact, and transport demands both accuracy and stability. Reinforcement learning handles such tasks but trains slowly and unevenly.

Their framework maps skills into a low-dimensional space to shrink the search. A curriculum then stretches competence across longer horizons step by step. Gradients flow through the simulated grains, so trajectories improve end to end. Experiments beat the reinforcement learning baseline on success rate and stability. Photocatalysis and synthetic chemistry motivate the laboratory setting. Contact-rich motion is where naive controllers shake loads apart. Skill parameters compress whole trajectories into tunable knobs. Stability across the long horizon is the headline improvement. End-to-end gradients replace trial-and-error search. Powder handling is a small task with outsized difficulty.
arxiv-2510-01938:
Li, Sajadmanesh, Li, and Lyu add geometric discipline to low-rank fine-tuning in this 2025 paper. LoRA adapts big pretrained models by training small low-rank matrices instead of all weights. It saves compute, yet it still trails full fine-tuning on many tasks. One weakness is that LoRA ignores the geometric structure of the low-rank space it works in.

Their method, StelLA, splits the adapter into three factors that mirror a singular value decomposition. Two factors hold the input and output subspaces, and a diagonal factor holds the scaling. Both subspace factors are constrained to the Stiefel manifold, which keeps their columns orthonormal throughout training. A modular design converts any ordinary optimizer into a geometry-respecting Riemannian one. Across reasoning, math, code, image classification, and image generation tasks, StelLA beat LoRA and its recent variants. The gains come with the same small training footprint.
arxiv-2510-02338:
Jhaveri and co-authors train language models to write clinical notes that stay factual and complete. Their 2025 paper joins reinforcement learning with a claim level checker. Long clinical summaries often drop key facts or invent them. Human reference notes are costly to write for training. Their checker, DocLens, scores each claim against the source dialogue. Those scores become the reward signal directly. No separate reward model is needed. A gating trick also cuts training cost by reaching the same quality in fewer rounds.

Tests ran on two clinical summarization benchmarks. Precision, recall, and combined scores all improved under the method. An independent GPT-5 review compared outputs side by side. It preferred the trained model on factuality, completeness, and brevity. Hallucinations and omissions both fell in that review. Cleaner benchmarks may understate the real world gain.
arxiv-2510-02438:
Domcke and co-authors bound how lopsided the early universe could have been. Their 2025 cosmology paper limits the total lepton number. Lepton number measures the excess of matter leptons over antimatter ones. Below a key temperature, only neutrinos could carry that excess. The team solved neutrino kinetic equations with a new averaged framework. They then ran the full network of early element forming reactions. Primordial element abundances and microwave background data set the limits. The allowed band sits near zero for both neutrino mass orderings.

Flavor specific asymmetries face even tighter limits in places. The bound complements older limits from baryon overproduction arguments. It rests on lower temperature physics and independent reasoning. The team released their solver code publicly as COFLASY-C. Other groups can rerun or extend the analysis freely. A nearly balanced lepton universe is now an observational fact, within these bounds.
arxiv-2510-02538:
Wang and co-authors move robot skills from simulation to real arms with far less expert data. Their 2025 robotics paper tackles imitation learning under scarcity. Offline imitation breaks when demonstration coverage is thin. Performance often collapses during real world fine-tuning. Their recipe pretrains a world model through online imitation in simulation. A reward model separates expert from ordinary behavior. That signal trains the world model without true rewards. Offline fine-tuning on a few real demonstrations follows. Domain transfer then starts from a much stronger base.

Six simulation transfer tasks tested the recipe first. Two hand built domain gaps stressed those transfers. Three real robot tasks completed the evaluation. Success rates rose by at least thirty one point seven percent in simulation transfer. Real transfer gains reached at least twenty three point three percent. Both margins beat strong offline imitation baselines. Scarce expert data stretches much further this way.
arxiv-2510-02638:
Bui Thi Ha Giang and Dang Van Soa compute exotic boson decays at future muon colliders. Their 2025 particle physics paper works inside the Randall-Sundrum model. That model adds warped extra dimensions to known physics. The team studies Z and W bosons decaying exclusively. The final state holds two charged leptons plus two neutrinos. Scalar unparticles and tower gravitons enter the calculation. Beam polarization and anomalous couplings vary as knobs. Collision energies reach the multi tera electron volt scale. Feynman diagram methods drive the numerical evaluation.

Cross sections depended strongly on every knob tested. Polarizing both beams the same way maximized the rates. Mixed polarization made rates grow with collision energy instead. Charged W decays far out-produced neutral Z decays. The benchmark unparticle setting framed the numbers. Future muon colliders could test extra dimension ideas directly. Careful polarization choices sharpen that test greatly.
arxiv-2510-02738:
Li and co-authors teach robots contact rich tasks by generating force aware training data from one human demo. Their 2025 robotics paper builds a simulation to policy pipeline. Visuomotor policies stumble when tasks need continuous contact. Ignoring force leads to crushing grips or fragile behavior. Force data is scarce and costly to gather. Their framework synthesizes force data in simulation. A single human demonstration seeds generation. A flow matching policy learns compliance from that data. The policy reads point clouds plus force signals. It adjusts stiffness as conditions change.

Zero-shot deployment ran on real Franka robots. Block flipping and another task executed. No real world training data was used. Passive impedance control cut energy injection during rollouts. Success rates improved under the compliant rollout. Simulation effort for complex scenes remains a limitation. Color information is ignored by the design. Contact skills without real data change the economics of training.
arxiv-2510-03138:
Martinet and co-authors put honest error bars on how stars forge heavy elements. Nucleosynthesis models predict element yields from nuclear inputs. Many inputs far from stability rest on theory alone. Model flaws have been charted, but parameter wobble has not. Their method anchors parameter spread to known data. A backward-forward Monte Carlo pass does that anchoring. Two capture processes test the machinery.

The i-process in metal-poor giant stars came first. Neutron capture rates drove its parameter study there. Odd-charge elements showed the widest yield spread. Single isotopes carry those elements, so one rate rules them. The r-process in neutron star mergers came second. Nuclear mass errors drove the spread in that case. Parameter effects matched model effects in total size. More lab data on key nuclei would shrink both kinds of doubt. The authors name the rates worth measuring first.
arxiv-2510-03338:
Huet and Prosdocimi present a 2025 arXiv paper on fitting extreme value models when a few data points can spoil the fit. Flood planners use the generalized extreme value distribution to judge rare peak flows. Yearly maxima give small samples, so fitting methods bend too easily toward outliers. The authors build a robust estimator based on density power divergence. A tuning knob slides it between the classic method and a tougher, outlier resistant one.

The team proves the estimator settles near the truth and behaves in a regular way for large samples. Its response to any single bad point stays bounded, which the method cannot promise. Simulations showed strong accuracy when data stayed clean and firm resistance when outliers crept in. A United Kingdom flood case study showed good results with no need to hunt outliers first. Water agencies could use the method to plan defenses on messy real records.
arxiv-2510-03438:
Kim, Eddy, Srinivas, and Kochenderfer present a 2025 arXiv paper on choosing ground stations for large satellite fleets in low Earth orbit. Operators rent antenna time from shared ground station services and must pick sites that cut cost and data gaps. Exact optimization over all sites collapses under its own weight as fleets grow. Their framework splits the globe sized puzzle into single satellite, short window subproblems. Winning sites from those slices are clustered, then matched back to real candidate stations.

On synthetic fleets, the method landed within ninety five percent of the exact optimum in every test. Real fleets from Capella, ICEYE, and Planet, with up to ninety six satellites, ran where exact solvers failed to scale. Quality stayed near optimal, reaching ninety seven percent or better on downlink goals in the study. Fleet operators gain a planning tool that keeps pace with mega constellations now launching.
arxiv-2510-03538:
Mele and Lami present a 2025 arXiv paper on hiding classical data inside quantum states in the strongest known way. Quantum data hiding uses state pairs that global measurements can tell apart easily. Local measurements plus phone calls between the holders, though, should learn almost nothing. Past examples forced trade offs: separable states, which use no entanglement, could not also be perfectly distinct globally. Random states hid more bits but needed entanglement and stayed only roughly distinct.

The authors construct a new group symmetric family that achieves every wish at once. Their states are separable, perfectly orthogonal, and even stable under partial transpose. That trio exhibits so called nonlocality without entanglement to its utmost extent. The analysis also brings fresh numerical tools to convex problems in quantum information. Beyond the puzzle value, hiding limits what separated parties can learn, a fact with echoes for quantum networks and cryptography.
arxiv-2510-03638:
Liu and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper proving that implicit neural models grow more expressive the longer they iterate at test time. An implicit model applies one learned block repeatedly until its output settles at a fixed point. Such models act like infinitely deep networks while training with constant memory. Practitioners knew iterations let small implicit models beat feedforward ones, without understanding why. The authors analyze expressive power without assuming a task or data distribution.

They show that iterating a simple operator can express progressively richer mappings. In the limit, the reachable fixed points cover the class of locally Lipschitz functions. Three case studies, in image reconstruction, scientific computing, and operations research, back the theory. As iterations rose, the learned mapping's complexity grew toward the target's, and accuracy improved before stabilizing. The result gives designers a dial: buy capability with test time iterations instead of parameters.
arxiv-2510-04038:
Pham and Ahn present this 2025 arXiv paper on coordinating two kinds of traffic control across a whole city network. Signal timing alone cannot stop congestion when more cars enter a network than it can hold. Perimeter control meters inflow at boundary junctions, but earlier combined schemes never fully optimized the signals under the metered flow. The authors join both controls in one model predictive framework with a strict priority order.

The first objective regulates inflows at the boundary to maximize network capacity while keeping operation smooth. Only then are internal signal timings optimized together under those regulated inflows. The predictive controller respects safety and road capacity constraints throughout. To keep computation manageable, the network is split into subnetworks run by local agents. An ADMM-based distributed method lets each agent decide using only its own and neighbors' information. Simulations in VISSIM and MATLAB showed clear improvements in network management.
arxiv-2510-04138:
Guo, Li, and Weng present this 2025 arXiv paper on learning dynamics of high-dimensional systems without knowing their hidden low-dimensional structure. Neural ordinary differential equations model continuous dynamics well, but in high dimensions they demand heavy computation and accumulate solver error. Real data usually lies near a low-dimensional manifold, yet earlier manifold methods needed that manifold given in advance. In practice it is unknown.

The authors learn the manifold instead of assuming it. A structure-preserving encoder maps data onto a graph that approximates the underlying manifold. The neural ODE then evolves on that constrained structure rather than in the full ambient space. Across several datasets, the approach beat baselines on accuracy. It also needed fewer function evaluations and converged faster. The method suits physical, biological, and engineering systems whose true state space is far smaller than their measurements suggest.
arxiv-2510-04338:
Laï-king and Paroubek present this 2025 arXiv paper testing whether language models can judge how completely clinical trial reports follow reporting standards. Poorly reported trials distort the evidence clinicians rely on, and checking abstracts against the CONSORT standard is slow manual work. The authors built CONSORT-QA, an evaluation corpus drawn from two published studies of abstract reporting quality. They release the corpus publicly for reuse.

Several generative models were tested, spanning general-purpose systems and biomedical adaptations. Prompting strategies included few-shot examples and chain-of-thought reasoning. The best model and prompting combination reached eighty-five percent accuracy on the criteria judgments. Chain-of-thought outputs also exposed the model's reasoning, which helps human auditors verify individual decisions. Automated screening at this accuracy could triage manuscripts for editors and systematic reviewers. It also creates a benchmark for tracking model progress on structured research-quality assessment.
arxiv-2510-04938:
Shiwen Qin and six co-authors aim to speed up the search for good neural network designs in this 2025 arXiv paper. That search, called neural architecture search, is slowed by the cost of training each candidate. Fast predictors exist, but most only work inside one narrow family of designs. The team wants one predictor for almost any architecture.

They built ONNX-Bench, a shared collection of more than 600,000 networks with known accuracy scores. Each design is stored in the common ONNX format and rewritten as a text string. A language model reads that string and predicts performance instantly. Tests showed strong zero-shot accuracy across very different design families after light pretraining. The catch is that narrow graph-based tools can still win inside their home territory.
arxiv-2510-05138:
Gregory Hok Tjoan Go and five co-authors automate the writing of literature reviews in this 2025 arXiv paper. Scientific output grows so fast that reviews go stale quickly. Earlier automation focused on finding and screening papers. The actual writing, where readability and citation accuracy matter most, stayed largely manual.

Their system, LiRA, mimics how human teams write a review. Specialized agents outline the content, draft subsections, edit, and review the result. On the SciReviewGen benchmark and a ScienceDirect dataset, LiRA beat AutoSurvey and MASS-Survey in writing and citation quality. Its text stayed competitive with human-written reviews in similarity. Tests also probed robustness when the reviewer model changed. The results suggest agentic workflows can write trustworthy reviews without domain-specific tuning.
arxiv-2510-05338:
Asli Karacelik reviews how Bayesian methods pair with neural-network controllers in this 2025 arXiv paper. Model predictive control steers a system by predicting its future behavior. Neural networks supply flexible models for hard nonlinear processes. They carry uncertainty, though, and Bayesian tools promise to measure and propagate it.

The review surveys individual studies across modeling, control design, and uncertainty quantification. Most reported that Bayesian methods improved their systems, but some found poor results. Reported gains remain fragmented, with inconsistent baselines and limited reliability analyses. Few studies tested models far outside their training region. Karacelik argues for standardized benchmarks, ablation studies, and transparent reporting before the field trusts these claims.
arxiv-2510-06038:
Li and co-authors teach a car to drive with help from a human teacher in a 2025 robotics paper. Reinforcement learning can master driving by trial and error, but real-world trials are slow and sometimes dangerous. Their method, called H-DSAC, lets expert guidance steer the learning process without a hand-written reward function.

A proxy value function stores the teacher's intent as expected returns, rewarding expert-like actions and penalizing actions that forced the human to intervene. Those labels spread to similar unlabeled states, so the policy learns expert habits while still exploring on its own. Tests in simulation and on a real ground vehicle show the system learned safe, robust driving within practical training times. The approach offers a route to real-world training that wastes fewer samples and takes fewer risks.
arxiv-2510-06238:
Lekhak and three co-authors add uncertainty estimates to landmine and unexploded ordnance classification in a 2025 computer vision study. Deep learning could speed humanitarian demining, but deterministic networks stay silent about their confidence. Noise and adversarial attacks can cause missed detections or wrong labels, with dangerous consequences.

The team integrates Monte Carlo dropout into a fine-tuned ResNet-50 and tests it on a simulated dataset. Repeated stochastic passes reveal epistemic uncertainty, giving operators a reliability score per prediction. On clean, adversarially perturbed, and noisy images, the model flagged predictions that deserved distrust. The authors frame it as a proof of concept. It highlights how badly demining networks need uncertainty quantification and how exposed they are to attack. For field teams, a classifier that knows when it is guessing beats one that always answers confidently.
arxiv-2510-06338:
Yang and Lee introduce exceptional-bound band engineering, making topology depend on system size, in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Non-Hermitian physics is famous for the skin effect, where states pile at boundaries. Their mechanism is entirely different, hinging on critical scaling near exceptional points.

Through ansatz models, they derive analytically and confirm numerically how transitions shift with system size. The resulting phase boundaries grow increasingly sophisticated. The approach designs scaling-dependent bands in multi-dimensional lattices, gapped or gapless. The mechanism works because exceptional points amplify finite-size effects instead of washing them out. It challenges established expectations for critical and entanglement behavior. Experiments need no exotic platform. Photonic crystals and classical or quantum circuits can all demonstrate the effect. That sensitivity is usually a nuisance in non-Hermitian devices, not a resource. Growing or shrinking the sample itself becomes a knob switching topological phases.
arxiv-2510-07038:
Wenxun Wu and four co-authors train language models to call tools while they reason. Their 2025 paper presents TAPO, a reinforcement learning framework for tool-augmented models. Reasoning helps on math, but many tasks need fresh facts or exact computation. Search engines and code interpreters fill those gaps when invoked.

TAPO adapts a policy optimization method for tool-calling scenarios. The model interleaves multi-step reasoning with on-demand tool use. Two training sets mix knowledge retrieval with mathematical computation, one easy and one hard. Models of three and seven billion parameters trained strongly on them. Tool calls proved especially efficient for computation tasks. Ablations showed that spelling out reasoning steps improves tool use a great deal. The effect was strongest for code interpreter calls. Trained models resisted distraction from irrelevant tool outputs. The work gives small models a way to punch above their weight.
arxiv-2510-07238:
Jiang, Chang, McAuley, and Xu show that the tests used to grade model truthfulness are themselves going stale. Their 2025 paper examines five popular factuality benchmarks. Facts change, and models keep improving, but static test sets sit still. That mismatch, called temporal misalignment, can distort every score drawn from them. The team built a pipeline that fetches current facts to check test items. Three new metrics quantify how badly a benchmark has aged.

Eight models from different release years took part in the study. A considerable share of items in the widely used benchmarks proved outdated. Scores from those items misjudged what the models actually know today. The authors offer their testbed so others can audit a benchmark before trusting it. Benchmark designers, they argue, must plan for renewal from the start. Otherwise leaderboards reward memorizing yesterday's world rather than tracking today's.
arxiv-2510-07538:
Meshram and Chandrasekaran present D2RA, an attack that strips watermarks from generated images with a single forward pass. Their 2025 paper stress-tests the provenance defenses the AI industry is racing to deploy. Recent semantic watermarking hides signals in latent or frequency representations for robustness. D2RA needs no training, no model access, and only one image. It projects the watermarked image onto natural image priors in two complementary domains at once. That dual projection suppresses the watermark signal while preserving what the picture looks like, both structurally and semantically, to a degree that surprises.

Across six watermarking schemes and two datasets, the attack beat regeneration and optimization-based removal methods. The schemes shared a common frequency-domain weakness the attack exploits. The authors argue future watermarks must spread their signals jointly across spatial, spectral, and semantic cues, or add cryptographic verification on top.
arxiv-2510-07638:
Parikh and three coauthors present this 2025 computer graphics paper on variable fonts. Variable fonts let a typeface change smoothly along settings such as weight or width. Designers still adjust those settings by hand, which makes text animation slow and skilled work. The team wants software to optimize letter shapes automatically. Their goal is to keep text readable and attractive while making it easy to reshape.

The authors compress the variable font rules into a compact mathematical form. That form yields gradients, so standard optimization tools can tune font settings directly. They show direct shape editing, overlap-aware modeling, and physics-based text animation. They also show automatic font design driven by target images. The team plans to release the code. Their framework could bring automated design tools to a format that artists have mostly used by hand. Logos and titles are natural early use cases.
arxiv-2510-07838:
Lin and six coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on evaluating full-duplex speech agents, systems that listen and speak at the same time. Natural overlap makes such agents feel human, but multi-turn behavior is barely tested. The authors present Full-Duplex-Bench-v2, a streaming evaluation framework with an automated examiner. The examiner drives staged goals at fast and slow pacing. Four task families cover daily chat, correction handling, entity tracking, and safety.

The framework scores turn-taking fluency, instruction following across turns, and task competence. It runs both commercial services and open-source models through one protocol. Tested systems often grew confused when speech overlapped. They handled corrections awkwardly and lost track of who or what was under discussion. Performance also decayed as conversations lengthened, with open models struggling most on correction and tracking under fast pacing. The authors release the protocol so new task families can be added.
arxiv-2510-07938:
Troude and Sornette wrote this 2025 paper on a new kind of phase transition in complex systems, where classical theory says abrupt change needs an instability, where an equilibrium loses stability. The authors study non-normal systems, whose internal directions are not perpendicular. In such systems, noise gets transiently amplified by the flow's shear. That amplification acts like an extra temperature on the system, even though every equilibrium stays formally stable.

Once a non-normality index passes a threshold, escapes between states become easy and transitions turn abrupt. The mechanism extends the classic Kramers escape picture beyond energy barriers. The authors apply it to DNA methylation, where cells keep long-term epigenetic memory yet switch states quickly. The same logic may explain tipping points in climate, ecology, finance, and engineered networks. Their claim is bold: a universality class of change hides where linear analysis sees stability.
arxiv-2510-08338:
Benjamin Maier and a large team test whether language models can mimic consumer surveys, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Firms spend billions on consumer research, yet panels are biased and hard to scale. Language models could play synthetic shoppers, but asked directly for number ratings they answer unrealistically. Their reply distributions look nothing like those of real people.

Their method, semantic similarity rating, first asks the model for a free-text reply. It then maps that text to a Likert scale distribution by comparing embeddings with reference statements. Embeddings are numeric codes that capture the meaning of a text. The team tested it on fifty-seven personal care surveys with nine thousand three hundred human responses. The method reached ninety percent of human test-retest reliability. Its distributions also stayed close to real ones, while giving rich written feedback.
arxiv-2510-08638:
Thomas Fel and a large team dissect what the DINOv2 vision model actually perceives in a 2025 arXiv paper. DINOv2 is deployed everywhere for recognizing objects, scenes, and actions, yet its internal concepts were unknown. Taking the Linear Representation Hypothesis as a baseline, they train overcomplete sparse autoencoders on its features. The result is a dictionary of thirty-two thousand visual concept units.

Different tasks recruit the dictionary in functionally specialized ways, they find. Classification exploits 'elsewhere' concepts, which fire on everything except the target object itself, a learned negation. Segmentation leans on boundary detectors forming coherent subspaces, while depth estimation uses three monocular cue types matching visual neuroscience. Representations prove partly dense rather than strictly sparse, contrary to the hypothesis. Within an image, tokens sit on a locally connected set of low dimension in concept space.
arxiv-2510-08738:
Caden Ginter, Kamal Choudhary, and Subhasish Mandal predict how materials interact with light straight from crystal structure in a 2025 arXiv paper. The dielectric function governs a material's optical response and its solar cell potential. Computing it with density functional theory for every candidate is far too slow for screening. Their atomistic line graph neural network learns the mapping from structure to spectrum.

The model trained on roughly seven thousand dielectric functions stored in JARVIS-DFT, where a meta-GGA functional produced them. The model reproduces spectral features, peak intensities, and overall line shapes accurately, they report. Applied to the Alexandria database of over four hundred thousand insulating materials, a clear elemental trend emerged. Vanadium flags materials with high spectroscopic limited maximum efficiency, a key solar metric. Vanadium-based perovskites show a substantially higher fraction of high-efficiency compounds than the database average.
arxiv-2510-08838:
Song and co-authors build a clustering method whose groups stay apart by design, in this 2025 arXiv paper on Bayesian statistics. Mixture models sort data into clusters, each described by its own bell curve. Because standard versions place cluster centers independently, the centers often pile up or duplicate each other, which muddies interpretation. Earlier fixes that push centers apart were hard to compute with or lacked solid theory.

The team's prior for center locations comes from a random process built to repel its own points, with the special virtue of exact sampling. That choice yields clean formulas for what the data imply and what new points should look like. It also supports two practical fitting algorithms, including the first fully workable version of one classic style. The authors prove the method settles on the truth and sheds spare clusters. On brain-response data it found subgroups that clinicians could interpret.
arxiv-2510-09038:
Wu and co-authors give screen-operating AI agents a visual memory that grows without drowning them in text, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Agents that click through interfaces need to remember past runs, but writing them out as text inflates the prompt and drops exact visual details, like a button's size and place. Their memory instead encodes each trajectory into a short fixed-length stream of continuous embeddings, the model's own numeric language, using the vision model itself as the encoder.

Plugged into the model's input, these embeddings cost little context and keep fine visual cues. Adding more memory steadily improved performance, unlike text memory, which degrades as prompts lengthen. A self-running data flywheel gathered over one hundred thousand trajectories for about four thousand dollars, by discovering environments, inventing tasks, executing them, and verifying success. With light encoder tuning alone, a mid-size open agent matched top closed models.
arxiv-2510-09138:
Omrani and Sadeghi test how the choice of antenna shapes the images from a microwave scanner, in this 2025 arXiv letter. Microwave imaging of layered materials powers ground-penetrating radar and through-wall sensing. The reconstruction algorithm gets the credit or blame, yet the antenna delivering the waves matters just as much. The authors compare three directional designs at the same frequency band: a horn, an open waveguide, and a flat Vivaldi antenna.

They characterize each antenna's behavior up close and at distance, then feed their measurements through a diffraction tomography algorithm, which rebuilds the target's location inside the layered medium. Both single-position and multi-position data were used. The pattern was consistent: the more directional the antenna, the cleaner the reconstruction, with less shadowing smearing the layered structure. For builders of compact imaging systems, the letter offers a practical guide to how much antenna choice alone can buy.
arxiv-2510-09238:
Marwaha, Kryszkiewicz, and Jorswieck allocate power and antennas jointly in a massive MIMO system whose amplifiers distort the signal, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Energy efficiency decides whether dense 5G networks are sustainable. Most schemes pretend amplifiers are perfect, yet real ones bend loud signals, and that distortion limits how hard a system can be driven. The authors build it into the optimization, for ideal and realistic amplifier designs alike.

Their framework tunes each user's power and the number of active antennas together in a multi-user OFDM downlink. It imposes no explicit power cap, since distortion creates the practical ceiling instead. An alternating optimization solves the non-convex problem and provably settles at a stationary point. In a simulated five-kilometer cell serving sixty users, median efficiency gains over distortion-blind allocation reached about forty percent with ideal amplifiers and twenty percent with Class B ones.
arxiv-2510-09538:
Chhatra Bahadur Subba and six co-authors propose a new photocatalyst for splitting water in a 2025 arXiv paper. Cheap, efficient catalysts for clean energy conversion are a central goal of materials science, and platinum, the benchmark, is scarce and costly. The candidate here is a newly predicted monolayer material called SnSiGeN4, a member of the MXene family of layered compounds.

Using first-principles calculations, the team studied the material's electronic, vibrational, and optical behaviour under several levels of theory, including hybrid functionals. The results show a wide and tunable band gap, the energy window that controls light absorption. Simulated infrared and Raman spectra confirm the structure is dynamically stable and carries catalytically active sites. Computed overpotentials for the oxygen and hydrogen reactions match platinum-based catalysts and beat iridium-based ones. The authors position the material as a sustainable platform for photocatalysis driven by ultraviolet and visible light.
arxiv-2510-09638:
Yu Song, Zehua Song, Jin Yang, Kejin Chen, Kun Jiang, and Jizhou Tang combine physics-based learning with reinforcement learning to keep boreholes stable, in a 2025 arXiv paper. An open-hole wellbore can fail as seepage, heat, water-driven softening, and rock deformation interact over long exposure. Predicting that multiphysics instability and choosing drilling fluid settings to prevent it is a dual challenge.

The authors write coupled core equations for the four processes and build a flat model in polar coordinates with the COMSOL Multiphysics software. Simulations across rock types and parameter changes generate a dataset of stress, strain, pressure, temperature, and water content, checked for sound physics. Their physics-informed network embeds the equations and boundary conditions to predict the wellbore's evolution from sparse readings. A learning algorithm then tunes fluid parameters, rewarding low failure risk and smooth control.
arxiv-2510-09738:
Steve Han, Gilberto Titericz Junior, Tom Balough, and Wenfei Zhou benchmark language models as judges in a 2025 arXiv paper. Organisations increasingly let models grade the answers of other systems, such as retrieval pipelines, against ground truth. The authors ask how faithfully those judges replicate human judgement, using a two-step method they call the Judge's Verdict Benchmark.

First, a correlation test filters out judges whose scores barely track human scores. A second test classifies the survivors as human-like, mimicking natural variation, or super-consistent, agreeing more than humans do. Of fifty-four models tested, twenty-seven reached the top tier: twenty-three judged in a human-like way and four were super-consistent. Judge quality, the authors conclude, depends on training strategy more than size, and correlation alone cannot certify a judge.
arxiv-2510-10038:
Dovgoshey and Olga Rovenska study longest paths in trees in this 2025 arXiv paper in metric geometry. A tree here is a branching network with no cycles. Labeling its vertices with numbers generates an ultrametric space, a space where distances obey a stronger triangle rule than usual.

The authors collect all ultrametric spaces that labelings of one tree can generate. They relate the longest paths in the tree to how isometric those spaces are, meaning when two spaces count as the same up to distance-preserving maps. A special role goes to star graphs, trees with one central vertex. The results tie a simple path quantity to the full classification of the spaces a tree can produce.
arxiv-2510-10338:
Balagopal Unnikrishnan and co-authors argue that inclusive design pays in medical AI in this 2025 arXiv perspective paper. The ethical case for fairness in healthcare AI is strong and well known. What such design is worth in business terms, by contrast, has barely been studied.

The authors name the effect the inclusive innovation dividend. Tools built for diverse, low-resource settings, they argue, earn more when they reach broader markets. A tool made for a poor clinic must be cheap, robust, and simple, and those traits travel well. The paper reframes inclusion from a cost of compliance into a design strategy, giving health AI leaders a business case that stands next to the ethical one.
arxiv-2510-10538:
Amit Te'eni, Yaron Oz, and Eliahu Cohen revisit how much the quantum Fourier transform matters for classic quantum algorithms, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The hidden subgroup problem asks what symmetry a function hides, and several famous algorithms are special cases of it. The Bernstein-Vazirani problem, for instance, has a hidden subgroup of index only one or two, and one query suffices to solve it. The team generalizes this to subgroups of index one or an arbitrary value q.

They give a single query algorithm that always tells the two cases apart. With suitable unitary steps before and after the oracle, the same query identifies the hidden subgroup exactly, under stated minimal conditions. Those conditions hold automatically when q is two or three. By contrast, the sampling approach of Shor and Kitaev cannot guarantee exact recovery from one sample.
arxiv-2510-10638:
Aminata Sow and Tidiane Diallo apply machine learning tools to the near-infrared spectra of paracetamol, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Near-infrared spectroscopy measures how a substance absorbs light just beyond the visible range, here from 900 to 1800 nanometers. Such spectra are rich but hard to read directly. The authors test several dimensionality reduction algorithms, which compress the spectra into a few informative features while keeping their structure.

The methods compared are Principal Component Analysis, Kernel PCA, Sparse Kernel PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP. Each takes a different route: the PCA family finds linear or kernel based projections, while t-SNE and UMAP build maps that preserve local neighborhoods. The team evaluates how well each method models and reveals the spectral features. Their aim is simpler analysis and clearer visualization of the spectra, for pharmaceutical quality control, where fast checks of drug composition are valuable.
arxiv-2510-11138:
Software built around foundation models such as GPT, called FMware, is spreading fast, but little is known about what makes building it slow. Zitao Wang, Zhimin Zhao, and Michael W. Godfrey study that question empirically in this 2025 arXiv software engineering paper. They analyze FMware development across cloud platforms and open-source repositories, the first large-scale study of its kind.

Their data come from GitHub repositories and from leading FMware platforms including HuggingFace, GPTStore, Ora, and Poe. They find FMware concentrated in education, content creation, and business strategy work. Persistent technical challenges include memory management, dependency handling, and tokenizer configuration. On GitHub, bug reports and core functionality issues are the most common problems reported. Code review, similarity search, and prompt template design take the longest to resolve, pointing to where better tools and community support would help most in the years ahead.
arxiv-2510-11438:
Search is changing: generative engines like Google's AI Overview and ChatGPT now answer questions directly, so website owners want to know what content these engines favor. Yujiang Wu, Shanshan Zhong, Yubin Kim, and Chenyan Xiong study that preference learning problem in this 2025 arXiv paper. They introduce AutoGEO, a framework that automatically learns what generative engines prefer in retrieved content and rewrites web pages to earn more traction from them.

AutoGEO first prompts frontier language models to explain engine preferences and extracts preference rules from the explanations. The rules then serve two systems: a prompt-based optimizer that uses them as context, and a trained model that uses them as rule-based rewards. On GEO-Bench and two new benchmarks built from real user queries, AutoGEO improved content traction while preserving search utility. Analyses confirmed the learned rules are robust and capture preferences in different domains.
arxiv-2510-11538:
Diffusion transformers generate images of striking quality, and inside them researchers have noticed massive activations: a few feature values enormously larger than the rest. Chaofan Gan and co-authors investigate what those spikes actually do in this 2025 arXiv computer vision paper. They find the activations occur across all spatial tokens, modulated by the timestep embeddings.

Experiments show the massive activations are the key to synthesizing local detail, while having minimal impact on the overall semantic content of the output. Building on that, the authors propose Detail Guidance, a training-free self-guidance strategy. They create a degraded, detail-deficient copy of the model by disrupting its massive activations. That copy then steers the original network toward higher detail fidelity. The technique integrates seamlessly with classifier-free guidance. Across pre-trained models including SD3, SD3.5, and Flux, Detail Guidance consistently improved fine-grained detail quality.
arxiv-2510-11638:
Yijia Fang and five co-authors settle two open questions in Ramsey theory, the study of patterns that must appear in large structures. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies colorings of space where every point gets one of several colors. Earlier work showed that triangles, squares, and cubes have a special property. In high enough dimensions, a copy of the shape always appears in one color or in all colors at once. Whether all triangles and all rectangles share this property was unknown.

The team proves that they do. For triangles they chain together rotations on spheres in four-dimensional space. For rectangles they reduce the problem to simpler product patterns with bounded color complexity. They also add a perturbation framework, a method that nudges near-miss shapes into place. That framework extends the property to a natural family of three-dimensional simplices, the pyramid-like shapes of the geometry.
arxiv-2510-11738:
Simone Carnemolla and five colleagues introduce SeeingSounds, a system that turns sound into images. Their paper appeared at ACM Multimedia Asia 2025 in Kuala Lumpur and was posted on arXiv the same year. Existing methods usually need paired recordings and pictures for training. SeeingSounds needs none. It works by aligning sound with both language and vision at once.

A frozen language encoder first maps each sound into a semantic space of words. A vision-language model then grounds that meaning in the visual world. Only small adapter pieces are trained, while the big image generator stays frozen. The system also converts sound changes into descriptive text, so a fainter rumble becomes a prompt about distant thunder. In benchmark tests, SeeingSounds beat existing methods in zero-shot and supervised modes alike. The authors call it a new state of the art for controllable audio-to-visual generation.
arxiv-2510-11838:
Xu Yang and seven colleagues present Lingxi, a framework that helps AI agents fix software bugs across whole repositories. Agents powered by large language models still struggle with such repository-level repairs. The team's 2025 arXiv paper blames two gaps: agents lack procedural knowledge about how fixes proceed step by step, and they waste computing power exploring blindly.

Lingxi mines old issue-fixing records offline and distills them into reusable procedural knowledge. When a new issue arrives, it scales up effort by consulting knowledge from similar past issues and analyzing the problem from several angles. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, Lingxi resolved about three quarters of the bugs on the first attempt. It beat five state-of-the-art rivals by roughly five to fifteen percentage points. Ablation tests confirmed the knowledge does the heavy lifting; scaling without it gained almost nothing. Design patterns and coding practices proved most valuable.
arxiv-2510-11938:
Yanying Lin and four colleagues present FlexPipe, a system that reshapes how large language models are served in the cloud. Production traffic arrives in bursts, and serverless clusters leave graphics processors fragmented into unusable scraps. Static serving pipelines cannot adapt, so capacity sits idle while latency climbs. Their 2025 arXiv paper lets the pipeline reconfigure itself while requests are still flowing.

FlexPipe chops models into fine-grained stages while respecting the wiring of the computation graph. It then adjusts pipeline granularity from live request patterns, moves cached data consistently during the switch, and places work with awareness of the fragmented hardware map. On an eighty-two-GPU cluster, FlexPipe delivered up to eight and a half times better resource efficiency than leading systems. Latency fell by about thirty-eight percent at the same time. Reserve GPU capacity dropped from seventy-five percent of peak to thirty percent.
arxiv-2510-12038:
Jean-Pierre Fouque, Tomoyuki Ichiba, and Ka Lok Lam build a bridge between quantum walks and classical probability. A discrete-time quantum walk spreads a particle across the integer line with wave-like interference. Their 2025 arXiv paper writes an explicit Feynman-type formula connecting such walks to a four-state Markov additive process, a classical random process with internal states.

Through that lens, the spectral decomposition of the classical process yields the homogeneous quantum walk's limiting density, where the particle ends up after many steps. The authors then rescale space and time together. The walk converges to a system of quantum transport equations in continuous space and time, carrying a phase interaction term that remembers the quantum origin. Their probabilistic representation of those equations doubles as an efficient Monte Carlo technique for computing solutions.
arxiv-2510-12238:
Zhang and co-authors introduce GGDOpt, a diffusion based method for optimization under uncertainty, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Chance constrained programming asks for decisions that satisfy constraints with high probability when some inputs are random. Such problems are hard because the feasible region is often nonconvex and the exact distribution is often unknown.

GGDOpt needs only a set of samples, not the true distribution. It recasts the problem as sampling from a product of two distributions. One sits on the nonconvex feasible set, the other is shaped by the objective, and both use first and second order gradient information. Adding noise during a forward diffusion gradually convexifies the feasible region, and guided reverse sampling then produces near optimal solutions. The authors prove convergence guarantees and error bounds. On synthetic data and a wireless waveform design task, GGDOpt beat existing methods in quality and stability, cutting overhead by nearly eighty percent.
arxiv-2510-12438:
Hooper, Hooper, and Horsley extend the theory of quasinormal modes to photonic time crystals, in a 2025 arXiv physics paper. Quasinormal modes describe the ringing, transient response of an optical cavity. A photonic time crystal is a material whose properties oscillate rapidly in time rather than varying in space, which changes how light behaves inside it.

The authors define Floquet quasinormal modes for these time modulated systems. Unlike their static counterparts, these modes show exceptional points, special parameter values tied to symmetry transitions, as an inherent feature. The modes spontaneously lock their phase to the material's oscillations in a non perturbative way, meaning the effect cannot be captured by small corrections. The authors also study large cavities, where new behavior appears. As a time crystal cavity grows, its modes come closer to the maximum gain predicted from the bulk band structure, revealing how finite size limits amplification.
arxiv-2510-12538:
Huang, Peng, and Tang redefine a monotonicity notion for operators in Banach spaces and use it on a splitting algorithm, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Such operators generalize increasing functions and underlie many methods. Their alpha monotone variant adds a numeric twist, classically built in Hilbert spaces, where geometry is simplest.

Working in real two uniformly convex and smooth Banach spaces, the authors give a new definition of the alpha variant. They establish structural and key properties of such operators. These extend Hilbert space results and reveal new facts about Banach space geometry. The resolvent of alpha maximal monotone operators behaves in line with the firmly nonexpansive property known from Hilbert spaces. They then analyze the forward reflected backward splitting method under the new assumption. It converges strongly, with a linear convergence rate in their setting, showing the theory pays off in practice.
arxiv-2510-12638:
