Asadulaev, Karray, and Takac estimate the quality of an offline reinforcement learning dataset before training any agent on it, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Offline learning uses static logs of past behavior, which in practice mix expert, mediocre, and random trajectories. Which algorithm suits a dataset depends on its fidelity, but provenance is usually unknown, so quality is hard to judge.

They study proxies from simple cumulative scores to learned value based estimators. Their main proposal, the Bellman Wasserstein distance, measures how dissimilar the dataset's behavior policy is from a random policy, using a behavioral critic and an optimal transport formulation. It needs no environment interaction or full policy training. Across standard benchmark tasks the score correlated strongly with an oracle measure of how well offline algorithms actually perform on each dataset. Used as a regularizer during training, it also pushed learned policies away from random behavior and improved returns.
arxiv-2510-13038:
Martínez-Pérez and Mendonça study pure symmetric automorphisms of right-angled Artin groups in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. These groups are built from a graph, and their pure symmetric automorphisms send each generator to a conjugate of itself. The authors ask when the associated graded Lie algebra, built from the group's descending central series, is Koszul, a strong algebraic regularity property.

They characterize the answer with a purely combinatorial condition on the defining graph. When the condition holds, they prove the automorphism group and its outer version are iterated extensions of right-angled Artin groups, and in particular poly-free, built from free groups in stages. They also show the automorphism group for free groups on four or more generators is not poly-finitely generated free. They prove that a broader class containing these groups is one-formal, linking group structure to rational homotopy theory.
arxiv-2510-13238:
Mikami introduces a stochastic optimal transport problem for Langevin dynamics in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Optimal transport finds the cheapest way to reshape one probability distribution into another, and its stochastic version guides noisy particle motion. Langevin dynamics adds friction and thermal noise to particles with mass, and Mikami asks what happens as that mass shrinks to zero.

The new formulation fixes only the initial and terminal distributions of particle positions, deliberately leaving velocities free in view of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. In the zero-mass limit, he shows the transport problem's minimizer stays tight, meaning it does not escape to infinity, exactly when the initial momentum, mass times velocity, converges to zero. He also shows the limit of a minimizer is itself a minimizer of the standard stochastic optimal transport for continuous semimartingales, tying the massive and massless theories together.
arxiv-2510-13438:
Glaser, Huang, and Gretton analyse contrastive divergence, a training algorithm for unnormalized probability models. Their 2025 arXiv paper asks how fast this method converges as data grows. Earlier work had shown a slow convergence rate for models in the exponential family. The authors test whether a faster, parametric rate is actually within reach. Unnormalized models assign scores that need not sum to one as probabilities.

Under stated regularity assumptions, they prove the faster rate does hold. Their non-asymptotic analysis covers several ways of batching data during training. Both fully online updates and minibatch updates fall under the same results. They further show the method is near-optimal in a precise statistical sense. Its long-run variance sits close to the Cramér-Rao lower bound, a floor no unbiased method can beat. That closeness means little accuracy is lost by using this simpler algorithm.
arxiv-2510-13538:
Ponticello and co-authors interview blind and low-vision users about how they manage their passwords. Their 2025 arXiv paper, from a security conference, reports a qualitative study with thirty-three participants. Password managers promise both safety and convenience for sighted users. Whether they serve blind users equally well was largely unstudied.

Every participant used a password manager to some extent and found them fairly accessible. Convenience, not security, drove that adoption in most cases. The strong-password generation features went largely unused, because using them accessibly proved impractical. Participants said managers ignore their need for agency, shaped by years of inaccessible software. Underuse pushed some toward risky habits, like reusing predictable passwords. Others wrote key credentials in braille, relying on obscurity for safety.
arxiv-2510-13838:
Kitazawa, Esumi, Niida, and Nonaka derive exact formulas for fixing per-event means when sensors miss some of the particles. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves heavy-ion crash tests, where event-by-event means of momentum or flow are key measures. Every sensor catches each particle only with some chance below one. Fixing that catch-rate loss for means is subtler than for simple sums.

The authors assume each particle's chance of being caught stands on its own. Under that assumption they derive exact rebuild formulas for particle-averaged quantities. Event-by-event spreads, not just overall means, fall under the same treatment. Notably, the exact formulas clash with the naive fixes people commonly use in the field. That clash implies some printed means may carry hidden biases. The proof covers the mean transverse momentum and flow anisotropy numbers as worked cases.
arxiv-2510-13938:
Writing again on gravity's foundations, Jaume de Haro and Emilio Elizalde ask whether the equivalence principle, the idea that gravity and acceleration feel identical, can by itself generate spacetime geometry. They pose the question in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their historical-critical account tries to derive the metric, the rule that measures distances in spacetime, without using Einstein's field equations.

For still sources, they start from a relativistic form of D'Alembert's principle and treat the inertial force as a real force that exactly cancels gravity. This produces a metric whose free-fall paths reproduce a relativistic version of Newton's second law. Applying a Lorentz transformation, the standard change between moving observers, extends the result to moving matter. The moving-source metric matches the weak-field limit of general relativity, suggesting gravity can emerge from the structure of inertia at least where fields are weak, as in the Solar System.
arxiv-2510-14038:
Junsong Peng and co-authors review progress on breathing-soliton lasers, fiber lasers whose pulses rhythmically swell and shrink instead of holding shape, in this 2025 arXiv paper. These mode-locked lasers, which emit ultrashort pulses, serve as model systems for nonlinear science because their dynamics are rich yet controllable.

Drawing on advanced diagnostics and control strategies such as genetic algorithms, the review catalogues a spectrum of phenomena. There are breathers locked to frequencies. There are fractal hierarchies of Farey sequences, Arnold tongues, the resonance regions of nonlinear dynamics, with anomalous features. And there are complexes of bound breathers acting like molecules. The authors identify a route to chaos passing through modulated subharmonic states, where the breathing locks to fractions of a rhythm before breaking down. They argue these findings open opportunities for ultrafast laser control and for studies of dissipative systems, systems that lose energy as they evolve.
arxiv-2510-14338:
Yuanhong Zeng and Anushri Dixit train controllers at different levels of risk aversion, then let a bandit algorithm pick the right one on the fly, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Locomotion policies that are too cautious waste performance, while bold ones fall on unfamiliar terrain, and the environment is unknown.

Training uses constrained policy optimization based on Conditional Value-at-Risk, a tail-risk measure, producing risk-conditioned policies with stability and sample efficiency. At deployment, a bandit selects among the policies using observed returns, no privileged information about the environment. In simulation across eight settings varying dynamics, contacts, sensor noise, and terrain, the risk-aware policy achieved nearly twice the mean and tail performance of baselines. On a Unitree Go2 robot in new terrain, it did the same. The bandit adaptation settled on the best-performing policy within two minutes of operation.
arxiv-2510-14438:
Rui Wang and co-authors present WebAggregator, a data synthesis pipeline that teaches deep research agents to reason compositionally instead of retrieving, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Research agents answer hard questions by gathering scattered evidence, but current systems are retrieval-heavy and reasoning-light, succeeding by entity-seeking rather than by aggregating information into insights.

The pipeline first sends a Proactive Explorer to collect interconnected knowledge. A Compositional Logic Proposer then weaves that knowledge into complex questions. It uses more than a dozen composition guidelines derived from dissecting the research task. From ten thousand verifiable question-answer pairs grounded on fifty thousand websites, rejection sampling curates a fine-tuning data set. Fine-tuning on it transformed agent behavior toward compositional reasoning with less tool use. The thirty-two-billion-parameter model surpassed GPT-4.1 and matched Claude-3.7-Sonnet on the GAIA, WebWalkerQA, and XBench benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-14538:
Marconato and co-authors offer, in a 2025 arXiv overview, a gentle introduction to a failure mode in neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence. Such systems pair a neural network, which turns raw input into concepts, with symbolic reasoning that checks predictions against prior knowledge. The catch is that the network can attach the wrong meaning to a concept. The system then scores well for the wrong reasons, a problem called a reasoning shortcut.

Shortcuts are hard to spot because the final answers still look right. They quietly damage the value of the model's explanations and its behavior on new kinds of data. Direct supervision of the concepts would prevent them, but that supervision is usually missing. The overview explains causes and consequences in plain terms and gathers the scattered theory. It also reviews methods that reduce shortcuts or make users aware of them, noting each method's benefits and limits.
arxiv-2510-14638:
Sanna, Regano, Maiorca, and Giacinto survey, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how artificial intelligence can strengthen the fight against cybercrime in Europe. Europol reports that cybercrime remains common, and prevention depends on tools such as automated network and malware analysis. Digital forensics, the careful extraction of evidence from devices, also matters, because what investigators learn can train better detection systems.

The authors argue that AI should be woven into both detection and forensic procedures as an added instrument, not a replacement. They also warn that the same tools cut the other way. Criminals can use AI systems to sharpen their skills and slip past automatic detection. As a case study, they show how three popular chatbots can be combined to write Python code that hides data inside images with steganography. The code itself is not proof of a crime, but the exercise shows how easily such techniques are now produced.
arxiv-2510-14938:
Sunyaev and colleagues present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, an X-ray panorama of one of the Galaxy's strangest neighborhoods: the microquasar SS 433 embedded in the radio nebula W50. SS 433 is a binary pouring out more energy than the Eddington limit, and its outflows have sculpted the nebula. The eROSITA telescope aboard the SRG observatory imaged the complex in X-rays.

The images span a large dynamic range and support spectral analysis of the emission. They reveal a close connection between the nebula's thermal and non-thermal parts. The link runs from narrow bright filaments under a parsec long to the nebula's extent beyond a hundred parsecs. The team characterized a pair of symmetric, sharp-edged elongated structures aligned with the binary's orbital axis. These have no radio counterparts, yet shine in very-high-energy gamma rays. The authors offer the picture as a guide for future observations and simulations.
arxiv-2510-15038:
Kong and co-authors improve, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how flow-based generative models learn to turn noise into data. Coupling noise samples to data points through optimal transport during training straightens the flow paths, making generation more effective. But estimating that coupling from mini-batches of samples scales poorly to large, high-dimensional datasets.

Their method, AlignFlow, uses semi-discrete optimal transport instead. The noise space is partitioned into Laguerre cells, regions each assigned to one data point, which yields an explicit transport map with guaranteed convergence. During training, noise samples are routed through this map, so every noise point arrives pre-aligned with its partner. The alignment adds negligible overhead, and it scales to large datasets and model architectures. In experiments, AlignFlow improved a range of state-of-the-art flow algorithms, and it drops into training pipelines as a plug-and-play component. Code is released.
arxiv-2510-15138:
Anthony Bilic and eight colleagues work on computer diagnosis from pathology slides, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Whole slide images are far too large to feed to a model at once, so software studies small patches and pools the results, a method called multiple instance learning. Patch-only views miss the broad structures across a slide, and that gap weakens predictions.

The team adds a branch that reads the slide in the frequency domain, using the fast Fourier transform to pull out low-frequency crops that summarize global patterns. That compact summary is fused with the usual patch features and can plug into many existing systems. Across three public datasets and six leading methods, the addition raised F1 scores by about three and a half points on average. The authors call frequency data a cheap route to whole-slide context.
arxiv-2510-15438:
Vincent Knight and four colleagues rebuild a famous cooperation experiment from the 1980s and rerun it with modern tools. Their 2025 arXiv paper revisits Robert Axelrod's second tournament of the iterated prisoner's dilemma, the game that made the simple Tit for Tat strategy famous. The original code is lost, though the submitted Fortran strategies survive, leaving a gap in checking a landmark result.

The team restored those Fortran strategies to compile on modern systems and wrapped them, unmodified, in a Python interface. Rerunning the tournament reproduced Axelrod's main findings, with Tit for Tat prevailing and rankings mostly unchanged. Successful play again looked cooperative, quick to answer defection, and willing to forgive. Adding newer strategies and running one of the largest such tournaments to date complicated the picture, though. The original field was unusually favorable to Tit for Tat, and several lesser-known old submissions shone in more diverse, noisy fields.
arxiv-2510-15638:
A robot hand modeled on the human hand can teach children how modern robotics works. Jared Lepora and three colleagues, including his father Nathan Lepora, built one entirely from LEGO MINDSTORMS. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents the Educational SoftHand-A, copied from the Pisa/IIT SoftHand design family. Two motors per finger drive opposing tendons, giving reactive and fine control of each finger. Clutch-gear differentials link the fingers into soft synergies, so they move together naturally.

Only standard LEGO pieces are used, and tests rely on equipment found at home. The hand still grasps a broad range of objects with simple actuation and control. The authors aim to inspire children toward engineering through hands-on building.
arxiv-2510-15738:
Nora Elisa Chisari reviews a research field in a 2025 paper. The field is intrinsic alignments of galaxies. Galaxies tend to point in related directions. The Universe's large-scale structure causes this tendency. These alignments contaminate gravitational lensing measurements. Lensing maps dark matter by how it bends light. But alignments also carry useful information. They speak to cosmology and galaxy evolution.

The review covers twenty-five years of work. It surveys modelling approaches across scales. It sums up what observations have constrained so far. It covers predictions from large cosmological simulations. It also reviews ways to remove the contamination from lensing data. Statistical measures beyond the standard ones are included. The paper closes with open problems in the field.
arxiv-2510-16138:
Dung V Nguyen and eight co-authors rethink how to merge the specialist sub-networks inside a sparse mixture-of-experts language model. Merging usually averages expert weights by simple rules, with no principled way to decide how much each expert should count, even though experts cooperate and compete at the same time.

Their framework, NAMEx, imports Nash bargaining from game theory to strike a balanced deal among experts, and adds complex momentum to speed expert propagation with proven convergence. Across language modeling, text and image classification, and corrupted-data tests, it beats rival merging methods and plugs into popular architectures. Applied to the fourteen- and sixteen-billion-parameter Qwen and DeepSeek mixture models, it holds up in both zero-shot and fine-tuning use.
arxiv-2510-16438:
Aidyn Ubingazhibov leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on matching points and lines across photos. Points and line segments give clues about place and shape. Tools that match them guide robots and build 3D maps from images. Past tools matched points and lines apart, or used one heavy joint tool.

Their tool, LightGlueStick, is a light joint matcher built for speed. A new part lets lines share facts about how they connect. Tests across standard data sets set a new best score. The tool is fast enough for live use on small devices. Shared code lets other teams build on it.
arxiv-2510-16538:
Mehrdad Nasernejad and Jonathan Toledo define a new ideal link in a 2025 paper. In a commutative ring, all parts swap order when combined. An ideal is a set closed under ring acts and sums. They call one ideal a demotion of a larger one when a power rule holds. The rule ties mixed powers of both ideals to their meet, for all powers.

The pair study demotions mostly in polynomial rings, where terms are power sums. They link the demotion trait to normal torsion-freeness, a health trait of powers. Torsion-free means no part is killed by a non-zero ring mate. They also set demotions side by side with reductions of ideals. The links may give new tests for when ideal powers stay clean.
arxiv-2510-16638:
Ekaterina Nistiuk and Yulia Zaitseva, writing together, describe a family of affine monoids whose invertible elements form an active semidirect product. A monoid resembles a group but its elements need not have inverses. Here the invertible part combines a unipotent group with a torus, two standard building blocks in algebraic geometry.

The pair characterizes these monoids through multiplication rules on their algebras of regular functions. They introduce root monoids, built from sets of Demazure root pairs on an affine toric variety. The paper then studies the properties of these new monoids. The work gives algebraists a concrete recipe for recognizing and building this class of objects.
arxiv-2510-16738:
Matteo El-Hariry, Vittorio Franzese, and Miguel Olivares-Mendez study how to measure the inertia of small satellites while they are in orbit. Inertia controls how a satellite rotates, and it can shift as fuel drains or parts move. Their simulations couple rotation dynamics with reaction wheels, actuator limits, and outside disturbances.

The team excites the simulated satellites with eight torque profiles that differ in frequency content. They compare a batch least squares estimator with an extended Kalman filter across three satellite setups and cases where inertia changes over time. Findings show that the signal richness and the estimator assumptions together decide accuracy. Open-source code accompanies the practical guidance.
arxiv-2510-16838:
Yu Guo, Jinfeng Liao, and Shuzhe Shi use heavy-ion collision data to test whether quark-gluon plasma holds chromo-magnetic monopoles. These monopoles are knot-like excitations of the strong force field. They have long been suspected of driving quark confinement and the strongly coupled behavior of the hot plasma, but they were usually put in by hand as model assumptions.

Working inside the CUJET3 jet-quenching framework, the team runs Bayesian inference on a broad set of measurements of hadron suppression and flow. The monopole share of the plasma comes out substantial at one to two times the transition temperature. The inferred share also matches extra data checks and predicts transport properties of the plasma.
arxiv-2510-16938:
Alok Das and Kiseop Lee speed up machine-learned hedging in a 2025 paper. Hedging means offsetting risk from a financial product with trades. In incomplete markets, no trade plan removes risk fully. Deep hedging trains a neural network to choose the trades.

Training such networks normally needs very large batches of market paths. That makes each training run slow and expensive. Das and Lee add topological features, summaries of the data's overall shape. With those features, far smaller batches train effective models. Hedging quality barely drops despite the smaller batches. The change makes deep hedging practical for more research groups. It also shortens the path from experiment to usable risk tools.
arxiv-2510-17138:
Marta Sewilo and thirteen co-authors report frozen complex molecules near a young star in this 2025 paper. The star, called ST6, sits in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a nearby galaxy. That galaxy is poor in heavy elements and has harsh star light. Its state mimics star birth in the early cosmos.

Space telescope spectra found five complex organic ices on dust near the star. One, acetic acid ice, had never been firmly seen in space before. Three others had never been firmly seen past our own galaxy. Plain ices like water and carbon dioxide also crowd the spectra. Shares differ from young stars at home, which hints at local effects.
arxiv-2510-17338:
Wildlife cameras must name known animals yet also admit when an animal is new and unknown. Jiahao Huo, with three co-authors, notes that strong classifiers trained only on known species stay overconfident when a strange animal appears. Open-set recognition aims to sort the known species while rejecting the unknown ones, without retraining the whole model.

Huo and his co-authors compare two views of each image: how close it sits to the average example of its nearest class, and what the model output layer predicts. When those views agree, the answer is trusted. The method placed in the top three on two animal data sets covering African and Swedish species, with steady scores on both.
arxiv-2510-17638:
Qingchuan Yang, with Simon Mahns and four co-authors, tests whether language models can forecast real events in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their benchmark, Prophet Arena, collects live forecasting tasks on an ongoing basis. Each task is split into stages, so researchers can see where predictions succeed or fail. The setup supports large, controlled comparisons across many models.

Many models already forecast surprisingly well in the tests. Their confidence levels matched outcomes closely, and their market style returns looked promising. Weak spots also stood out clearly. Models recalled past events with errors and misread some data sources. They also folded in fresh news more slowly than markets near a deadline. The benchmark frames forecasting as a measurable model skill.
arxiv-2510-17738:
Fabian Jaensch, Giuseppe Caire, and Begüm Demir work on faster setup for 5G networks. In 5G, each user must be matched to a beam from the base station. That matching step, called beam training, can waste time and capacity. The team predicts good beams from maps and station position.

Their neural network reads geospatial data, meaning data tied to real places. It predicts a beam map for all user spots at once. The method works in new places without fresh on-site training. It also needs no special sensors at each site. Tests show it cuts the candidate beams that stations must try.
arxiv-2510-17838:
Hector Giacomini reexamines how special relativity was born between 1895 and 1913. He places Lorentz, Poincaré, and Einstein inside their shared scientific context. German review journals spread Lorentz's 1904 results quickly across Europe. One concise 1905 review by Richard Gans gave many readers easy access.

Poincaré named the relativity principle and interpreted local time clearly. He also proved the group property of the Lorentz transformations. Against that background, Einstein's 1905 paper looks like a powerful reformulation. It answered problems already posed by Maxwell's electrodynamics and failed ether tests. Later histories then sidelined Poincaré from the standard canon.
arxiv-2510-18238:
Bryan Wilder and Angela Zhou argue for broader evaluation standards in a 2025 position paper. Their topic is artificial intelligence for social impact, meaning AI projects meant to help communities and public causes. Current review rules, they say, reward only projects that both deploy a system and invent new methods.

That narrow reward, the authors argue, harms partners whose needs fit single-front work better. They urge reviewers to value wider forms of impact beyond deployment alone. They also urge stricter checks on whether deployed systems truly help in practice. The paper speaks to researchers and reviewers who shape what social impact work gets published.
arxiv-2510-18538:
Aleksandr Azatov works with Mohamed Mahdi Khalil and Motoo Suzuki. They propose two models for composite axions. Axions are hypothetical particles. They may explain dark matter. A composite axion forms as a bound state inside a stronger force. That origin avoids delicate tuning. It also protects the particle's key trait. Less is known about such particles after cosmic inflation. Problems remain, such as leftover domain walls and exotic relics.

Both models make the domain wall problem vanish. A short extra burst of inflation dilutes the relics. One model rests on a chiral gauge theory. The other uses a gauged symmetry in a family of like theories. The authors map the working ranges of the models. Some cases have axion strings re-enter view early. Some have them return after a key cooling stage. In those cases, most dark matter comes from the decay of the string and wall network.
arxiv-2510-19938:
Foad Namjoo and eight co-authors describe MotionPI, a smartphone system for collecting behavioral and health data from study participants securely and with little effort on their part. Real health studies need continuous data under messy conditions: dying batteries, weak cellular signals, and unsupervised users. MotionPI gathers passive sensor data, including location and wristband motion, and prompts short in-the-moment surveys, triggered randomly or by activity.

Data are encrypted in transmission and storage, kept both on the phone and on a secure cloud server. A Bluetooth wristband buffers raw data and sends motion summaries and trigger events to the phone. The design aims at practical, scalable data collection for cyber-physical health research without burdening participants.
arxiv-2510-20238:
Runsong Zhu and seven co-authors present COS3D, a collaborative framework for open-vocabulary three-dimensional segmentation, where regions of a 3D scene must be labeled from free-form language. Gaussian-splatting methods either lean on a single language field and segment poorly, or reuse pre-computed segments and pile up errors. COS3D instead couples an instance field and a language field throughout its whole pipeline.

During training, a new instance-to-language feature mapping and a two-stage strategy build the joint field effectively. During inference, an adaptive step refines language prompts against instance evidence for cleaner segmentation. Experiments on two widely used benchmarks show leading performance, and the authors also demonstrate uses in image-based segmentation, hierarchical segmentation, and robotics.
arxiv-2510-20538:
William Samuelson and six co-authors gauge how tough and local Majorana bound states stay in systems where parts act on each other. In clean cases with no such acts, the links of split, twin ground states, and safe braid moves are well known. Short dot-based Kitaev chains now press the need to set those links with care when acts are in play.

The team states the bound states from group ground states in a direct way. They show how the local reach of a state caps its link to the world near it. That cap then gauges how safe the twin ground gap is, and if braid moves can be done at all. The frame serves new tests on live gear.
arxiv-2510-21038:
Gereon Elvers leads two co-authors on non invasive neural keyword spotting in the LibriBrain data set, a brain computer interface task pitched between basic detection and full brain to text. Keyword spotting is practical and privacy aware, since only chosen words trigger action rather than open decoding.

The fifty two hour within subject corpus gains standardized splits for reproducible benchmarking, with an evaluation protocol built for extreme class imbalance. Precision recall area serves as the main score, suited to rare keyword events. Solid keyword results would mark a step toward usable thought driven controls that respect user privacy by design.
arxiv-2510-21338:
Liang Ma and fifteen co-authors report a new superconductor made under extreme pressure from bismuth and hydrogen. Hydrides poor in hydrogen were not expected to superconduct at high temperatures, since hydrogen contributes few electronic states and weak coupling in such materials, yet the team found the opposite here.

At pressures near one hundred fifty gigapascals they formed a compound with two hydrogen atoms per bismuth atom, arranged as a bismuth framework of open channels holding hydrogen molecules as guests. Resistance fell to zero at about sixty-two kelvin, and the transition shifted as expected under magnetic fields. Analysis credits the bismuth channels themselves with the metallic conduction and about half of the pairing strength, a route that differs from known hydride superconductors.
arxiv-2510-21538:
Likun Tan and three co-authors detect hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, where a model answers from fetched documents yet still strays from them. Prior detectors blur two sources of error: the supplied context and the model's built-in knowledge, though fixing each calls for different remedies.

Tracing the mechanism, they find hallucinations flare when late-layer feed-forward modules pump too much built-in knowledge into the stream of computation. From that insight they build two scores per layer and attention head, one for context use and one for built-in knowledge use. Train small regression classifiers on those signals from a compact open model. The detector rivals giant commercial systems and standard toolkits, and its signals transfer to answers from a much larger model, suggesting proxy-based checking can be cheap and portable.
arxiv-2510-21638:
Tala Aljaafari and three co-authors detect when a reinforcement learning agent has wandered into situations unlike its training, using almost embarrassingly little machinery. Deployed agents in safety-critical jobs break under such distribution shift, and existing detectors lean on heavy learned representations that cost a fortune to run.

Their detector, DEEDEE, keeps just two statistics per episode: the average of a suitable episode summary. A kernel similarity score against a stored summary of training behavior, catching global and local departures respectively. Across standard test suites it matches or beats contemporary detectors while using about six hundred times less computation, and adds roughly five points of accuracy over strong baselines on average. The lesson is that many anomalies stamp themselves onto trajectories through a few simple statistics.
arxiv-2510-22038:
The Electron-Positron Alliance, a collaboration of nineteen named researchers including Anthony Badea and Austin Baty, remeasures a classic quantity from archived particle collision data. Thrust describes how pencil-like or spherical the debris of an electron-positron collision looks. Such event shapes historically gave some of the sharpest values for the strong coupling, a basic constant of nature.

The data come from the ALEPH detector at the former Large Electron-Positron Collider, recorded at the Z boson energy. Modern machine learning corrects for detector effects without binning, so the thrust distribution emerges in finer detail than the original ALEPH analyses achieved. The new curve shifts slightly toward larger values of the spread measure. The team illustrates what that shift could do to extractions of the strong coupling, which currently disagree between methods.
arxiv-2510-22338:
Aritra Mitra and five co-authors, Srijoni Majumdar, Anamitra Mukhopadhyay, Partha Pratim Das, Paul D Clough. Partha Pratim Chakrabarti, feed design documents to language models so the comments they write for code actually help. Comments guide everyone who maintains a program later, but novice programmers, now producing more code than ever, often write comments that are useless or worse. Maintainers already fall back on design documents when comments fail.

The study tests whether giving the model that same design context, the intent and structure behind the code, produces more useful comments than code alone could support. The feasibility question is deliberately narrow and practical: does design-aware context beat the naive approach on real codebases. If it does, comment generation stops being a paraphrase of the code and starts carrying the reasoning a future maintainer cannot see in the code itself.
arxiv-2510-22538:
Retrieving graphs that contain a query pattern shows up in scene search, molecule screening, and circuit design. Ashwin Ramachandran, Vaibhav Raj, Indrayumna Roy, Soumen Chakrabarti, and Abir De present IsoNet++ in 2025, improving an earlier late interaction model for subgraph matching.

Unlike the older model, their network lets the two graphs talk early while embeddings are built. A matching between nodes updates slowly over several rounds, and each round reruns the network under the current match. They also compare node pairs, not just single nodes, as partners. The design aims for sharper matches between query and candidate graphs.
arxiv-2510-22638:
Modal logic deals with what is possible and what must hold in a given setup. Tenyo Takahashi wrote a 2025 paper on rules in that field, and he wrote it alone. His tool is a broad form of filtration. Filtration shrinks a model while it keeps key truth facts intact. The rules he studies are called stable canonical rules.

He shows that systems with this tool can be fully set out by such rules. He gives an algebraic view of Gabbay's filtration too. Past results on formulas are pushed to a wider family of logics. A finite model trait holds for the stable logics. He also maps which logics split from the rest. New, stronger formulas sharpen the results.
arxiv-2510-23238:
A Barsode, K N Maity, and P Ajith assess how well strongly lensed gravitational waves can be detected, arguing the challenge is lensing, not luck. A small share of signals will be split by a galaxy or cluster into multiple copies arriving at different times. Those copies could probe astrophysics and cosmology in new ways.

Finding true pairs among many unrelated events is hard, and false alarms grow faster than the lensed rate as detectors improve. The authors weigh detection prospects against that background. Their analysis guides searches so that claimed lensed pairs are real, not chance matches.
arxiv-2510-23438:
Lingxiao Huang and four co-authors study coresets, small stand-in datasets that let clustering algorithms run fast while barely changing the answer. Their twist is noise: the input data is corrupted by random errors from a known pattern, so the true clean dataset is never seen. Judging whether a coreset still works well becomes tricky when the ground truth is hidden.

The team compares an older stand-in error measure with a new one that tracks the true clustering cost more closely, even though it ignores the noise pattern itself. They build a construction method around the new measure and prove it gives smaller coresets and tighter guarantees than the classical route. Under mild assumptions, coresets can shrink by a factor tied to the number of clusters. Tests on real datasets back up the theory.
arxiv-2510-23538:
Qiushi Sun and eight co-authors tackle a growing gap in artificial intelligence: models read code as text, yet programs also produce pictures, charts, and interactive pages. Good training data that pairs code with its visual output is scarce, because making and grading such pairs is hard. Their work attacks the problem from both the data side and the model side.

The team built a toolkit that uses each form of data to help create the other, producing a corpus called JanusCode-800K, the largest of its kind so far. On that data they trained JanusCoder and JanusCoderV, models that write code from text, from images, or from both together. In their tests, the mid-size models matched or beat commercial systems on text-based and vision-based coding tasks.
arxiv-2510-23638:
Songyuan Li and nine co-authors build a neural network that computes entirely in analogue hardware, with no digital help. Analogue in-memory chips do matrix multiplication cheaply, but they lack learnable nonlinear steps, the curves that give networks their power. The team turns to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, which place trainable one-variable functions on each connection instead of fixed activations.

Their design, KANalogue, realizes those functions directly in devices with negative differential resistance, where current falls as voltage rises over a range. Using cold-metal tunnel diodes, they shape varied nonlinear curves and sum them through a crossbar array, keeping the whole signal path analogue. On MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 the system reached strong accuracy with far fewer parameters than rival analogue designs, nearing digital KAN performance. The approach works for a broad class of such devices, pointing toward larger, low-energy analogue AI.
arxiv-2510-23738:
Camilla Mupo and a co-author study the cosmic defect networks of high-quality axion models. The QCD axion can solve the strong CP problem only if its Peccei-Quinn symmetry holds to an extreme standard, and Barr-Seckel models supply such axions. In these models, tangled networks of axion strings and domain walls must vanish early enough, or they would wreck the standard cosmology.

For models with domain wall number one, the authors show that axion strings with winding above one always split apart. They break into unit-winding axion strings plus pure gauge strings, which lets the whole string-wall network collapse in time. The leftover gauge strings then decay into gravitational waves. That decay generically prints a double plateau across frequencies in the wave spectrum. Upcoming detectors could see that two-step shape, turning an abstract quality requirement on the axion into a testable signal.
arxiv-2510-23938:
Marcin Spoczynski and a co-author present a framework for checking the integrity of very large machine learning models directly on the GPU that runs them. Security verification usually lives on separate CPU processes, while the models themselves run on graphics accelerators. That split creates bottlenecks and mismatches exactly when models grow past a hundred gigabytes.

Their design co-locates the checks with execution and runs the cryptography on the GPU's own matrix units, such as Intel's XMX blocks or NVIDIA's Tensor Cores. High memory bandwidth and parallel hardware let verification keep pace with the model itself. The mechanism is standardized to behave the same across vendors and hardware generations. The authors also look ahead to secure channels between trusted execution environments and accelerators. Their aim is a hardware-agnostic foundation that enterprise teams can deploy on whatever CPU and GPU mix they own.
arxiv-2510-24438:
Abdullah Mushtaq and seven co-authors pilot an agent based evaluation of Islamic content generated by large language models. Such models are increasingly used for Islamic guidance but can misquote texts, misapply jurisprudence, or produce culturally inconsistent answers. The team tests GPT-4o, Ansari AI, and Fanar on prompts drawn from authentic Islamic blogs.

A dual agent framework pairs a quantitative agent, which verifies citations and scores six dimensions, with a qualitative agent comparing tone, depth, and originality side by side. GPT-4o scored highest on Islamic accuracy and citation, Ansari AI followed, and Fanar lagged. All models still fell short of reliably accurate, faithful religious content.
arxiv-2510-24538:
Venkata S Govindarajan and Laura Biester study deliberately bad humor through sentences from the Bulwer-Lytton Fiction Contest, which rewards awful opening lines for imaginary novels. Textual humor is hugely diverse, and computational work must account for intentionally bad jokes as well as good ones. The authors curate and analyze a new corpus of contest sentences.

Standard humor detection models perform poorly on this corpus. Analysis shows the sentences mix devices from existing humor data, like puns and irony, with metaphor, simile, and metafiction. When language models imitate the style, they exaggerate it, overusing certain devices and inventing far more novel adjective noun pairs than human writers do.
arxiv-2510-24638:
Sabrina Haque leads a team with eleven co-authors who built and tested a phone app to help older adults move more. Their app, Senior Fit, had to work with no lab gear and no in person training. The group ran long tests with twenty five adults aged sixty five to eighty five.

Feedback led to fixes that made the app more clear and easy to use. Users liked video guides and nudges that made tasks feel in reach. Some disliked typing in their own logs and wanted more choice to fit their needs. A group chat page helped some users but shut out those new to it.
arxiv-2510-24838:
Ilin Lazar leads a team with eleven co-authors who map how many dwarf stars sit in galaxies by place in the web of space. They ask if the count of small galaxies by mass shifts with how close a galaxy is to the big threads and nodes of that web. They also ask if a lack of dwarfs is a real flaw in the main dark matter view.

Deep shots from two sky fields were matched with fine code worlds. Near the big threads, the dwarf share fell and the knee of the mass curve moved to higher mass. Samples were full down to low masses and out to a fair depth. On the whole, no broad lack of dwarfs showed as a flaw.
arxiv-2510-24938:
Yiran Li, Mobin Alipour, and Amir Pahlavan find a twist in how chem grades move small bits out of dead end pores. Such pores trap dirt and drug bits in rock and soil. Salt or chem fronts can push bits by a drift called diffusiophoresis, but real fronts smear as they cross mixed flow.

One might think a smeared front would kill the drift. In a one line dead end model, backed by code runs and lab chips, the team finds the reverse: smear boosts how many bits get pulled out. Their math tracks bits under a slow front over space and time. The find may help clean ups and drug dose plans.
arxiv-2510-25138:
Yuxiang Yan leads a team with seven co-authors who teach a robot the right order to move things in a clump. In a tight pile, a bad pick order can block a path or cause a crash. Past tools oft skip those space ties, which caps their range and bend.

Their frame, OrderMind, learns pick ranks straight from the space lay of the pile. A graph built from near peers pools shape facts, while a time part sets the ranks. To get true marks, a sight and word model is led by a space prior to write sound pick orders for training. Tests on a new pile set check the frame in real time.
arxiv-2510-25238:
Qianqian Qiao leads a team with nine co-authors who built VADB, a large set of films marked for their look and feel by pros. Looks in film are hard to score: time flow and mixed modes break tools made for still shots. Their set holds more than ten thousand films, marked by a large pro team.

Marks span a whole score, scores by trait, rich word notes, and plain tags. Their net, VADB-Net, pre trains on two modes in two stages. It beat past film grade tools on score tasks, and can serve more look tasks in film work. The set and code are shared in the open.
arxiv-2510-25838:
Hrant Gharibyan and five co-authors report a test of quantum advantage using circuits designed to peak on one target output. A peaked circuit is built so that one bit string, a string of zeros and ones, should appear far more often than others. They run their circuits on Quantinuum System Model H2, a commercial quantum processor.

Their largest run used two thousand two qubit gates and produced the target in under two hours. By extending results from leading classical methods, they argue the same task would take years on top supercomputers, which hints at a large gap. They also prove a related decision problem is hard for quantum verification in a formal sense.
arxiv-2510-26038:
Jiali Cheng, Chirag Agarwal, and Hadi Amiri ask whether a small student model can inherit a teacher model defense against misleading shortcuts. Knowledge distillation trains a student to copy a teacher, which compresses the model. A debiased teacher resists spurious correlations, patterns that predict the label in training but fail on new data, and the question is whether that resistance transfers.

Across language inference and image tasks, Cheng and the team find that debiasing is mostly undermined after distillation. Training a debiased student does not gain from teacher knowledge, and robustness can shift unevenly across bias types even when the average holds. They trace the change to an attention pattern and circuit inside the model, then propose fixes.
arxiv-2510-26238:
Duc-Hai Nguyen, Vijayakumar Nanjappan, Barry O'Sullivan, and Hoang D. Nguyen test how well language models can work with questionnaire data. Millions of people answer surveys daily, and the resulting tables cross many questions with hundreds of respondent rows. Models excel at open ended text, but their skill at structured survey tables is largely unexplored, and standard survey tools assume a human in the loop.

Their benchmark, QASU, probes six structural skills, including answer lookup, respondent counting, and multi hop inference, across six ways of serializing the data and several prompt strategies. Experiments on current models show that representation choice has a strong effect. The study aims to give scientists and survey users evidence based guidance on feeding questionnaires to models.
arxiv-2510-26338:
Z. M. McIntyre, A. Kasman, and R. Milson construct phase linked states for rational extended forms of the harmonic oscillator. The harmonic oscillator is the basic model of a particle in a curved trap, and its rational extended forms add exactly solvable structure. Using Maya diagrams, a counting picture of splittings, and ladder operators that raise and lower energy, they describe the algebra of lowering operators for this class.

From that algebra, McIntyre and the team build the phase linked state in the Barut Girardello sense, as a joint special function of the lowering operators. The resulting time dependent function exactly solves the time dependent Schrodinger equation. An argument based on Schur functions shows the new states in the large limit cut position momentum spread, a hallmark of classical like quantum states.
arxiv-2510-26438:
Konark Jain, Nick Firoozye, Jonathan Kochems, and Philip Treleaven study market making in a 2025 paper. A market maker posts buy and sell prices and earns from the gap between them. Their market is a limit order book, a list of waiting buy and sell orders.

Prices move in a Hawkes process, a model where past trades make new trades more likely. The maker acts at set times, not at each event, by placing, ending, or filling orders. Two learning methods are tested, and one earns strong risk-adjusted gains in tests. A hard math form is also solved for comparison. The work links control theory with deep learning for fast, jumpy markets.
arxiv-2510-26538:
David Williams, with five co-authors, reflects on how software engineering research is coping with large language models. Studies that use these models face new worries: benchmark quality, contamination, where test data leaks into training, hard replication, and the money and energy costs of running big models.

Williams and the team survey current practice at ICSE, a leading venue in the field. They give a structured picture of what researchers are doing well and where gaps persist. Their closing advice aims to firm up benchmark rigour and make studies easier to repeat. It also asks the field to face the financial and environmental costs of model-based research head-on, rather than treating them as side notes.
arxiv-2510-26638:
Dave van der Meer, with four co-authors, presents REALMS2, a multi-robot system for exploring and mapping the Moon. The system was built for a challenge run by the European Space Agency and the European Space Resources Innovation Centre, which asked teams for fresh ideas in space prospecting with robot teams.

Van der Meer and the team base the system on ROS 2, the standard robot software frame, and add visual mapping that builds maps from camera views while tracking position. A mesh network keeps rovers in touch without fixed infrastructure, and one interface controls the whole fleet. In the challenge's second field test, three identical rovers mapped about sixty percent of the test area. The system coped with communication delays and blackouts, which are routine hazards off Earth.
arxiv-2510-26838:
Amine Razig, Youssef Soulaymani, Loubna Benabbou, and Pierre Cauchy build a system that listens for marine mammals under noisy water. In the St Lawrence Estuary, calls range from low moans to ultrasonic clicks, overlap often, and sit inside shipping and environmental noise. Their framework first segments spectrograms, pictures of sound, to make soft masks of biologically relevant energy.

Razig and his three co-authors fuse those masks with the raw input at a mid level, so classification focuses on salient regions while keeping global context. Recordings come from the Saguenay St Lawrence Marine Park Research Station in Canada. The mask-guided method cut false positives and beat baseline architectures in every setting. It also held up when the sound was transformed in new ways, where high-capacity baselines lost accuracy, a sign it learns transferable traits.
arxiv-2510-26938:
Ajinkya Gaikwad, with five co-authors, studies a family of graph editing problems called F-vertex splitting. Given a graph, the task is to turn it into a member of a target class F using at most k vertex splits. They examine four target classes: constellations, cycle graphs, linear forests, and bipartite graphs, in both inclusive and exclusive splitting variants.

Gaikwad and the team show the problem is solvable in polynomial time for cycle graphs and linear forests, in both variants. For constellations and bipartite graphs, it is NP-complete in both variants, meaning it is almost certainly hard in the worst case. The results sort a whole family of modification problems by difficulty, class by class. The splitting variants follow definitions introduced by Abu-Khzam and collaborators in 2018.
arxiv-2510-27038:
Fatima Muhammad, Shamsuddeen Hassan, and Isa Inuwa-Dutse create the first dataset for detecting sexism in Hausa, a widely spoken West African language. Sexism online sustains stereotypes and exclusion, yet detection tools lag for low-resource languages where data are scarce and expression is shaped by local culture. The team built the dataset through community engagement, careful coding, and data expansion.

A two-stage study with native speakers explored how sexism is defined and voiced in daily talk. The team then tests both classic classifiers and pretrained multilingual models, including few-shot learning with only a handful of examples. Nuance proves hard to capture, especially clarification questions and idiomatic phrases, which trigger many false positives. The resource gives future work a grounded starting point.
arxiv-2510-27338:
Arun Jose, in a 2025 study, checks whether AI reasoning traces can still be read. Reasoning models write a chain of thought, a step-by-step scratchpad, before their final answer. Watching the scratchpad could reveal bad intent early. That only works if the scratchpad is legible, written in plain readable form.

Across fourteen reasoning models, Jose found training often makes the scratchpad unreadable. Models think in garbled text yet answer in clean prose; one model family was the exception. Forcing models to use only the readable parts cut accuracy sharply, by over half. Harder questions brought worse legibility. He weighs causes like hidden codes, training quirks, and leftover tokens. The warning: without care, reward-based training hides how models think.
arxiv-2510-27438:
Muhammad Garba, Alwell Nwachukwu, and four other co-authors simulate a magnetic way to sort metal ions in this 2025 paper. The paper is part two of a study of magnetophoresis, the drift of particles in a magnetic field. Even weakly magnetic ions move when the field is uneven and the material is porous, full of tiny holes. The team models that drift on a computer.

Their simulations couple fluid flow, spreading by diffusion, and the magnetic field itself. They try two views of the porous stuff: a simple Stokes view and a Brinkman view that adds drag and permeability. The Brinkman view matched recent lab data; the simple one missed key trends. Both a manganese salt and a zinc salt formed clusters under field slopes. In mixed salts, clusters of one kind dragged the other along.
arxiv-2510-27538:
King L. Ng, Luís H. Carnevale, and four other co-authors chart how droplets dance on shaking surfaces, in a 2025 study. Droplets on vibrating plates matter for microreactors and for sorting single cells. The shakes set the droplet swinging, and the swing can end in breakup. They simulate many-particle fluids across wide ranges of shake speed, shake size, and surface wetting.

Observed swings sort into phases, grouped by the capillary number, a ratio pitting flow forces against surface tension. Phase one settles into a steady state. Phase two breathes in a metastable way, then swings lopsided and can split; they measure how fast that instability grows. Phase three stays out of equilibrium. Spin and vorticity, local swirling, mark each phase. Contact counts between droplet and plate complete the picture.
arxiv-2510-27638:
Sivaraman Balakrishnan, Nika Haghtalab, Daniel Hsu, Brian Lee, and Eric Zhao formalize panprediction in 2025, a way to train one model for many future tasks and losses at once. Classic training fixes one task and one loss, which is a score for error. New practice instead asks one model to hold enough signal to serve many later uses.

Panprediction extends two prior ideas that each covered only half the goal. The team gives methods that learn such models from sample counts close to the single-task case. Both fixed and random forecast rules are covered under mild conditions. The finding is striking: serving endless tasks and losses can cost little more than serving one.
arxiv-2511-00138:
Giulia de Meijere and Hugo Martin model how incentives for self-staying home, based on incidence rather than prevalence, could flatten an outbreak curve. Their box model couples outbreak spread with single uptake of staying home, described through copying motion. People weigh the current outbreak state against the length and social cost of staying home, and may defy advice as staying home drags.

Analytical results are derived for the coupled system, comparing incentives keyed to new cases against those keyed to total active cases. Public health readers get a timing insight: incidence reacts faster than prevalence, so backing staying home on incidence could trigger earlier group action when it matters most.
arxiv-2511-00238:
Alexander Leithes examines small ripples on a rotating, expanding model universe based on Gödel's spacetime. Gödel's model is famous for rotation, and this version adds expansion as well. Leithes asks which features of the ripples are real and which depend on the coordinate choices used to describe them, a problem known as gauge dependence.

He builds quantities that stay fixed under those coordinate changes. From the energy balance equation he finds a conserved quantity, a trace measure of the spatial ripples, that holds on large scales for pressureless dust. He then extends the result to a perfect fluid, giving cosmologists clean variables for this unusual universe.
arxiv-2511-00338:
Yuhao Fang, Zijian Wang, Yao Lu, Ye Zhang, and Chun Li combine two neural tools to solve inverse problems, tasks where the hidden cause must be inferred from measured effects. One tool, DeepONet, learns operators that map inputs to solutions. The other, the neural tangent kernel, describes how a network's behavior changes during training. Their hybrid targets source finding under fluid flow equations and image reconstruction from sparse, noisy data.

Physics rules and task-specific penalties are built into the training loss, so answers stay both accurate and physically sound. Tests on synthetic and real datasets show the framework holds up under noise and sparsity. The authors present it as a flexible route for imaging and computational physics problems where data is scarce.
arxiv-2511-00438:
Yu Qiu and Yu Zhou connect three worlds that meet on decorated marked surfaces with vortices: punctures carrying an extra flip symmetry. Decorating the surface adds marked points. The symmetry then lifts to a rule: the braid twist along any path joining a decoration to a vortex, raised to the fourth power, is the identity. Groups built from such braiding encode deep geometry.

The authors prove three groups are in fact the same. One is the cluster braid group defined by King and Qiu for the surface. The others are the braid twist group of the decorated surface, and the fundamental group of a moduli space of framed differentials built by Bridgeland and Smith. They also give finite presentations for these groups, concrete generator-and-relation descriptions that make the isomorphism usable.
arxiv-2511-00738:
Maksim Konoplia and Dmitrii Khizbullin reframe place recognition, the task that lets a self-driving car know where it is from sensor data. Nearly all methods learn by contrast, pulling matching LiDAR scans together and pushing others apart. The authors instead treat the problem as multi-class classification: each location gets a discrete label, and an encoder-decoder learns to name the place of each scan directly.

Evaluated on the NuScenes dataset, the classification approach reaches performance competitive with contrastive learning methods. It also brings practical advantages in training efficiency and stability, two properties that matter when models are retrained often on growing fleets. The study widens the design space for localization, showing that a plain classification head can rival a contrastive pipeline built with far more machinery.
arxiv-2511-00838:
Avijit Pal and Bhaskar Paul work in operator theory on dilation. Dilation is the idea that a shrinking map on a Hilbert space can be realized as part of a length preserving map on a larger space. A classic theorem of Sz.-Nagy covers one operator. Their setting is multivariable, with the unit disk replaced by two special domains and the pentablock.

They prove necessary conditions for isometric dilations to exist in each of the three settings. They also construct classes of contractions on the two special domains that always dilate, and give examples built from the theory's fundamental operators. Those examples probe the gap between the known sufficient conditions and the necessary ones established here.
arxiv-2511-01138:
Raymon Watson and Karen Kheruntsyan study quantum Otto cycles, the quantum version of a classic heat engine cycle, when several control parameters are quenched at once. Sudden quenches, abrupt jumps of the controls, make the cycle tractable while still capturing how quantum working media behave.

They work within the sudden quench approximation. The authors argue it applies broadly to controllable many body systems. They test the protocol on a one dimensional Bose gas and on the transverse field Ising model. Run as an engine, the multi parameter cycle beats each of its single parameter counterparts in both work and efficiency, and even beats the sum of those cycles run separately. The same enhancement appears in reverse, raising the coefficient of performance when the cycle runs as a refrigerator.
arxiv-2511-01238:
H. J. Elmers and colleagues examine a kagome metal, CsV3Sb5, in which five percent of the vanadium atoms are replaced by niobium. Using angle resolved photoemission spectroscopy, they map the low temperature electronic structure of the substituted crystal and compare it with the pure material.

The substitution acts as chemical pressure: band widths grow and the gaps at Dirac like crossings open wider. That strengthens the magnetic circular dichroism signal, letting the team analyze orbital magnetic moments band by band near the Fermi level. The results support a predicted coupling of those orbital moments to three van Hove singularities at the zone corners. Earlier work had shown niobium doping lowers the charge density wave temperature while raising the superconducting transition temperature.
arxiv-2511-01438:
Jacob Poschl, in a single author paper, measures how sharply a neural network's output curves in input space. Curvature affects generalization, robustness, and how reliably a network responds to small input changes. But standard sharpness metrics live in parameter space, where they can be costly, hard to interpret, and sensitive to reparameterization.

His curvature rate is the exponential growth rate of higher order input derivatives, estimated as the slope of log derivative size against derivative order. For classical functions it recovers the inverse radius of convergence, and for bandlimited signals the spectral cutoff. On neural networks it tracks high frequency structure emerging in the decision boundary during training. A simple regularizer based on it matched a leading sharpness method's accuracy while giving flatter input space geometry and better calibrated confidence.
arxiv-2511-01638:
Mazen Alamir designs partial estimators, algorithms that reconstruct only part of a system's hidden state, for nonlinear systems whose parameters are not known exactly. Instead of a neural network, he proposes learning the estimator as a sparse multivariate polynomial: a compact formula relating measured data to the quantities that need estimating.

A general design framework is presented first, then tested on two illustrative examples against several machine learning and deep learning alternatives. The sparse polynomial scheme came out ahead, at least when the amount of learning data is small, the regime where big flexible models tend to overfit. The result argues for structured, interpretable formulas as serious rivals to black-box learners in estimation problems with limited data.
arxiv-2511-01938:
Tiberiu Musat explains grokking, the strange training pattern where a neural network memorizes its training data perfectly, sits at zero loss for a long time, and only then suddenly generalizes. Earlier work tied the delay to representation learning driven by weight decay, but the dynamics stayed murky.

Musat frames post-memorization training as constrained optimization: once the loss is zero, gradient descent effectively minimizes the weight norm while staying on the zero-loss manifold, the surface of perfect fits. He proves this formally in the limit of infinitesimal learning rates and weight decay. An approximation then decouples a subset of parameters from the rest, yielding a closed-form expression for the post-memorization dynamics of the first layer in a two-layer network. Simulations using the predicted gradients reproduce both the delayed generalization and the representation learning that define grokking.
arxiv-2511-02738:
Wrong labels in training data quietly hurt machine learning systems. Ilies Chibane, Thomas George, Pierre Nodet, and Vincent Lemaire study a popular fix in a 2025 paper: train a base model, then use its confidence to flag labels that look false. The flagging is only as good as that base model, they note.

The team asked whether calibrating the base model first, so its confidence scores mean what they say, makes the flags sharper. Their experiments say yes. Calibrated models flagged bad labels with better accuracy and more robustness across settings. The gain needs no exotic machinery, which suits industrial teams. The paper offers a practical recipe: calibrate first, then hunt for mislabeled examples with more trust in the scores.
arxiv-2511-03438:
V A Allakhverdyan and the Baikal-GVD team describe a fast data pipeline for a neutrino telescope sunk in Lake Baikal. Speed matters because a high-energy neutrino may mark a fleeting cosmic event that other telescopes should chase at once. The telescope's clustered layout lets files be processed in parallel across dedicated machines.

A quick pipeline turns raw hits into usable reconstructions within minutes, with delay set by glowing water levels. A fuller pipeline folds in live detector geometry and quality checks within about a day. Together they let the team alert partners fast, then refine the picture later. Fast alerts are how multi-messenger astronomy catches bursts before they fade.
arxiv-2511-03638:
Yili Wang and colleagues model the sideways flow of the f0(980) particle in proton-lead collisions to test its inner makeup, here in a companion study focused on momentum spectra. The particle's structure is still debated, with a kaon-antikaon molecule as a leading candidate. Their coalescence model assumes the molecule forms only at the last freeze-out moment, when the fireball cools enough for it to survive.

Kaon maps from a tuned hybrid model feed the forming calculation, with a sensible molecular size assumed. Output spectra match one LHC detector's data and flow matches another's across a wide momentum range. Agreement on both fronts strengthens the molecular reading. Two companion analyses together make flow and spectra a joint structural test.
arxiv-2511-03738:
Pranav Bhandari and colleagues steer the personality of language models by nudging their internal activations at chosen layers. Models show implicit traits in their writing, yet aligning those traits to a task has lacked a stable dial. Their pipeline reads hidden states tied to the Big Five traits, openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, and the rest of that classic set.

A hybrid rule picks which layers to steer, balancing strength against steadiness of the output. Steering at well-chosen layers shifts trait expression while keeping text coherent, where naive nudges often degrade quality. Stable trait control could tailor assistants for coaching, tutoring, or negotiation without retraining. The work also maps how personality constructs sit inside transformer layers at all.
arxiv-2511-04238:
Raju Kumar Gupta, Sourav Sarkar, and Samir Shukla study Vietoris-Rips complexes of integer lattices under the Manhattan metric, simplicial complexes whose pieces collect lattice points within a chosen diameter. Such complexes serve data analysis, geometric group theory, and sensor networks, and whether the lattice complex eventually becomes contractible has driven a sequence of results.

A conjecture that contractibility holds once the scale reaches the dimension is proved for dimensions up to five. Contractibility for all lattices at scale ten or more is also shown, improving earlier thresholds substantially. The homotopy type at scale two is determined as well. Shrinking the unknown range brings a full classification of these lattice complexes closer.
arxiv-2511-04538:
Cyril Vallez and three colleagues test how vulnerable the code from language models still is. AI coding assistants now write code that ships, so their bugs carry real security weight. Benchmarks exist, yet it is unclear whether leading models improved on known flaws.

The team finds even the latest open-weight models fail on the earliest reported scenarios. A realistic use setting exposes the same old weaknesses, they argue. To help, they propose a severity metric that reflects the true risk of a model-made flaw. Their claim is that safety trade-offs have so far blocked real patching of these holes.
arxiv-2511-04638:
Satchel Grant and three colleagues question whether intervening on neural networks distorts what it studies. Mechanistic interpretability often pokes internal representations to see what they encode. Such pokes may push the network into states it never visits naturally.

The team shows, in theory and in tests, that common interventions do shift representations off distribution. They then separate two kinds of divergence. Harmless shifts sit in the behavioral null space of the layer and change nothing downstream. Pernicious shifts alter real behavior, so explanations drawn from them may mislead. The distinction helps researchers judge which intervention results to trust.
arxiv-2511-04838:
Brenda Nogueira leads five authors with SPECTRA, a generative fix for lopsided molecular data. Property regression fails most where data are rarest, yet those rare ranges often matter most. Oversampling just copies molecules and produces meaningless variants.

SPECTRA generates fresh graphs guided by spectral structure instead. A rarity-aware budget focuses effort where examples are scarce. Target-neighbor alignment keeps new graphs structurally tied to real ones. Laplacian spectra, node features, and targets are interpolated together for each synthetic case. A spectral graph network with edge-aware filters then learns from the enriched set.
arxiv-2511-04938:
Davar Khoshnevisan and co-authors prove uniform dimension results for a system of parabolic equations driven by space-time white noise. The system runs on a ring, starts from a smooth fixed profile, and has set rules for drift and noise strength.

They show that, with high dimension of the output, the image of any compact set at a fixed time has twice its Hausdorff dimension, with full certainty. If the noise matrix does not depend on the state and is not singular, the same result holds in lower output dimensions too. Such laws pin down how rough the random field is.
arxiv-2511-05538:
Sarah Wyse, Eric Foxall, and Rebecca Tyson link social change and climate change in one shared model. Extreme weather shapes how people act, and human choices in turn shape the climate. Most past models kept the two apart or fixed human behavior in advance.

Their work joins three parts: a social model, a climate model with natural swings, and a combined feedback model. A key finding is that a committed minority can flip a social norm toward climate action. When that flip happens also matters a lot for later temperatures. The authors say leaving out the feedback loop can skew forecasts of future warming.
arxiv-2511-05638:
Wan Chang and co-authors explore what a second interaction region at the Electron-Ion Collider could do for imaging light nuclei. The collider will smash electrons into protons and nuclei to probe their inner structure. A second detector site, set up unlike the first, would catch particles scattered at very small angles.

That reach matters for processes where a light nucleus stays intact after the hit. Tagging the whole nucleus lets physicists map how its partons are spread in space. The authors study which events the second region could detect and chart the accessible range of energies and angles. They argue the site would widen the collider's exclusive and diffractive physics program.
arxiv-2511-05738:
D Rivera and co-authors use a trick called symmetry breaking to explain odd magnet-like traits in two rare materials, EuB6 and SmB6. Letting a model break its own symmetry on purpose can catch strong effects that a plain mean-field model misses. The team asks how an inner field, the exchange field, drives those states.

With spin-based density models, they compared four setups for the atoms' tiny magnets: fully even, two ordered forms, and a mixed form built from a random-like frame. The mixed form gave each rare-earth atom its own local field. Those fields then broke the symmetry of the charge and magnet traits. The authors say this explains past X-ray test results on both materials.
arxiv-2511-06038:
Rumen Bachev and co-authors report a fresh flare season of BL Lacertae, the blazar that named its whole class. In the fall of 2024 the object brightened sharply and flickered fast, with large swings in brightness and polarization from night to night and within single nights. Three observatories in Bulgaria and Greece monitored it over forty nights.

The campaign caught some of the most dramatic within-night flickering ever seen in a blazar. Colors changed together with no measurable delay, down to about a minute. Oddly, polarization stayed fairly steady on those short scales, unlike past episodes. The team explored links between polarization, brightness, and flicker speed to constrain how the relativistic jet produces its light.
arxiv-2511-06138:
Hossein Askari, Yadan Luo, Hongfu Sun, and Fred Roosta work on inverse problems, where a clean image must be recovered from partial or noisy measurements. Flow-based methods have lately beaten diffusion methods at this task, yet most still work in full pixel space, which is costly. Their method, LFlow, moves the work into a compressed latent space.

LFlow is training-free and samples along an efficient flow path using a pretrained latent flow model. It also introduces a posterior covariance derived from the flow itself, which guides reconstruction more faithfully than standard choices. Experiments show better reconstruction quality than leading latent diffusion solvers on most tasks tested.
arxiv-2511-06738:
Hyunjae Kim and colleagues put retrieval-augmented generation for medicine under expert review and find it wanting. Medical language models are supposed to gain currency and verifiable grounding by fetching evidence before answering. Eighteen medical experts produced more than eighty thousand annotations on eight hundred outputs spanning real patient questions and exam-style queries.

Each pipeline stage was graded separately: the passages fetched, the evidence chosen, and the final answer. Standard retrieval often hurt, with only about a fifth of passages relevant, weak evidence selection, and factuality and completeness slipping against no-retrieval models. Filtering evidence and reformulating queries recovered much of the loss on two medical question benchmarks, a call for stage-aware design.
arxiv-2511-06938:
Shunichiro Kittaka and six co-authors measure how the superconductor Sr2RuO4 changes length in strong magnetic fields, using high-quality single crystals. This substance is Pauli-limited, meaning its superconductivity is destroyed by electron spin effects rather than orbital motion. Under in-plane fields the team observed a first-order superconducting transition with pronounced hysteresis, and relative length changes of only about one part in a hundred million.

Great care was taken to remove magnetic torque artifacts through field-angle-resolved readings. Inside the hysteresis region, just below the upper critical field, a hump-like anomaly appeared in the magnetostriction coefficient, with a matching double-peak structure in its angular derivative. The anomaly might signal the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov state, though a broadened first-order transition remains possible, and it sits off the boundary earlier NMR work suggested.
arxiv-2511-07038:
Kizito Salako and Rabiu Tsoho Muhammad work on cautious reliability assessment for safety-critical software, where an estimate must not overstate how dependable the software is. Their Bayesian approach considers not one inference problem but a whole collection of them. It reports the worst case across the collection: the predicted probability that the software runs without failure in the future. Software failures are modeled as a Bernoulli process.

The authors determine these worst-case posterior predictive probabilities explicitly and deduce asymptotic features of those probabilities and their priors. They then show how the results feed into useful assessments of high-stakes systems. The work extends robust Bayesian inference and earlier cautious Bayesian methods, giving assessors a sound way to keep reliability claims honest under prior uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-07138:
Theron Guo, Kento Kaneko, Claude Le Bris, and Anthony T Patera analyze the thermal dunking problem: a solid suddenly plunged into a fluid at another temperature. Engineers care about how the solid heats and cools and about the Biot number, the dimensionless coefficient governing heat exchange at the surface. The full description couples fluid flow and energy equations to heat conduction in the solid, but full conjugate simulations are expensive, so the lumped-capacitance model, a single simple equation, is used instead.

The authors decompose the reduction error into time homogenization and lumping parts. They derive an asymptotic bound for the lumping error for heterogeneous solids with varying heat transfer coefficients, and a computable upper bound in measurable quantities. They also propose learning characteristic length scales from data so Biot correlations extend to new geometries, checking everything against simulations.
arxiv-2511-07338:
Zhen Wang and seven co-authors generate fake people with truly deep profiles. Persona-based simulation is transforming behavioral research and AI personalization, but most such personas are shallow sketches of a few traits. DeepPersona builds a taxonomy of hundreds of human traits organized in a hierarchy, mined from thousands of real user conversations with ChatGPT. It then samples from that taxonomy step by step, generating coherent personas conditionally so the details agree with each other.

Each persona averages hundreds of structured traits and roughly a megabyte of narrative text, about a hundred times deeper than earlier work. Breadth and uniqueness beat state-of-the-art baselines by wide margins. Personas improved a model's custom question answering by about twelve percent on average.
