Modeled national citizens tracked real human survey responses and Big Five personality results noticeably more closely than previous fake citizens.
arxiv-2511-07638:
Jack Guo, Thomas Roy, and Nitish Govindarajan arrange two catalysts to turn carbon dioxide into valuable products more efficiently. Silver converts carbon dioxide to carbon monoxide, and copper then upgrades carbon monoxide further. Placing the metals in the right pattern inside a flow reactor should align both steps.

Continuum transport modeling feeds an optimizer that reshapes the silver-copper surface pattern using adjoint methods. The simplified two-dimensional reactor serves as proof of concept. Better patterning raises overall yield without new chemistry. Electrochemical carbon recycling needs such design tools because reactor geometry often decides whether tandem catalysis pays off.
arxiv-2511-07738:
Donglai Xu, Hongzheng Yang, and Yuzhi Zhao train multimodal models with rewards that survive noisy labels. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards needs trusted labels, yet real annotations err often. Pure entropy tricks can lock onto wrong labels and blunt the ranking signal group-based training depends on.

A two-stage token-level entropy method first encourages exploration, then shifts toward exploitation. The schedule guides learning dynamically instead of fixing one pressure throughout. Noise tolerance improves because early openness resists premature commitment to bad labels. Practical multimodal training data is messy by nature, so methods that expect mess are likelier to survive deployment.
arxiv-2511-07938:
Chuanqing Pu, Feilong Fan, and Nengling Tai keep port scheduling forecasts useful as conditions keep changing. Seaport power and logistics scheduling usually predicts first, then plans, but forecasts tuned to one task fail when vessel arrivals reshape the task stream. Decision-focused learning ties prediction training to decision quality, at the cost of narrow fit.

Continual learning with Fisher penalties adapt online while protecting what earlier tasks taught. The method generalizes across varying scheduling tasks instead of restarting. Ports run around the clock under shifting arrivals, so schedulers that learn continually match the real port setting better.
arxiv-2511-08438:
Shivam Pandey and co-authors present Galactification, a transformer based model that paints galaxies onto dark matter only model runs. Hydrodynamical runs model galaxy traits faithfully but cost far too much to run over survey sized volumes. Dark matter only runs are cheap, so learning the galaxy layer on top of them would unlock realistic mock catalogs for interpreting cosmological observations at scale.

The multi modal transformer reads three dimensional dark matter density and velocity fields. It outputs a point cloud of galaxies with their physical traits, positions included. The trained model reproduces varied galaxy summary statistics and tracks how they shift when cosmological and astrophysical parameters change, a first for accelerated forward models of this completeness.
arxiv-2511-08738:
Will Stephenson and three co-authors explain strange wave behavior in disordered mechanical systems using Lyapunov exponents, numbers that measure how fast nearby motions diverge. Their systems are built like Markov processes laid out in space, where each site's traits depend on its neighbor in a random but ordered way.

Disorder, it turns out, tends to polarize the system's zero modes, pushing them to one side, and the exponent framework explains why. In the nonlinear regime those same modes become mobile solitons that travel while every other mode stays localized. They even teleport across barriers in a reflectionless, direction-dependent way. The authors argue the Markov viewpoint can guide the design of tunable metamaterials with built linear and nonlinear responses.
arxiv-2511-08938:
Yuxi Liu and seven co-authors improve neural compression of B-frames, the video frames predicted from both a past and a future reference. Two references should help, but in hierarchical coding the far-apart frames at some levels make the two references contribute unevenly, wasting one of them.

Two new modules harmonize the pair. Bi-directional Motion Converge merges the multiple optical flows used in motion compression, giving more accurate compensation over larger spans. Bi-directional Contextual Fusion then weights the reference contexts explicitly, guided by how accurate that compensation proved. On standard HEVC test sets the system outperforms earlier neural codecs and even passes the traditional VTM reference encoder in random access configuration. Source code is released, and the authors frame the work as closing a gap between B-frame and P-frame neural compression research.
arxiv-2511-09238:
Joschka Haltaufderheide and five co-authors examine the ethics of multimodal digital biomarkers. These tools fuse physiological, behavioral, and contextual data into continuous pictures of health. Such biomarkers reach further than earlier digital measures in variability, complexity, and abstraction. The authors argue this amounts to a change in what health itself is taken to be.

They describe an ontological shift, in which health becomes data, and an epistemic shift, in which what counts as health-relevant changes. Together these shifts reshape knowledge, responsibility, and governance in data-driven preventive medicine. When everyday signals can be read as health data, the boundary of medicine moves into daily life. The paper maps the ethical consequences that follow from that move.
arxiv-2511-09438:
Sai Puppala and four co-authors propose letting large language models assist graph learning when data must stay private and personal. Their method targets node classification and link prediction in low-resource settings, where graphs are sparse and labels scarce. Language models add data, tuning signals, and few-shot reasoning about graph tasks.

Those language-model signals parameterize a dynamic UMAP manifold of client-specific graph embeddings, inside a variational objective for personalized federated learning. A cross-modal regularizer aligns language representations with graph structure. The authors outline a convergence argument for the aggregation procedure and a privacy threat model using a moments accountant. Uses discussed include knowledge graph completion, recommendation-style link prediction, and citation and product graphs.
arxiv-2511-10338:
Guduru Manoj and ten co-authors build BhashaKritika, a synthetic pretraining dataset for Indic languages, where high-quality text is scarce compared with English. Synthetic data has become a serious alternative for pretraining, and the team generated 540 billion tokens across ten languages with five different techniques. They vary grounding in real documents, personas, and topics, and test how the prompt language and document language affect quality.

A modular evaluation pipeline checks script and language identity, metadata consistency, repetition, and perplexity-based filtering with KenLM models, keeping quality control workable across many scripts. Model training runs exposed trade-offs between translation of English content and native generation. The authors distill best practices for building multilingual corpora in low-resource settings.
arxiv-2511-11338:
Stéphane Girard and Cambyse Pakzad extend Extreme Partial Least Squares, a dimension reduction method for extremes, to data with missing entries and weak time dependence. The method models how a response depends on many covariates when the action sits in the tails, under heavy-tailed laws. Real data add two wrinkles the base method lacked: values go missing, and nearby observations lean on each other.

Their frame uses a single-index inverse regression model, with a missing-at-random rule whose chance grows with the response's extremeness. Limit theory under a mixing frame yields consistency when tails vary regularly. Simulations over eleven dependence schemes show robust behavior even with much data missing, and an environmental case study confirms the method.
arxiv-2511-11838:
Mina Sarem and three co-authors extend a phase-field model of cracking in quasi-brittle materials. Concrete is the model case. The model must now handle cyclic loads that slowly stretch the material. This ratcheting effect drives low-cycle fatigue failures. Standard fatigue models miss that steady strain growth.

Ratcheting strain is built into the free energy and the dissipation terms. The plasticity frame is pressure based and non-associative. Each load cycle adds its share of strain. Damage then grows toward final failure in a consistent way. Grounding the values in microstructure keeps the model honest. Engineers who judge structures under repeated load gain a model that matches the true failure path.
arxiv-2511-11938:
Sebastian A. R. Ellis and four co-authors improve neutrino energy estimates with a simple idea. First, classify what kind of interaction made each event. Distinct channels hide distinct amounts of energy in a systematic way. Plain calorimetric methods ignore that structure. Long-baseline oscillation tests need precise energy values to succeed.

Supervised machine learning sorts the events by channel. It trains on labeled simulated events. Channels include quasi-elastic scattering and meson-exchange current. Each channel then gets reconstruction matched to its missing-energy pattern. Next-generation tests are limited by interaction modeling errors. Using known channel structure attacks their dominant error at the source.
arxiv-2511-12338:
Felix Eder, Catherine Witteveen, Enrico Giannini and Fabian O. von Rohr show how a simple change in cooling can select among three related magnetic crystal phases. The material is a potassium chromium selenide with a layered delafossite-type structure, a promising setting for magnetism on triangular lattices. Controlling composition and structure in such materials is a known challenge.

Starting from the same self-flux mix, the team isolates phases with different potassium shortages. Each has a distinct structure. The key choice is the quenching temperature, the point at which the sample is cooled fast. That insight lets them grow full-composition single crystals. Magnet tests along different directions then reveal a strong field dependence of the ordering temperature. They also show a weak metamagnetic transition at low fields.
arxiv-2511-12638:
Benjamin Driscoll and five co-authors tackle a trust problem in modern chip computing. Graphics processors run the heavy math behind deep learning, and their small programs, called kernels, are now often written or sped up by large language models. Those optimized kernels come with no formal proof that they still compute the right thing. The authors present the first checker that can prove two GPU kernels are equivalent.

Their tool, named Volta, verifies kernels optimized by hand, by a language model, or by a compiler. The checker is shown to be sound, and complete for a well-defined class of kernels that covers many programs of real interest. It handles core machine learning work such as convolutions, matrix multiplication, and attention, giving optimized code a checkable guarantee instead of blind trust.
arxiv-2511-12738:
Parsa Esmaeilkhani and Longin Jan Latecki study a puzzle inside vision-language models: the image tokens most relevant to a question get almost no attention in the model's final layers. Since all tokens are treated alike there, answers can drift away from what the picture actually shows. The standard training signal, predicting the next word, does not teach the model where to look. The authors propose fixing that with direct supervision of attention itself.

Their loss, called KLAL, pushes the attention of answer words toward the image regions that truly correspond to them, using ground-truth maps from task geometry or existing annotations. Combined with ordinary training, it improved geometric tasks, pointing, and referring expression understanding on synthetic and real data. They also add a dataset for line tracing, a task on which even commercial models performed surprisingly poorly. The lesson is that grounding can be taught explicitly.
arxiv-2511-13038:
Bo Peng and Yu Zhang unify the mathematics of quantum systems that remember. Open quantum systems leak into what surrounds them, and the standard Lindblad equation describes the memoryless case. Many real platforms are not memoryless: they relax algebraically and show coherence flowing back, signatures of long memory. Fractional calculus, with derivatives of non-integer order, produces power-law memory kernels, and the authors build a unified framework placing fractional master equations inside the hierarchy of open-system accounts.

In their construction, the fractional equation is a structured subclass of memory-kernel models. It reduces exactly to the Lindblad form when the order is one, and it can be written as an average over plain Lindblad evolutions through Bochner-Phillips subordination, which guarantees physical validity. Its resolvent connects it to non-Markovian tools. The result is a language for long-memory quantum systems, meant for analysis and simulation.
arxiv-2511-13538:
Nailya Manatova proves blow-up results for the quintic, mass-critical generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation across a full range of rates. Earlier work built solutions that blow up with an infinite-point rate, but only under a tight technical restriction on the exponent. Manatova removes that restriction for every exponent strictly between one half and one.

Her solutions live in the energy space, stay arbitrarily close to the soliton family, and concentrate a soliton that races off to spatial infinity as the blow-up time nears. A modified virial-energy functional carries the proof and simplifies the energy estimates. The borderline case at exponent one half is left for separate treatment.
arxiv-2511-14038:
Lijie Chen, Yang Hu, and Hanlin Ren prove new limits on a classic proof strategy for circuit lower bounds. The algebrization barrier, named by Aaronson and Wigderson, explains why many arithmetization-based techniques cannot settle big complexity questions. The authors attack the barrier through a communication problem about finding a string that no pairwise XOR of two lists can produce.

They construct oracles whose algebraic extensions let certain randomized classes solve problems with tiny circuits, on all or infinitely many input sizes. Results of this form show those classes' lower bounds cannot come from algebrizing methods alone. The paper extends the barrier's reach, including toward lower bounds for the class MA with exponential time.
arxiv-2511-14238:
Yan Huang, Yongyi Su, Xin Lin, and two co-authors squeeze more accuracy out of depth estimation foundation models using only weak labels. Models in the Depth Anything line already generalize well with no target-domain training, but a little downstream data might do better. Their framework, WeSTAR, adapts a model with self-training plus regularization while updating only a small set of added parameters.

A dense self-training objective supplies structural supervision, and segmentation-aware normalization stabilizes it across scales. Cheap pairwise labels saying which of two points is closer add ordinal constraints that fix local ordering errors. A weight penalty anchors the updates so the model's broad knowledge survives adaptation to new domains.
arxiv-2511-14438:
Mahdi Etumi, Hazel M. Taylor, and Marie Farrell catalog reusable requirement patterns for space robot missions. Safety-critical requirements are usually written in natural language, which is ambiguous and resists formal verification. Specification patterns give logic-based templates instead, and a general robotic pattern suite already exists inside NASA's FRET requirements tool. The question is whether those patterns fit space missions.

The team reviewed flown missions, rewrote their requirements in FRET, and sorted them against the existing patterns. Most fit, showing the suite transfers to space. The exceptions yielded five new patterns plus several variants, all contributed back. The resulting corpus gives mission engineers a tested starting library for formal requirements.
arxiv-2511-14838:
Madyson G. Barber, Andrew W. Mann, and 13 co-authors measure the tilt of a very young planet's orbit. The planet TIDYE-1 b is only about three million years old and crosses a star whose outer disk sits at an angle. For mature systems, planet orbits show every tilt, but the few known young planets look nearly aligned with their stars' spin.

The team uses the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect, the wobble in a star's spectrum during a transit, to find the sky-projected tilt. Missing data at the transit start makes the fit tricky, so spectra and brightness data from a mass campaign supply the missing baseline. The orbit looks likely aligned, adding weight to the idea that planets start out orderly.
arxiv-2511-14938:
Jack Collard and twelve co-authors test proton specific entropy as a proxy for a key solar wind composition ratio. The slow solar wind source remains uncertain, unlike the fast wind from coronal holes. Oxygen charge state ratios freeze in near the Sun and reveal source regions. Direct heavy ion measures were once limited to far distances.

Solar Orbiter data now cover the inner heliosphere from near the Sun outward. The team confirm a strong anti correlation between entropy and the oxygen ratio across that range. They also separate fast, slow, and slow Alfvénic wind by entropy traits. The proxy extends composition inference where direct measures are sparse.
arxiv-2511-15038:
Dorien Herremans and Abhinaba Roy argue that generative music systems must be aligned with human preferences through systematic methods. Modern music generators achieve high quality and style range, yet often miss what listeners truly value. Standard training losses optimize technical traits, not musical appreciation. Taste learning methods from other fields offer a remedy.

The paper reviews large scale taste learning for music and multi taste diffusion methods. Inference time tuning techniques are also discussed. Music poses special challenges: long term coherence, harmonic agreement, and subjective quality. Scaling to long works and modeling preferences reliably remain open problems. The authors map a research agenda for taste aligned music creation.
arxiv-2511-15138:
Hyo-Jeong Jang, Hye-Bin Shin, and Kang Yin propose agreement guided active learning for emotion recognition from brain signals. Electroencephalogram signals are noisy and vary greatly between people. Emotion labels are subjective and often inconsistent, compounding the problem. Active learning must decide which samples deserve expert labeling.

Their approach judges uncertainty jointly with cross modal agreement between brain and face features. A shared latent space aligns both modalities semantically. Remaining mismatches are treated as noise driven, and those samples are queried selectively. That distinction separates true cognitive ambiguity from sensor noise. The goal is more robust affective decoding for brain computer interface systems under limited, noisy labels.
arxiv-2511-15238:
Ihab Tabbara, Eliya Badr, and Hussein Sibai make a standard safety analysis honest about its own grid errors. Hamilton-Jacobi reachability computes which states a control system can steer to a target while avoiding danger, by solving for a value function over the state space. Grid-based solvers quietly ignore the error from chopping continuous space into cells, so their safe sets can be wrong in the dangerous direction.

The authors give an algorithm that computes guaranteed lower and upper bounds on the value function itself. Those bounds certify that backward reachable sets are over-approximated and reach-avoid sets under-approximated, exactly the safe directions. A refinement step splits grid cells where the bounds are loose, so precision is spent only where it matters.
arxiv-2511-15638:
Yang Cui and three co-authors learn from imperfect labels with a physics aware neural operator, applied to denoising distributed acoustic sensing data. Supervised models degrade when labels carry errors, yet perfect labels are costly. Their physics aware loss penalizes violations of known physics to offset label flaws. A modified operator network blends U-Net strengths with function space operator learning.

The combined framework is tested on seismic sensing data from a geothermal field site. Labels from an integrated filtering method still hold residual coupling noise near the well. The physics guided model cleans data more faithfully than label fitting alone would allow. High fidelity feature representation supports that gain. The approach generalizes to other sciences where labels are imperfect but physics is trusted.
arxiv-2511-15738:
Chao Yu, Qixin Tan, and eight co-authors propose a three-dimensional view of test-time scaling for reasoning models. Reasoning models improve at answer time as their chain of thought grows, but a fixed context window caps that gain far below training scale. The authors revisit enhancement techniques and sort them into three scaling dimensions: context length, batch sampling in parallel, and turn-by-turn self-refinement.

Each dimension helps on its own but has bounded capacity. Combining all three raised performance substantially on hard testbeds from computing, math, and physics olympiads, and human preference feedback added further gains. The framework also extends naturally to a human-in-the-loop setting and to embodied tasks, where an agent acts in a physical or simulated world.
arxiv-2511-15938:
Pierre-Louis Taillat and Hadrien Kurkjian build a low-energy theory for Landau quasiparticles in Fermi liquids. Such liquids are interacting fermion systems found in liquid helium and in metals. Quasiparticles are dressed particles that carry the low-energy behavior. A shared account must cover the state equation, transport, and superfluidity at once. Their scheme removes resonant couplings above an energy cutoff by a unitary change.

The resulting Hamiltonian ties three things together. It holds the Landau interaction, the pairing behind superfluidity, and the collision term behind transport. As the cutoff changes, its flow recovers a known link between two of those parts and proves a new parallel link for pairing. One use is corrections to quasiparticle lifetimes beyond standard theory.
arxiv-2511-16138:
Weiping Yu, Ye Jiarui, and three co-authors present SGLANG-LSM, a storage system that makes large language model key-value caches scale far better. The cache stores attention data that speeds up first-token replies, but disk systems that keep one file per cache object suffer metadata overhead, inefficient input-output, and poor locality. Their design borrows log-structured merge-tree architecture from databases.

A prefix-preserving engine keeps token sequence locality while storing large cache tensors separately from keys. An adaptive controller retunes the storage configuration as workloads shift, and runtime services add batch operations and automatic resource management for production use. On large dynamic workloads, cache hits rose substantially and time to first token fell by up to about a quarter against leading systems.
arxiv-2511-16238:
Arshyn Altybay and Gulzat Nalzhupbayeva study an inverse problem for the heat equation: recovering a source coefficient that changes with time, in a setting where diffusion is governed by a fractional Laplacian. The only data is a weighted integral measurement, so the unknown must be pulled out of indirect evidence.

The authors recast the problem as a Volterra equation under a nondegeneracy condition, then build a numerical scheme from a fractional matrix power discretization plus a Crank-Nicolson time step. They prove stability and a second-order convergence rate, and give a formula that reconstructs the coefficient directly. Tests with one to five percent noise in the data show stable recovery that matches the theory.
arxiv-2511-16338:
Zoltan Bajnok and Apor Roth compare two integrable models: the elliptic Ruijsenaars-Schneider model, a relativistic many-body system, and the finite-volume sine-Gordon quantum field theory. The question is how closely their energy spectra match across coupling regimes and limiting cases.

Working in the two-particle sector, the authors compare analytically at the free point and numerically elsewhere, using a truncated Hilbert space method adapted to difference operators. They test the method in the trigonometric limit, where answers are known, and study the non-relativistic limit covering the Calogero-Moser-Sutherland family. Momentum quantization rules from scattering phases prove exact in the rational and trigonometric cases. They pick up finite-size corrections in the hyperbolic and elliptic cases, and those corrections differ between field theory and many-body systems.
arxiv-2511-16438:
Sherine George and Nithish Saji present ESGBench, a benchmark for explainable question answering over corporate sustainability reports. Environmental, social, and governance claims need answers that show their evidence. Their benchmark pairs domain grounded questions across many ESG themes with human curated answers. Supporting evidence passages enable fine grained scoring of model reasoning, not just final answers.

Leading language models are analyzed on the benchmark for factual consistency, traceability, and domain alignment. Each proves challenging for current systems in distinct ways. Transparent scoring exposes where models assert without support. The resource aims to accelerate accountable ESG focused AI. Investors and regulators need sustainability answers they can audit back to source documents.
arxiv-2511-16638:
Jordan Bounds and Ellis Edinkrah characterize commuting linear maps on the Heisenberg algebra, the matrix algebra of upper triangular matrices with ones on the diagonal in spirit. A linear map is commuting when it commutes with every element it is applied to. For many algebras every such map has a standard form, a scalar multiple of the identity plus a center-valued additive map.

For the n-by-n Heisenberg algebra the authors determine the commuting maps explicitly. The headline is that the standard form does not always suffice: this algebra admits linear commuting maps that cannot be written that way. The result adds a concrete counterexample to the catalogue of algebras where commuting maps are automatically standard, and gives the full description in its place.
arxiv-2511-16738:
Kevin J. Joven and five co-authors write a perspective on what scalable quantum computational science will require. They argue that recent hardware and error correction progress still leaves a gap between abstract quantum methods and practical science uses. Their candidate unifying framework is block-encodings with polynomial transforms.

The article surveys how block-encodings are built and combined. It also covers how quantum signal processing extends to perform polynomial transforms of encoded operators. Scaling to parallel and distributed quantum machines gets special attention. Promising uses span simulation and measuring observables in chemistry, physics, and optimization. The authors lay out traits that scalable methods should have and present the framework as a gentle bridge from quantum algorithm theory to applied science.
arxiv-2511-16838:
Anup Budhathoki, Leonardo Rydin Gorjão, Pedro G. Lind, and Shailendra Bhandari model how the joint distribution of traded volume and price for New York Stock Exchange equities evolves in time. Sampling the empirical distributions every ten minutes over nearly a thousand trading days, they fit Gamma, inverse Gamma, Weibull, and log-normal forms and track each fit's shape and scale parameters.

After removing daily average behavior, the parameter time series are dissected with Kramers-Moyal coefficients up to sixth order. For most families the shape parameter diffuses plainly while the scale parameter shows dominant jump-diffusion dynamics, with jumps accounting for a large share of its variance; the log-normal fit reverses the roles. The classification gives risk modelers a precise statement of which parts of volume-price dynamics move smoothly and which move by rare leaps.
arxiv-2511-17038:
Hao Chen, Renzheng Zhang, and Scott S. Howard rethink how diffusion models solve inverse problems, such as restoring a damaged image from partial measurements. The standard account says a learned prior and the measurement data guide sampling together, in one coupled process. The authors argue this picture is misleading, and that practice works differently than the theory suggests.

They show the diffusion prior mainly serves as a warm start that places an estimate near plausible images, while agreement with the measurements does nearly all the reconstructive work. Their method, DAPS++, separates the two stages openly, letting the measurement term drive refinement while keeping the numbers stable. It needs fewer model evaluations and still restores images robustly across varied tasks. The paper also explains why the older unified solvers worked despite the confused picture.
arxiv-2511-17238:
Anshul Singh, Rohan Chaudhary, Gagneet Singh, and Abhay Kumary probe how vision and language models handle real-world tables. Standard tests give models clean, English-only tables, while real tables come in many languages and often as noisy scans. To close that gap, the team builds MirageTVQA, a test set with nearly sixty thousand question and answer pairs across twenty-four languages, using tables with realistic flaws.

When leading models face the noisy tables, scores fall steeply, by more than a third for the best systems. A second pattern also shows: skill in English does not carry over evenly, and reasoning in other languages lags behind. The work gives builders a harder, fairer yardstick and names the two failures that most need fixing.
arxiv-2511-17338:
Paul A Draghis, Jon M Miller, Erin Kara, Elisa Costantini, Oluwashina Adegoke and Javier A Garcia present the first high-resolution X-ray view of reflected light from Cygnus X-1. It is a famous black hole system. The XRISM satellite's Resolve tool separates a broad iron line, stretched by motion near the black hole, from the smooth glow beneath it and from narrow features in the same band.

The clarity shows the excess light is one broad feature, not a pile of narrow ones that older tools could not split. Fitting its shape points to a black hole spinning near the top of the allowed range and a disk tilted at a steep angle. The spin value agrees with earlier reflection studies, which strengthens trust in that method.
arxiv-2511-17638:
Pratham Sorte proposes sending knowledge between neural networks as concept packets instead of data. Distillation and transfer learning still revolve around examples: a teacher must emit outputs, logits, or gradients for a student to absorb. The proposed framework, Model-to-Model Knowledge Transmission, has models exchange packets containing structured concept embeddings, abstraction graphs, reasoning traces, and provenance records. It operates in concept space rather than example space, with no labeled dataset or teacher outputs needed during transfer.

Sorte formalizes concept manifolds, defines an alignment mapping between teacher and student latent spaces, and derives a composite loss enforcing geometric, structural, and reasoning consistency under explicit safety constraints. Algorithms cover packet creation, ingestion, and checking. In symbolic reasoning experiments with large language models, the student reached roughly 85 to 90 percent of teacher performance while using over 98 percent less data than standard distillation.
arxiv-2511-17938:
Jianghao Wu and five co-authors improve test time reinforcement learning for reasoning models, where a model adapts at use time using its own majority votes as rewards. Such methods often collapse: responses shorten, the majority answer dominates, and accuracy falls.

They trace the collapse to updating every token equally, when a few high uncertainty tokens actually decide the reasoning path. Their SPINE method updates only those branch point tokens and keeps their uncertainty within a healthy band. Across eight benchmarks for text and multimodal reasoning, it improves first try accuracy and trains more stably.
arxiv-2511-18638:
Chidi Elijah Nwakpa, Chinedu Izuchukwu, and Chibueze Christian Okeke set a flow in time that solves mixed variational inequalities. Such problems blend an operator with a convex cost and arise in mechanics, transport, and game models. Their system steps forward, back, then forward again, in a loop that mimics a well known split method.

Lyapunov analysis shows the paths meet the solution weakly when the operator is Lipschitz and monotone in a broad sense. With a stronger pseudo monotone claim, the balance point is globally stable at an exponential rate for all starting paths. Numeric cases show the paths home in on the balance point. A time flow view can ease both proof and design of solvers.
arxiv-2511-18938:
Evie Ladbrook, Mark S. Senn, and Jon Wright image the hidden domain structure inside a cuprate superconductor in three dimensions. Phase changes breed complex microstructures that rule how a material acts, yet bulk 3D maps of them are hard to get. Their sample is a layered copper oxide doped at the famed one eighth level, where structure and electron behavior tangle.

Scanning 3D X-ray diffraction resolves broad domain wall zones with a tetragonal like cast inside the nominal orthorhombic crystal. On cooling to a low set point, fine orthorhombic like stripes appear inside that matrix. The maps recast how structural and electronic patchiness link in this cuprate class. The method proves its worth for bulk microstructure at large.
arxiv-2511-19238:
Ariel Caticha extends entropic dynamics, a framework that derives quantum theory from information geometry and maximum entropy reasoning, to quantum electrodynamics. In that framework quantum motion appears as a special flow on a statistical manifold, which explains why the theory is linear and uses complex numbers. Gauge symmetries, which act locally, were the missing piece.

With suitable choices of basic variables and constraints, Caticha derives the quantum theory of radiation fields interacting with charged particles. As a check that the unorthodox starting point still matches experience, he also derives Maxwell's equations, the classical laws of electromagnetism. The result tests whether the entropic route can support a full gauge theory.
arxiv-2511-19638:
Haokun Zhou turns the failure of simple weather models into a measuring tool for climate change. Data-driven forecast models assume the statistics linking predictors to outcomes stay fixed, an assumption a warming climate breaks. Zhou trains plain linear models of sea-level pressure and near-surface temperature, place by place, on data from the nineteen fifties and from the two thousands, then tests them on recent years. The performance gap between the two vintages defines a local, readable measure of concept drift.

Splitting errors by frequency, weather regime, and region shows the drift is dominated by slow, low-frequency change and depends strongly on the prevailing circulation pattern. Over the North Atlantic and Europe, drift peaks in one phase of the regional oscillation. The diagnostic maps how the atmosphere is reorganising beneath the averages.
arxiv-2511-20038:
Hongjian Jiang, Michael Hahn, Georg Zetzsche, and Anthony Widjaja Lin settle an open question about the power of transformers. Hard-attention chain-of-thought transformers were already known to be Turing-complete, meaning they can carry out any computation given enough steps. Whether the softmax attention used in real models has the same power was unknown.

The authors prove a stronger result: length-generalizable softmax chain-of-thought transformers are Turing-complete. Their proof routes through C-RASP, a counting language matched to such transformers. For letter-bounded languages the plain system suffices, and adding relative positional encoding extends completeness to arbitrary languages. They also train transformers on languages needing complex, non-linear arithmetic reasoning to check the theory in practice.
arxiv-2511-20338:
Adamson, Mertzios, and Spirakis price the chore of keeping a changing network two-colored. Their 2025 paper studies bipartite colorings on temporal graphs. Temporal graphs rewire themselves step by step. A proper two-coloring must survive every snapshot. Recoloring vertices fixes clashes but costs effort.

The budget question asks if few enough recolorings suffice. Static bipartite coloring is trivially easy by contrast. On temporal graphs the problem turns NP-hard. Worse, no constant-factor approximation exists in general. That hardness holds unless the Unique Games Conjecture fails. A positive result exploits snapshot structure instead. Few connected components per snapshot make it tractable. An exact algorithm runs in time exponential only in components. An approximation algorithm achieves a root-log factor guarantee. It runs in roughly cubic time in problem size. Longer palettes are the natural next question. Matching-only snapshots leave approximation open. Time-varying networks inherit deep coloring complexity.
arxiv-2511-20538:
Colombo rebuilds plasma physics inside one geometric structure. His 2025 paper recasts the Maxwell-Vlasov system, the core equations of collisionless plasma. Particles and fields usually get separate treatments. The Skinner-Rusk scheme handles both on a single space. A constraint algorithm then pulls out the full equations.

Gauss's law, Faraday's law, and gauge structure emerge naturally. Vlasov advection joins the same chain of constraints. Shrinking the system by its relabeling symmetry transforms the picture. The reduced system recovers the known Euler-Poincaré form. It also yields the classic Lie-Poisson Hamiltonian form. States that partly break the symmetry get a shifted version. That version clarifies Goldstone-type neutral modes in plasmas. The energy-Casimir stability method gains firm geometric ground. Antenna fields enter as controls on the Hamiltonian. Shaping conserved quantities suggests a route to stability.
arxiv-2511-20738:
Dmitry V. Fedorov and colleagues work in 2025 on a weak force with outsized influence: van der Waals attraction, the faint pull between molecules arising from correlated flickers in their electron clouds. In molecular crystals these feeble forces are the main glue between building blocks, so predicting a crystal's structure means computing them well. The standard tool, density functional theory, fixes this with van der Waals density functionals, recipes that add the missing attraction.

The team analysed the formalism behind the two functional families, DF1 and DF2, and built a scheme combining them into one optimisable tool. They proved the scheme on the X23 dataset, the standard set of 23 molecular crystals. Their combined functional beat existing approaches on unit cell volumes and lattice energies, the two numbers crystal predictions are judged by. Accuracy matched the many-body dispersion method, a respected but heavier technique, at far lower cost.
arxiv-2511-21038:
Anantha Padmanaban Krishna Kumar tests in 2025 whether examples shown in a prompt can teach small language models to use words against their learned meanings. He ran eight classification tasks across eight open-source models of 1 to 12 billion parameters, from the LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen, and Gemma families. Demonstrations came in two flavours: natural labels, and inverted labels that systematically flip meanings, such as tagging positive reviews as negative.

With natural labels, in-context learning improved accuracy while predictions stayed aligned with the models' prior instincts. With inverted labels, no model learned a coherent anti-semantic classifier. The semantic override rate, correctness under the flipped scheme, stayed at exactly zero in every few-shot run. Prompt alignment rose only by sacrificing accuracy. Kumar concludes that in-context learning re-aims inputs onto stable semantic directions from pretraining rather than remapping them, so flipping label meanings at this scale needs interventions beyond prompting.
arxiv-2511-21338:
Julianna Piskorz and five coauthors at Cambridge and Qualcomm probe a new kind of language model and find old habits, in 2025. Masked diffusion language models generate text by unmasking tokens in parallel, reading context from both sides, unlike standard models that write left to right. That global view should make them use distant context evenly, but the team shows it does not.

Piskorz and her coauthors find a strong locality bias: answers depend heavily on where the key information sits, favoring nearby text. They also show that the many mask tokens the model must carry during generation act as distractors, measurably degrading comprehension. Their fix is a mask-agnostic loss, training the model to give the same predictions regardless of mask count. Fine-tuning with it substantially restores robustness, and the authors urge benchmarks to report mask counts and test mask sensitivity routinely.
arxiv-2511-21538:
Finnian Gray, David Kubizňák, Hryhorii Ovcharenko, and Jiří Podolský probe the hidden symmetries of a new family of black holes, in 2025. The Ovcharenko–Podolský spacetimes describe black holes bathed in an electromagnetic field that is not aligned with the geometry, a class beyond the classic Plebański–Demiański family. Hidden symmetries, encoded in mathematical objects called Killing–Yano forms, are what make motion around rotating black holes exactly solvable.

Gray and his coauthors prove the whole class carries a non-degenerate conformal Killing–Yano 2-form, the seed of hidden symmetry. One wrinkle: unlike the aligned family, this seed does not grow the full tower of symmetries, thanks to the field's non-alignment. It still does heavy lifting, separating variables in the massless Hamilton–Jacobi, conformal wave, and Dirac equations, and making perturbations tractable. The spacetimes also test Penrose charges, quantities tied to hidden symmetries.
arxiv-2511-21638:
Daniel Jiang, Jalaj Bhandari, Yukai Yang, Rémi Munos, and Tyler Lu reduce a hard alignment problem to a solved one, in a 2025 technical note. Training chatbots for multi-turn outcomes, like a sales agent closing a deal over many messages, suffers from sparse, delayed rewards. Direct multi-turn reinforcement learning is unstable and tooling-poor.

Their Iterative PPO reframes the task: learn a multi-turn Q-function, a value estimate for conversation states, and use it as the reward model for an ordinary single-turn RLHF problem. They prove that solving that single-turn problem with standard token-level PPO is exactly a policy improvement step in the original multi-turn problem. The algorithm alternates between fitting the Q-function on logged trajectories and improving the policy with off-the-shelf tools. It sits between fully online and fully offline training, keeping adaptability with offline stability.
arxiv-2511-21738:
Single author Luke Tonon rethinks circuit complexity, the study of how large a circuit a computation needs, through information theory, in 2025. Since Claude Shannon introduced them in the 1930s, Boolean circuits have been viewed as machines that transform inputs into outputs through logic gates. Tonon proposes viewing them instead as descriptions.

On this reframing, a circuit's size measures how compactly the function it computes can be described. The paper draws analogies to Kolmogorov complexity, the theory of shortest descriptions, and develops the title's idea: truth, embodied in a function's full table of outputs, resists compression. Circuits become a special case of a general description problem, letting information-theoretic limits speak to computation limits. The framework aims to give fresh purchase on the field's fundamental open questions about efficient computation. Rather than counting gates mechanically, it asks what a function's structure permits any description to achieve.
arxiv-2511-21838:
Carpenter and colleagues tackle a blind spot in judging frontier AI risks. The worst harms may be events no one has seen or imagined yet. Standard risk analysis assigns odds to a list of known bad outcomes. That fails when the list itself is incomplete. The team proposes a process they call dark speculation. Analysts first invent and refine detailed disaster stories. Underwriters then attach odds and damage estimates to each story.

Decision makers then combine the results into summary numbers. A simplified model of rare, heavy-tailed shocks formalizes the cycle. The process beats a naive baseline that relies only on past events. It yields fuller and better calibrated risk estimates. Keeping story writers separate from underwriters improves the results. Studying several risk classes in parallel also improves the estimates. Writing thick stories rich in causes and possible fixes helps as well.
arxiv-2511-22038:
Chaturvedi and a large team of clinicians and computer scientists build tools for spotting type 2 diabetes risk early from the free-text notes in electronic health records. Notes carry timing and reasoning that structured data miss, but they are long, irregular, and privacy-sensitive. The team proposes two methods: HiT-Gnn, a hierarchical graph neural network modeling events within and across visits. ReVeAL, which distills a large language model's reasoning into small verifier models.

On carefully time-filtered cohorts from private and public hospital data, built so no post-diagnosis notes leak in. HiT-Gnn achieves the best predictive accuracy, especially for near-term risk, while ReVeAL raises sensitivity to true diabetes cases and keeps its reasoning explainable. Ablations confirm both the temporal structure and the medical knowledge augmentation matter, and fairness analysis shows HiT-Gnn performs more equitably across patient subgroups than baselines.
arxiv-2511-22138:
Haque, Rahman, Gupta, Shujaee, and George systematically test whether small language models under three billion parameters can run AI agents on edge devices, calling tools and APIs without any cloud connection. Using the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard, they evaluate models including TinyAgent, TinyLlama, Qwen, and xLAM across simple, multiple, parallel, and multi-turn function-calling categories. They compare optimization recipes: supervised fine-tuning, parameter-efficient tuning, reinforcement learning, direct preference optimization, and hybrids of them.

Model scale mattered clearly: medium models of one to three billion parameters significantly outperformed sub-billion models, reaching up to 65.74 percent overall accuracy and 55.62 percent multi-turn accuracy with hybrid optimization. The team details a preference-optimization pipeline built from AgentBank data, converting supervised examples into chosen-rejected pairs. Their conclusion is that hybrid tuning makes accurate, private, low-latency on-device agents practical, provided the model is not too tiny.
arxiv-2511-22538:
Kim and Kottas build a more flexible model of earthquakes and aftershocks. The Hawkes process captures self-excitation: each event temporarily raises the rate of future events, producing clusters like a main shock followed by aftershocks. Their marked version also tracks each quake's magnitude. Unlike the standard ETAS model, which forces one aftershock pattern for all magnitudes, their Bayesian nonparametric approach learns the excitation pattern from data. It uses basis functions over time lag and magnitude with gamma process prior weights.

The model also learns a time-varying background rate, and its Monte Carlo inference uses the exact likelihood without approximations. Tested on synthetic data and Japanese earthquakes from 1885 through 1980, it beat ETAS at forecasting and at recovering who triggered whom. The key finding: larger main shocks produce aftershocks concentrated closer in time to the parent, a magnitude dependence the older model cannot express.
arxiv-2511-22738:
Burniol Clotet proves that for many chaotic flows, the pattern of fastest divergence determines the flow itself. Anosov flows split motion into stable, neutral, and unstable directions; the unstable directions organise into a foliation, surfaces along which nearby trajectories separate. Two foliations are equivalent if a homeomorphism carries one to the other. The question is how much dynamics that topological data remembers.

The answer, for transitive Anosov flows on compact 3-manifolds, is nearly everything: if two such flows' strong unstable foliations are equivalent, the flows are topologically conjugate after a constant rescaling of time. This generalises rigidity theorems for horocyclic flows going back to Ratner, where equivalence forced the surfaces to be homothetic. The contrast is sharp: a nonconstant change of time destroys foliation equivalence, so the space of inequivalent unstable foliations is infinite-dimensional even though nearby Anosov flows are always orbit equivalent.
arxiv-2511-22938:
Ji and colleagues work on teaching neural networks to simulate fluids, so engineers can skip slow traditional solvers. Their base tools are graph neural networks that track a fluid as moving particles. But each particle only talks to its close neighbors. So these models miss the long-range pushes and pulls that shape a whole flow at once, such as pressure acting across a tank.

Their fix, CoRGI, briefly moves particle information onto a fixed grid. It runs cheap convolutional updates there so every region can affect every other. It maps the result back to the particles. Added to a standard particle simulator, it cut rollout error by 57 percent while adding only 13 percent more inference time. Against a rival design, it was 49 percent more accurate while running nearly twice as fast, a useful trade for cheaper fluid simulation.
arxiv-2511-23038:
Tyagi and Bhattacharya use computer simulations to study a family of layered hybrid perovskites, crystals that alternate organic and inorganic sheets and are already prized for solar cells and light emitters. The family has four members, combining lead or tin with iodine or bromine, and its layered structure breaks a symmetry that normally forbids a built-in electric polarization.

With density functional theory and model calculations, they find all four members have indirect bandgaps and strong spin splitting, where electron energies separate by spin direction. Their in-plane ferroelectric polarization holds electron spins in a stable out-of-plane pattern called a persistent spin texture. Reversing the polarization with an electric field flips the spin orientation of both spin branches at once. This means spin information could be written electrically and kept without power, a useful property for future spintronic memory and logic.
arxiv-2511-23338:
Loaiza-Brito and colleagues manufacture new cosmological spacetimes out of black holes. Using coordinate swaps and complex mappings that turn static black hole metrics into time-dependent universes. The point is quantum field theory, since only metrics passing the Kontsevich-Segal allowability criterion can host a consistent quantum theory. And the authors check which of their constructed dynamic metrics qualify, and for how long in each case.

Swapping the radial and time coordinates maps a static black hole's interior onto the Kantowski-Sachs cosmological model. While the rotating Kerr case lands on a specific Gowdy-type cosmology, both then tested against the criterion after complex deformation. For a Wick-rotated metric describing an accelerated universe, allowability holds only for a finite lapse of time. Of order the inverse Hubble rate, and the paper offers physical interpretations of what that window means in the examples.
arxiv-2512-00238:
Spinors describe particles with spin, and their duals are a subtle part of quantum field theory. Cavalcanti and Hoff da Silva present a unified approach to spinor duals in 2025, built on Clifford algebras and related symmetry groups. Recent work has revealed several distinct algebraic formulations of generalized Dirac duals.

Different dual constructions can lead to different physical models, so a unified view helps theorists compare them safely. The authors locate these formulations inside the structure of a complex Clifford algebra. The work is mathematical physics, aimed at readers who build field theory models from algebraic first principles. Clifford algebras unify rotations and reflections, which is why spinor theory leans on them.
arxiv-2512-00538:
Large optimization problems often exist at several resolutions at once, from coarse grids to fine ones. Robert Baraldi, Michael Hintermüller, and Qi Wang present a multilevel proximal trust-region method for nonsmooth optimization in 2025, with applications. Multilevel methods exploit that hierarchy to converge faster.

Combining coarse and fine information has proved highly effective for partial differential equations and related problems. Trust-region methods control step sizes, while proximal terms handle nonsmooth structure that gradients alone cannot. The method targets science and engineering problems whose scale defeats single-level algorithms. Nonsmooth problems include contact and friction, where gradients jump or fail to exist. Proximal methods are the standard toolkit for exactly that structure.
arxiv-2512-00738:
Paul Oamen, Robert Wesley, and Pius Onobhayedo wrote a 2025 paper on loyalty programs in the age of smart commerce. Reward schemes have grown from copper tokens to complex digital systems. Yet most programs stay closed, with one brand controlling the points, rules, and rewards.

Coalition programs let points work across brands, which should help everyone. Still, the authors note that many such coalitions fail within ten years, despite the network gains theory predicts. Their paper asks how rewards should be orchestrated so partners share value fairly. The lessons matter for retailers building joint programs that last.
arxiv-2512-00838:
Md Muzakkir Quamar, Ali Nasir, and Sami ELFerik present a planning framework for drones in a 2025 paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles must plan missions in complex, uncertain settings, from shifting weather to failing parts. Good plans are often computed with Markov decision processes, which weigh actions, chances, and rewards together.

Those processes grow too large to solve directly as missions scale up. The team's two-stage decomposition breaks the big problem into smaller pieces that can be solved and recombined. The framework is built to be scalable and fault-tolerant. Faster, sturdier planning would let drone fleets take on bigger jobs.
arxiv-2512-01038:
Hetvi Shastri and four coauthors present FMTK in a 2025 paper on time series tools. Foundation models adapt to new tasks with little or no extra training, and time-series foundation models do the same for data that unfolds over time. They have shown strong results on classification, regression, and filling missing values.

FMTK is a modular toolkit for building composable pipelines from such models. Users can mix and match stages instead of rebuilding a whole system for each job. Modularity matters because time series work spans forecasting, monitoring, and health signals, each with its own steps. A shared toolkit lowers the cost of trying foundation models on real problems.
arxiv-2512-01138:
Search tasks that always have an answer sit at the heart of this study. Some can be solved fast by a chance-based method. The work starts a close study of that class of tasks. It groups tasks that a fast random method can always solve.

Examples include finding a prime in a fixed range. They also include tasks that test claims about circuit limits. The study maps what sits in the class and how its parts link. A clear map helps show which hard search tasks may yield to fast random methods and which may not.
arxiv-2512-01338:
Sanjeeda Sultana, Chayan Ranjit, and Surajit Chattopadhyay rebuild a dark energy model. The model mixes a Chaplygin gas with holographic dark energy in the Barrow frame. That frame tweaks how entropy works at the edge of space. Such models try to explain why the cosmos grows faster over time.

The team checks if the rebuilt model obeys the broad law of thermodynamics. They also bound its values with fresh data from space probes. A model that passes both checks stays in the race. One that fails helps rule out paths for dark energy theory.
arxiv-2512-01538:
Marco Romanelli, Gabriel Gil, and Stefano Corni quantize light modes of metal nanoparticles. Tiny metal bits can trap light as plasmons. Their shape can be any form, not just spheres. The metal's response shifts with light tone in ways set by real data.

Their method handles odd shapes with that real response built in. Quantized modes let scholars compute quantum effects of plasmons. Those effects matter for sensors and light tools at tiny scales. A general method frees the work from shape-by-shape hand math. Experimental dielectric data anchor the modes, so predicted resonances can be checked against measured spectra for real metals, not ideal ones.
arxiv-2512-01638:
Zvirzdin searches for ultra-high-energy photons with the Telescope Array. Such photons can test astrophysics models and new physics. The array's surface detector has run for many years. Its data holds a vast set of air shower events.

A neural network sorts showers by their likely source particle. Photon showers differ in shape from proton showers. The sort yields updated caps on the diffuse photon flux. Tight caps rule out models that would flood the sky with such photons. They also bound exotic ideas about dark matter decay. Fourteen years of data give the caps weight, since rare photon showers need huge exposure before a null result means anything at all.
arxiv-2512-01738:
Pedro Curvo, Jan-Willem van de Meent, and Maksim Zhdanov scale neural solvers to industrial physics. Large simulations must capture fine local acts and long-range links at once. Millions of spatial elements make both hard. Attention over all elements is too costly.

Their Multi-Scale Patch Transformer splits the task. Local attention works inside patches of elements. Global attention works on coarse patch summaries. That split keeps fine detail without full cost. Industrial users could run larger, truer physics models with learned speed. Patch summaries carry the far field cheaply, much as multigrid solvers do, which is why the design scales near linearly in tests.
arxiv-2512-02138:
Networks of machines, from drone swarms to power grids, are often built from parts that are individually easy to control. Fengjun Yang, Jake Welde, and Nikolai Matni study in 2025 what happens when those parts are coupled: the whole network can lose the flatness property that made each part simple.

Differential flatness lets engineers plan motion and design controllers with unusual ease for a single subsystem. The authors seek distributed control that survives coupling designed to preserve flatness across the network. Their results matter wherever many nonlinear units must cooperate, because a control scheme that only works in isolation fails exactly when the system becomes interesting.
arxiv-2512-02238:
Roger Penrose held that time's arrow is writ in the shape of space. As things form, one kind of curve in that shape, Weyl curvature, should come to dwarf the other kind. Four authors led by R. A. Sussman take a fresh look in 2025 at what they call a long-held false take on this Weyl claim.

A claimed counter-case by Bonnor used exact math for hot spheres that fall inward in a Vaidya setting. The team rechecks that case and what the claim in fact says. The stakes are high. The claim ties the smooth start of the cosmos to the rule that disorder must grow.
arxiv-2512-02538:
Nathanaël Berestycki gives a concise tour of the hidden sound spectrum of Liouville quantum gravity. That theory describes a random, fractal like geometry meant to model quantum space. On it runs Liouville Brownian motion, the natural random walk for such a strange landscape.

Berestycki lays out how the motion's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions are built, forming the spectrum of the geometry. He also summarizes a recently proved Weyl law, which counts those tones at high frequency. Work in progress on the heat trace is reported too, linking the spectrum to how heat would spread on quantum geometry. The talk also serves as a map for those who want to learn this young field from the ground up.
arxiv-2512-02738:
Joel Nyholm, Wojciech Mostowski, and Christoph Reichenbach profile energy use down to single lines of code. Energy demand grows from phones to huge data centers, and developers need detail to fix waste. Older profilers blame whole programs or single functions, which is too coarse to act on.

Their probabilistic profiler targets statically typed JVM based languages, including Java. It estimates energy per source statement, with uncertainty stated openly. Line level feedback could help teams cut the energy cost of common software, a growing share of global electricity use. Line by line costs show staff the exact line that eats the watts, not just the app as a whole blob.
arxiv-2512-02838:
Ridha Horchani drafts an experiment to tell two explanations of the classical world apart. Quantum theory allows macroscopic superpositions, yet daily life never shows them. Either the environment steadily erases them, a process called decoherence, or the wave function collapses on its own.

Both stories predict similar everyday behavior, so telling them apart takes care. Horchani's blueprint lays out how a real experiment could distinguish the two mechanisms. A working test would strike at one of the deepest open questions in physics, the border between quantum and classical. Two tales that match on all past tests can still split on the next one, and this plan names that next test in full.
arxiv-2512-02938:
Maksymilian Kuna and seven co-authors show that a weak magnetic field brightens valley control in a tungsten diselenide sheet. The monolayer was grown by molecular beam epitaxy on hexagonal boron nitride. Valley polarization measures which of two electron valleys the light emission favors.

Circularly polarized photoluminescence measurements track that balance as a field is applied. A field on the order of a tenth of a tesla already enhances the polarization, the authors report. Easy valley control in grown monolayers supports valleytronic devices, which store information in electron valleys. Weak fields are cheap to add and safe for the flake. So a boost at low field is worth more than one that needs a huge rig to run.
arxiv-2512-03038:
Giulio Fabbian and six co-authors remeasure a faint distortion in the cosmic microwave background's spectrum. The y type distortion records the pressure of hot gas trapped in galaxy groups and clusters. Archival data from the FIRAS instrument still holds untapped signal for this measurement.

With improved cleaning of astrophysical foregrounds, the team extracts a new mean distortion value. The result carries implications for feedback models in galaxy formation and for cosmic shear measurements. Old satellite data, reanalyzed well, can still sharpen how we model gas in the universe. Old tapes with new eyes is a cheap trick with real yield. This yield is a mark that gas rich clumps must match in their own tales of growth.
arxiv-2512-03238:
Synthetic data can train AI without exposing real records. Natalia Ponomareva and a large team offer a practical guide in this 2025 work. They focus on making such data with differential privacy, which bounds what can be learned about any one person.

Good data are vital for AI, yet fresh human data are getting scarce. The guide, called how to DP-fy your data, walks through the process step by step. Clear guidance helps firms share and use data safely. It also helps meet privacy rules while still training useful models. Step-by-step guidance lowers the barrier for teams with data but no privacy experts.
arxiv-2512-03438:
Rewarding only final answers can starve agent training. Reuben Tan and a large team address that in this 2025 work on multimodal reinforcement learning. Agentic models are capable, yet sparse outcome rewards dominate their training.

Rewards computed from reasoning tokens give finer guidance during learning. The authors add an agentic verifier to supply those richer rewards. Finer feedback can teach agents to plan and check their work. That may raise reliability in tasks that mix text, images, and tools. Reasoning-token rewards teach process, not just outcomes, which may curb lucky but flawed answers in multimodal agent training.
arxiv-2512-03738:
Doctors predicting how long a patient will survive need honest uncertainty ranges, especially when a wrong call is costly. Jaeyoung Shin, Chi Hyun Lee, and Sangwook Kang work on that problem in a 2025 statistics preprint. They use conformal prediction, a model-agnostic method that promises correct coverage in finite samples, and extend it to survival data where many outcomes are cut short by censoring.

Earlier conformal methods for censored data either assumed narrow settings or demanded heavy computation. One recent approach builds censoring-adjusted p-values, but its coverage depends on heuristic tuning and it breaks when the patient population shifts. Shin and colleagues supply the missing theory for how its prediction sets are built, then extend the method to handle such covariate shift. Simulations and a real dataset show robust coverage and sensible interval shapes across censoring levels and shift strengths.
arxiv-2512-03838:
Medical prediction models can be accurate yet untrusted, because doctors need reasoning they can check, not just a score. Michael Staniek, Artem Sokolov, and Stefan Riezler teach language models to reason from clinical consensus guidelines step by step. Their 2025 preprint turns written guidelines into training data by applying the rules to real electronic health records.

Because the rules are explicit, the model's reasoning can be graded automatically, checking conclusions against premises and values against measurements. The team demonstrates the approach on the complex Sepsis-3 definition. Small fine-tuned models beat much larger models that were merely shown the definition, and nearly perfect rule-following appeared on unseen patients from the same area. The remaining bottleneck is forecasting sparse clinical variables into the future. Adding a time-series model's output to the language model improved that part as well.
arxiv-2512-04138:
When a dataset contains errors, fixing them well depends on knowing how they got there, yet most monitoring tools only flag that something looks wrong. Philipp Jung and colleagues present MechDetect in a 2025 preprint, a simple algorithm investigating how the errors were generated. It builds on the statistics literature about missing values, where mechanism has long mattered.

Given a table of data and a mask marking which entries are erroneous, MechDetect trains models to test whether the errors depend on the data itself. That distinction, data-dependent versus data-independent corruption, guides very different repairs. The method generalises classic missing-data tests and applies to other error types whenever an error mask exists. Experiments on benchmark datasets show the approach identifies mechanisms effectively. The authors pitch mechanism detection as the missing diagnostic step between noticing dirty data and cleaning it correctly.
arxiv-2512-04238:
Vision-language models are entering clinical workflows, yet their benchmarks mostly show them typical anatomy. Leon Mayer and colleagues probe the blind spot in a 2025 medical imaging preprint. Rare anatomical variants, such as six fingers or a single kidney, act as natural adversarial examples. They violate the expectations the models have learned.

The team introduces AdversarialAnatomyBench, the first benchmark of naturally occurring rare variants across modalities and body regions. Testing twenty-five state-of-the-art models brought three findings. Mean accuracy on perception tasks collapsed, from about seventy-one percent on typical anatomy to twenty-eight percent on atypical anatomy. Even the strongest models lost between roughly two-fifths and half their accuracy. Their errors mirrored anatomical biases, and neither scaling nor bias-aware prompting or test-time reasoning fixed the problem. The benchmark gives the field a systematic way to measure and mitigate anatomical bias.
arxiv-2512-04338:
Biagio Montaruli, Luca Compagna, Serena Elisa Ponta, and Davide Balzarotti present one detector for harmful Python packages that fits both public stores and company systems. Malicious packages are a rising path for supply chain attacks. Current tools miss two things: tricks that rewrite code to dodge scans, and the distinct false-alarm limits that distinct users can accept. A public store needs very few false alarms; a firm can accept more. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles both gaps.

The team built a method that crafts sneaky package variants with fine code scrambling. Training on such variants made the detector far harder to fool. They then tested it on a huge daily haul of real packages from PyPI, gathered over eighty days. The tests show the hardening works but needs care, since it can shift false alarms. The result is a single tool that adapts to each setting's risk line.
arxiv-2512-04438:
Tu Nguyen, Tuan Nguyen, and Vu Le give an explicit algorithm that reads off the type of a Lie algebra from a single invariant. Lie algebras encode the local rules of continuous symmetry groups. Sorting them into types is a basic step in algebra and physics. The invariant they use, named Jordan-Kronecker, packages the algebra's structure into data that a computer can check. Their 2025 arXiv paper turns that package into a decision method.

The algorithm takes the invariant of any finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra as input. It then walks through fixed steps to name the algebra's type. The authors built the method into a working Matlab program. Such a tool lets researchers sort new algebras without hand proofs for each case. It also gives students a concrete way to test how the invariant reflects structure, and it supports wider computer algebra work on symmetry.
arxiv-2512-04638:
Kei Beauduin presents a new formula for umbral operators, a tool from a quirky corner of algebra that treats sequences as if they were powers. Umbral calculus has long given shortcuts for handling polynomial families. The new formula does three things at once. Its 2025 arXiv paper ties the field to iteration theory, the study of repeated function application. It also gives a natural meaning to fractional powers of umbral operators, which had lacked a clean definition.

The proof gathers a wide spread of older results in operational calculus and shows their combined force. As a sample payoff, Beauduin extends the classic Laguerre polynomials in a new and natural way. Fractional exponents could let researchers interpolate between known operators, opening paths that integer steps cannot reach. The work renews a classical subject by linking it to modern dynamics.
arxiv-2512-04738:
Zhuoyue Wan, Wentao Hu, Chen Jason Zhang, and co-authors present OsmT, an open model that turns plain questions into queries for OpenStreetMap. The map's data answers through OverpassQL, a structured language few casual users can write. Big closed models can translate, but they cost much, hide their workings, and resist small deployments. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a lean, open alternative tuned for map tags.

A mechanism called Tag Retrieval Augmentation feeds the model relevant tag knowledge while it writes a query. Tags are the map's vocabulary, arranged in layers from broad classes to fine details. With the right tags in context, generated queries stay valid and precise. The team reports gains over generic open models on their tests. A trustworthy translator could open the world's largest open map to journalists, planners, and aid workers who think in words, not code.
arxiv-2512-04838:
L. D. M. S. Sai Teja, N. Siva Gopala Krishna, Ufaq Khan, and co-authors present DAMASHA, a framework for finding the seams where a text switches between human and machine authorship. Mixed-authorship documents now appear in classrooms, newsrooms, and courts, and knowing who wrote which span matters for trust and oversight. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds a detector, called Info-Mask, that segments such texts at their transition points.

Info-Mask blends three signal kinds: stylometric cues from writing style, perplexity signals that flag machine-like smoothness, and structured boundary modeling. To stress the system, the team built and released an adversarial benchmark of mixed texts with deliberate perturbations. The framework also exposes human-interpretable attributes behind each call, so users can see why a seam was drawn. Reliable segmentation could help editors and teachers judge collaborative writing fairly.
arxiv-2512-04938:
Raquel Norel, Michele Merler, Pavitra Modi, and co-authors propose watching the brain through the voice: continuous cognitive monitoring from smartphone speech, fused with other records by a relational graph transformer. Patients with rare neurological diseases report brain fog that standard tests cannot see. Clinic visits are snapshots months apart. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests the idea in phenylketonuria, a metabolic condition where blood chemistry swings affect thinking.

A speech measure, Proficiency in Verbal Discourse, tracked blood phenylalanine levels with a clear correlation. Standard cognitive tests showed no such link. The authors argue a graph transformer can weave speech, lab values, and assessments into one model, dodging the bottlenecks of mixed medical data. The prize is alerts weeks before a patient crashes. Validation across diseases and languages remains the hard road ahead.
arxiv-2512-05038:
Cassandra Goldberg, Chaehyeon Kim, Adam Stein, and Eric Wong uncover a quirk in how transformers handle concepts. Concept vectors are directions inside a model that stand for human ideas, a tool for reading what the model is thinking, but their signals are often noisy. The authors find that transformers systematically sharpen the signal instead of spreading it evenly across many tokens.

Attention heads tuned to a concept multiply the gap between matching and non-matching inputs, so the already-strong activations grow fastest and the best evidence piles into a few tokens they call SuperActivators. In large models those tokens stand out from the noise, appear reliably whenever the concept is present, and are few — a small slice of the top activations does the job. Detection built on them beats standard scoring across images and text, and the tokens carry sharper, more local meaning than global concept vectors.
arxiv-2512-05138:
Sakshi Agarwal, Wei Xiong, and Rampi Ramprasad present polyRETRO, a language-model tool that works backward from a target polymer to how it could be made. Machine learning now designs promising polymers quickly, but deciding how to actually synthesize one still rests on expert intuition, and automated retrosynthesis — routine for small molecules — barely exists for polymers. That gap slows the move from computer designs to real materials.

Given only the target's chemical string, polyRETRO first predicts which class of polymerization reaction most likely built it, then identifies the reaction template and the starting monomers, working largely in natural language. Framing the problem for a large language model makes the reasoning readable to chemists rather than a black box. The authors present it as a first step toward polymer retrosynthesis tools that scale — and toward lab validation at the speed designs are proposed.
arxiv-2512-06138:
N. T. Nguyen-Dang and twenty co-authors stack faint X-ray signals to weigh galaxy clusters that optics found and X-rays barely see. eROSITA supplies X-rays; Subaru supplies the optical catalogue. Nearly a thousand clusters are stacked into measurable profiles. Weak lensing calibrates the mass scaling relations.

The luminosity relation runs slightly steeper than self similar prediction. No extra evolution is required. Detected clusters are a biased subset, with brighter centers. Optical and X-ray samples are different populations; cosmology depends on knowing it. Combining deep surveys is the value shown.
arxiv-2512-06238:
Yuping Zheng and Andrew Lamperski study how to measure cause and effect flowing between two streams of data. Their tool of choice, directed information, gauges how much one stream helps predict the next step of another, step by step in time. Labs must guess this value from a finite run of data, so they need to know how far off the guess might be.

Work on error bounds had covered data drawn from a fixed set of symbols, but not smooth real valued data. The authors fill that gap for data that follows a bell curve pattern. They write the target rate as a clean formula built on best guesses of the next value, then build an estimator from it. They prove its error shrinks at a known rate as more data comes in. Such bounds help engineers trust causal measures drawn from real sensors.
arxiv-2512-06438:
Ramazan Fazylov and four co authors present AGORA, a system that creates moving three dimensional head avatars that can be driven in real time. Such avatars serve virtual reality, remote presence, and film. Older methods were slow to render or stiff in motion, while fast splatting methods, which paint a scene with soft three dimensional blobs, mostly made still heads with no control over expression.

AGORA grows splatting inside a generative contest setup, where one network makes avatars and another grades them. A light branch, steered by a standard face model, nudges each blob so the face can change expression while keeping its identity. Two graders, fed with synthetic renders of the face mesh, police realism and expression alike. The avatars render at high speed on a graphics card and, notably, at a usable rate on a plain processor alone. On expression accuracy the system beat leading rivals.
arxiv-2512-06638:
Isha Karn and David Jensen show that two favorite data sets for testing fake news detectors cannot judge the very thing they are used to judge. Graph neural networks detect fake news by modeling both article content and how stories spread between accounts. The benchmarks, GossipCop and PolitiFact, pair articles with their spread graphs, so they look ideal for grading such models.

The authors benchmark five graph architectures against a plain network that ignores spread entirely and reads only article features. The plain network matched or nearly matched the graph models, with gaps inside the noise. Shuffling the article features wrecked performance, while randomizing the spread links changed almost nothing, a sign the graphs carry no useful signal. Most nodes sit one hop from the root, so the graphs are shallow fans with little structure. On synthetic data where spread truly informs, graph models pulled clearly ahead.
arxiv-2512-06738:
