M Yashwanth and four co authors adapt image models across sites that cannot share their data or even reveal their labels. In federated source free domain adaptation, each client holds unlabeled images from its own world, and the only starting point is a model pretrained elsewhere. The source data itself is off limits. Clients' worlds differ sharply from each other and from the source, so local training drifts, and the guessed labels that guide it go unreliable.

Their framework, FedSCAl, steadies clients by aligning their predictions with the server model's predictions, a mechanism they call server client alignment. After alignment, the clients' guessed labels measurably improved, which cuts the drift at its root. Across benchmark vision data sets, FedSCAl consistently beat leading federated methods in this strict setup. The work matters wherever privacy or ownership bars data pooling, from hospitals to fleets of cameras.
arxiv-2512-06938:
Ivanhoé Botcazou and co-authors work on a mundane but stubborn problem: making a language model write a text of exactly the requested length. A recent method counts down the tokens left to write, but the authors show it wobbles badly when asked for lengths outside its training range. Tying control to an absolute remaining count, they argue, is the weak point.

Their fix replaces the countdown with a progress ratio, the share of the target length already written. That ratio feeds the model as a smooth signal built from wave-like functions, which the authors liken to a sense of impatience. The method slots into standard transformer designs without fuss. In tests on two news-summarization benchmarks, length was held steady and text quality did not drop. It also worked for target lengths the model had never seen in training, the very case that broke the older approach.
arxiv-2512-07138:
Emi Cora Valmai Hughes, Avinash Upadhya, and Kishan Dholakia survey a detector technology that counts single particles of light, and its promise for seeing inside living tissue. Superconducting nanowire detectors offer extreme sensitivity, timing precise to trillionths of a second, and reach across a broad range of wavelengths. This perspective weighs them against established photon-counting devices for the biomedical imaging tasks where light is scarce and every photon counts.

The advantages are concrete: better signal against noise, sharper timing, and wider bandwidth enable deeper tissue imaging and exact measurements of how long fluorescence lingers, a signature of tissue state. Quantum-enhanced imaging schemes also come into reach. Barriers remain at the system level, since the detectors need deep cooling and careful collection optics. Arrays are scaling up and cryogenics are shrinking, lowering those barriers.
arxiv-2512-07638:
Mohammad Farhoudi, Masoud Shokrnezhad, and Tarik Taleb wrote this 2025 survey paper on future mobile networks. Sixth-generation networks will fuse edge and cloud computing with very fast links. Services will multiply, shift, and surge in ways today's systems cannot handle.

Four tasks sit at the heart of running such services. They must be registered, indexed, discovered, and selected, a chain the authors call SRIDS. The survey first lays out the theory and the end-to-end workflow. It lists design goals from reliability and scale to privacy and trust. A broad review then exposes gaps that block a unified approach. The authors sort known mechanisms into centralized, distributed, decentralized, and hybrid kinds. Each study is graded against the design goals they set out. Their own proposal is a hybrid architecture for the field. Central data management keeps consistency, while distributed coordination supplies scale. Generative AI is woven in as support.
arxiv-2512-07738:
Dengjia Zhang and seven co-authors wrote this 2025 report from Johns Hopkins' HLTCOE team. They entered the TREC 2025 track on video question answering. The task, answer generation, asks a model to answer questions about a video.

Their approach works in two stages built around ranking. A base multimodal model first drafts several candidate answers. A second model then reranks those candidates into a final order. The reranker trains on a new loss designed for this listwise job. That loss mixes pointer-based selection with weights that depend on rank. A masked cross-entropy term, restricted to a set vocabulary, completes it. The blend gives stable and interpretable training for the reranker. Generative fluency and discriminative ranking thus pull together. Experiments show steady gains in accuracy and ranking stability. Questions needing temporal reasoning benefit most from the design. Semantic disambiguation, another hard case, improves as well.
arxiv-2512-08038:
Elifnur Sunger, Tales Imbiriba, Peter Campbell, Deniz Erdogmus, and colleagues, researchers in machine learning and medicine, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their topic is retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of premature infants that neural networks can help classify from fundus images. Doctors, however, need explanations they can trust before acting on a model output.

Their method, called SSplain, explains a classifier pixel by pixel while keeping the explanation smooth and sparse. Earlier explainers often broke up the natural structure of the image, producing unrealistic maps. SSplain poses the task as an optimization problem with combined constraints and solves it with a standard splitting method. In experiments it beat common explainers on accuracy and smoothness checks. It also highlighted features that match what clinicians themselves treat as signs of the disease, and it carried over to other public datasets.
arxiv-2512-08138:
Kyriakos Lotidis, Panayotis Mertikopoulos, Nicholas Bambos, and Jose Blanchet, researchers in game theory and learning, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is the Nash equilibrium, the standard solution idea for games, and whether equilibria survive when conditions shift. They examine robustness in two senses: against small changes to game payoffs, and against noise in the learning process that leads players to an outcome.

The authors define robust equilibria as those unchanged by any small payoff disturbance, and describe them geometrically. They then study a learning rule called follow the regularized leader, asking which equilibria it settles on under randomness. Despite their different origins, the two robustness notions match: strategic robustness implies dynamic robustness, and weakening the first breaks the second. They also show how fast learning converges to robust equilibria, with entropy based regularization giving geometric speed in many games.
arxiv-2512-08238:
Mahathir Monjur and Shahriar Nirjon, computer scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about judging speech quality with a language model. Phone, voice over internet, and streaming services must monitor huge amounts of degraded audio. Classic measures mimic human opinion scores but need controlled tests, while learning based scorers give numbers without explaining themselves or answering questions.

Their system, SpeechQualityLLM, pairs an audio encoder with a language model trained on the NISQA corpus. Training uses question and answer pairs about overall quality and four traits: noisiness, coloration, discontinuity, and loudness. The model writes textual answers, from which numeric scores are read back. On held out clips, its error on overall quality was small and its ranking matched human ratings well. Users can also ask free form questions and request the ear of different listener types, cutting the need for costly listening panels.
arxiv-2512-08438:
J Maes, Gavin J Pringle, and Hannah P Menke, earth scientists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They simulate fluid flow through rocks using full resolution scans, with no shrinking of the images to fit the computer. Their two rock samples, a sandstone and a carbonate, were imaged by micro CT at billions of voxels each, the carbonate full of fine porous patches.

Running on the United Kingdom ARCHER2 supercomputer, their solver treats the rock surface through a simple volume indicator rather than a complex fitted mesh. That choice allows plain grid meshes built in parallel, scaling cleanly as the machine grows. Scaling tests show full resolution flow simulations are now feasible on such giant images, opening true scale modeling for geology and engineering.
arxiv-2512-08638:
Anthony Manni and coauthors study a variant of the Michelson interferometer designed to sense tiny strains, such as those from gravitational waves. In place of normal beam splitters, the design uses special four port scatterers called Grover coins, which are unbiased in direction. That change is meant to sharpen phase readings.

The team works out the noise to signal ratio for sideband tones created when a gravitational wave shifts the phase. They explain how the Grover setup boosts the signal, and how adding light recycling can improve it further. The work is a careful quantitative case for the design. It shows where the gains come from and what limits remain, giving builders a clearer path to more sensitive detectors.
arxiv-2512-08738:
Samuel Johnny, Blessed Guda, Emmanuel Aaron, and Assane Gueye define a new task called Sign Language Spotting. Automatic sign recognition helps bridge deaf and hearing communities, but finding one specific sign inside a longer signed sequence has barely been studied. Their task asks whether a query sign appears in a sentence level target video.

Instead of using raw video frames or gloss text, their model works directly on pose keypoints taken from the videos. An encoder only design with a binary head decides whether the query sign is present. Pose input cuts compute cost and reduces visual noise. On a shared task data set for word presence, the system reaches moderate accuracy and F scores. The authors present the result as a first step toward full sign retrieval and verification tools.
arxiv-2512-09538:
Ekaterina Fadeeva leads a team improving how the uncertainty of a language model's answers is measured. Consistency-based methods sample answers to the same question and gauge how much they agree; disagreement signals uncertainty. In short-answer tasks, random sampling often produces duplicate answers because the model's distribution is peaked, and its randomness makes uncertainty estimates vary from run to run.

Their alternative uses beam search, a deterministic decoding method, to generate the answers instead. The resulting family of methods performs better and with less variance than sampling-based ones. The authors also prove a lower bound on the probability mass a beam set captures, under which beam search is guaranteed smaller error than random sampling. Across six question-answering datasets, the beam-based approach improved on multinomial sampling and reached uncertainty quantification performance. The message is in the title: do not throw away the beams a model computes.
arxiv-2512-09638:
Cristiano Longarini and Cathie Clarke investigate a bottleneck in how stars gain mass from their protoplanetary discs. They work with a sample of discs where the star's mass, the disc's mass, and the disc's size have all been measured dynamically. From those data they infer each disc's viscosity, the parameter summarizing how fast material spirals inward.

The inferred viscosities span a broad range, over a thousandfold. That spread tracks the star's rotation period: systems whose stars spin faster show lower accretion rates, as if their inflow is choked. The authors interpret this within magnetospheric accretion models. The balance is between the co-rotation radius, where the star's magnetic field rotates with the disc, and the magnetospheric radius, where the field takes over. It decides whether material accretes steadily or is held back in the propeller regime. They conclude stellar spin is a key regulator of disc-to-star transfer.
arxiv-2512-09738:
Tanja Amerstorfer leads a team testing whether heliospheric imagers watching from the L5 Lagrange point can improve forecasts of coronal mass ejection arrivals at Earth. These solar eruptions drive space weather that can damage satellites and power grids, so arrival time and speed predictions matter. The study prepares for the European Space Agency's Vigil mission, which will observe from L5.

Using the ELEvoHI model, they feed in imager data from the STEREO mission, adding observations progressively as would happen in real time, and measure how forecast accuracy changes. They also test human factors: predictions based on tracking by three scientists expose how manual choices bias results. Direction estimates from imager methods are compared with coronagraph-based ones. The findings show imager data improves forecasting when combined with other observing platforms, especially once data extend beyond an elongation from the Sun, laying groundwork for Vigil-era prediction methods.
arxiv-2512-10138:
Raymond Chu, Inwon Kim, and Sebastian Munoz analyze the supercooled Stefan problem, the mathematics of water freezing below its melting point. Supercooled liquid can freeze in jagged ways, with ice nucleating suddenly at scattered points. The authors first study general solutions, proving with a new Markovian gluing technique that fractal freezing and nucleation are the generic pattern. They then single out maximal solutions, obtained by maximizing a suitable average freezing time, and prove this marked class is far better behaved.

For maximal solutions, the transition zone between liquid and solid is open except for a low dimensional leftover set, letting obstacle problem methods deliver finer regularity. Maximal solutions are generally not universal: unlike constructions can give unlike answers. Yet sharp stability under perturbations holds for each. In radial and one dimensional settings, the picture cleans up fully: the maximal solution is universal and minimizes nucleation, matching what physicists observe.
arxiv-2512-10238:
Antu Saha surveys a research program on resolving software issues with artificial intelligence. Fixing reported bugs is central to software quality, yet developers struggle with poor quality issue reports, limited knowledge of real workflows, and little automated help. The program attacks on three fronts. First, it improves the reports themselves, using language model reasoning enriched with application specific information. Second, it studies how developers actually resolve issues, in both traditional and AI augmented teams, to ground the tools in real practice rather than assumptions.

Third, it automates the cognitively hardest resolution tasks: locating the buggy user interface element behind a report, and identifying the right solution. Machine learning, deep learning, and language model methods are all brought to bear. The document is a compact three page research overview rather than a single study. It presents empirical findings, practical tools, and automated methods as one agenda.
arxiv-2512-10438:
Jacob Fox, Benny Sudakov, and Yuval Wigderson work on a Ramsey theory question about tournaments, round-robin style directed graphs where every pair of vertices has exactly one arrow between them. Colour the arrows with many colours, and the question is how long a directed path can be guaranteed that avoids one chosen colour entirely. Questions of this shape feed into vector sequences, convex geometry, and hypergraph theory.

The authors prove a clean threshold result. Once the number of colours is large enough, any coloured tournament holds a colour-avoiding directed path nearly as long as the whole tournament. It misses the full length only by a small power. That settles a question of Gowers and Long, strengthens several of their results, and extends earlier work by Loh.
arxiv-2512-10538:
Shubham Ghatul and co-authors present NUTEx, a small near-ultraviolet telescope riding on a CubeSat platform to watch the sky for brief, flashing events. CubeSats are cheap and compact, and this payload is built for a micro-satellite bus. Its Ritchey-Chrétien telescope feeds a photon-counting detector that is blind to sunlight, giving a wide field of view in the near-ultraviolet band.

The instrument aims to catch transient phenomena such as supernova remnants and flaring M-dwarf stars, events that unfold too fast for slow survey schedules. The paper lays out the optical design, the home-built readout electronics, and the mechanical structure with its analysis. Sensitivity reaches faint magnitudes in a twenty-minute exposure, and launch is scheduled for the second quarter of 2026, making the paper a full design report for a mission still under development.
arxiv-2512-10638:
Sepideh Adamiat, Wouter Kouw, and Bert de Vries ask whether spikes can do statistics. Bayesian inference gives a principled account of how natural agents process information, but how neurons might carry out its steps is unknown. The team tests a concrete hypothesis: that belief propagation, the message-passing algorithm on factor graphs, can run inside a network of spiking neurons.

They encode each incoming message to a factor node as a spike-based signal, pass it through leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, and decode the result as the outgoing message. Three core operations, branching, addition, and multiplication, are each realised in such networks. Checked against the standard sum-product algorithm, the message updates come out accurate. And the framework handles Kalman filtering and Bayesian linear regression, covering both still and moving inference problems on the road to neuromorphic reasoning hardware.
arxiv-2512-11438:
Tariq Berrada Ifriqi and colleagues present Flowception, a video generation method that builds films by inserting frames rather than predicting them one after another. Autoregressive generators extend a video step by step, so errors accumulate and long clips drift. Generating the whole sequence at once avoids drift but costs far more computation and cannot decide how long a video should be.

Flowception learns a probability path that mixes two operations: dropping new discrete frames into the sequence and continuously cleaning up frames already there. Insertions compress long term context efficiently, cutting training computation roughly threefold compared with full sequence flows. The model learns video length jointly with content. Scores on standard quality benchmarks beat both autoregressive and full sequence baselines. The same machinery handles image to video generation and filling in missing frames between two known ones.
arxiv-2512-11538:
Gergely Bérczi and Felix Minddal introduce a non associative model for the Hilbert scheme of points, a central object in algebraic shape that parametrises clusters of points on a space. Nested versions of these schemes, tracking clusters inside clusters, are notoriously singular, which blocks the building of virtual invariants, the corrected counts modern shape relies on. Their idea is to embed the problem in a smoother, larger space.

In the non associative Hilbert scheme, the standard nested scheme appears exactly where an explicit associativity condition holds, cut out by a section of a purpose built bundle. That description yields canonical obstruction theories and virtual fundamental classes in every dimension and for every cluster pattern. Virtual localisation then produces closed formulas as sums over admissible nested partitions. Over the most singular locus, these collapse into a single iterated residue formula. That formula governs all the virtual integrals at once.
arxiv-2512-11638:
Juan Andrés Urrea-Niño and co-authors, with Sinéad M Ryan, ask what heat does to an exotic form of charmonium. Charmonium is a bound pair of a charm quark and its anti partner. The exotic state here, labeled 1 minus plus, cannot be a plain quark pair, so it hints at richer structure.

Using lattice simulations from the FASTSUM group, the team tracks this state above zero heat for the first time. They use a distillation method with a wide set of probes. Heat adds a flat background to their signals, which needs care. They also try tuned distillation shapes built for hot systems. Early reads on the state heat response are reported.
arxiv-2512-11938:
Jason Hanson gives two recipes for building a quantum circuit that enacts any permutation of basis states. A permutation just shuffles items; on n qubits it shuffles 2 to the n labels. Both recipes use only multi controlled Toffoli gates, the workhorse swap like gate of quantum computing.

The first recipe starts from any split of the permutation into swaps, but needs one spare ancilla qubit. The second needs no spare, yet demands swaps between labels at Hamming distance one, meaning labels differing in a single bit. Hanson proves every permutation admits such a split and gives a way to trim the swap count. The circuits suit tests of quantum algorithms and error checks.
arxiv-2512-12038:
Antonio Olivas-Martinez, Peter B Gilbert, and Andrea Rotnitzky extend proximal causal inference to a richer kind of intervention. Proximal methods handle hidden confounding by using two proxy sets: negative control treatments and outcomes. Past work covered fixed or randomized treatment rules for a single exposure.

The new target is a modified treatment policy, where each person dose is shifted by a set rule, a natural what if for drug and vaccine studies. The authors give identification and estimation that avoid assuming all confounders were measured. Modern debiased machine learning handles the nuisance parts. The method is motivated and tested on COVID-19 vaccine immunobridging data, where hidden immune strength confounds the read.
arxiv-2512-12138:
Shan-Ping Wu, Peng Cheng, and Shao-Wen Wei study gravity and heat in a 2025 physics paper. They ask how a fixed volume changes the gravitational partition function. That function links the Euclidean action, a key quantity in gravity theory, to heat based results.

Going past the massless case, they build solutions with mass and find a new class of shapes with a boundary and a horizon. Extending those shapes gives forms with two horizons, each often with a cone-like flaw. Only at one critical mass can both flaws vanish. The work ties these forms to the Schwarzschild de Sitter static patch.
arxiv-2512-12238:
Yinzhu Cheng and four co-authors propose a new way to measure how close two texts are in meaning in a 2025 paper. Semantic distance supports search and text sorting, but most measures are fixed rules. Fixed rules adapt poorly to new data or to the needs of a given task.

Their measure treats a hidden meaning function as a Gaussian process. Its kernel mixes Matern and polynomial parts, and its settings are learned from labeled data, not set by hand. They test it on fine grained sentiment sorting with large language models that learn from examples. Results show the learned measure works well for that task.
arxiv-2512-12338:
S Ozum, T Akkurt, R Erdem, and N Guclu study a ferroelectric crystal through geometry in a 2025 paper. The crystal, Sn2P2S6, switches between ferroelectric and paraelectric phases as temperature and pressure change. Ferroelectric materials hold a natural electric polarization that an outside field can flip.

The team models the crystal as a quantum lattice with multi-well local potentials. They track mean and Gaussian curvature, curvedness, and shape index of free energy surfaces across the phases. Near the phase change, three measures show a cusp, a sharp point, while Gaussian curvature tends to zero. That pattern helps map how the two phases meet at critical points.
arxiv-2512-12538:
Martin J Gander, Yao-Lin Jiang, and Hui Zhang propose a new coarse solver for the Helmholtz problem in a 2025 paper. The Helmholtz equation models oscillating waves, and solving it on fine grids needs many degrees of freedom. Coarse problems inside Schwarz methods, a divide and conquer scheme, inherit that size, so they become too large to help.

Their form of Schwarz method adds coarse correction in two parts: a randomized SVD of the interface iteration and hierarchical domain decomposition. SVD is a matrix factorization that finds dominant patterns from random sampling. The resulting coarse problem is hierarchical and splits into decoupled pieces at each level, making large wave problems more tractable.
arxiv-2512-13038:
Milind Sarkar and co-authors build a machine learning system that sorts gamma-ray bursts by distance using optical data alone. These bursts are among the brightest events in the cosmos and can probe the early universe. Their afterglows fade fast, so quick distance calls matter for follow-up.

The system uses plateau and prompt traits from 171 long bursts, cleaned with robust statistics, careful gap filling, and feature selection. An ensemble learner combines several model types. At a redshift split of 2.0 it reached a true positive rate of 74 percent. On a separate sample it hit 97 percent overall accuracy. A public web app offers the classifier for real-time use.
arxiv-2512-13238:
Francesco Ragusa and co-authors present Ego-EXTRA, a video and language data set for expert help given through a trainee's own eyes. It holds 50 hours of unscripted first-person video of people doing hands-on procedures. A real expert guides each trainee by voice, playing the role of a wearable assistant.

The expert sees only the trainee's view, answers questions, and offers tips unprompted. Those dialogues were transcribed and turned into over 15,000 visual question answer sets for benchmarking. Current multimodal models scored poorly on the benchmark, the authors report. The gap shows how far egocentric assistants still have to go.
arxiv-2512-13838:
Adam Brček, Ryosuke Hirai, Ilya Mandel, and Harmony Lower present a new framework for how massive main-sequence stars evolve. Stars spend most of their lives on the main sequence, where hydrogen burning sets the internal structure that shapes all later stages. In massive stars, winds and binary interactions can change that structure during this phase.

Implemented in the COMPAS code, their framework tracks the convective core under any mass-loss or mass-gain history. It also treats stellar rejuvenation and main-sequence mergers. The model yields more massive helium cores at the end of the main sequence and more compact radii in stripped stars. It also gives systematically higher black hole masses than common prescriptions, improving rapid population synthesis.
arxiv-2512-14338:
Michael Murray, Tenzin Chan, Kedar Karhadker, and Christopher Hillar study how Hopfield networks learn symmetry in a 2025 paper. Many learning problems are organized by group symmetries, and invariance is usually built into the model by design. The authors ask when it can emerge from training on part of an orbit instead.

In classical Hopfield networks, memorization can be written as a linear margin problem. Their main result shows that samples from a finite permutation orbit concentrate fast around the full orbit solution. A polynomial number of samples, independent of orbit size, can give near invariance and memorize every orbit element. For graph isomorphism orbits, invariant parameters form a three dimensional subspace, and every such orbit is memorizable.
arxiv-2512-14538:
Riku Ikarashi, Yuji Koike, and Shinsuke Yoshida check that two rival calculation schemes in quantum chromodynamics agree where they overlap. Both describe how a polarized hyperon, a heavy cousin of the proton, emerges when an electron smashes into a target. One scheme tracks transverse momentum in detail; the other, called twist-3, works with collinear quantities and special fragmentation functions.

In the middle momentum range both schemes should hold, and the authors show they do. The polarizing fragmentation function can be rewritten using the twist-3 functions, including purely gluonic ones. The two cross-section formulas then coincide, confirming they capture the same physics from different angles.
arxiv-2512-14738:
Zhengxu Yan, Han Li, and Yuming Feng, researchers at Stanford University, built NoveltyRank to judge how original a research paper really is. With AI papers pouring out faster than anyone can read, spotting a truly new idea among small updates is hard. Their 2025 system compares a paper against earlier literature to score its conceptual novelty.

NoveltyRank treats the job two ways: labeling one paper as novel or not, and ranking two papers against each other. The team tested three model sizes, from a compact encoder to a large frontier model used with no training. Small models fine-tuned for the task beat the big untrained one, showing that focused training matters more than size. The best model now runs as a public online scoring tool.
arxiv-2512-14838:
Marianne Moore and Stefano Profumo rescue a dark matter candidate that standard theory left for dead. The candidate is the sexaquark, a tight bundle of six quarks: two up, two down, and two strange. If the early universe cooled in the usual thermal way, far too few sexaquarks would survive to explain dark matter.

The authors show that a non thermal path can make enough of them. Late decaying particles called reheatons can flood the young universe with strange rich matter that clumps into sexaquarks. They give compact formulas for the final amount, set by how much strange matter is made and how well it clumps. Worked examples use reheating heats of 10 to 100 MeV. The study maps where the idea works and checks it against collider and detection limits.
arxiv-2512-14938:
Zhenzhi Wang and four coauthors release TalkVerse, a large open dataset for making talking head videos from audio alone. The field has been hard to compare fairly, since top systems train on closed data or huge private models. TalkVerse offers 2.3 million high resolution clips, 6.3 thousand hours in all, drawn from over 60 thousand hours of raw video.

Each clip passed checks for clean cuts, looks, and tight sync between sound and lips, and carries notes like body skeletons and style captions. With it, the team trains a 5 billion parameter model that can generate a full minute of video with little drift. It matches a 14 billion parameter rival on lip sync and looks, at one tenth the cost. The data, recipes, and model are all open sourced.
arxiv-2512-15338:
Chloe E. Fisher leads twenty four authors reporting that a hot rocky planet shows no clear sign of air. The planet, TOI-1685 b, orbits an M dwarf star, the class of systems most promising for studying rocky planet atmospheres. The team watched four transits with the Webb telescope's NIRSpec instrument and added a fifth from an earlier phase curve study.

The combined spectrum is flat, and statistical retrievals favor a plain flat line over any atmosphere model. A hydrogen dominated atmosphere is firmly ruled out. Heavier secondary atmospheres must have a mean molecular weight of at least about 10, at roughly five sigma significance. Pure carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide, water, or methane air, or a mixed secondary air, could still fit if clouds sit high. The authors judge the planet is likely a bare rock, and they weigh escape and stellar activity as causes.
arxiv-2512-15538:
Taichi Aida and co authors present a method for tracking how sets of vectors change over time in a 2025 paper. Such sets appear in ecology, crime mapping, and word embeddings, where each set has its own structure that also shifts. Comparing sets across time is hard because both members and structure move.

The team models the distribution behind each set with infinite dimensional Gaussian processes. Approximating the latent function with random Fourier features gives compact representations that can be compared across time. Plotting those representations in low dimensions shows transitions clearly. Tests on crime distributions and word embeddings show the method captures change in an interpretable and robust way.
arxiv-2512-15738:
Abraham Itzhak Weinberg presents a hybrid quantum classical ensemble for predicting S&P 500 direction in a 2025 paper, dated December 6. Market direction models rarely beat 55 to 57 percent accuracy because prices are noisy and non stationary. Even small gains, though, can carry real value.

The framework combines quantum sentiment analysis, a decision transformer, and strategic model selection, reaching 60.14 percent directional accuracy, a 3.10 point gain over single models. Mixing different algorithms on the same data beat mixing data sets, and a 4 qubit quantum circuit added up to 1.5 points per model. Filtering out weak models lifted the top seven ensemble well above all 35 models combined. Backtests gave a Sharpe ratio of 1.2.
arxiv-2512-16238:
Yifeng Cai and seven co-authors protect expert knowledge in AI services in a 2025 arXiv paper. Owners of valuable professional data hesitate to feed it into language models: they earn little from it yet keep the legal risk if it leaks. Existing tools hide the data from its owners and bake it into the model, beyond their control.

Their system, PKUS, treats each provider's knowledge as a separate adapter that runs only inside a hardware-sealed trusted execution environment, while the base model stays on graphics cards. Tests on sentiment, inference, and question answering tasks with two models matched full fine-tuning quality. Per-request speed beat CPU-only secure setups by 8.1 to 11.9 times. The design gives providers a trustworthy, controllable way to license knowledge.
arxiv-2512-16938:
J. E. Hirsch writes a comment on a recent paper about the Meissner effect, the expulsion of magnetic fields that marks superconductivity. Markos and Hlubina had argued that standard theory does describe the dynamics of that expulsion, contrary to Hirsch past claims.

Hirsch replies that their arguments carry flaws that void the result. He walks through where the reasoning breaks, in his view, and proposes a lab test that could shed light on the dispute. The note, marked as a comment on arXiv:2511.03384, keeps alive a long debate over whether textbook theory truly explains how the Meissner state forms in time.
arxiv-2512-17038:
Brandon Marks and coauthors test whether generalized-gamma scale mixtures of normals fit large image data sets. Such mixtures, normals blended by variances drawn from a generalized gamma law, are popular priors for Bayesian image reconstruction, yet their realism was unproven at scale.

The team draws data from remote sensing, medical imaging, and image classification, then checks the fit on Fourier and wavelet coefficients and on first-layer AlexNet filter outputs. Augmentation tricks and rules for finding exchangeable coefficients help. Best-fit parameter zones run far broader than the zone past computing work stressed. The family beats Gaussian, Laplace, and Student t priors on every set, though some image traits still fit poorly.
arxiv-2512-17238:
Aprup Kale, Rucha Kulkarni, and Navya Garg study how to split goods that cannot be divided, such as houses or jobs, among people who value them in their own ways. A perfect split would leave no one jealous and waste nothing, but such splits do not always exist. The team asks whether they exist in the typical case, where values are drawn at random.

Their answer is yes, with high chance, once the numbers of people and items grow large. Better still, the split can be found fast. Sampling just a few values per item, rather than asking everyone about everything, is enough to compute it. Tests on small random cases already came close to the ideal split.
arxiv-2512-17638:
Pavel Mnev and Konstantin Wernli review their extension of a deep invariant that Chern-Simons theory assigns to three-dimensional spaces. The older perturbative invariant, built by Witten, Axelrod, and Singer, only worked at acyclic flat connections, special points where a key operator has no quiet modes. Most spaces offer messier connections where that tool falls silent.

The new construction integrates a Chern-Simons volume form over a whole smooth island of flat connections, not just one point. The result is a higher-loop invariant for framed three-manifolds that tolerates the generic case. Reviews like this one fix the construction in one place, signs and conventions included, so other researchers can build on it without chasing scattered papers.
arxiv-2512-17838:
Roshan Kenia, Xiaoman Zhang, and Pranav Rajpurkar ask whether today's coding agents can handle real medical imaging work. They built ReX-MLE, a benchmark of 20 challenges drawn from major medical imaging contests. The tasks span many scan types and demand full workflows, from raw data to a finished submission.

The team tested leading agents paired with several large language models. Most entries landed near the bottom when ranked against human experts. The failures came from missing medical knowledge and weak engineering under tight time and compute limits. The benchmark gives builders a clear map of what domain aware agents still lack.
arxiv-2512-18138:
Yihao Zhao, Yang He, and Zhonghan Hu study the Madelung problem for finite crystals. The classic problem asks for the electric potential at one ion inside an ionic crystal, a sum over all its neighbors that fixes the crystal's lattice energy.

For a finite crystal of size p, they show the potential splits into a sum over displacement vectors to the neighbors. Each pair term breaks into three parts: a bulk term, a boundary term, and a finite size correction with a known leading form. Adding the parts gives a direct summation scheme that converges fast. It stays accurate even at p equal to 1, a block of just 27 unit cells. The scheme puts Madelung constants for many ionic crystals within reach of hand calculation.
arxiv-2512-18238:
Ding Jia leads a seven author team lining up time series that have holes. When several sensors log the world, missing values and drifting clocks leave the records out of step. Many fixes first fill the gaps with guesses, which can bend the match that follows. Their method syncs the records under firm time and shape rules, with no filling at all.

They state the sync problem in exact terms and offer three fast shortcut methods that trade a little accuracy for scale. On varied real data sets, their approach beat past methods on match quality and on how many rows could be lined up, across a range of loss rates. The work gives messy sensor data a cleaner joint reading.
arxiv-2512-18338:
Antonio Palamara, Francesco Plastina, Antonello Sindona, and Irene D'Amico build a first principles way to count work in a driven quantum crowd. When many interacting particles are pushed out of balance, the work done spreads over a range of values, and each moment of that spread tells part of the story. Past accounts often rested on fitted stand ins.

Their method rebuilds the core easing function from thermal density theory, so every moment of the work spread can be scored in a consistent way. On the Hubbard model under a staggered push, the easing shifts shape as the system crosses from a Mott state to a band insulator. The frame should carry to other tangled quantum materials out of balance.
arxiv-2512-18438:
Didier Sornette and Virgile Troude argue that living things are built to speed up chemistry. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, starts from the standard picture of life as a system that holds internal order by consuming free energy and dumping entropy. They claim this waste is not a side effect but a shaped feature of living networks.

Using calculations on real biochemical reactions, they show that living systems act as non-normal chemical accelerators. The lopsided, layered wiring of their reaction networks amplifies energy flow and entropy export, even while the system stays stable overall. The framework makes testable predictions about dissipation rates and robustness. It also suggests an evolutionary principle: life tends to build ever more non-normal reaction architectures.
arxiv-2512-18538:
Takeshi Fukuyama finds the same hidden structure in two distant arenas: nuclei forming in heavy-ion collisions and Bose-Einstein condensation in the early universe. In both, a short-lived middle sector shapes the outcome, and removing it from the equations leaves a memory of its past behavior. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, works out that shared pattern.

In the collision case, dropping the Delta hadronic sector produces an exponential memory kernel. In the cosmological system, the collapsed component feeds back through the expansion rate, and dropping it also gives a history-dependent equation. Together they define a universality class, plus a time-scale test for when memory matters. As an application, he predicts the sequential-to-direct ratio in hypertriton formation grows with the hadronic stage's lifetime, a shift of about 40 percent against a 20 percent change in total yield.
arxiv-2512-19138:
Matteo Fael, Jack Jenkins, Enrico Lunghi, and Zachary Polonsky sharpen the Standard Model forecast for a rare B-meson decay. In the decay, a B meson turns into a strange hadronic system plus a neutrino pair that escapes unseen. Precise forecasts let experiments spot any excess that hints at new physics.

The update uses a state-of-the-art short-distance coefficient with quantum chromodynamics and electroweak effects included. Heavy-quark methods organize the mass terms and power corrections up to high order. The branching ratios for neutral and charged B mesons land near three and a half parts in one hundred thousand, with errors near three percent. Cuts matched to Belle II are included.
arxiv-2512-19338:
Claudia Neves and Chang Xu heal a long split in extreme value statistics. Two schools compete: block maxima, which keep only the largest value in each block, and peaks over threshold, which keep everything past a high line. Block maxima fell from favor as wasteful, since it discards data.

Their hybrid-Hill estimator joins the two. A new universality class of extreme distributions drops the old demand that blocks be huge before a maxima fit makes sense. Inference focuses on the larger block maxima, from which the peaks-over-threshold method emerges naturally. The hybrid's asymptotics promise more than efficiency, and extensions to dependent and non-stationary data are sketched.
arxiv-2512-19838:
Fayçal Drissi, Xuchen Wu, and Sebastian Jaimungal model the business of supplying liquidity to a decentralized exchange. Their setup is a game played in steps. First, a risk-averse provider sets how much liquidity the exchange holds, and runs a costly hedge on a central exchange. Next, price-aware traders pick their volumes. Then arbitrageurs pull prices into line. The team proves an equilibrium exists for broad trading rules.

Depth of liquidity turns out to be the provider's main risk dial. It is set in advance to cap exposure. Two more forces shape whether the role pays. One is the ratio of risk aversion to hedge cost. More caution in that ratio means thinner markets and less mean profit. Private information is the other force, and its effect is not one-way. For mild price moves, it can draw liquidity in. For large moves, it thins the market.
arxiv-2512-20038:
Wen-Ji Hua and four co-authors demonstrate group quantum key distribution that trusts no source. Multipartite entanglement lets several users share one secret key. Source-independent conference key agreement stays safe even if the source is rigged. That is a strong draw. Past demos hit snags, though. Making and sharing multipartite entanglement was slow and hard to scale.

Their build uses polarization-entangled photon pairs. Three users sit in a star network. Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger correlations are assembled after the fact, by a post-matching method. The team reports a secure group key rate above twenty thousand bits per second. That is under the stated channel transmission, in a symmetric-loss network. Six sets of tests vary the channel and the basis-choice odds. They map how the key rate answers. The path looks scalable for large multi-user quantum networks.
arxiv-2512-20238:
Luigi Ruggiero and co-authors built microwave resonators directly on germanium quantum-well structures. Such devices are needed for hybrid quantum devices that pair superconductors with semiconductors. On the usual Ge-on-silicon bases, photon losses had kept quality factors disappointingly low.

Their resonators are patterned in an aluminium film grown together with the semiconductor stack on a bought Ge wafer. Quality factors pass one thousand routinely and reach about forty-nine thousand at single-photon levels, roughly ten times better than earlier Ge devices. The resonance also survives in-plane magnetic fields up to 850 millitesla. The advance removes a materials bottleneck for Ge-based quantum circuits.
arxiv-2512-20338:
Valentin Féray and Kelvin Rivera-Lopez build a general theory of up-down chains. Each step of such a Markov chain first grows an object, then shrinks it back to the original size. The approach unifies scattered results in the literature and adds explicit conditions for constructing well-behaved, integrable examples.

The payoff is a family of scaling limits. Applied to permutations and graphs, the chains converge to diffusions whose values are permutons and graphons, continuum limits of those discrete objects. Both chains and diffusions are ergodic with diagonalizable semigroups, and the maximal distance to stationarity has an explicit formula. For the diffusions, that distance involves the Dedekind eta function. The stationary measures are new recursive objects the authors introduced earlier.
arxiv-2512-20638:
Maty Bohacek and co-authors go looking for what benchmarks hide. Standard test suites report one aggregate score per model, masking the specific concepts where a model is weak and the concepts a benchmark itself under-covers. Their method reads concept activations from sparse autoencoders inside the model to map gaps concept by concept.

Applied to five open models across more than a dozen benchmarks, the unsupervised method rediscovered documented weaknesses, including sycophancy, without being told to look for them. It also found novel model gaps and flagged benchmark gaps, core concepts a benchmark claims to cover but barely tests. Because the analysis grounds evaluation in internal representations, comparisons across benchmarks come naturally. Developers get a finer instrument for improving both models and tests.
arxiv-2512-20838:
Abhishek Samlodia and four co-authors place a classic magnetism model inside curved anti-de Sitter space, a geometry central to holography. Using tensor networks, a compact way to store quantum states, they tile the hyperbolic space and scan the model's phase diagram. They look for ordered and disordered magnetic phases and the boundary between them.

Both phases appear, separated by a true phase transition. Deep in the disordered phase, boundary spin correlations fall off as a power law, matching holographic expectations. At the critical point, boundary entanglement grows logarithmically, while the whole system follows a volume law. The team also measured correlators that reveal how fast information scrambles.
arxiv-2512-21238:
Mohammed Latif Siddiq, Joanna Santos, and four co-authors grade five leading language models as if they were students in a security curriculum. Using Bloom's taxonomy, the ladder from remembering up through understanding, applying, analyzing, and evaluating to creating, they test GPT-4o-Mini, GPT-5-Mini, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Llama-3.1, and Qwen-2.5 on multiple-choice questions, vulnerable code from the SALLM collection, real course exams, XBOW case studies, and project-based design tasks.

The pattern is consistent: models recall facts and spot known vulnerabilities well, then degrade sharply when asked to reason about architecture, evaluate designs, or create secure systems. The authors formalize each model's ceiling as a software security knowledge boundary, the highest cognitive level with reliable performance, and catalog fifty-one recurring misconception patterns across the levels. Teams adopting AI coding assistants gain a sober map of where supervision is optional and where it is indispensable.
arxiv-2512-21938:
Boltzmann equations with inverse power potentials approach the hard-sphere equation as the power stiffens. Quantitative rates for that limit were missing. Zheng-Nan Hu, Jin Woo Jang, Zheng-An Yao, and Yu-Long Zhou prove a sharp pointwise estimate for the collision kernel. The inverse-power angular part differs from its hard-sphere limit by an error proportional to the small parameter, blowing up only mildly at grazing angles.

The estimate delivers the optimal linear convergence rate for solutions of the homogeneous Boltzmann equation with large initial data in suitable Sobolev spaces. It is measured in weighted norms. Earlier work had the kernel convergence and weak solution convergence; this paper makes both quantitative with the best possible rate, closing the estimate for the classical grazing-collision limit.
arxiv-2512-22038:
Competitive platforms rate players whose skills drift over time, and matchmaking shapes what each match reveals. Wataru Nozawa studies controlled rating dynamics in the mean-field limit. A kinetic description tracks the joint evolution of skills and ratings, and an exact Gaussian moment closure yields low-dimensional dynamics for rating accuracy.

Three lessons emerge. Skill drift caps long-run accuracy no matter the policy, a Red Queen effect. Under signal-matched scaling, one-step accuracy gains are invariant to matchmaking intensity. And the optimal policy separates cleanly: greedy filtering sets the gain and rating scale, while matchmaking becomes a static trade-off between match utility and sorting costs.
arxiv-2512-22338:
Prantik Sarmah, Sovan Chakraborty, and Xilu Wang predict the neutrinos expected when the recurrent nova T Coronae Borealis erupts. Gamma-ray telescopes caught near-TeV output from the 2021 eruption of RS Ophiuchi, proving recurrent novae accelerate particles, but whether the output is hadronic or leptonic stays unclear without neutrinos. T Coronae Borealis sits much closer to Earth, giving a rare spotting chance.

The authors compare two proton acceleration sites: an outer shock far from the star, and magnetic reconnection near the white dwarf's surface. The shock model's neutrinos mostly escape detection, while the reconnection scenario yields a flux within reach of IceCube and KM3NeT. Its neutrinos would also arrive hours before shock signals, a timing fingerprint for telling the physics apart.
arxiv-2512-22538:
Qingyang Li and five co-authors present MultiConf, a tool that pinpoints which source files inside a compiler cause a bug. Compilers are enormous, so localizing a fault is notoriously hard. MultiConf builds multiple pairs of adversarial compilation configurations: in each pair, one configuration triggers the failure and its twin passes, differing only in a few fine-grained options it selectively disables.

Every pair independently ranks the compiler's source files by suspiciousness using a spectrum-based fault localization formula. A weighted vote then merges the rankings into one final list. On a benchmark of sixty real GCC bugs, MultiConf localized twenty-seven bugs to the single most suspicious file. That beat the two leading current approaches by wide margins in both effectiveness and efficiency.
arxiv-2512-23038:
Sarah Packman, Justin Finkel, Dorian Abbot, and Eli Tziperman work out cheaper statistics for extreme El Niño events. Events like the one in 1997 and 1998 trigger severe weather worldwide, but they are so rare that even very long simulations contain too few of them to characterize return times reliably. Rare event sampling fixes that by steering computer time toward the extremes.

The team uses the TEAMS algorithm, which grows a branched ensemble of related trajectories through successive targeted perturbations, suiting El Niño's mix of predictability window and event duration. They test it on the Zebiak-Cane model, an intermediate ENSO model where a five hundred thousand year direct simulation exists for validation. TEAMS reproduced that simulation's return time estimates at about one fifth of the computational cost. The authors argue the method can plausibly scale to full-complexity climate models, where brute-force statistics are unaffordable.
arxiv-2512-23138:
Yuan-Sen Ting tackles a flaw in data-driven astronomy: models trained on noisy measurements chronically underestimate extreme values. The cause is attenuation bias, the shrinkage that measurement error in inputs inflicts on regression, long understood for linear models but largely unaddressed for neural networks. Ting shows neural networks suffer the same bias and that the classical cure, treating true input values as latent variables to be estimated, transfers directly.

The resulting method, LatentNN, optimizes the network's parameters and the latent true inputs by maximizing the joint likelihood of inputs and outputs together. Demonstrations cover one-dimensional regression, multivariate inputs with correlated features, and stellar spectroscopy, a flagship astronomical use case. Across signal-to-noise levels where standard networks show large bias, LatentNN cuts the attenuation substantially. The correction works best when measurement errors stay below about half the data's intrinsic range, the regime covering much real survey data.
arxiv-2512-23538:
J. Sumaya-Martinez and J. Mulia-Rodriguez propose a new way to judge structured light beams, the laser beams whose intensity patterns form rings, lattices, and other shapes. Such beams are usually described by entropy measures of complexity, but complexity alone does not say how useful a beam is for measuring something. The authors instead use Fisher information, a statistical quantity that captures how sensitively a measured pattern reacts to a parameter change.

Treating the recorded intensity pattern as statistical data, they compute Fisher information for parameters such as sideways displacement. Beams with nearly equal entropy turned out to carry very different Fisher information, with the pattern's nodes and curvature explaining the gap. Tests on Hermite-Gaussian, Laguerre-Gaussian, and Bessel-Gauss beams showed higher-order modes consistently carry more metrological content.
arxiv-2512-23838:
E. S. Moreira and J. P. A. Paula test thermodynamic stability in a toy cosmos: Einstein's static universe, a closed sphere of constant radius filled with radiation. They compute the finite-temperature Feynman propagator for a neutral massive scalar field coupled arbitrarily to the spacetime curvature, then use it to get the mean square fluctuation, internal energy. Pressure of scalar blackbody radiation as functions of that coupling.

For massless scalar fields, the thermodynamic analysis singles out one coupling value, one sixth, the conformal coupling, as the only choice giving stable equilibrium at every temperature and every radius. The authors then show that in the high-temperature or large-radius regime with electromagnetic and neutrino radiation present, at least one scalar field must also exist for stability to hold. The version here matches the published Physical Review D article apart from styling.
arxiv-2512-24138:
Haoran He and colleagues confront reward hacking in the fine-tuning of image-generating diffusion models. Reinforcement learning can sharpen how well images match text prompts, but the score it optimizes is only a proxy for quality. Models learn to game the proxy: scores climb while real quality worsens and the variety of outputs collapses.

The usual fix, penalizing drift from a reference model, protects quality but slows learning and blocks exploration, since the reference is itself mediocre. Their framework, GARDO, regularizes selectively, penalizing mainly the samples that show high uncertainty, and it periodically refreshes the reference model to match the improving policy. It also boosts rewards for outputs that are both good and diverse, encouraging coverage of modes. Across many proxy rewards and held-out measures, GARDO curbed hacking and preserved diversity without giving up sample efficiency.
arxiv-2512-24438:
Akshad Shyam Purushottamdas and five colleagues probe how vision transformers organize images. Most insight into transformers comes from language tasks. Vision transformers may structure information differently. The question is compositionality: do parts combine into wholes in the model's latent space? The team builds a test for exactly that.

Their primitives come from the discrete wavelet transform. A one-level wavelet split gives input-dependent building blocks. The test asks whether composed part representations reproduce the whole image's representation. For the vision transformer encoder, they roughly do. The composition holds approximately in latent space. That finding offers a new angle on the model's inner order. Images, it suggests, are stored as near-composable assemblies of wavelet parts. The framework adapts an older compositionality test from representation learning to vision.
arxiv-2512-24538:
Livia Zhu, R J Graham, and Dorian Abbot compute how long Earth's land biosphere can last. As the Sun brightens, the carbonate-silicate cycle draws down carbon dioxide. Plant life eventually dies from heat or from carbon starvation. Recent coupled models stretched the expected lifespan well past a billion years. Two neglected processes might shorten it again.

Seafloor weathering is the first. If it responds more strongly than continental weathering and carries much of the global load, the lifespan shrinks. A lifespan beyond a billion years still looks likely, though. Random swings in volcanic outgassing are the second process. They matter only if larger than anything seen in the past billion years. Weak weathering and modest swings change little. The lengthened lifespan survives, provisionally.
arxiv-2512-24738:
Michael Hilke studies the disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a basic model of quantum topology with two phases, one holding zero-energy edge states and one holding none. A gap around zero energy suppresses transmission through the system, and that suppression grows with length at a rate set by a Lyapunov exponent. Disorder can be diagonal, off-diagonal, or both.

An analytical expression gives that exponent as a function of energy under both disorder types. Readers in condensed matter get an exact handle on how transmission fades in a topological chain. The formula helps separate effects that disorder has on edge physics from effects on bulk transport.
arxiv-2512-24838:
Md Ahmed Al Muzaddid, Jordan James, and William Beksi present CropTrack, a system for tracking many objects in farm settings where appearances repeat and occlusions are constant. Crops look alike, light changes suddenly, and plants hide targets, so motion-only trackers lose identities. Appearance-based association is hard for the same reason, since objects barely differ.

Combining appearance and motion cues in a re-identification framework keeps identities through frequent, strong occlusions. Precision agriculture readers get tracking suited to counting and monitoring in the field. Reliable identities over time support yield estimation, growth tracking, and robot guidance among near-identical plants.
arxiv-2512-24938:
Kemal Aziz, John Ekpe, and Augustine Okekeoma study why a single layer of tin telluride in its 1T structure conducts heat so poorly despite being metallic. Two-dimensional metals with low lattice thermal conductivity are rare and valued for energy and electronic uses. First-principles calculations confirm the single layer is stable, with strong cohesion, favorable formation energy, and no unstable phonon modes.

Metallic pattern comes from strong mixing of tin and tellurium p orbitals. Small-scale analysis of phonons and bonding explains the ultralow heat transport. Materials readers get a new sheet material where electronic conduction and thermal insulation coexist, useful for thermoelectric and device design.
arxiv-2601-00038:
Shane A McQuarrie, Mengwu Guo, and Anirban Chaudhuri develop a smarter way to train reduced-order models of systems governed by parametric differential equations. Their 2026 method matters for digital twins, where a fast, explainable stand-in for a costly simulation is only as good as its training data. Instead of sampling training parameters at random, they ask which new data would most improve the model.

The team builds a probabilistic version of operator inference, treating the learning step as Bayesian linear regression. Uncertainty in the resulting model then drives a sequential sampling scheme that picks new parameter values aimed at stability and accuracy across the whole parameter range. On several nonlinear test systems, adaptively trained models beat randomly trained ones under the same computing budget, consistently. The work gives simulation practitioners a principled route to better surrogates without simply buying more training runs.
arxiv-2601-00438:
Kaili Cao and seven colleagues forecast what NASA's Roman Space Telescope will reveal about the universe. Roman's High Latitude Imaging Survey will measure cosmic shear, galaxy-galaxy lensing, and galaxy clustering. Combining those three signals, known as a three-by-two-point analysis, tests cosmological models in several ways at once. The team worked within the survey's first data challenge.

Using Fisher forecasts, a standard method for predicting how well parameters can be measured, they focus on two key quantities that scale the lensing signal. Their forecasts agree well with a fuller statistical analysis of the same mock data. They also test how assumptions about unknown biases in galaxy distances and shape measurements change the expected results.
arxiv-2601-00738:
Aleksei Adadurov and five co-authors ask, in 2026, what faster Ethereum blocks would do to a kind of trade. The trade buys a coin cheap on one exchange and sells it dear on a chain-based one. On the chain, trades wait for the next block, now twelve seconds apart. A proposed change would add one-second subslots inside each block. The authors model a trader whose chain trade may fail to land.

Their model is tuned to real data from a big exchange and a chain exchange, over three months of 2025. With one-second subslots, the count of such trades rose by 535 percent on average. The total value traded rose by 203 percent. Fast slots cut the spread of both wins and fails. That made the trade safer per unit of risk. The paper gives a clear case in a live debate on chain design.
arxiv-2601-00938:
Faruk Alpay and Bugra Kilictas study, in 2026, how a small AI agent can hand hard steps to a bigger outside helper. Small agents have a tight working memory, and long chains of thought overflow it. Their scheme, compressed query delegation, squeezes the agent's state into a slim query tensor. The answer then updates the agent's state along a curved space of fixed-rank forms.

The authors frame the scheme with rate-distortion theory, which weighs code size against error. For a natural squared-error task, they show a sharp cutoff rule is the best squeeze. They also prove the update steps settle, under bounded noise from the oracle. Tests used a suite of two thousand five hundred hard reasoning items. The scheme was set against plain chain-of-thought runs at fixed cost. The work gives small agents a principled way to borrow big help.
arxiv-2601-01138:
Ameya Uday Nagdeo, Sharanya Sur, and Bhargav Vaidya simulate how weak seed magnetic fields grow in fast, turbulent plasma like that between the stars. This growth, the fluctuation dynamo, works differently when the gas is squeezed hard by supersonic motion. The team runs detailed three-dimensional simulations at about eleven times the speed of sound and varies how easily the field slips through the gas.

When that slip is low, growth is slow, ends weaker, and is driven mostly by compression of the gas. When it is higher, swirling stretch takes over, growth speeds up, and the final field is stronger. The link between gas density and field strength flips from strongly positive to weak across the range. The team also estimates the coherence scale a telescope would see through rotation of light polarization. The results help explain magnetic fields in young, gas-rich galaxies.
arxiv-2601-01238:
Kalyaan Rao studies how statisticians weigh evidence for one model over another. Standard shortcuts assume a model's effective size equals its raw count of parameters. That assumption breaks for singular models, which are overbuilt or rank-deficient, where a quantity from singular learning theory gives the true effective size instead.

Rao works with linear models where the exact evidence can be computed in closed form, so errors can be measured rather than guessed. He shows the standard shortcut's error grows in a clean pattern set by the gap between raw size and effective size. A correction that uses the effective size restores the right evidence slope and ignores mere re-labelings of the same model. Tests back the theory. The work gives a concrete picture of where the common shortcut fails and offers evidence slopes as a practical way to estimate effective size.
arxiv-2601-01338:
Ye Yan and five co-authors study how two exotic particles, the Omega baryon and the phi meson, interact. Both are built from strange quarks, so their interaction tests models of the strong force in a clean setting. The team works within a quark model that lets quarks spread between particles while screening their color charge.

Their calculations find no bound state in any channel they checked. One spin arrangement gives a weakly attractive pull; the others, and a related pairing with a different meson, are repulsive. They then compute correlation functions of the kind measured in heavy-ion collisions, where two particles' momenta are compared. Because spins average out, the overall signal depends only weakly on the size of the emitting source. That stability makes the prediction a useful target for future experiments, which can confirm or refute the model directly.
arxiv-2601-01638:
Lancelot and 3 co-authors sharpen what a classic model of program meaning can say about resource use. The relational model of linear logic tracks how programs consume resources, but the orderings it induces speak only of qualitative sameness, through tree-like forms of programs. Counting how much two programs interact with their surroundings is beyond that older view.

Using a newer calculus based on checkers, the team gives the ordering a quantitative, context-based reading. They show the relational model refines the ordinary contextual ordering by also bounding the number of interactions between a program and its context. The work, in a version with full proofs, links meaning, context, and cost.
arxiv-2601-01738:
Paul Boisseau, Weixiao Lu, and Hang Xue close their three-paper series proving the Gan-Gross-Prasad conjecture for Fourier-Jacobi periods on unitary groups, along with a refinement of Ichino-Ikeda type. The proof strategy, carried through the earlier papers, compares relative trace formulae formulated by Liu.

Here the authors compute the spectral expansions of those formulae, the side of the identity that encodes representation-theoretic data. Finishing that computation reduces the whole conjecture to the corank zero case, which completes the proof as presented. The result settles, by the authors' argument, a central prediction linking periods of automorphic forms on unitary groups to special values of L-functions, a theme at the heart of the Langlands program.
arxiv-2601-01938:
Measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree between the early cosmos and today's neighborhood, a mismatch called the Hubble tension that hints dark energy may not be static. Arpit Kottur, Jui Mahajan, and Raka Dabhade propose the source. It is a dilaton. The dilaton is the particle born when scale invariance breaks spontaneously. Scale invariance is symmetry under stretching distances.

A simple quadratic mass term becomes, after coupling to gravity, a thawing exponential potential in the Einstein frame. Recent reconstructions from Planck, Pantheon+, and SH0ES data pin the potential's slope to a small value. That value matches a specific tiny non-minimal coupling. The field's equation of state evolves to about minus zero point eight five today. That is the behavior needed to ease the tension. An approximate shift symmetry protects the field's small mass.
arxiv-2601-02438:
Yun Bian and four co authors question a common recipe for detecting security flaws in code, which fuses two views of a program. Its token sequence as read by a pre trained model and its code property graph as read by a graph network. The recipe assumes a second view always adds information. Their analysis shows pre trained models already encode much structural information, so the two views overlap heavily, and graph encoders are usually weaker feature extractors.

Naive fusion can therefore dilute the strongest warning cues with noise instead of sharpening them. Their answer is a task conditioned complementary fusion strategy guided by Fisher information, a measure of how much a feature tells about the label. Fusion then keeps what the second view genuinely adds for the vulnerability task, rather than blending everything by default.
arxiv-2601-02638:
Madison Gerard and a team of co authors report observations of SN 2024abfl, a faint Type IIP supernova caught shortly after it exploded. Such supernovae hold a flat brightness plateau for months, and this one lasted about one hundred twenty five days, peaking well below typical events. Its late time light curve implies only a small mass of radioactive nickel was made, in line with other low luminosity events.

Simple shock cooling models cannot reproduce the fast early rise, so material shed by the star before the explosion, struck by the blast, likely powered the first light. Spectra show the narrow metal lines and slow expansion, a few thousand kilometers per second at most, typical of the class. A broad ledge feature appeared within three days, read as blended lines from shocked gas, and the main hydrogen line later split into peaks as ejecta met that material.
arxiv-2601-02838:
Giacomo Abbasciano, Balázs Endrész, Gábor Stépán, and George Haller use spectral submanifold theory, a data driven reduction method. With it they capture global bifurcations and chaos in a mechanical system whose controller suffers delay and coarse digital steps. Their test system is a Furuta pendulum, a rotating arm driving a free pendulum.

A parameter dependent reduced model built on spectral submanifolds predicts global heteroclinic shifts and local bifurcations in the delayed system, and numerical work confirms them. With the controller's spatial grid added, the same approach reproduces a microchaotic attractor. That attractor had been seen in simulation and experiment.
arxiv-2601-03338:
Fernanda Roman-Oliveira, Francesca Rizzo, and Filippo Fraternali dissect the rotation of three disc galaxies seen at cosmic noon, when the universe was a few billion years old. Rotation curves trace the gravitational potential and the dark matter distribution, but decomposing them at high redshift was long blocked by data limits. The team combines sharp ALMA observations of cold gas with near-infrared JWST imaging of the stars for three galaxies from the ALPAKA program.

The galaxies look like extended, symmetric stellar discs with spiral arms. Their dynamical models reproduce the outer rotation well but systematically underpredict the inner rotation speeds. That deficit of central motion points to extra central concentration: more stars, more dark matter, or a massive black hole packed into the middle than the models assumed.
arxiv-2601-03738:
An Huang and Christian B. Jepsen explore how the spectrum of a string-like system changes when built on ultrametric, p-adic geometry instead of ordinary numbers. In the standard non-relativistic string, integer-spaced energy levels plus the Hardy-Ramanujan partition formula reproduce ordinary two-dimensional thermodynamics at high temperature. The authors test deformed versions motivated by p-adic string theory, including Lorentzian variants with unusual spectra.

Linking oscillators with tree graphs instead of strings fails to give the expected scaling. But two other spectra do recover it, from the derivative map on the p-adic circle and from a Neumann-to-Dirichlet map. Energies and their degeneracies both grow exponentially in a balanced way, modulated by log-periodic fluctuations. The result hints that p-adic models can mimic thermal behavior of ordinary strings in surprising detail.
arxiv-2601-04038:
Tord Sjödin, writing alone, adds a new closure fact about a family of probability distributions called generalised gamma convolutions. The family was already known to stay closed under changes of scale, weak limits, and adding or multiplying independent variables. Sjödin asks what happens under powers.

He proves the family also stays closed under taking q-th powers for exponents above one. The proof uses exact density formulas for finite sums of gamma variables, a special class of monotone functions, and the Laplace transform. He then applies the result to sums and products of independent gamma variables. A symmetric extension of the family is treated as well, which broadens where the closure fact can be used.
arxiv-2601-04238:
Lingkai Kong, Cheol Woo Kim, Davin Choo, and Milind Tambe ask how generative AI can help social impact work scale. Projects in health, conservation, and security have scored real wins, yet growth stalls at deployment. The authors trace the stall to three linked gaps that hold projects back together.

Data are scarce or unreliable, planning must handle combinatorial choices in shifting settings, and expert knowledge is hard to fold in as conditions change. Language model agents can turn plain-language guidance into clear goals and limits for planners, easing the alignment gap. Diffusion models can make realistic synthetic data and support uncertainty-aware planning, easing the data and policy gaps. Together, the four authors argue, these tools could yield systems that are scalable, adaptable, and aligned with human judgement in high-stakes resource choices.
arxiv-2601-04438:
Alan Lujan removes an apparent roadblock in computational economics in a 2026 arXiv paper. The endogenous grid method is a beloved shortcut for solving dynamic models, because it inverts the key optimality equation and skips slow root-finding. But with Epstein-Zin preferences, the fashionable kind that separate risk aversion from patience, the value function itself sits inside that equation, and the method seemed not to apply.

A power transformation of the problem, Lujan shows, dissolves the difficulty. The resulting algorithm needs no root-finding at all, runs one to two orders of magnitude faster than value function iteration. is more than ten times as accurate; at matched accuracy the speedup grows to two or three orders of magnitude. Where the older methods trade speed against precision, he argues, the transformed grid method escapes the trade entirely.
arxiv-2601-04538:
Kumar Utkarsh and three co-authors lend strength to datasets too small to trust, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Ecologists, biologists, and clinicians often hold many short, sparse time series that individually cannot pin down a model's parameters. Their augmentation method combines series from different sources when the series share similar statistical properties, building one effectively longer record for estimation and model choice.

Validation studies show the pooled data can reliably tell apart point-process models, distinguishing bursty Hawkes dynamics from memoryless Poisson behaviour. The motivating application is pain in sickle cell disease, a condition affecting millions, especially people of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern. Indian descent, where each patient's diary of pain events is short and subjective. Pooling across patients with similar statistics sharpens the analysis of how pain events cluster and recur, without pretending any single diary says more than it does.
arxiv-2601-05638:
Malgorzata Warecka and 2 co-authors propose, in a 2026 paper, a new exact approach to wave scattering inside waveguide junctions containing conducting cylindrical posts. Waveguides channel high-frequency waves through hollow structures, and posts inside a junction scatter the waves in ways designers must predict accurately. Their method builds on mode matching, a technique that fits wave patterns together at boundaries.

Local projection functions improve the numerical conditioning of the calculations, making results more stable. The approach also shrinks the boundary region where such sums are needed, raising speed. Several cases, including multi-section microwave filters, test convergence and accuracy. Comparisons with finite element results from a commercial simulator validate the method for real-world of such parts design. The tests span several worked cases, not just one.
arxiv-2601-05938:
L F Calazans de Brito and 2 co-authors develop in 2026 an analytic theory for localized pulses in the defocusing modified Korteweg-de Vries equation, a model of nonlinear waves. Some pulses evolve into dispersive shock waves, patterns of rapidly oscillating wavefronts, instead of separating into clean single solitons. Predicting that evolution analytically is difficult.

Working in the Gurevich-Pitaevskii approach, the authors solved the Whitham modulation equations for a class called quasi-simple dispersive shock waves. Concrete initial pulses illustrate the answer. Direct numerical model runs matched this theory closely, with the exact description staying accurate even down to scales of a single wavelength. Such agreement supports modulation theory as a reliable shortcut for this wave regime. The match holds even at the scale of a single wave, where such shortcuts often fail.
arxiv-2601-06338:
How does an image model place one object to the left of another? Binxu Wang and 2 co-authors trace the internal circuits in a 2026 mechanistic study of diffusion transformers. These models generate images from text but often get spatial relations wrong, and the internal reason was unclear.

The team trained models from scratch on prompts specifying two objects, their attributes, and their spatial relation. Every model learned the task nearly perfectly, but the mechanism depended on the text encoder. With random embeddings, two cross-attention heads separately read relation and object information in a two-stage circuit. With a pretrained encoder, the model fused both into a single token and read them together. The two circuits also differed in robustness to unfamiliar prompts.
arxiv-2601-06438:
Is the push of the cosmos due to dark force, or to a tweak in how gravity works? S. A. Kadam and 2 co-authors test a tweaked gravity in a 2026 paper. In their frame, gravity comes from how space fails to stay flat in a length sense, not from its bend.

A chain-based fit matched the model to three data sets: old star clocks, a big blast-star set, and fresh sound-wave marks from a sky survey. The best fit gives a growth rate for space that fits local marks well. It also shows the cosmos slowed in its youth, then sped up, with the flip at a mid past date.
