Zhikai Li and four co-authors propose a method for quantising large language models to very low bit widths without the usual accuracy loss caused by outlier weights. Post-training weight-only quantisation shrinks models and speeds generation by easing the memory bottleneck, but a small set of systematically large weights resists compression.

Their approach suppresses those outliers additively. A second-order property guides it, one the authors observe in the data. The curvature matrix of the loss is consistently low-rank across inputs. Certain directions show almost no curvature. They identify that stable flat subspace and build a weight transformation from it. The transformation absorbs outliers into directions where they do little harm. Only then does quantisation proceed.
arxiv-2605-04838:
Thomas Robinson and Ranjit Lall address causal discovery when some data are missing, a setting where standard tests can badly mislead. The usual route fills in missing values first, then tests whether variables are independent given others. Errors from filling in can create false links, so true absences get rejected far too often.

Their test, PAIR-CI, builds multiple imputation into the test itself with a paired permutation design, so imputation error cancels out. In simulations where data were missing for reasons tied to the values, older tests gave many false positives while PAIR-CI stayed near the target rate. Used inside the PC algorithm, it also recovered graph structure more accurately.
arxiv-2605-05038:
Euijoon Kwon and three co-authors build a unified theory linking fluctuations and responses for systems held away from equilibrium, worked out band by band. Such systems follow noisy Langevin dynamics or random jump processes and never settle to equilibrium. The central result is an exact relation that builds the full fluctuation spectrum of what is measured from local reactions measured at the same frequency.

From that result the authors derive a family of known links, including uncertainty bounds and the classic equilibrium fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Uses on stochastic networks and driven diffusive systems show how spectra split into local parts. The framework also exposes trade-offs among swings, response, and energy loss that change by band.
arxiv-2605-05438:
Fine-tuning a small transformer on causal reasoning can go badly wrong. Pratik Deshmukh and Atirek Gupta show that a Gemma model trained on transitivity and separation tasks collapsed completely. It learned to answer yes or no regardless of the problem, reaching misleading scores while learning no real reasoning.

Their fix adds a semantic loss built from graph-based logical rules, with a weight that changes over training. The treated model kept stable, context-sensitive answers and scored about seventy percent on both task types. That was a large gain over the collapsed baseline, and the result held up under adversarial checks.
arxiv-2605-05638:
A classifier that cannot say "this is unfamiliar" will fail silently on shifted data. Brett Barkley, Preston Culbertson, and David Fridovich-Keil revisit whether detecting out-of-distribution inputs really needs labeled training or fine-tuning. Their claim: modern pretrained models already carry the needed geometry in their frozen representations.

Across 59 backbone-and-task pairings in vision and language, they test two label-free detectors. One fits a global Mahalanobis estimator on unlabeled representations; the other, ReSCOPED, estimates typicality with a light diffusion model. Both performed strongly without any fine-tuning, reframing the problem as one of reading representations well.
arxiv-2605-05738:
Traffic keeps growing into roads that did not exist when a prediction model was trained. Mei Wu and four co-authors propose CoMemNet, a continual learning framework for forecasting on evolving traffic networks. Static graph structures cannot capture the expansion, so the model must keep learning without forgetting old patterns.

Two branches split the work. A fast online branch handles the main predictions, while a slowly updated target branch mines historical information through a dynamic contrastive sampler with memory replay. The pairing aims at forecasts that adapt to new roads and regimes while staying stable.
arxiv-2605-05938:
Yuhang Wang and five co-authors build a benchmark for a growing privacy task in large multimodal models. People often send deletion requests one after another, so a model must forget new private material while keeping earlier deletions in place. Older benchmarks test mostly single or short rounds of forgetting, which hides long term failure.

ICU-Bench holds 1,000 synthetic private profiles drawn from medical reports and labor contracts. It spans 9,500 document images, 16,000 question answer pairs, and 100 sequential forget tasks. Tests on two models show that methods good at the newest target often lose earlier forgetting or damage kept skills. Some score well only by badly degrading the model itself.
arxiv-2605-06138:
S. Mallik, F. Gulminelli, and two co-authors review efforts to pin down how nuclear symmetry energy changes with density. That dependence shapes exotic nuclei, heavy ion collisions, neutron stars, and supernovae, yet it remains a key uncertainty in nuclear physics. Robust progress needs observables that transport models predict reliably and that final state effects barely touch.

The review centers on isospin diffusion in heavy ion reactions at Fermi energies as such a probe. It gathers recent results from the INDRA-FAZIA collaboration, including isospin transport ratio data, beside transport model calculations. Confidence regions for the symmetry energy come from both first principles and phenomenological nuclear functionals. The resulting limits should feed future statistical studies of the nuclear equation of state.
arxiv-2605-06738:
Lars Kersten Kroehl tackles a trust problem for autonomous agents. When a marketplace or consortium sets admission rules behind its own border, how can outsiders verify the rules were actually applied without trusting anyone new? Signed credentials alone do not answer that, since the border owner could bend its published rules in private.

His Combined Evidence Protocol turns rule compliance into a five-condition check that any party can recompute from anchored data, borrowing the recompute-it-yourself logic of optimistic rollups. The intended setting is a consortium of equal, mutually distrusting peers under a shared charter. The underlying credential infrastructure, Kroehl notes, is already live on a public blockchain layer.
arxiv-2605-06838:
Fernando Tinaut-Ruano and four co-authors classify over fourteen thousand asteroids by their reflected sunlight spectra from the Gaia mission's third data release. Spectra constrain surface composition, and Gaia observed more than sixty thousand asteroids, but instrumental systematics make direct comparison with older taxonomies risky. The team built a scheme tailored to Gaia, then linked its classes back to established ones.

Strict quality cuts and albedo information shrink the sample before clustering in reduced dimensions. The final taxonomy has thirteen classes, three more objects classes than previous spectral efforts covered, with the largest relative gain in the K class. Near-ultraviolet coverage separates primitive types inside the carbon-rich complex. Geographic trends match expectations across the main belt.
arxiv-2605-07338:
Ziheng Zhou and four co-authors release ShellfishNet, a benchmark for naming sea molluscs in photos. That naming supports ecology work and shellfish farming, but real images vary widely in setting, look, and posture. The dataset holds over forty thousand images across one hundred classes, built so that study groups never leak between splits.

Models are judged on labeling, image search, error patterns by family, and response to controlled condition changes. Rankings from search add to those from labeling, and many exact-class errors remain correct at higher family levels. Models with similar clean scores can react very differently to altered conditions, warning against single-score comparisons for marine vision.
arxiv-2605-07638:
Adrien Dubouloz and two co-authors study families of algebraic varieties that are contractible in a specific homotopical sense, called A1-contractibility, relative to a base scheme. The basic question is whether this property of a morphism can be checked one fiber at a time, on the geometric pieces over each point of the base.

For bases of finite Krull dimension, they prove it can: a smooth morphism is A1-contractible exactly when all its geometric fibers are. Applying this to spaces fibered by affine spaces gives a description via towers of vector-bundle torsors. In relative dimension one the contractible maps are exactly locally trivial line bundles, and dimension two brings rigidity results plus counterexamples in positive characteristic.
arxiv-2605-07738:
Hamidreza Eivazi and Henning Wessels speed up physics-informed operator learning for hyperelastic materials, the stand-in models used inside multiscale finite-element simulations of microstructures. The bottleneck is the cost of scoring the training loss over full volume elements in 3D, which makes proper fitting impractical.

They combine the Equilibrium Neural Operator with a QR-based sampling method. The operator learns reduced displacement and stress modes that satisfy periodicity and equilibrium by construction. The sampling method restricts basic evaluations to a few selected points. Training cost per step fell by roughly a thousandfold against full-field scoring, and the reduced model ran thousands of times faster than direct simulation. The surrogate filled in and extended stress fields well from few loading snapshots.
arxiv-2605-07938:
Sachini Weerasekara and four co-authors add a missing middle stage to single-cell foundation models, which read gene expression by treating genes as tokens and cells as sentences. These pretrained models stumble on the long-tailed distribution of cell types and on shifts in expression data, and ordinary fine-tuning only partly helps.

Their method, CellRefine, operates between pretraining and fine-tuning, refining the model's latent map of cells with a multi-part objective that uses marker-gene sets as structural prior knowledge. Across multiple computational biology tasks, CellRefine consistently improved downstream performance over the pretrained models, with gains up to fifteen percent. The idea borrows the language model playbook while respecting the biology that makes cell data different.
arxiv-2605-08038:
Bartolomeo Fanizza and Florent Renac design a limiting method for simulations of conservation laws, the equations behind gas flow and similar systems. High-order schemes are accurate but can produce values outside the physical range, such as negative density. A good limiter pulls the solution back without ruining its accuracy.

Their method blends a high-order solution with a low-order one that is known to stay inside the allowed region. It extends the classic flux-corrected transport idea to full systems and works with both explicit and implicit time stepping. The limited solution is written as a convex mix of safe quantities, which makes the preservation property provable.
arxiv-2605-08238:
Farhana Yasmin, Mahade Hasan, Haipeng Liu, Amjad Ali, and coauthors search automatically for heart MRI segmentation networks that respect a compute budget. Outlining the ventricles is central to measuring cardiac function, but low contrast, fuzzy borders, and scan differences make it hard, and hand-designed networks may waste resources.

Their CardiacNAS framework evolves architectures from a UNet-like supernet over a cardiac-aware search space covering depth, width, kernels, attention, fusion, dropout, and residual scaling. Candidates are scored jointly on overlap accuracy and boundary distance against model size and floating point cost. The search runs under fixed budgets and is evaluated on the ACDC dataset against six leading methods.
arxiv-2605-08538:
Doga Kerestecioglu and four coauthors give language model agents a memory system modeled on the human brain. Current agents pile up past events with no clear way to keep what matters. Their design uses six linked parts, among them sleep like consolidation, forgetting through overlap, and knowledge graphs for named entities, plus search that uses several cues at once.

On a large coding issue dataset, merging duplicate memories kept recall near perfect while cutting storage by more than half. On a long personal chat test, the system matched plain search accuracy while using far less space. Agent builders gain a principled way to remember more without storing everything.
arxiv-2605-08638:
Yinwei Dai, Zhuofu Chen, Lijie Yang, and Ravi Netravali make robot action generators more reliable by sampling several futures and picking the consensus. Diffusion based physical AI drafts action chunks from noise, so a single draft per round can be brittle, and errors stack across a long task. Their KeyStone method draws parallel candidate chunks, groups them by closeness, and returns the middle member of the biggest group.

Action chunks live in a geometric space where distance truly means physical likeness, so no trained judge is needed. Spare memory bandwidth runs the extra drafts with almost no added delay. Across robot and world models, success rates rise clearly at no training cost.
arxiv-2605-08738:
Shengkun Tang and many coauthors study how to compress giant mixture of experts language models during pretraining, using pruning and teaching from a larger model. Three questions guide the work: whether pruning beats fresh training, how expert cuts play out after long continued training, and which teaching strategy works best. Their large scale tests answer each in turn.

Pruned starts beat scratch training at equal budget, rival expert cuts converge to similar ends, and merging experts with partial preservation helps most tasks. Teaching combined with normal training beats teaching alone, and gradual pruning beats one shot cuts. Their compressed model shrinks an eighty billion class system dramatically while staying competitive.
arxiv-2605-08838:
Jiayi Liu, Jiaxing Zhang, Bowen Jin, and Jennifer Neville build benchmarks for retrieval augmented generation that models cannot pass from memory alone. Many current test sets leak: their questions are answerable from a model's built in knowledge, and reuse for training makes the leak worse over time. Their SeedRG pipeline extracts a reasoning graph from a seed set's question and context pairs, then swaps entities under type rules to mint fresh, structurally similar tasks.

Two checks guard quality: a consistency check keeps difficulty honest, and a leakage filter drops anything solvable without retrieval. Evaluation of retrieval systems gains tests that stay novel as models absorb older benchmarks, keeping the measurement aimed at retrieval itself.
arxiv-2605-08938:
Ali Baheri and Ignacio Laguna Peralta ask whether neural surrogates for partial differential equations can be formally verified, not just tested. Once weights and grid are fixed, a small Fourier neural operator's forward pass is piecewise linear, so it compiles exactly into a solver's arithmetic. They compare that exact encoding against a lighter frozen shortcut that replaces the spectral path with a constant.

On ten tiny surrogates, the exact route produces sound proofs and counterexamples about positivity and mass behavior, beating sampling based falsification at finding worse violations, though some queries time out. The frozen route scales further but certifies only an approximation. Verification research gains an honest map of the soundness versus scale trade.
arxiv-2605-09038:
Jinchao Hu and three co-authors address a weak point of language models that answer questions by searching: the queries they write are often broad or copied from the question. SearchSkill teaches models to plan each search step by first picking a reusable skill from a growing bank of skill cards.

The bank is not fixed. When the same kind of failure keeps appearing, the system adds or sharpens skills, rebuilds the affected practice examples, and trains again. Across open and closed models, the method raised exact-match scores on hard question-answering tests. It also produced fewer copied first queries, more focused follow-up queries, and more correct answers within a small search budget.
arxiv-2605-09138:
Avantika Agarwal leads six co-authors in raising the known capacity thresholds for two basic quantum noise models, the depolarizing channel and Pauli channels. Their 2026 paper concerns quantum capacity, the rate at which a channel can carry quantum information, a value unknown for most channels. Even deciding whether a channel has any nonzero capacity is hard, and bounds often sit far apart.

Building on a recent representation theory framework, the authors extend it to the full symmetric subspace and optimize over rank-two states there. Their calculation shows very many noise operators vanish on that space, sharply cutting environment entropy and boosting coherent information through degeneracy in the resulting codes. For the depolarizing channel they report the first threshold improvement in eighteen years, larger than all earlier gains past the hashing bound combined. Symmetry, in short, buys real communication power.
arxiv-2605-09738:
Chiriac and Jorza studied the rational coefficients that appear when an Eisenstein series Gk is written as a polynomial in the basic series G4 and G6. Eisenstein series are central objects in number theory, tied to modular forms and the zeros studied by Rankin and Swinnerton-Dyer. The paper proves a conjecture giving an exact formula for the smallest 2-adic valuation among those coefficients, expressed through the binary expansion of the weight.

The proof runs through lacunary recurrences, sparse relations among Eisenstein series, and refines what is known about the first valuation levels. As an application, the authors prove irreducibility results for Faber polynomials built from dyadic combinations of Eisenstein powers. Exact valuation formulas, the paper shows, can settle algebraic questions about these polynomials.
arxiv-2605-10338:
Alfio M. Bonanno and Emiliano M. Glaviano ask whether quantum gravity itself limits hypothetical fifth forces. Such forces would appear as Yukawa corrections to Newtonian gravity, set by a strength and a range. Experiments from torsion balances to lunar laser ranging already bound those parameters tightly. Their 2026 paper adds a theoretical bound from ultraviolet completeness.

The authors study a scalar multiplet coupled non-minimally to gravity and follow its renormalization-group flow near an interacting, UV-complete scaling regime. Requiring regular trajectories that reach that regime restricts the low-energy data to a finite wedge, mapping onto a narrow region in strength-range space. Its complement is ruled out by UV completeness alone. Strikingly, part of that excluded domain lies below current experimental limits, so sharper fifth-force searches could put this class of models to a direct test.
arxiv-2605-10438:
Xiang Chen and Alexander Binder argue that 3D tokenization has the wrong job description. Current 3D tokens treat encoding as spatial compression: compact codes rebuild surface geometry but leave part owners and join validity implicit. In open-world assets with intersecting parts and noisy topology, local shape, part identity, and assembly tangle. Their 2026 paper proposes interface-first generative states instead.

In that view, tokens build a working state, not a passive code, exposing geometry, owners, and joins to query, constrain, and repair during decoding. The authors build it with Component-Conditioned Canonical Local Tokens, or C2LT-3D, splitting it into standard geometry, group context, and seam factors. Each factor targets a distinct failure: pose leakage, cross-part interference, or invalid local joins. Trained on single-object CAD models, tested zero-shot on open-world assets, C2LT-3D improved robustness, with latent variables usable under adversarial joins.
arxiv-2605-10638:
Wladimir Silva reports a disparity between stochastic noise models and performance in NISQ-era classifiers. On the ibm_kingston chip, he measures the Kingston Constant at about seven hundredths, a 93 percent drop. Despite this decay, a digital twin shows the Hadamard Test Perceptron at about 94 percent MNIST accuracy. His 2026 paper backs the new Hadamard Resilience Law under depolarizing noise floors.

Through simulation, he establishes a gate noise phase transition at lambda-critical about two-thirds, where rank preservation breaks down. Physical execution at depth N equals 256 reveals a divergence, the Coherence Gap, about nine-tenths in size. Machine scoring accuracy collapses to 53 percent there. That collapse stems from a Coherence Wall at depth about 10 thousand. That exceeds its depth limit about three and a half thousand. The gap isolates coherent phase errors, not depolarizing noise, as the main barrier to scaling quantum layers.
arxiv-2605-10738:
Max Studt and Georg Schildbach build a spread-out backup model predictive control plan for multi-agent sets with nonlinear moves, reaching crash-free motion when agents share state facts alone. Spread-out crash dodging stays hard with no path sharing, since old plans lean on wary teamwork or pledge little on repeat use and settling. Each agent keeps the same agreed rule set, giving safe planning with no chatter.

Each agent solves a local tune-up tying a base path to a backup pledge that keeps a safe fallback in hand under step-by-step use. A new shape-based safe-set refresh stops use loss between back-to-back steps. The end plan pledges repeat use, with crash dodging, and proves a Lyapunov-type settling result to a safe rest. Runs show strong work in thin, dense sites, with jammed pinch spots and plug-and-play use.
arxiv-2605-10838:
Sanjoy Patra and seven colleagues report the first experimental sighting of a null point in a tunable molecular aggregate, a 2026 result with promise for solar materials. Theory says null points flatten energy bands and filter charge the way photosynthesis does, favouring electrons or holes selectively, but the defining signal had never been observed.

Using a simple donor-acceptor pair as a minimal model, fast pump-probe laser shots catch charge splitting through a fleeting mixed excited state that appears as the solvent steadies the charge-transfer state. Polarization data reveal both localized states and selective filtering, from balanced transfer to hole-only filtering. Chemists gain a design rule, backed by a new vibronic theory, for building null points shielded from vibration.
arxiv-2605-10938:
Keya Hu and seven colleagues present ELF, a diffusion language model that works in continuous embedding space instead of discrete tokens. Diffusion models dominate image and video generation, but leading language versions still step through tokens, missing tricks that work well for pictures.

ELF stays in continuous space until the final step, where a shared-weight network maps embeddings to tokens, making image-style tools like classifier-free guidance easy to adopt. In tests it beats leading discrete and continuous rivals on generation quality while using fewer sampling steps. Language-model builders get a credible path to continuous diffusion models that rival token-based designs.
arxiv-2605-11038:
Zheng Xing and five colleagues construct radio maps without site surveys, using only unlabeled signal-strength readings placed into a known indoor layout. Traditional radio mapping demands laborious collection and precise location labels, and this approach targets corridor spaces with dominant one-way foot traffic.

A hidden-Markov-model coarse-to-fine method lines up placed readings with measurement spots despite random signal swings, producing maps without manual surveys or motion sensors. Corridor spaces give the structure that makes unlabeled alignment workable. Building operators get indoor radio maps at survey-free cost for suitable layouts.
arxiv-2605-11538: Wang and three colleagues propose a tuning-free, covariance-weighted method for GRPO, group relative policy optimization. GRPO lifts language-model reasoning but struggles to balance search and use, often landing on weak results. Their insight is that entropy shifts follow covariance between token odds and their advantages. The method down-weights extreme token updates via a Gaussian kernel, easing instability while keeping useful signals. It lifts downstream reasoning over GRPO and steadies entropy as training goes on.
arxiv-2605-11838: Alexander Yukhimchuk and three colleagues extend gradient clipping to matrix-valued parameters. Standard clipping treats all weights as vectors, yet data outliers often amplify only a few leading singular values inside per-layer gradient matrices. Their spectral clipping clamps singular values above a threshold while keeping directions, with layer-wise self-tuning thresholds from moving means or sliding-window cutoffs. They prove an optimal rate for heavy-tailed noise and clip only the top values via random short SVD.
arxiv-2605-11938: Cosmin Burtea and David Gérard-Varet derive reduced models for gas bubbles moving in an ideal liquid from Hamilton's least action principle. They first recover the standard sharp interface model with matching pressure across bubble skins. They then trim surface shapes to a finite-knob family, spheres being the simplest case, and work out the surface rules in place of pressure matching. A soundness analysis for curl-free flow and even bubble pressure ends the work.
arxiv-2605-12338: Braun, Burghoff and Toussaint tackle sampling evenly from curved, constrained spaces that split into separate pieces. Standard guarantees assume one connected feasible region, yet real problems in robotics and optimisation often break into disconnected parts. Their MASEM method resamples to maximise entropy, judged by nearest-neighbour density estimates, and they show the gap to the even target shrinks exponentially with resampling steps. Tests on synthetic and robotics cases show fast mixing across components.
arxiv-2605-12438: Touchent and de la Clergerie improve domain adaptation for encoders with a short detour through causal language modelling. The usual route continues training with masked modelling alone. They switch briefly to causal modelling, then decay back to masked modelling, and test the recipe on biomedical French and English tasks with ModernBERT. Gains reach a few points in French and under a point in English, depending on model size. The benefit traces to low layers, persists through the decay phase, and grows with model size.
arxiv-2605-12538: Girin and seven colleagues build a silicon photonics platform that makes quantum graphs on a chip. Light guides on silicon chips at telecom bands set out graphs to probe ray-wave links and quantum chaos. Third-harmonic light in silicon images single optical wave functions straight, without harming them, in detail. Two graphs with unlike motion show varied spectral patterns. One is strongly chaotic, the other ergodic but non-mixing. Those patterns match random matrix theory. The platform opens a scalable route to optical quantum circuits in complex networks.
arxiv-2605-12938: Jin, Kim, Park and Ye introduce CRePE, a positional encoding that gives video world models unified camera control across pinhole, wide-angle and fisheye lenses. Each image token becomes a depth-aware distribution along its camera ray, and the encoding integrates the expected rotary signal along the curved path it traces. Built as a light adapter on a frozen video diffusion model, it improves camera, lens and orientation fidelity. It also transfers without tuning to unseen fisheye footage.
arxiv-2605-13038: Shao, Cui and Ren present CoGE, a framework for online geometric estimation during monocular colonoscopy, giving surgeons 3D spatial perception and navigation. True labels are hard to obtain inside the narrow, closed colon, and simulated data differs sharply from real footage in artifacts and lighting. CoGE counters with illumination-aware supervision from Retinex theory and structure-aware perception via wavelet decomposition. Trained only on simulated data, it still leads on both simulated and real scenes.
arxiv-2605-13138: Loose and four co-authors rigorously re-evaluate code language models for detecting vulnerability-fixing commits, which advisory databases often record late or never. Consolidating 20 fragmented datasets spanning over 180,000 commits and training 270 models, they isolate the code-only signal under group-stratified evaluation. Model size helps but not enough, and extra code context gives no reliable gain under strict false-positive budgets. At a 0.5% false-positive rate every fine-tuned code-only model misses at least 80% of fixes. A manual audit finds label error concentrated in commits lacking CVE links.
arxiv-2605-13538: Anuj Sadani and Deepak Kumar propose an on-device pipeline swapping personal data for fake values. It combines a token classifier, a small model for surrogates, and a rule-based generator. With naive fixed demonstrations, the small model copies demo outputs verbatim. That failure comes from prompting, not quantisation, and locale-based rotating demonstrations fix the echoes. All 482 test calls succeed, though the model still copies from a small same-locale pool. On entity recognition, fake values give natural text but a narrow training set, and variety matters more.
arxiv-2605-13738: Gareth Cabourn Davies and Ian Harry demonstrate two techniques for premerger identification of massive black hole binaries in realistic LISA data. They apply both to the LISA Data Challenge dataset Sangria-HM, recovering all 14 signals expected visible at least half a day before merger. The inpainting method identifies premerger signals even with data gaps, recovering a signal despite 3 day-long gaps added to the 14 days before merger.
arxiv-2605-13938: Bouzenada builds a relativistic take on the q-deformed Dunkl-Fokker-Planck equation in one space and one time dimension, inside a mirror-warped quantum frame. Warped Dunkl tools and mirror symmetry shape a broad change law for quantum setups. A q-Wigner-Dunkl supersymmetry set then springs from warped ladder tools and SUSY links, giving a sound spectral picture. The harmonic oscillator with a centrifugal push yields exact algebraic answers and closed energy spectra.
arxiv-2605-14038: Cheng and four co-authors redefine tool necessity per model, exposing a knowing-doing gap in language-model tool use. Past work treats the need for tools as fixed across models, judged by people or models, and mostly on obvious cases like fetching weather versus rewording text. In truth, a task a strong model solves alone may still need tools for a weaker one. Grounding necessity in each model's own measured performance, the paper compares need against observed tool calls across four models on arithmetic and factual questions.
arxiv-2605-14138: Chen, Clemen and Noel study tournament anti-Sidorenko orientations of trees. An oriented graph has the property if its homomorphism density in any tournament stays below that in a large random tournament. Every oriented path with at least three arcs and exactly one non-leaf source or sink vertex has the property. An oriented path also has it when leaf vertices sit at least two from source or sink vertices, and distances between non-leaf source or sink vertices are multiples of four. Three-legged spiders admit such orientations.
arxiv-2605-14338: Liu and Wang turn adaptive stopping into a two-part reliability problem for Krylov-shadow estimation. Krylov order sets population resolution, while sample count controls uncertainty. Treating them as one risks false stops, with a width rule giving a narrow interval around a biased estimate. AKS-QFI, a component-aware stopping interface, separates truncation from finite-sample uncertainty. On a benchmark, width-only stopping gives false-stop rates between 16 and 68 percent. AKS-QFI returns no false success declarations, and after recalibration, it returns accurate declarations at true 5 percent tolerance.
arxiv-2605-14538: Walleghem asks whether free choices stay absolute once they are internalised in an extended Wigner friend scenario, where one observer sits inside a sealed lab and another reasons about them from outside. Building on the Pusey-Barrett-Rudolph theorem, he argues against absoluteness under a locality assumption. Similar arguments from other contextuality or nonlocality models are noted as possible.
arxiv-2605-14738: Sharma, Naim, Saha, Jain, Chadha and Asher ask when task-aware layer pruning helps and why. Across controlled polynomial regression tasks plus large language models, pruning gives no benefit on in-distribution data but consistently lifts out-of-distribution accuracy. Out-of-distribution inputs distort layerwise norm and distance profiles away from in-distribution profiles. Pruning layers that create or amplify that distortion realigns inputs with the task-adapted geometry. Causal evidence comes from controlled shifts and residual-scaling interventions.
arxiv-2605-15338: Sidharth Pulipaka and six others expose sleeper memory poisoning in language-model agents with persistent memory. An attacker corrupts outside context, such as a document or repository, so the helper stores a fake memory about the user. Unlike prompt injection, the poison can lie dormant and reappear across later chats. Across memory-holding helpers, tainted memories were written up to 99.8 percent of the time on one model and 95 percent on another, and recalled poisons steered foe-planned actions in 60 to 89 percent of evaluations.
arxiv-2605-15438: Ali Bouland and Jeff Borggaard tackle control of the fluidic pinball. This test case joins three cylinder wakes in complex ways. They shrink a finite-element flow model by interpolatory reduction. Then they pair it with a quadratic-quadratic regulator, a feedback law fit for the flow equations' squared terms. At one speed it hits its goal faster than a linear law. At a higher speed it steadies the wake where the linear law fails.
arxiv-2605-15538: Anik Kumar Paul and Shalabh Bhatnagar study stochastic mirror descent with state-linked Markov noise. Here the sample law hinges on the current choice, and samples flow through a Markov chain. That mix adds bias and time links that break standard independent-noise tools. They prove almost-sure convergence for convex and nonconvex tasks under Lipschitz continuity alone, with no need for differentiability. Finite-time concentration bounds follow for smooth goals. In convex tasks the sample cost matches the classic independent-noise rate.
arxiv-2605-16338: Migliorini Filho and three colleagues built Vidya at LAMUHDI to meet NOBRADE and ISAD(G) while cutting archival processing from decades to days. The problem is dark data: digitized objects with too little metadata to be found or reused, while manual description stays slow and costly. Vidya orchestrates language models with free and open-source tools, binding each generation to YAML-defined ontologies and Pydantic validation, so probabilistic models yield structured JSON. The modular pipeline aims at low-cost use in memory institutions on modest hardware, following Maker principles.
arxiv-2605-16638: Cheng and colleagues speed up reasoning-aware multimodal embeddings by replacing explicit chain-of-thought traces with latent think tokens. The tokens are trained with generation loss, while later embedding tokens learn from contrastive loss, holding inference cost constant. Their TTE-Flash-2B model beats its explicit-reasoning counterpart on the MMEB-v2 benchmark. Zero-shot tests across 15 video datasets show gains as the number of think tokens grows.
arxiv-2605-16838: Hoang and colleagues characterize graphs both alpha-critical and in class Wp, in three languages. In the graph itself, it is well-covered, with fibers of size at least p covering every edge. In the independence complex, it is a flag complex with ridges of degree at least p and missing edges from ridge links. In the complement, it is a Kr+1-saturated graph with maximal cliques of size r and codegree at least p. The work gives an exact formula for the maximal such p and examples.
arxiv-2605-17338: Pei proves a structural cap for the Chayes-Machta-Redner picture of the Edwards-Anderson spin glass: in any subsequential local weak limit, the blue subgraph holds at most two infinite clusters. If two exist, they share one infinite grey cluster and carry opposite overlap signs. The proof builds an abstract multicolour Burton-Keane claim from finite-box coalescence, plus finite energy and a percolation shift for the grey subgraph.
arxiv-2605-17638: Sophokles Ktistakis and colleagues introduce TouchMap-OR, a multi-view system for hand-surface contact reconstruction in operating rooms. Hand-surface contacts drive pathogen transmission yet stay largely unobserved. The system builds multi-person body tracks across cameras and estimates MANO hand meshes from RGB views aligned to depth. Fused reconstructions attach to clinicians, yielding hand paths mapped onto a 3D room model. Timing closeness infers contact episodes naming clinician, surface and time. On three anesthesia cases it beats tracking-based baselines on contact F1 and identity scores.
arxiv-2605-17738: Lillian Thiel and colleagues demonstrate a wafer-scale quantum light platform. It bonds light-emitting III-V layers directly onto factory-made silicon nitride circuits. The nitride layer guides light with under 1 dB per meter of loss, while the III-V layers supply strong nonlinear effects for making entangled photons and converting frequencies. With efficient couplers, lasers, and detectors reaching up to 99% quantum efficiency, the platform points toward large, low-noise quantum photonic systems built at wafer scale.
arxiv-2605-18138: Kazuhiko Kakamu's 2026 paper models shifting income distributions from grouped data with a Bayesian state-space model for the GB2 law. By letting latent shape terms borrow strength across adjacent years, the fit beats fitting each year on its own. A counterfactual layer then isolates what demographic shifts add while holding the rest of the path fixed. On Japanese household data from 1969 to 2007, ageing and shrinking households push on different parts of the spread, and ageing grows as a driver of inequality after 2000.
arxiv-2605-18438: J. R. Goicoechea and eight co-authors present the first velocity-resolved maps in a 2026 paper of atomic oxygen fine-structure emission from the Orion BN/KL explosive outflow, the nearest such outflow. SOFIA data separate quiescent cloud gas from outflow gas, traced by a broader component matching shock-excited molecular hydrogen seen with JWST. Total oxygen line luminosity reaches 86.5 solar luminosities, implying a mass-loss rate near 9.1 thousandths of a solar mass per year, consistent with dense, warm postshock gas in dissociative J-type shocks.
arxiv-2605-18538: Daniele Corradetti offers, in a 2026 paper, integral planes tied to crystal and non-crystal systems in real composition algebras. For ten crystal orders one uniform construction recovers root systems including 2A1, A2 plus A2, 4A1, D4 plus D4, 16A1, and E8 plus E8. For two non-crystal orders it yields H2 plus H2 and H4 plus H4 over the golden integers. A rank-obstruction theorem proves no indecomposable rank-eight golden octonion order can exist.
arxiv-2605-18738: Payal Chandak and thirteen co-authors audit value pluralism in medical AI, in a paper from 2026. Medicine is plural: autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice often clash, splitting good doctors over hard cases. Their tool pairs clinician-checked dilemmas with a method reading value priorities from decisions. Top models span doctor variety and weigh rival values before deciding. Yet single decisions stay near-fixed across repeats and rewordings, missing doctor-panel spread. Most priorities fall in the normal doctor range, but some slight patient autonomy.
arxiv-2605-18838: Adil Amin finds a hidden phase change in how reasoning and truthfulness relate as language models scale. Below a family-dependent critical size, the two skills pull against each other; above it, they cooperate. That critical size sits near three and a half billion parameters, though design, data curation, and training method each move it on their own. Curated training, distillation, and design can thus move a small model into the cooperative regime. A single truth-direction vector at one layer also fixes many misaligned outputs without retraining.
arxiv-2605-18938: Selim Hotinli and six colleagues report detecting the moving lens effect for the first time, a subtle background pattern caused by sideways motion of gravity wells. Their Fourier-space estimator keeps the signal's scale dependence and is applied to Atacama Telescope maps crossed with DESI red galaxies. Amplitudes reach 4.8 sigma for the extended sample and 3.7 sigma for the main sample, both matching halo-model predictions. The result opens transverse velocities as a new probe, and with the kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect it points toward mapping the universe's velocity field.
arxiv-2605-19038: Lorenzo Bonin and four colleagues build STRELGen to brew safety first scenes for self drive tests. Mass road exposure costs much and rarely nets rare edge cases. STRELGen joins a multi agent path spread model with space time logic rules. Rule scores read as slopes, so run time search tunes the model core to max them. The yield is sound yet risky scenes inside the learned data spread.
arxiv-2605-19338: Jiaao Wu and colleagues build STAR-PólyaMath, a multi-agent system for long math reasoning that fights hallucination buildup and memory loss. Its orchestrator runs challenge, step, and replan loops, while a persistent Meta-Strategist keeps memory across attempts and issues guidance or mandatory orders. That supervision lets the system escape dead loops instead of stagnating or leaning too hard on tools. It tops eight elite contest benchmarks, with perfect scores on several and a wide margin over the strongest baseline on one flagship set.
arxiv-2605-19638: Jahangir and Ishii introduce the Accessibility Capability Boundary, a framework for the working limits and growth room of self-running access systems. They model access as a dynamic, many-sided ability space limited by latency, mental load, infra needs and interaction load. Browser systems built as single-file HTML pages, they argue, push those limits outward by cutting setup friction near zero and enabling rapid adaptation to context. Two prototypes test the theory: one interface for a blind user in Nepal and one webcam helper for blind users.
arxiv-2605-19738: Shi and team present TERGAD, a framework enriching structural meaning for graph anomaly detection using language reasoning. Existing text-rich approaches feed raw textual traits into vectors yet neglect structure, missing outliers where content clashes with topological role. TERGAD translates node properties into natural language stories, turned by a language model into meaning vectors. These fuse with raw node traits through a gated decoder that rebuilds graph structure and node traits. The anomaly score follows from total rebuild error, and six real sets show it beats rivals.
arxiv-2605-19838: Andersson and Elmqvist examine twin agents, digital twins of individuals that stand in for them with colleagues when they are away. They identify a trust calibration problem. When a colleague doubts a twin's output, three failure modes may apply: a schema gap, an epistemic gap, or a model artefact. There is no reliable way to tell which one is at fault. Forcing functions that curb overreliance assume a clear human AI boundary, but twin agents dissolve that boundary. The paper names the concept and poses research questions.
arxiv-2605-19938: Zabolotnii asks if a new density guess can sharpen even spread sampling on curved spaces. The host method weights resamples by near neighbour density, but sharp resampling can blow up small density slips. His gated guess uses shell gaps and falls back to the plain guess on flat ground, where the plain guess is already best, bounding the win.
arxiv-2605-20138: Larry Hui and three co-workers build a Hamilton-Jacobi framework for satellites sharing one circular orbit at risk of collision. Relative motion uses a radial-tangential-normal frame and Hill-Clohessy-Wiltshire dynamics, with unsafe states set by FCC minimum-separation rules. The encounter is cast as a zero-sum differential game, pitting the controlled satellite against a bounded disturbance. Reachable sets mark states where collision cannot be dodged at worst. Outside states admit collision-free paths, and hybrid control decides when to move evasively.
arxiv-2605-20338: Baerman and two co-workers solve the connection problem for higher-order linear equations linked to the quantum Toda chain. With several decaying solutions at each singularity, they derive the weakest quantization rules fitting decay at both ends. Those rules are stated through monodromy data, proving conditions predicted by topological string and spectral theory duality. The results hint at a hierarchy of spectral problems running to the full Toda chain's maximal-decay conditions.
arxiv-2605-20538: Prashant Pandey and three colleagues study continual segmentation when classes, input types, and label supply all shift at once. Prior work usually studies one shift alone, yet real streams mix all three at the same time. They steady learning under drift with a rule that scales random nudges by gradients, parameter by parameter. Unlabeled data are also used, with semi-supervised learning and supervision anchored on class prototypes.
arxiv-2605-20638: Xu Du and three colleagues extend the ALADIN optimization framework to distributed consensus problems. Such problems arise in smart grids, control, and machine learning, where many parts must agree on shared values. Their Consensus ALADIN version uses a central coordinator and comes in first-order and second-order forms, the latter using a Hessian approximation. A decentralized version runs over directed graphs with quantized messages, and both gain global convergence for convex problems.
arxiv-2605-20738: Yaoteng Zhang and three colleagues present STAR-IOD, a framework for incremental object detection in remote sensing imagery. Imagery arrives as a continuous stream, and standard detectors forget old categories when learning new ones. Their method also faces scale variation within classes and missing labels that make old objects look like background. A subspace-decoupled topology distillation module aligns class relationships across scales, while pseudo-label refinement recovers missing old-class labels.
arxiv-2605-20838: Haoyue Cheng and five colleagues present USV, a dataset of user-generated short-form videos for high-level semantic video understanding. Such videos are rarely studied, though large-scale video datasets have advanced the field. USV holds around 224,000 videos gathered from user platforms by label queries, without added manual verification or trimming. Most prior work focuses on instance-level recognition, which misses high-level semantic representation, so the authors add topic recognition and video-text retrieval tasks with two unified baseline methods.
arxiv-2605-20938: Elsa Baby, Manoj Gopalakrishnan, and Vishwas Vasisht study why confined active matter keeps moving at its edges. Active matter under confinement shows steady surface motion and strong edge affinity, yet how it points, its orientational behaviour, has received less attention than where it sits. With molecular simulations of an active Brownian particle in a hard circle plus the Fokker-Planck rule, they show where it sits couples directly to how it points. Confinement creates two preferred tangential pointing states linked by random flipping paths.
arxiv-2605-21238: Wei Minn and colleagues study self-admitted technical debt in Dockerfiles, viewed alongside related code. Dockerfiles build portable container settings, but they can hold quick fixes that hurt reliability, security, and upkeep. Past work looked at one file alone, yet code change spans production, test, build, and config files. The team finds about twenty-seven percent of debt admissions and forty percent of repayments link to non-Dockerfile files, with link sources varying by subtype.
arxiv-2605-21338: Yuefeng Shi, Nedjma Ousidhoum, and Jose Camacho-Collados present a question-based test framework for language models on long unstructured text, focused on social media. They curate four hundred seventy questions probing semantic understanding and reasoning over aggregated text. Applied to diverse Twitter sets spanning sentiment, hate speech, and emotion tasks, scores hinge heavily on input scale and data complexity. Scores fall clearly in multi-label or target-dependent cases, and drop steadily as task complexity rises from basic to advanced tasks.
arxiv-2605-21438: Hugo Duminil-Copin and co-authors present a random walk approach to high-dimensional critical phenomena. They present a black box proof of mean-field near-critical behaviour for functions on lattices in dimension greater than two, satisfying a short list of assumptions. The functions are two-point functions of a lattice model in subcritical or critical regimes. They decay as distance to the minus d plus two plus epsilon times exponential decay with correlation length. This applies to self-avoiding walk, percolation, spins, and lattice trees above critical dimensions.
arxiv-2605-21838: Allan Moreira and coauthors study fermion localization in a five-dimensional braneworld within modified teleparallel gravity. A non-minimal coupling between a Dirac spinor and torsional invariants yields Schrödinger-like equations for Kaluza-Klein modes. The teleparallel Gauss-Bonnet term changes the potentials and thus localization. Zero-mode analysis shows only one chiral part localizes on the brane, with the model setting its hold, while the massive spectrum stays continuous with resonant states from potential structure. Information-theory tests show torsional changes shift information toward stronger localization.
arxiv-2605-21938: Benjamin Kim, Lav Varshney, and Daniel Alabi study auditing of machine learning methods that claim Renyi differential privacy guarantees. They build a testing method that estimates Renyi divergence between neighboring runs with the Donsker-Varadhan variational estimator. Their math gives confidence intervals that hold for finite samples, splits statistical error from optimization error, and yields the first optimal guarantees for this estimator class. Auditing DP-SGD on MNIST and CIFAR-10, their auditors strongly improve Renyi lower bounds over prior black-box methods, most of all at small and moderate orders.
arxiv-2605-22138: Deng and co-authors argue efficient agentic work gains from self-regulated simulative planning. Dominant agents act as reactive policies with adaptive computation, expecting planning to emerge implicitly, but without control over planning, length balloons without reliable accuracy gains. The authors split decision-making into simulative reasoning grounding deliberation in future-state prediction, self-regulation deciding when and how deeply to plan, and reactive execution. Their SR2AM model matches systems of 120 to 355 billion and 685 billion to 1 trillion parameters while using far fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-22238: Ekne tests language models as live players in timed, multi-phase games of Risk, where planning and execution repeat under strict rules. In a 32-game championship across providers, one Gemini model won 20 games, a spread far from equal strength. Yet when execution was standardised on a cheaper scaffold, planner results looked near equal, suggesting system behaviour, not planning alone, drove the gap.
arxiv-2605-22438: Foscari, Tullii and Perchet study first-price auctions with feedback-only shilling. Shilling means fake bids feigning stronger competition. After a loss, the learner sees the larger of the real and shill bids, so learning changes but not the outcome. Their algorithm pairs a robust branch with an optimistic branch. The robust branch ignores the shilled report and hits the dynamic-pricing rate. The optimistic branch debiases losing reports, using suffix information when reliable for the first-price rate. Validation and racing let optimistic updates run blind to scale.
arxiv-2605-22638: Beurdouche and Knopp describe a heavy 5G virtualized radio access deployment built on the open OpenAirInterface software stack. They adapt the stack to exploit hardware accelerators and general purpose processors, and work out how to scale by sharing one server across several virtual radio instances. The paper reports their stack improvements, measured performance effects, and notes on how computer architecture shapes the deployment. It closes by naming deployment limits and next steps toward better virtual radio rollouts.
arxiv-2605-22738: Thies and others present ProxySHAP, a tool for Shapley and Banzhaf interactions that joins tree proxy speed with a sound path to consistency through residual fixes. They extend interventional TreeSHAP to polynomial time exact interaction indices for tree ensembles, dodging exponential depth effects in earlier methods. Analysis pins down when maximum sample reuse corrects proxy bias without variance exploding with size. Benchmarks show it setting a new top mark for quality at small and large budgets, beating ProxySPEX and KernelSHAP-IQ on downstream uses.
arxiv-2605-22838: Thron and Jafari detect a sample-by-sample distortion in RNA sequencing data, where measured gene expression shifts with expression level in ways standard normalization misses. Studying datasets from TCGA, SU2C, and GTEx, they found such biases throughout, and showed by simulation that they corrupt gene-gene correlations and group comparisons. Two new nonlinear transforms removed the biases, lowered sample variance, and raised test sensitivity and specificity by roughly three to five percent.
arxiv-2605-23238: Shadarevian and three coauthors introduce GENSTRAT, which uses generated games to test strategic reasoning in language models. GENSTRAT generates two-player zero-sum imperfect-information card matches. They sample 50 games from a 2,000-game pool and test nine frontier and open-weight LLMs in over 36,000 matches. Newer models score higher, but models with near-identical strength show different profiles, and two of the top three models are more volatile than the third.
arxiv-2605-23338: Mondelin and four coauthors measure own lines in the Perseus-Pisces cluster by system shape and outward extent into the low surface brightness regime. They detect positive own-lining signals for both early- and late-type systems out to 1 Mpc/h, with a clear signal for spirals. They find strong shape link: late-type systems lead the shape-shape signal, mostly living in threads and showing higher stretch matching edge-on tilts.
arxiv-2605-23438: Gong and three colleagues map spin-momentum locking in relativistic altermagnets, where symmetry loss can cut nodal planes. Non-relativistic g-wave locking need not survive relativity. In centrosymmetric CrSb and noncentrosymmetric wurtzite MnTe, the dominant spin part keeps its g-wave character only when the Néel vector points along the z-axis. Weaker parts show d-wave symmetry in CrSb and p-wave symmetry in MnTe. Ferroelectric cases can host one guarded nodal plane plus an accidental surface, or two accidental surfaces.
arxiv-2605-23538: Papadopoulos and colleagues speed up dark siren cosmology with a GPU-accelerated gwcosmo pipeline, which infers cosmic expansion from gravitational waves without light counterparts. Population-level work grows costly as detections mount, since each source needs integration over its localization volume. Their vectorized code processes the whole catalog in parallel each round, running 1000 times faster than the prior version. That pace makes O5-scale event counts doable in hours, keeping quieter but numerous sources in the analysis instead of dropping them.
arxiv-2605-23738: Sethi and colleagues speed up parallel runs of commuting Pauli product rotations for fault-proof quantum work. Per-qubit access point limits force commuting groups over budget to split, growing circuit depth. They propose two tricks: clique shuffling, permuting products into port-limited groups, and set restructuring, rewriting each group with reduced per-qubit port pressure. On QASMBench circuits, mixing both heuristics cuts average hardware-limited depth by 10 to 20 percent over a fixed-order baseline, up to 50 percent. Gains scale with per-qubit port budget and level off near 20 ports.
arxiv-2605-23838: David Perconte and colleagues track how disorder reshapes superconductivity in amorphous indium oxide resonators under strong magnetic fields. With microwave tests, they watch superfluid density fall only slowly, in a slow crawl across nearly three orders of field. That defies the fast power law drop expected for neat vortex lattices. Pinning that grows as vortices crowd together explains the drag. Density then dies linearly at the critical field, marking a continuous quantum critical point. A large positive Kerr response appears beside it.
arxiv-2605-24138: Basu and seven co-authors study Designer and Programmer agents building a Fibonacci game across twelve pairings from seven open models. They track how fast pairs settle and hold, how well roles align, and how often builds succeed with errors fixed. Only the DeepSeek-R1 pair settled from the first round and held the correct answer to the last. LLaMA 3.2 and Qwen3 pairs held strong role alignment despite drifting from the correct answer. Other pairs drifted off task and never settled, showing loose talk does not yield correct results.
arxiv-2605-24738: Owen Miller and Francesco Monticone offer a tutorial on limits in photonics and electromagnetics. Limits like Shannon capacity bounds, Bennett and Landauer thermodynamic limits, and Godel incompleteness anchor fields. Photonics and electromagnetism hide many physical bounds found over decades. The tutorial reviews rules constraining light-matter interaction, discusses limits across scales, from how materials respond to how waves propagate, scatter, and perform optical functions. By joining these results and flagging open questions, it aims to bring readers to the frontier and advance a universal framework for light-matter limits.
arxiv-2605-24838: Haoran Li leads a method for spotting many shifts in the mean of high-dimensional data streams. The target is dense shifts where dimension rivals sample size. The team builds ridge-regularized CUSUM statistics on an adaptable ridge-regularized Hotelling test. Ridge regularization steadies covariance handling while adapting to the true covariance shape. Scanning multi-scale adjacent segments needs no prior count or place for shifts. Pooling across ridge settings by taking the maximum test value adds adaptability, with limiting laws proved under null and local alternatives.
arxiv-2605-24938: Jianrui Zhang leads SMART, a trick coaxing multi-vector retrieval skill out of ordinary single-vector embedding models. Single-vector retrievers squash rich token sequences into one global vector. That is fast but drops fine local evidence dense retrieval needs. Multi-vector rivals need fresh training and often drop the global summary. The team notes pooled contrastive gradients already reach earlier hidden states, already arranged for cosine matching. Direct late interaction over frozen states at inference lifts scores, with gains focused on fine-grained and visual-document tasks.
arxiv-2605-25038: Festus Kahunla presents TRACE, a synthetic tuning dataset for Applied Behavior Analysis, a clinical field whose real session data cannot be shared under privacy rules. The 2,999 examples cover teaching programs and multi-session interpretation, spanning discrete trials, natural environment teaching, task analysis, twelve path patterns, and thirteen target behaviors. Each comes from a deterministic generator grounded in canonical ABA literature, with full sampling provenance. Splits run 2,549 training, 149 validation, 281 testing, and 20 sanity. The dataset is a research product, not tested in clinics.
arxiv-2605-25338: Akash Bonagiri and colleagues turn failed agent runs into lessons instead of just logging or retrying them. Their CausalFlow framework treats each failed trace as a chain of dependent steps, scoring steps by testing what changes when one is altered. Steps that cause failure get edits that flip the outcome to success, forming wrong-and-corrected step pairs. Those pairs support quick test-time repair with little drift, and training supervision for later improvement. Across four benchmarks in math, coding, question answering, and medical browsing, causal attribution beats heuristic fixes.
arxiv-2605-25438: Alexander Quispe and Kevin Xu model how agentic AI expands a developer's usable languages. Conversational AI mainly helps in known languages, while agentic tools add delegated execution that developers specify and check. The model predicts new-to-them languages that only an agent makes feasible. Testing on a monthly panel of 5,346 developers and 57 million changed files, adoption expands language breadth: active languages rise 2.5 against a 0.9 baseline, with new languages up 1.2 and entropy up 0.38. The pattern survives strong robustness checks, though voluntary adoption means associations, not causal proof.
arxiv-2605-25538: Chanwut Kittivorawong and colleagues cut the cost of turning still-camera video into reusable object tracks. Earlier systems sample whole frames over time, spacing detections too widely to trace true paths. Tetris instead splits frames into tiles, groups useful tiles into polyomino shapes, prunes repeats with an integer program under an accuracy cap, and packs survivors for detection. Across seven still-video sets it stays within five percent of full-frame accuracy while running about seventeen times faster than prior systems.
arxiv-2605-25838: Kanchinadam, Menachery and Deshpande test the robustness of language model text-to-SQL when the same data sits under varied schemas. Their framework generates schemas from one entity relationship model, varying shredding choices while questions and data stay fixed. Four models answer the same questions across variants in two domains. Schema shifts model behavior, with very varied answers across equivalent schemas. Adding the original specification improves performance but does not fully remove the inconsistencies.
arxiv-2605-25938: Kolomeisky works out the exact outer shape of an Abrikosov vortex in the extreme type-two limit. An Abrikosov vortex is a swirl of magnetic flux inside a superconductor. Outside a shrinking core, the theory becomes a closed set of rules for superfluid flow with a density constraint. Field and density then vary over one length only, the London penetration depth, so the familiar two-length picture fails here.
arxiv-2605-26038: Shi and five colleagues shore up small vision-language models for crowded scenes, where many objects, traits and links must be grounded and reasoned over in steps. Light models do well on plain benchmarks yet fail in dense scenes, partly because training never ties reasoning steps to visual items. The authors first build DRBench, with 14,573 questions over 2,943 images in five task types across three reasoning layers. Their DRScaffold training scheme then splits supervision into grounded parts. Results lift dense-scene reasoning while keeping the model light.
arxiv-2605-26438: Igor Ivanov and David Demitri Africa tackle evaluation awareness: language models acting differently once they sense a test. Their LURE method replays realistic tracks from live use and appends the test prompt, so the model meets a lifelike scene. A pipeline gauges realism by catching spoken test awareness and judge-model odds that a log is a test, validated on large live and test transcript sets. LURE tests prove far harder to tell from real deployment than standard benchmarks or synthetic generators. Trials cover scheming, sabotage, and sycophancy.
arxiv-2605-26738: Scott and Roberts build KARMA, a framework that teaches language models conversational pragmatics, the tone and norms that shape how messages land, from Reddit karma signals. A reward model trained on Reddit conversations guides reinforcement learning, and the tuned models behave more appropriately in pragmatics-heavy tasks. Surprisingly, the best downstream gains come from a context-only reward model, while factuality drops in every condition, a tension the authors trace to the reward signal itself.
arxiv-2605-27038: Li, Liu, and Ma present TPS-Drive, a system that cleans vision-language model views of space for autonomous driving planning. Text-aligned methods flatten spatial states into symbols and cause spatial mirages, while dense visual methods drown token makers in background texture. An agent-centric token maker shifts code room from static backgrounds to dynamic agents, and a split chain runs scene reading, foresight, and acting. Tests set new safety records on NAVSIM benchmarks and cut crashes on nuScenes.
arxiv-2605-27138: Pan and Wang propose ICCU, an in-context ongoing unlearning method. It induces readable refusal rules from unlearning datasets. It applies them at run time as a filter or via the system prompt, without changing model weights. Since rules gather as an order-free union, the method is modular and free of cross-request clashes. The source forget-set data can be dropped after rule mining. Tests show ICCU blocks target knowledge while keeping utility, scales across serial requests, and stays robust to rephrased and cross-lingual queries.
arxiv-2605-27238: Meng and co-authors build an agentic repair frame that lets execution evidence steer each repair stage. Their EviACT system uses three guardrails: a retrieval scaffold that grounds context, a compile gate that drops invalid edits, and a test-driven gate that checks target-test recovery before full regression runs. Across four benchmarks, resolve rates rise by a few points over the strongest comparable baselines, and reported per-bug API cost falls sharply where baseline costs exist. Ablations tie the gains to the coordinated evidence-to-action chain.
arxiv-2605-27538: Arpan Pal and Preshanth Jagannathan speed up Bayesian QU-fitting for radio interferometry with simulation-based inference. Their VROOM-SBI uses neural posterior estimation to fit Stokes Q and U spectra, matching Faraday synthesis and QU-fitting accuracy. The speedup reaches about 500-fold over classical QU-fitting, with open code and trained models for four depolarization models.
arxiv-2605-27938: Cen and colleagues teach 3D models to keep the meaning of parts steady across varied objects in plain photos. SEMAGIC pairs a standard template mesh with a learned warp field, tying shape change to meaning alignment while training. The result keeps part matches steady across varied cases and lifts semantic match scores by a clear margin.
arxiv-2605-28138: Abhishek Sahu removes chance from a combinatorial tool, the Separation Lemma, which guarantees unique set sums. Where earlier hardness proofs leaned on random weight assignments, his fully deterministic construction supplies the needed weights with proofs and examples. The swap derandomizes existing hardness results for path-packing problems and widens the lemma's reach.
arxiv-2605-28238: Scott Kim, Mathis Lechaume-Robert, and Anatole von Lilienfeld show that label symmetries, exact or rough, make learning need less data. Tests on hydrogen orbitals, water shakes, and its full energy surface give steeper learning curves, with gains lasting up to floors set by roughness. A Hessian fix squeezes more gain from rough symmetry.
arxiv-2605-28538: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for pair-produced vector-like T-quarks decaying to a Higgs boson plus a top quark, in lepton-plus-jets events. Using 139 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at 13 teraelectronvolts, boosted resonances are rebuilt with variable-radius reclustered jets, and a neural network separates signal from Standard Model background. A profile-likelihood fit to the effective mass distribution finds no excess above Standard Model prediction. Exclusion limits at 95 percent confidence set lower mass limits of 1.40 teraelectronvolts for singlets, 1.56 for doublets, and 1.66 at full branching fraction.
arxiv-2605-28738: Matthew Fickus, John Jasper, and Dustin G. Mixon prove no complex equiangular tight frame exists with vector count strictly between d squared minus d plus one and d squared. The proof, which grew from an internal model at OpenAI, echoes the link between real equiangular tight frames and strongly regular graphs. This addresses the Singer-Zauner gap for this family of frames, ruling out dimensions in the stated range. The argument connects frame theory with graph theory through the shared structure of equiangular lines and regular graphs.
arxiv-2605-28838: Veysel Kocaman and five colleagues build a specialty medical model for immune-mediated diseases. Pulling fine clinical information from medical notes is hard, and terms for immune-mediated and infectious diseases vary across sources, curbing general language systems. They assemble and label by hand 371 case reports with two experts, setting twelve classes covering immune-mediated and infectious cases plus symptoms. A transformer model trained on clinical-domain embeddings reaches F1 0.89, beating baseline and zero-shot rivals, and expert labels plus expert vectors prove most key for disease terminology.
arxiv-2605-28938: Christian Aoufia, Gonzalo Casas, and Fernando Marchesano examine approximate axionic shift symmetries in gravity-decoupling limits of type II Calabi-Yau compactifications. Each shift symmetry carries an axionic string whose tension limits the slope of the Kähler potential. The tension gradients form vector fields on moduli space much like those from BPS particle masses. Bounding the inner products of these fields splits them into mutually orthogonal groups, one of which decouples from gravity. The authors also link string-tension curvature to a divergent moduli-space curvature.
arxiv-2605-29238: Lianyan Fu proposes a graph neural network version of the generalized Mundlak estimator. It removes bias from group-level heterogeneity while allowing dependence within groups. Fixed-effects models use group intercepts but demand linear additivity and independence within groups. They support only within-group comparisons. Instead, balanced group-level sums control bias between groups, so groups can be compared fairly. Graph message-passing learns nonlinear forms and captures interaction effects within groups. Theory shows double robustness and a normal limit as samples grow.
arxiv-2605-29438: Ye Li proposes ElegantVLA, a tool that speeds up vision-language-action models. Such models are strong for robotic control, but high cost and low control rate hinder real-time tasks. Current methods tune single parts or rely on fixed rules, and miss that reasoning needs vary by stage. It learns when to invest full work and when to reuse prior work. A lightweight planner spreads work across the vision encoder, language model, and action head. It gives speedups and higher rate without changing the base model.
arxiv-2605-29838: Yunfeng Jiang and three colleagues use gate-parameter Lee-Yang zeros to probe dynamical phases in finite circuits. In Floquet circuits built from identical fSim gates, the Loschmidt amplitude turns rational in gate parameters after a variable change. At fixed size and depth, zeros in one complexified parameter gather onto limit curves, with state-dependent and universal parts. As the other parameter shifts, the universal zero set reorganizes abruptly, marking a dynamical phase transition in finite qubits. Tests on a solvable brickwork and longer-range variants back the mechanism.
arxiv-2605-30438: Jiguang Yu and Louis Shuo Wang study the base of indirect signal making in Keller-Segel chemotaxis models. In a multi-stage signaling cascade, they prove a sharp split between instant equilibration and kinetic memory. They show the equilibrating PES cascade collapses into one static fourth-order elliptic interaction. At dimension four, cancellation of the Newtonian singularity yields a logarithmic kernel, moving the mass-critical dimension from two to four. They show the mixed MEP cascade keeps a Volterra memory effect defying reduction.
arxiv-2605-30538: Xiao and colleagues build DisasterLex, a system that helps analysts query disaster databases in plain language. Ordinary text-to-SQL tools stumble on disaster data because queries span many geospatial tables and demand reasoning about causes. DisasterLex inserts an expert knowledge graph of concepts and causal links between the question and the database, routing each query through entity spotting, domain routing, causal planning, and SQL grounding. Across seven base models it beat four leading baselines by wide margins on a seventy-five-query test set.
arxiv-2605-30738: Ghugarkar and colleagues present MAVEN, a scaffold for decomposition, orchestration, and verification in tool calling. Large language models score strongly on benchmarks but struggle to compose strategies, preserve states, and coordinate tools across domains. MAVEN is evaluated across tool-calling benchmarks, plus MAVEN-Bench, a test for multistep mathematical and physical reasoning. MAVEN-Bench exposes a gap between quality and end-to-end success. In runs, MAVEN lifts its base model from 48 percent to 71 percent accuracy without training, staying competitive at a tenth of the cost.
arxiv-2605-30938: Yin builds a unified scaling theory for driven quantum critical dynamics at any driving rate. Classic Kibble-Zurek scaling holds only for slow drives starting far from the critical point. Studying drives confined to the critical region, he develops a finite-time scaling form. It bridges Kibble-Zurek scaling for slow drives and De Grandi-Gritsev-Polkovnikov scaling for sudden quenches. Simulations at quantum critical and tricritical points match the theory, supporting an account for all driving rates.
arxiv-2605-31038: Teixeira and colleagues build a brain-like microfluidic platform for multi-spectral classification and tracking of microparticles. Standard systems trade throughput, speed, and bandwidth, limiting fast-flow tracking without motion blur or huge output. Their platform extracts motion and spectral information from samples by pairing an RGB filter mask with an event-based sensor, coding signature and motion at sensing. It reaches sub-millisecond timing and robust sorting across sizes and speeds, including non-laminar flows, while cutting data bandwidth by over two hundred times versus standard imaging.
arxiv-2605-31338: Darji and colleagues build bundesrecht, an open library and corpus for German statutory reference processing. Legal cites appear in compact, variable forms. They may combine targets, use special short forms and point to fine-grained units, beating generic tools. The library parses, tidies and fixes raw cites into neat objects. It expands compact forms and links them to rules, while the corpus preserves statute ladder down to sub-rules. Tested on 2,944 marked cites, it groups real cite variants far better than string matching.

arxiv-2606-04238:
Devleena Das and colleagues present a recovery trick in 2026 for heavily quantized language models. Quantization stores weights with very few bits. It shrinks models for cheap deployment, but at two bits the quality drop is steep.

Their method first quantizes only two key layer types to two bits and leaves the rest at four. Then it reclaims the lost quality by distilling from the full model on synthetic data. Recovery brought back much of the accuracy that raw two-bit quantization had lost. Speed analysis showed a solid throughput gain from the mixed scheme. The authors frame mixed precision plus recovery as the practical path to tiny models. Tests spanned several model sizes.
arxiv-2606-04338:
Xixi Tian and co-authors test in 2026 whether hospitals can train a sepsis early-warning model together without pooling patient records. The method is federated learning: each site trains locally and shares only model parameters.

Their data held six hundred forty-eight screened cases from three Chinese tertiary hospitals. The federated setup matched the accuracy of a central model trained on all the data at once. Raw records never left their hospitals. Security checks also showed that attackers could not rebuild the original patient data from the shared parameters. The authors offer the setup as a workable template for privacy-preserving medical modeling across centers.
arxiv-2606-04638:
Di Marco and colleagues extend a classic 1964 framework for analyzing nonlinear electrical circuits to circuits that also contain memristors, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Brayton and Moser's mixed potential describes circuits of resistors, inductors, and capacitors through one scalar function. This enables compact state equations and convergence results. Memristors resisted this treatment. Their resistance depends on past current. The authors show a mixed potential exists for such RLCM circuits. The analysis must move from the traditional voltage-current domain into the flux-charge domain.

A flux-charge analysis method plays the crucial role. The authors compute the mixed potential explicitly for several examples. These include Chua's circuit with a memristor and large-scale memristor arrays with a neural architecture. A companion paper uses it for systematic Lyapunov-style convergence results.
arxiv-2606-04838:
Mismar and colleagues build an explainable AI framework that predicts which mobile subscribers are about to leave, and explains why, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Churn prediction helps telecom operators retain customers, but black-box models give retention teams no story. Their framework covers the data-driven pipeline with explainable machine learning.

Their central finding is that subscriber quality-of-experience indicators provide stronger churn signals than network counters alone. How the service feels to the user predicts departure better than raw engineering measurements of the network. For operators, the practical message is to aim retention analytics at quality.
arxiv-2606-05138:
Konrad Mueller and co-authors generate realistic financial time series by matching random convolutional features in this 2026 arXiv paper. Markets offer only a single observed history, so training a generator on it invites overfitting, especially with adversarial training where a critic can memorize the samples. A recent remedy trains generators to match fixed features of real and synthetic series, but the signature features used there can miss key traits at usable depths.

The team instead introduces SOCK, short for Soft Competing Kernels, a fully differentiable random convolutional feature map, since existing maps like Rocket and Hydra cannot train a generator by gradient descent.
