Generators trained by matching SOCK features beat signature and diffusion baselines across a wide range of small-sample market datasets. SOCK also matched or beat existing feature maps on two-sample testing and time series labeling, showing its features are useful beyond generation.
arxiv-2606-05238:
Yuanli Wang and colleagues introduce DeployBench in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for how well language model agents can deploy research artifacts, the code released alongside papers, from a fresh machine. Agent benchmarks assume a working environment exists. Yet setting one up means wrestling multi-language toolchains, system-level dependencies such as GPU configuration, and legacy code that no longer builds.

DeployBench holds 51 deployment tasks across AI and machine learning, computer systems, and scientific computing. Every task is graded by a hidden pipeline that runs the paper's experiment and checks its outputs. Evaluating four leading language models through the OpenHands agent framework gave pass rates from 7.8 percent up to 51.0 percent. Failures were dominated by a completion-judgment problem. In 97 of 154 failed runs the agent stopped after pre-finish checks that validated a different or weaker target than the task required, mistaking setup for success.
arxiv-2606-05438:
Dongruo Zhou settles the exact difficulty of a core optimization problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The problem is finding an approximately stationary point, a point where the gradient is nearly zero, of a smooth but nonconvex function using function values and gradients.

Zhou proves a new dimension-free lower bound valid for every finite order of smoothness. It matches the best known algorithms in the two cases: when the Hessian is Lipschitz continuous, no method can beat the known rate, and when third derivatives are Lipschitz. The hard example uses a block-chain construction that reveals information to the algorithm block by block while preserving the smoothness the hard instance needs. The construction was discovered with assistance from a frontier AI model and then verified by the author. The result closes the gap between what first-order methods achieve on higher-order smooth problems and what is provably possible.
arxiv-2606-05538:
He and co-authors look for a safer way to shrink very large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. The models use a mixture-of-experts design, where only some parts switch on for each input. That design gives strong results but a huge memory load. Past attempts to trim such models broke down on broad tests. The team traces the failure to trimming at too coarse a scale.

Skill in these models sits in tiny slices inside the expert parts, the authors find. In one model, removing just twelve of more than a million slices wrecked math scores while leaving fact recall mostly intact. Their method ranks slices by a statistical importance score and cuts the least needed ones. At half size, the trimmed model kept its skills, used about forty-five percent less memory, and ran about a fifth faster.
arxiv-2606-05638:
Jing-Yi Yan, Zhang, and Tang estimate the mass of a guessed exotic particle in a 2026 arXiv paper. The candidate is a hexaquark, a bound state of six quarks with hidden charm. Its quark content matches a known three-particle system. The authors model it as three tight quark pairs joined into one color-neutral whole. They test six current forms that could create such a state.

Their tool is the QCD sum rule method, which links quark-level physics to particle masses. The math includes perturbative terms and condensate terms up to high order. Inside windows that pass standard quality checks, the mass lands between three point nine and four point four GeV. That band gives experimenters a target range. Finding a state in that window would support the compact picture over looser molecular ones. The paper offers the estimate as a reference for future searches.
arxiv-2606-05738:
Longhua Qin and colleagues hunt for axion-like particles in blazar light in a 2026 arXiv paper. These guessed particles would let photons swap identity in magnetic fields, dimming distant sources in patterned ways. The blazar Mrk 421 shines across a huge energy range, ideal for the test. Two observatories watched it together over five epochs. The team fit photon-particle mixing and background light absorption together.

A copula method handled the weak links between epochs in one joint likelihood. Two jet models framed the source emission. No mixing signal appeared. The team set upper limits on the photon coupling at ninety-five percent confidence. In the lightest mass range the limit sits below eight ten-trillionths per GeV. Across the full mass scan, cautious limits land near ten to the minus twelve per GeV for both jet models. The framework suits future multi-messenger hunts.
arxiv-2606-06038:
Choksi, Kareliya, Malviya, and Mishra route an unsupported classical language through a modern relative's door in a 2026 arXiv paper. Prakrit, the Middle Indo-Aryan family of Jain scriptures and Ashokan inscriptions, lacks any slot in the IndicTrans2 translator. Rather than rebuild the model, the team maps Prakrit onto the Hindi language tag. Tokenizer, vocabulary, and architecture stay untouched. Script compatibility does the heavy lifting.

Training used a parallel corpus of under fifteen hundred Maharashtri Prakrit sentence pairs. Testing used a tiny twenty-sample set in the Ardhamagadhi dialect. Corpus BLEU improved over the untuned baseline, showing real transfer through the borrowed tag. The authors are candid about limits: data scarcity and dialect mismatch cap the gains. Released code and models invite others to push further. The broader lesson serves many classical languages. A script-compatible living relative can smuggle a dead language into modern multilingual systems.
arxiv-2606-06438:
Kartik Hans, Kaiwen Zhao, and Stephen Lee ask when replacing computers actually cuts carbon in this 2026 arXiv paper. New hardware runs faster and sips less power, but making it carries an embodied carbon cost paid upfront. If the old machine is lightly used, or the local grid is already clean, an early upgrade can raise total emissions instead of lowering them. Intuition is a poor guide here.

Their framework, CarbonSim, simulates the full lifecycle. It combines workload profiles, machine power draw, embodied carbon inventories, scheduling choices, and the grid's changing carbon intensity over time. It also supports different ways of spreading the embodied cost across a machine's life. Calibrated on several CPU generations, the simulations show that keeping older hardware longer often wins under light loads or clean electricity. Refresh decisions, they argue, should be workload aware, location aware, and lifecycle aware at once.
arxiv-2606-06738:
Big language models speak many languages, but the small ones inside them get squeezed, and rare languages suffer. Kumar and Dusek test a leaner way to teach a pretrained model one new language in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instead of retraining everything, they swap in a tokenizer built for the target language, freeze the word embeddings, the stored word meanings, and tune only the rest of the network.

Trials on Scottish Gaelic, Irish, and Quechua put the idea to the test. Quechua had only about eight thousand five hundred training examples, a truly tiny supply. The frozen embedding approach beat or matched full retraining on word prediction, while using fewer trainable parts and costing less to run. On name finding and grammar tagging tasks it performed about the same as full tuning, and the authors credit the frozen parts with curbing overfitting when data are scarce.
arxiv-2606-06938:
Vision language models like CLIP can be fooled by tiny, crafted changes to an image. Kim and Um fight back at test time in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their defense needs no retraining. An earlier counterattack method nudged corrupted images back toward safety. It weakened under strong attacks, though, because it trusted one corrupted view.

Their MAC method looks at the image from many angles at once. Augmented views give diverse embeddings of the same picture. Each view gets its own counterattack. A corruption estimate sets how hard each view should fight. Soft weighting replaces the old all or nothing gate. The defended views then merge into one prediction. Experiments spanned twenty data sets and many attack styles. Robustness rose substantially while speed and memory stayed lean. Clean accuracy survived as well.
arxiv-2606-07038:
A lattice can hide special states in its corners, protected by topology. Ning and Zhang control those corner states with a twist in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their lattice mixes a real resonator coordinate with a synthetic frequency coordinate. Periodic modulation drives a chiral walk across that hybrid plane. The system is non-Hermitian, so waves can grow or fade.

Corner pairs appear at two special quasienergies, zero and pi per period. Three mechanisms then act like separate dials. A non-Bloch construction decides whether the pair exists at all. Imaginary gauge fields choose which corner the modes pile into. The real flux decides whether the doubled period response shows up in light. The same sector can look bright, skin dark, or flux dark. A tunable exceptional point even changes the response's envelope shape. The result separates existence, location, and visibility cleanly.
arxiv-2606-07438:
Quarante, Chiang, Marenduzzo, and Negro simulate how a dry suspension of droplets flows under pressure, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such droplet assemblies model foams, emulsions, and biological tissues. At low forcing the suspension acts as a yield-stress material, sitting arrested until a critical force frees it. Their simulations suggest yielding is controlled by contacts between droplets, and the critical force depends on how deformable the droplets are.

Above yielding, flow does not steady; it turns intermittent, with stick-slip motion, caging periods, and velocity fluctuations far from bell-shaped. The authors interpret this as a self-pinned glass, where evolving droplet overlaps create a landscape that traps the droplets. At larger forcing, droplets deform enough to exchange neighbors continuously, annealing the overlap structure and triggering a transition to smooth, string-like flow. They propose overlap-network restructuring as a mechanism governing suspensions of deformable particles beyond this model.
arxiv-2606-07538:
Wang and a team fix a mismatch that breaks tool-finding for remote sensing agents, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language model agents processing satellite data need specialized tools, but tool documentation is too long to fit in context, so retrieval must pick the tools. Queries express broad intentions in plain language, while documentation describes technical details with no workflow context, a semantic asymmetry that defeats ordinary search. Their bidirectional method enriches both sides until they meet.

On the query side, a planning mechanism uses the agent's reasoning to decompose abstract intentions into logical subtasks, adding the vocabulary. On the tool side, a dependency graph learns how tools chain together and injects predecessor context into each tool's representation. Experiments on a remote sensing benchmark and a general API benchmark showed improved retrieval accuracy for complex tasks, with the method transferring robustly beyond its home domain. Code and data are released.
arxiv-2606-07638:
Lekshmi P, Arun, Syam, and Elgammal give photographers a dial for composition in an image generator, in this 2026 arXiv paper on landscape generation. Diffusion models absorb composition, so users cannot place the horizon or honor the rule of thirds, the guideline dividing a frame into 9 parts. Their framework extracts a 4-dimensional anchor from training images encoding facts such as horizon position and confidence, then injects it into a diffusion model through cross-attention with Fourier encoding. Three-way guidance dropout during training makes the anchor steerable at generation time.

Against a baseline and 3 ablated variants, the architecture achieved the highest horizon detection rate, near 0.85, and the highest rule-of-thirds alignment. A category ablation added nuance: training on uniform categories cut horizon deviation by up to 40 percent versus mixed training. Composition control, they conclude, is real but category-dependent, so controllability claims should be reported per scene type.
arxiv-2606-07738:
Artico and co-authors uncover a large new family of operators living on Wilson lines in this 2026 arXiv paper. Wilson lines are probes of gauge theories, the framework behind fundamental forces. They trace paths through the force field and serve as tools for studying confinement. The paper asks what structures such a line can carry when it transforms under a rich representation of the gauge group.

The answer is a broad class of operator insertions previously missed. In the highly symmetric N equals 4 super Yang-Mills theory, many carry the quantum numbers of the displacement supermultiplet, tied to how the line bends. The authors relate the deformations' beta functions, which govern how couplings change with scale, to correlation data. The deformations prove marginally relevant, meaning they grow slowly and reshape the line's distant behaviour, a claim backed by a weak-coupling calculation of four-point functions for any gauge group.
arxiv-2606-07938:
Swarna Chakraborty and co-authors build a dataset that teaches models to describe point cloud quality in words, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Point clouds, three-dimensional sets of sampled points, are degraded by compression and transmission. Judging that quality automatically is point cloud quality assessment. Existing datasets give one score per cloud, saying nothing about each distortion's severity.

The new dataset, DAL-PCQA, annotates clouds at the level of individual distortions. Each entry carries severity labels, quality categories, and natural-language descriptions of the damage. That richer supervision supports distortion-aware models that can explain a judgement, not just score it. Training with this distortion-level supervision substantially improves how well generated descriptions align with the actual distortions, in wording and meaning, over zero-shot and fine-tuned baselines. The dataset turns quality assessment from a number into an interpretable report.
arxiv-2606-08138:
Chinmaya Pradhan and co-authors simulate a yeast genome copying itself, base pair by base pair, under stress, in this 2026 arXiv paper. DNA replication must finish despite heat, chemicals, and DNA damage, yet its dynamics fluctuate wildly. Their lattice-based Monte Carlo framework models whole-genome replication in baker's yeast. It uses probabilistic origin firing, a spread of fork speeds, and a time-dependent limit on the cell's copying resources.

Benchmarked against experimental profiles, the model reproduces stress responses with only two effective parameters. Its central discovery concerns fork speeds: their variety explains why S-phase durations follow an Erlang distribution. It also explains the rare, very long events seen in bacteria and human cells, now predicted for yeast. The framework further predicts non-monotonic behaviour under heat stress and power-law scaling under hydroxyurea, a drug that starves forks. Simple ingredients generate the full repertoire of stressed copying.
arxiv-2606-08538:
Jannik Lübberstedt and a large clinical team show that routine blood tests, read as trajectories, foresee cancer care complications, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Laboratory panels drawn during cancer care form longitudinal recordings of organ function. Single-timepoint prognostic tools discard their temporal structure. The authors trained a transformer model on over two million lab measurements from nearly four thousand patients with myeloma or ovarian cancer. The model predicted the two-year onset of over one hundred sixty complications across eight clinical categories.

At the group level the predictions enriched complication rates several-fold above raw prevalence. The model matched or outperformed non-sequential baselines. Predictions generalized across both cancers. External validation on two independent datasets confirmed transfer across healthcare systems. The point is that care teams could watch for trouble weeks ahead, with no new tests at all.
arxiv-2606-08638:
Prasad and Sharma prove that tuning a fast linear programming solver is itself learnable with few examples, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Recent research has produced practical first-order methods for large-scale linear programming, the optimization workhorse behind logistics. Their performance depends heavily on hyperparameter selection. The authors derive generalization guarantees for hyperparameter tuning within a state-of-the-art graphics-processor solver built on the primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm.

First they pin down how the algorithm behaves as a function of its step size and primal weight. That leads to linear sample complexity guarantees for learning those parameters. They then analyze the full solver, which augments the core algorithm with preconditioning, adaptive step sizes, averaging, and restarts. Capturing the solution trajectory as a function of all hyperparameters, they obtain polynomial sample complexity guarantees for the full system.
arxiv-2606-08838:
Roy and Janquart improve the search for environmental fingerprints in gravitational-wave signals from merging binaries, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Some compact binaries form in crowded places, such as active galactic nuclei, where a third body's gravity accelerates the pair along our line of sight. That acceleration stretches the observed waveform in a characteristic way.The authors re-derive the effect fully and build it into waveform models with precession and higher harmonics, and into eccentric models across all harmonics.

Applying the model to selected events from the third observing run, they find no substantial evidence of line-of-sight acceleration. The work's sharper lesson is methodological. Treating the acceleration inconsistently between harmonics can bias the conclusions drawn from the same data. Their consistent implementation gives future runs a robust test of whether a merger's environment left a measurable mark, bearing on how these binaries form.
arxiv-2606-08938:
Li and colleagues train a medical AI to consult like a doctor who can reason in several styles without mixing them up, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diagnosis is a conversation under uncertainty: the doctor agent must ask follow-up questions, gather evidence, and switch among reasoning paradigms as the case demands. Teaching one model several paradigms from mixed dialogue data causes interference. Their framework, PACT, first synthesizes training dialogues under four paradigms using a Doctor-Patient-Supervisor setup that checks quality against full records while the doctor sees only patient-visible information.

Training then gives each paradigm its own adapter, called a LoRA Branch. Periodically the branches merge into a shared Anchor by sign consensus. The team built a dynamic multi-turn Chinese diagnosis benchmark. On it, PACT reached state-of-the-art results among the compared baselines, on diagnostic outcome and consultation-process measures.
arxiv-2606-09138:
Wang and colleagues build plumbing that turns AI agents' messy interaction logs into managed training data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agentic reinforcement learning trains language models through multi-turn interaction with tools and environments. Research focuses on training algorithms, while the data lifecycle, from producing traces to feeding them into training, gets little attention. Claw-R1 is a step-level data middleware bridging agent runtimes and training backends.

Two components do the work. A Gateway Server captures multi-turn steps through one API entry point. A Data Pool organizes them into step-level records with prompt IDs, response IDs, rewards, and metadata. In the demo, users inspect live trajectories, examine each step's state, action, and reward, curate data by quality, and assemble training-ready batches for downstream algorithms. The pitch: interaction traces are data assets to manage and audit, not temporary logs to discard. The code is available.
arxiv-2606-09338:
Karmim and colleagues pin down why language models fail questions whose answer requires chaining two facts they plainly know, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model can state when X was born and who Y's closest friend is, yet fail to say when that friend was born, in one forward pass. In a controlled biography setting, they separate people exposed to compositional contexts in pretraining from people never in any such context. The failure persists even at 97 percent one-hop accuracy, so the gap is a pretraining failure, not missing knowledge.

Nine data-centric augmentation formats were tested as remedies. Compositional pretraining transferred to unseen questions about exposed people, but never to people absent from compositional pretraining. Augmentation thus builds entity-specific associations rather than a reusable composition skill. Conclusion: exposure to compositional contexts in pretraining looks necessary for implicit multi-hop reasoning, a limit on later fine-tuning tricks.
arxiv-2606-09938:
Pierre-François Léget reports the shakedown of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's great camera in this 2026 arXiv proceeding. The eight point four metre scope in Chile began testing its main camera in April twenty twenty-five. Its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time is due to start in twenty twenty-six. A prime aim is to pin down dark energy through weak lensing, the slight warp of galaxy shapes by mass.

Such work needs the star image shape, the point spread function, modeled to a hair. Early sky data showed that task is harder than planned. Image quality and shape modeling both strain the shear measures the survey needs. The team log what they found once on sky, what they have since fixed, and what still waits. After one survey year, Rubin should match today's best dark energy bounds, if the flaws stay tamed.
arxiv-2606-10038:
Genel and colleagues release a new generation of the CAMELS simulation suite for learning cosmology with neural networks, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computational astrophysics. The new set holds one thousand one hundred ninety-two simulations varying thirty-five cosmological, astrophysical, and numerical parameters around the IllustrisTNG model. Each volume is eight times larger than the previous generation.

Training sets are built from matter power spectra, projected maps, galaxy distribution graphs, and halo properties, each fed to a matched network type. Larger volumes generally give tighter parameter constraints, thanks to lower sample variance and more diverse environments. The gains, however, grow more weakly than the square root of the added data, which the authors attribute to information loss from mode coupling or to parameter degeneracies. Four new parameters control the ionizing background, and their effects on intergalactic gas temperature are also studied.
arxiv-2606-10238:
Wu and his team argue that the brain's spatial memory system is shaped hyperbolically, and that the geometry itself improves computation, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computational neuroscience. The authors first propose a recipe for hippocampal tuning curves that induces hyperbolic geometry. They then connect neural decoding to associative memory by showing a modern Hopfield network update computes the minimum mean-squared-error formula.

Finally, they introduce an associative memory model defined directly in hyperbolic space that yields far larger capacity than leading models. The combined results suggest animals encode spatial information as a latent hyperbolic cognitive map, improving both memory capacity and decoding accuracy. Hyperbolic geometry expands fast with distance, matching the branching structure of settings and routes, which may explain why evolution settled on it. The picture links single-neuron tuning, group geometry, and memory theory into one account of hippocampal work.
arxiv-2606-10438:
Sonal and co-authors model a common business problem in this 2026 arXiv paper in economics: how far ahead should a firm plan an uncertain, staged search? Development proceeds through ordered stages with unknown rewards, and later stages require costly planning paid in advance. The authors frame this as an ordered Pandora's box problem, where each stage is a box with an unknown prize and an opening cost. A decision maker chooses an initial scope, and may later expand it at extra cost.

The paper proves that scope-dependent reservation values exist and are unique, so the optimal strategy is a threshold rule indexed by how much scope was prepaid. Three forces shape behaviour. A strong current offer encourages early stopping, prepaid scope encourages continuing because further access is cheaper, and a shrinking horizon discourages it. Examples with normal and fat-tailed rewards show the three forces producing distinct patterns.
arxiv-2606-10538:
James and colleagues improve how astronomers identify the home galaxies of fast radio bursts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes from distant galaxies, and matching one to its host underpins studies of cosmic gas and burst origins. The standard Bayesian tool, PATH, weighs candidates using radio position uncertainty and simple brightness assumptions. The authors extend PATH with three models predicting a host's apparent brightness from its expected redshift, itself inferred from the burst's dispersion measure, the smearing caused by ionised gas.

Fitted to thirty-two bursts from the Australian ASKAP telescope, all three models raise confidence in the most probable host for every galaxy examined. They agree at low redshift. Real hosts are fainter than a star-formation-weighted guess predicts, with a p-value of 0.12 percent against that model. A mass-weighted guess fits far worse still.
arxiv-2606-10638:
Kumar and Mandal find the minimum genus for a class of covers in this 2026 arXiv paper in algebraic geometry. The setting: a Galois cover of a projective curve in positive characteristic, its group a cyclic p-group, branching confined to finitely many points. A larger group, an elementary abelian l-group extended by the cyclic one, raises the question: among its covers dominating the given one and unramified outside the branch set, what minimum genus occurs?

The method runs through the Picard group of the covering curve, encoding its divisor classes. The authors find group-stable submodules inside the l-torsion of that Picard group, plus a generalisation, and use them to pin down the minimum genus. They also treat covers of the projective line unramified outside the affine line, a test case. The results feed the study of the étale fundamental group and its finite quotients.
arxiv-2606-11138:
Jha and four co-authors introduce First-Order Trajectory Matching in a 2026 arXiv paper, a surrogate for random systems. Many scientific systems behave randomly through chaos or unresolved detail, so honest prediction means propagating whole ensembles of paths. Standard operator learning averages futures away: trained on squared error, it collapses to the mean and loses fluxes and crossing currents.

FTM instead learns the probability current velocity, the local flow carrying probability mass, straight from paths. Matching the symmetric first-order motion of paths avoids estimating drift, diffusion, or scores. The learned flow preserves time marginals, so ensemble averages stay right, and captures current-like quantities too. A stability analysis shows the one-step, simulation-free loss is stable when time resolution and sample size are balanced. Across random dynamics and PDE examples, FTM gave ensemble predictions at plain-rollout cost, though it cannot reproduce full path statistics like hitting times.
arxiv-2606-11338:
Camacho-Guardian and four co-authors classify the critical behavior of ideal Bose-Einstein condensation in a 2026 arXiv paper. The ideal Bose gas near the transition is a classic continuous phase transition. They show its behavior falls into three distinct classes, set only by the low-energy scaling of the density of states, which dimensionality and confinement control.

In one class, susceptibilities diverge algebraically, as usual. In another, divergence comes with marginal log corrections. In the third, subtler class, only the correlation length diverges. The result is a unified framework for such transitions in ideal bosonic systems. It applies to atomic, photonic, polaritonic, and magnonic condensates, where dimension, confinement, and spectral design reshape the density of states.
arxiv-2606-11838:
Hyomin Kim leads a seven-author team improving how generated videos are scored in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reward models grade text-to-video outputs and guide further training, but they often miss fine-grained mismatches. A prompt may demand several objects, actions and timings, and a single global score cannot say which requirement failed.

Their model, SG-PVR, plans before it judges. The prompt is decomposed into atomic claims, one per requirement. A spatio-temporal scene graph is extracted from the video, listing entities, attributes and time-grounded relations. Each claim is then verified against both the graph and the raw video, anchoring judgments in explicit evidence. Scores for visual, temporal and physical quality come from the same trace. The model leads rivals on compositional and temporal alignment across three evaluation settings, and as a test-time reranker improves the alignment of generated videos.
arxiv-2606-12138:
Gerasimov and co-authors ask which learned features of a neural network survive retraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse autoencoders are small networks trained to split a model's internal activations into a large set of clean, readable features. Retraining with a different random seed often yields different features, threatening their use as evidence. The team defines feature stability as the chance that a feature reappears in an independently trained autoencoder.

Across seeds, models, layers, and dictionary sizes, stable features carried most of the signal used for reconstruction and prediction. Unstable features had weak impact and were dominated by rare surface-form triggers, such as odd spellings. Yet unstable features were not pure noise: they clustered in reproducible low-rank subspaces that each run splits differently. Stable features earned perfect detection scores about 4.5 times more often. Pooling unique features across seeds built steadier autoencoders without losing explained variance.
arxiv-2606-12238:
Bouobda-Moladje and co-authors build a model for a failure mode threatening the hydrogen economy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hydrogen stored inside metals can gather at weak spots and trigger sudden cracking, called hydrogen embrittlement. Their phase field model smears the crack over a small zone instead of tracking a sharp line, letting cracks grow on their own. Crucially, the model also tracks hydrogen segregation, its gathering on crack faces and grain boundaries, which lowers the energy holding those surfaces together.

Built inside a variational framework with strict energy bookkeeping, the model respects thermodynamics throughout. In polycrystal tests it reproduces the switch engineers fear. Without hydrogen, cracks cut through grains; as hydrogen content rises, grain boundaries weaken far more than grain interiors, because hydrogen collects there more strongly. The boundary fracture resistance ratio falls drastically. Cracking therefore reroutes along the boundaries, the intergranular mode seen in real hydrogen damage.
arxiv-2606-12338:
Cammarata and co-authors show that a wall's quantum jitter can entangle light fields that never touch, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two fixed conducting plates and one movable plate between them form two cavities, each holding a scalar field. A fixed wall would keep the fields perfectly independent. Here the middle wall has finite mass and sits in a harmonic trap, so its position fluctuates quantum mechanically. Those fluctuations couple the wall to both fields through a generalized Law Hamiltonian.

Working to second order in perturbation theory, the authors compute the ground state. Tracing out the wall leaves the two fields in a state whose negativity, an entanglement witness, is positive. Field modes across the wall are entangled, through the wall's motion. Total multimode negativity confirms it numerically. The entanglement's size depends on the wall's mass and oscillation frequency, its distances to the fixed plates, and the mode frequencies chosen.
arxiv-2606-12438:
Neumann and Schön track six years of a master's course slowly turning into a research apprenticeship, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Project-based software engineering courses usually apply known methods to practice cases. Their Information Systems course at Hannover began there in 2019. Year by year it grew more research-oriented: students framed questions, justified methods, and produced sound results with external partners. Raising demands like that usually risks student satisfaction.

A longitudinal mixed-methods study, using teaching evaluations, course documents, and artifacts, finds perceived quality stayed positive throughout. The stability rested on design choices. Authentic projects and collaboration with outside stakeholders kept work visibly relevant. Strong lecturer support and structured scaffolding caught students as tasks grew less certain. The course became broader, more demanding, and harder to coordinate, yet students kept rating it well. The paper offers a template: evolve in steps, protecting the transition with support, not just ambition.
arxiv-2606-12638:
Selagamsetty and co-authors build a ghost GPU that behaves just real enough to study AI supercomputer traffic, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Training large models spans many GPUs whose constant chatter, synchronization and peer-to-peer writes, can bottleneck everything. Simulating whole GPUs in detail is far too slow at that scale. Eidola, an extension to the gem5 simulator, instead models each GPU as an eidolon, a minimal stand-in keeping only what traffic modeling needs.

Annotated timing profiles from real applications drive the stand-ins, which emulate peer-to-peer writes with cycle-level precision. Traffic patterns are configurable per GPU, so scenarios can be isolated and compared. Eidola reproduces the variability seen in fused kernel execution, where compute and communication merge. Implementing a SyncMon-style synchronization scheme inside it confirms real reductions in polling-related memory traffic. Spin-wait traffic scales linearly with write delay, as predicted.
arxiv-2606-12838:
Jiang and colleagues present OCOO-T, a minimalist virtual cell model by design that predicts how a cell's gene expression responds to perturbations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowing transcriptional responses to gene knockdowns or drugs is central to building AI virtual cells. Current models lean on auxiliary cell-state encoders, hierarchical variational autoencoders, or gene-link priors, adding bulk that can limit scalability.

OCOO-T instead uses a plain Transformer stack working directly on continuous gene expression profiles, and frames prediction as a flow-matching denoising process over continuous time. Perturbation identity, dosage, and cell-type context enter through adaptive layer normalisation and in-context tokens, with no extra encoder gear. Tests on the Tahoe100M, Replogle, and PBMC benchmarks show state-of-the-art results across diverse perturbations and cell types. A patching scheme lets the model scale to long transcriptional profiles by handling cellular context in blocks.
arxiv-2606-12938:
Wang and colleagues develop a simulation-based inference pipeline that measures galaxy cluster masses from the projected phase-space information of member galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cluster masses carry cosmic information, but classical estimates rely on the mass-velocity-dispersion relation, which uses only a summary number for the galaxy motions. The pipeline joins a Deep Sets architecture with posterior estimation using normalising flows, and is trained to predict fixes to the classical relation, picking out information beyond velocity dispersion.

Trained and tested on the Uchuu-UniverseMachine simulation, the method is tested under an idealised interloper-free setup and a cylindrical setup. In the idealised case it reduces the scatter in mass values to as low as about 0.1 dex, a twofold gain over the standard mass-dispersion relation. In the cylindrical setup it reaches comparable performance at the high-mass end, above 10 to the 14.5 solar masses per h.
arxiv-2606-13138:
Biira and Doğan examine how the LIMITS computing community, founded to move computing away from growth-oriented values toward long-term well-being, engages with time and temporality, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Temporal frames shape which futures are imagined, which problems seem worth working on, and which solutions get pursued, yet assumptions about time stay implicit in research practice.

Through a literature review of the last decade of LIMITS scholarship, they find ways that explicit attention to concepts of time would enrich the field. Within the work that does engage with time, they find 5 recurring types of temporal engagement. These are computing time, methodological and design time, the politics and ethics of time, biological and ecological time, and afterlife and waste time. These types reveal how implicit temporal assumptions are embedded across research practices, design methods, and accounts of technological impact.
arxiv-2606-13838:
Alonso and Rivas give a simpler proof of a classic result about ordering in group theory. A group is bi-orderable when its elements can be lined up in a total order unchanged by multiplication on either side. The free product glues two groups together with no extra relations. Vinogradov proved in nineteen forty-nine that free products of bi-orderable groups stay bi-orderable. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves this again by dynamical means.

The proof views ordered groups as symmetries of the real line, each element acting as a sliding map. Modified ping-pong partitions keep the combined action faithful, so the built ordering is genuine. It extends the orders on both factor groups. A bonus follows: when each factor's order survives certain symmetries, the product order survives the combined symmetry too, recovering a result of Rolfsen.
arxiv-2606-14138:
Ding, Wen, and Li challenge a basic intuition: moving lots of heat requires violent turbulent stirring. In Rayleigh-Bénard convection, a fluid heated from below transports heat upward, measured by the Nusselt number. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses marginal energy-stability theory, asking which mean profiles saturate an energy-stability constraint. The selected profiles approach the best optimal transport states and rigorous bounds. They predict transport scaling as zero point zero two four five times the Rayleigh number to the one-half power.

The optimal profiles are hierarchical: conductive inner layers, logarithmic-like intermediate layers, and a stably stratified bulk. The striking step converts such a profile into an exact motionless conductive state through prescribed internal thermal forcing. In simulations, a turbulent flow relaxed to stillness while maintaining a large wall heat flux. Energy-stability saturation thus interprets transport limits physically: high-flux heat transfer without turbulence, by design.
arxiv-2606-14438:
Guo and co-authors present CADET in a 2026 arXiv paper on self-driving car software. End-to-end driving planners learn by imitating human drivers, but they can pick up statistical shortcuts, linking roadside objects or building fronts to steering choices instead of the factors that truly cause them. Standard scores like displacement error and collision rate cannot reveal this hidden reliance.

CADET audits a trained planner for such spurious reliance without any retraining or parameter changes. The framework is grounded in physics and causal reasoning, and it can also benchmark and repair the problem in already deployed planners. That training-free design matters because earlier causal fixes required retraining large models from scratch. The authors position CADET as a practical check for causal confusion that otherwise stays silent until rare, long-tail road situations appear.
arxiv-2606-14638:
Repasky and co-authors sharpen Moon maps with a generative model in a 2026 arXiv paper. Higher-resolution topography helps scientists read surface processes and landforms, but analytical super-resolution is expensive at large scales. Their approach adapts the Schrödinger bridge, a diffusion method that morphs one data distribution into another, to connect low-resolution lunar elevation to high-resolution elevation.

The model also conditions on optical imagery, echoing shape-from-shading methods that refine elevation using pictures at the target resolution. Training used a new dataset of rendered lunar terrain mimicking images from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's narrow-angle camera. Unlike fixed sharpening rules, the bridge produces samples, so each reconstructed pixel carries an uncertainty estimate. The authors present the method as a flexible route to large-scale lunar topography enhancement.
arxiv-2606-14738:
Fuchs and co-authors demo a tiny levitated gravity sensor in a 2026 arXiv paper. It can hear Earth tides. Gravity mapping reveals underground mass and its movement. But current gravimeters weigh over eight kilograms and cost over one hundred thousand dollars. Deployment stays limited. Their sensor instead levitates a small suspended mass. The diamagnetic design fits in a few cubic centimeters.

The device showed sensitivity of eighteen microgal, the standard gravity unit. Its integration time was six seconds, with far better projected performance. It resolved Earth tide signals. These are the daily gravity swelling caused by the Moon and Sun. Its stability matched state-of-the-art instruments. It acts as a true gravimeter, not a mere accelerometer. The authors foresee drone surveys and distributed sensor networks for cheap, high-resolution gravity monitoring.
arxiv-2606-15538:
Piñuelas and colleagues analyse the Jaynes-Cummings model in 2026 with Lie symmetry methods and conservation-law theory. The model, a cornerstone of quantum optics, describes a two-level atom exchanging excitations with a single quantized field mode. They recast its dynamics as a system of partial differential equations by projecting the von Neumann equation onto the atomic degrees of freedom.

From that system they determine the point and generalized symmetries and build invariant solutions that respect quantum mechanics. The dressed-state dynamics reappear, joined by a second family of solutions whose radial shape is given by Heun polynomials. Using generating functions, they derive laws beyond the conservation of total excitation number. New conserved currents involve atomic populations, coherence, reduced-state purity, and moments of the field. One balance law links purity and coherence to the atom-field coupling, tying the structure to entanglement dynamics in the coupled system.
arxiv-2606-15638:
Ali and colleagues present MambAdapter in 2026, a cheaper way to adapt speech and audio foundation models to new tasks. Full fine-tuning of transformer models is costly, so parameter-efficient methods tune only small adapter modules while the base model stays frozen. MambAdapter rebuilds those adapters around Mamba, a state-space sequence model, instead of the usual transformer-style blocks.

The design folds a lightweight Mamba module into low-rank bottleneck adapters and shares projections across adapters to cut the parameter count further. On four audio classification tasks and speech recognition in five languages, MambAdapter matches or beats strong parameter-efficient baselines. It does so even under reduced parameter budgets, where rival methods have more weights to work with. For teams adapting large audio models on modest hardware, state-space adapters offer a leaner route than shrinking transformer adapters, with no loss in accuracy.
arxiv-2606-15838:
Kang and colleagues report on I-GUIDE Smart Search in 2026, a retrieval system for spatial discovery inside a scientific gateway. Researchers must search datasets, maps, notebooks, software, and publications, plus the links among them. Conventional geoportals offer metadata and spatial filters but little semantic retrieval or graph traversal in one place.

Smart Search combines OpenSearch keyword, vector, and spatial indexes with a Neo4j provenance graph. Its pipeline augments queries, routes between methods, grades relevance, and checks answers for hallucination. On one A100 server it serves about a hundred users in parallel at 4.4 requests per second, despite each query taking dozens of model calls. On 170 real user queries, it improves evidence reach and judged answer quality over non-retrieval and naive baselines. The clearest gains come on exact-identifier, spatially constrained, and suggestion questions. The lesson: deployed search quality owes more to maintained metadata and validation than to model scale.
arxiv-2606-16038:
Ahmad and colleagues introduce Open-SWE-Traces in 2026, a large open dataset for training software engineering agents. Such agents fix real code issues by browsing repositories, running tools, and editing patches over many steps. Training them needs recorded trajectories, meaning step-by-step runs, and those records have been scarce. The team built the collection from real pull requests across nine programming languages.

The dataset holds 207,489 trajectories drawn from 20,000 real-world pull requests, gathered with OpenHands and SWE-agent harnesses. One teacher model produced traces with explicit thinking text, while another produced direct non-thinking traces. Fine-tuning the Qwen3-30B-A3B family on the data gives a best resolve rate of 61.7 percent on SWE-bench Verified in the reported runs. Scores also reach 57.1 percent on the multilingual benchmark and 36.8 percent on SWE-bench Pro. Open data at this scale lets smaller models learn long repair jobs.
arxiv-2606-16138:
Smith and co-authors close a hidden gap in 2026 in fast methods for fitting latent stochastic differential equations. Such equations model an unobserved state that evolves with noise and produces the data we see. Variational inference fits them, but classic algorithms must simulate the system step by step, trading accuracy for cost. Simulation-free methods skip the simulation by describing the posterior through its snapshots over time.

Smith shows that this shortcut quietly restricts which posterior processes the method can express, weakening both inference and learning. Their Helmholtz-SDE algorithm optimizes over full path laws that match a chosen set of time snapshots, removing the restriction. On the fluid-flow test reported, its forecast error of about 3.24 beats rival simulation-free methods at 4.07 and 3.99, with a better fit score as well. The fix keeps the speed of simulation-free fitting while restoring its reach.
arxiv-2606-16238:
Xu and Zhong prove in 2026 that the three-dimensional compressible Navier-Stokes equations stay well-behaved for all time, even when the fluid starts with vacuum regions. These equations govern gases whose density changes, and far-field vacuum means the gas fades to nothing at large distances. Global strong solutions can break down in such settings, so proving they persist is delicate. The key assumption is smallness of one specific initial quantity.

That quantity is scaling invariant, meaning it keeps the same size under the equations' natural rescaling, and it couples the system's coefficients together. Its smallness conditions depend on no initial data values or known parameters beyond the quantity itself. Notably, the proof needs no compatibility conditions on the initial data. Delicate energy estimates yield both global existence and uniqueness of strong solutions and their decay rates over time. The result improves previous theorems on compressible flow with vacuum.
arxiv-2606-16538:
Sopena-Gilboy builds new algebraic tools for complex geometry in a 2026 mathematics paper. Complex manifolds carry several kinds of cohomology, the invariants that count holes and twists in a space. Two of them, Bott-Chern and Aeppli cohomology, capture complex structure that the standard theory misses. They matter most for non-Kahler manifolds, where the usual shortcuts fail.

The work is set in algebras with two gradings and two differentials, compared up to a weak notion of sameness from pluripotential theory. In that setting Sopena-Gilboy sets up operadic calculus and Koszul duality, which organize operations with many inputs. The main result is a Pluripotential Homotopy Transfer Theorem. It gives a framework for Massey products, higher linking invariants, inside Bott-Chern and Aeppli cohomology for any complex manifold. The theorem lets algebraists move rich structures along weak equivalences without losing the higher product data that plain cohomology cannot see.
arxiv-2606-17138:
Fang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on pinning down a key weak-interaction parameter from B meson decays. The parameter, known as Vcb, sets the strength of transitions between bottom and charm quarks. It is extracted from semileptonic decays in which a B meson yields a D meson, a lepton, and a neutrino, using measured rates plus theory input on the decay form factors.

The team fits recent data with three common form-factor schemes, named BSZ, BGL, and HQET, under several fit scenarios. They show how the extracted value shifts with the scheme chosen and with how the data are treated in the fits. The BGL scheme reproduces the official world average quoted by the Particle Data Group. The HQET scheme tends to give a smaller value instead, and the authors also test whether new-physics effects are still allowed.
arxiv-2606-17238:
Hone presents a 2026 arXiv paper on vector peakon equations, a family of integrable wave equations built from a spectral problem in a Clifford algebra. The system can be read as a vector perturbation of the Camassa-Holm equation, a well-known model with peaked waves, and it keeps a residual orthogonal symmetry. Hone studies both the two-component case and the general case with any number of components allowed.

For two components, travelling waves match a Liouville integrable Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom, via a reciprocal transformation to a symmetry of another known system. A full symmetry classification of integrable two-component perturbations is given, and it turns up one new system not reported before. For many components, the short-pulse limit is governed by a vector Hunter-Saxton type system, whose measure-valued weak solutions are analysed in detail.
arxiv-2606-17538:
Bhadra, Rivas, and Martín-Delgado present a 2026 arXiv paper showing that bosonic pairing opens a second channel for chiral edge currents in a two-dimensional kagome lattice. Particle-conserving models have only the familiar hopping current, so anything extra is a genuine novelty of the paired setting. Starting from the continuity equation, the authors split the lattice current into that hopping part and an anomalous pairing part, each with its own microscopic source inside the material.

The hopping current is fed by on-bond single-particle coherence, while the pairing current draws on off-site anomalous coherence set by the pairing gap. A leakage ratio for the pairing current around a defect can be tuned from confined to strongly anomalous at fixed topology. The two channels leave distinct fingerprints around defects in real space. Driven photonic lattices and superconducting circuits could test the predictions directly.
arxiv-2606-17738:
Frank, Koskela, and Mishra present a 2026 arXiv paper in analysis proving Sobolev interpolation inequalities on extension domains, in the same shape they take on the whole space. Such inequalities bound a function's size by a blend of its gradient and a weaker norm, and they power many arguments in partial differential equations. On domains, the question is whether functions can be extended outward without losing control. The authors pin down the extra property that makes the whole-space form survive the move.

The key is a notion, the Lebesgue extension domain, defined through extension into Lebesgue spaces rather than Sobolev ones. The main theorem shows every Sobolev extension domain automatically has this Lebesgue property, for the full range of exponents. With that bridge, the interpolation inequalities follow in their whole-space shape. Applications follow where that shape, not a weaker variant, is what the argument needs.
arxiv-2606-17838:
Fernandes and colleagues automate the fiddly craft of prompt writing for language model game agents, in a 2026 paper. An agent's success in a game world swings wildly with its prompt, yet tuning prompts by hand is slow and specific to each task. Their framework splits the job between a descriptor agent that reads the scene against the goal and an action agent that picks the move, then improves both prompts in turns.

An evolutionary loop drives revisions, guided by scores from actually playing the game. A behavior analyzer blames specific prompt parts for each outcome, and a mutator proposes targeted edits, which rollouts then verify. On all five BabyAI tasks the method improved results with no change to model weights. One coordination task jumped from total failure to success in nearly three quarters of attempts.
arxiv-2606-18138:
Mandarapu and Kunkunuru ask when a database's self-tuning filters are worth their complexity, in a 2026 systems paper. Log-structured merge trees store data in runs, each guarded by a Bloom filter, and a fixed memory budget must be split among them. The best static split is known, yet a large literature makes the split adaptive, chasing shifting access hotness online. The authors question whether that machinery pays.

Three analytical results structure the answer. A log-law says optimal bits per key grow linearly with the logarithm of access frequency. A robustness law shows misjudging hotness costs little, since errors enter only through that logarithm. And an adaptivity frontier shows the gain from continuous tracking shrinks against simply recomputing at compaction time, which rebuilds filters for free. Sweeps, Twitter cache traces, and a real RocksDB engine validate the three-regime policy.
arxiv-2606-18338:
Stevenson and colleagues introduce ThousandWorlds, a benchmark dataset for machine learning emulation of exoplanet climates, in a 2026 paper. Reading faint atmospheric signals from a possibly habitable planet requires knowing its climate, because the same molecule can point to life on one world and plain chemistry on another. Global climate models supply that knowledge, but single runs can consume millions of core-hours.

The dataset holds roughly eighteen hundred simulations from five different climate models, mapping eight planet parameters to three-dimensional fields of temperature, humidity, winds, clouds, and radiation. Three nested subsets raise the difficulty from one simulator to many, including cases with structured missing data. Among seven baselines tested, Gaussian process methods performed best, ahead of deep learning approaches. The authors offer the benchmark as a shared test for faster, trustworthy climate emulation in a low-data setting.
arxiv-2606-18538:
Chowdhury and Weiner put a leading explanation for why neural network neurons seem to do double duty on rigorous mathematical footing, in a 2026 paper on mechanistic interpretability. The explanation is superposition. A network packs more features than it has neurons by representing features as overlapping, non-orthogonal directions, which works because any single input uses only a few features at a time.

Working with the simple autoencoder model where superposition was first demonstrated empirically, the authors analyze the mathematical basis for when it occurs and when it is optimal. For power activation functions they derive upper and lower bounds on the squared reconstruction loss, and show the bounds are tight in the very sparse regime where superposition is supposed to shine. The paper thus corroborates key empirical findings of the earlier work with proofs rather than simulations.
arxiv-2606-19138:
Detzel and colleagues introduce INDEQS in 2026, a graph-based neural differential equation method for time series forecasting. Neural controlled differential equations handle continuous-time data well. Their graph extensions usually learn spatial structure from data alone, even when a directed graph is already known from the domain. INDEQS instead builds prior graph knowledge into the model at distinct positions, so known flow structure guides learning rather than being rediscovered from scratch.

The method separates inner mixing of hidden states across graph nodes from outer mixing between vector field and control path. A light variant constrains the graph, while a richer variant learns extra links from data. To test when prior structure helps, the team builds a continuous advection simulation on directed graphs with known ground truth. Real tests cover river discharge on a hydrological network and traffic flow. Outer informedness improves error most on larger graphs.
arxiv-2606-19238:
Kulmaganbetov and colleagues introduce quantum ophthalmology in 2026, surveying how quantum technologies could reshape eye imaging and sensing. Four directions anchor the review. Photon-limited retinal imaging uses advances in optical coherence tomography and single-photon detection to image under tight photon budgets. That cuts light toxicity while preserving image quality, a key limit for repeated imaging of delicate retinal tissue in patients.

Correlation-based imaging, including ghost imaging, offers image formation in low light and scattering media, though detection efficiency and acquisition time still limit practice. Nanoscale probes such as quantum dots give tunable, photostable contrast agents, with biocompatibility and clinical translation still open. Last, single-photon and structured-light experiments show the visual system itself works near physical detection limits and can be probed with controlled optical states. Most approaches are early stage. Together they show how quantum optics could extend what eye care can measure.
arxiv-2606-19538:
Ashim Dhor, Rasel Mondal, and Pin-Yu Chen unify three neural network families under one mathematical object in 2026. Three network families carry unlike biases: local links, step-by-step memory, and content-based links between parts. ITNet treats all three as partial views of a learnable integral transform.

A small multilayer perceptron serves as the kernel, depending jointly on positions and features. Pairwise interactions thus adapt to data instead of fixed design rules. Convolution, multi-head self-attention, and recurrence families like LSTM, GRU, S4, and Mamba all arise as special cases. ITNet can also match any smooth operator in theory. Tiled kernel fusion, weighted Monte Carlo sums, and learned low-rank splits keep compute in check. One shared architecture matches or beats specialists on ImageNet-1K, GLUE, ModelNet40, VQA v2, and NLVR2. A single learned interaction mechanism can thus recover three architectural traditions.
arxiv-2606-19938:
Yi Xiao and five colleagues propose triangular consistency as a universal training constraint for optical flow in 2026. Optical flow estimates how pixels move between frames, and training usually leans on labels or model-specific tricks. The new rule composes two flow fields to induce a third, then demands that all three agree. Depending on the inputs, this yields cycle consistency, longer-range motion through chained frames, or a form of data augmentation from synthetic transforms.

The constraint adds almost no compute and needs no extra annotation, since it follows from flow geometry alone. Gains appear across supervised, unsupervised, and transfer settings, and the code is public. Because the rule is independent of architecture and dataset, it can slot into many existing pipelines. Motion estimation gets a cheap, principled regularizer.
arxiv-2606-20138:
Po-Chin Chang, Nicholas Hogan, Aske Plaat, and Michiel van der Meer build a tutoring system that learns which prompt to give a language model for each student and subject. Their 2026 paper notes that static prompts cannot adapt across disciplines. The team extracted fourteen teaching features, such as scaffolding and signs of understanding, from raw transcripts, and trained a prompt routing model inside a simulated classroom first.

Deployed with real high-school students, the router chose strategies that shifted between analytical work and guided scaffolding. In A/B testing over 656 conversations from 359 students, adaptive routing cut about three turns per exercise while holding teaching quality steady. A greedy router matched the baseline conversion rate near nineteen percent. A stochastic router that samples among strategies did better, reaching 28.1 percent of exercises converted. The gains show simulation-trained routing can transfer to live classrooms.
arxiv-2606-20438:
Zahra Asghari Varzaneh, Reza Khoshkangini, Thomas Ebner, and Lars Johansson build a sperm-shape classifier that can explain its own calls. Their 2026 paper targets male infertility workups, where judging sperm morphology by eye is slow and varies between observers. Deep learning grades sperm images well, but most models are black boxes, which limits clinical trust.

The framework pairs a pretrained EfficientNet-B0 network with a CBAM attention module that steers focus onto key areas of the sperm head. On the SMIDS and HuSHem datasets it reaches 90.2 and 93.9 percent accuracy, beating a simple CNN and the plain backbone. Grad-CAM++ heat maps show which features drove each decision. An accurate grader that can also show its reasoning is far easier for fertility clinics to adopt.
arxiv-2606-20638:
Sonali Goel and four colleagues at Oxford introduce RIZZ in 2026, a system for helping black-box language model agents adapt over time without access to model weights. Long-lived agents must handle new users, tasks, and feedback, yet single-prompt tuning or flat memory lets failures in one area spoil behavior in another. RIZZ routes interactions to near zero-interference zones, meaning separate memory branches where one task family is less likely to disturb another.

A context-aware router selects or creates a branch for each input. It compiles branch, global, graph, and working memory into a bounded prompt. Verifiers check results before lessons are stored. By keeping memories apart, RIZZ limits cross-task contamination and costly repeated search.
arxiv-2606-20838:
Jules Fowler and fourteen colleagues report on-sky results in 2026 for forecast wavefront control at Keck, aimed at imaging planets around other stars. Extreme adaptive optics corrects wavefront errors over a tiny field. Time lag is a leading problem. The wavefront changes faster than the lag between sensing and correction. Forecast control predicts where the wavefront will be when the fix lands.

Their setup uses learned patterns from past sensor states. It is built into the Keck-II real-time controller. On-sky tests compare it with a classic integral controller. The new controller improves results by about twenty percent. Gains on sky, not only in simulation, strengthen the case for forecast control at other sites chasing faint planets beside bright stars.
arxiv-2606-20938:
Linden Disney-Hogg proves a parity result in a solo 2026 mathematics paper about theta characteristics on Riemann surfaces that are invariant under a group of symmetries. A theta characteristic is a special line bundle whose square is the canonical bundle. Its parity, even or odd, is a key discrete invariant. The symmetries come from a group acting on the surface.

The method uses representation theory of a double cover of the symmetry group. That algebraic input forces the parity to be even for invariant characteristics. The result is applied to certain Hurwitz curves, which are highly symmetric surfaces. A recent conjecture by Broughton and Disney-Hogg is proved as a consequence. Parity results constrain which bundles can appear on symmetric curves. They also link geometry to group theory in a way that can be reused for other families of curves.
arxiv-2606-21238:
Yang Shen and four colleagues tackle a serving bottleneck for large language models in 2026: the key-value cache, stored attention data that speeds up text generation. The usual least-recently-used rule evicts blocks by age alone, so unrelated jobs sharing a server flush each other's useful cache entries. Their fix splits cache space adaptively between blocks that are recent and blocks that recur often.

On synthetic document question answering, the adaptive policy lifts the cache hit rate by up to 10.8 percent and cuts time to first token by up to 12.6 percent over plain vLLM. Gains shrink on real chat traffic but stay positive, at about two percent on both measures. The method also holds up for batch jobs, and the team released the code openly.
arxiv-2606-21538:
Jiashun Guan and four colleagues argue in 2026 that the accuracy wall hit by machine learning forecasts of chaotic flow is set by physics, not by model quality. Predictors of unsteady fluid motion always decay as the forecast horizon grows, and better architectures only postpone the drop. Working with bluff body flow, a classic testbed of spatiotemporal complexity, the team derives a scaling law for that decay from a framework inspired by Kolmogorov's turbulence theory.

High-fidelity simulations confirm the law, closing a loop between a transparent physical theory and black-box prediction. The ceiling on predictability follows from the turbulence itself, so forecast skill can be judged against a principled limit rather than against rival models alone. The authors frame the result as a compass for building trustworthy learning systems across the physical sciences.
arxiv-2606-21838:
Tao and colleagues tackle hierarchical image classification in 2026, where labels sit in a tree from broad groups down to exact species. Image-text models can name fine categories with no task training, yet their answers often contradict themselves across levels, predicting a species whose parent group they themselves ruled out. The authors trace the fault to false negative pairs created when contrastive training mixes categories from different levels.

Their fix restricts each contrastive comparison to categories within the same taxonomic level, and balances training so every level gets enough attention. Built on BioCLIP with the TreeOfLife-10M dataset, the model improved both consistency and accuracy from coarse to fine levels. On the iNaturalist 2021 benchmark, average accuracy across levels rose by 30.47 percent over the baseline, a large gain for hierarchical zero-shot classification. The team released both Euclidean and hyperbolic versions of the model publicly.
arxiv-2606-21938:
Wang and colleagues introduce Artic-O in 2026, a system that reconstructs articulated objects, things with movable parts like laptops and cabinets, from just a few images. The task demands full geometry, parts, and motion parameters at once. Earlier methods split those jobs into separate stages, which weakened consistency and slowed inference.

Artic-O works end to end in one feed-forward pass. It encodes sparse views, taken with joints in varied poses, into a geometry latent space learned beforehand, and a flow-matching decoder, kept frozen, provides a prior for complete shapes. A part-reasoning module then fuses image tokens, geometry codes, and decoder features to segment active parts and predict their motion. On the PartNet-Mobility benchmark it beat a strong prior method on reconstruction quality with similar or better joint accuracy. Inference time fell from nine minutes to about a third of a second per object.
arxiv-2606-22238:
Niu and Sekiyama build, in 2026, the classical powerdomains inside synthetic domain theory, and use them to model nondeterminism. Synthetic domain theory rebuilds domain theory inside a constructive universe where every definable map between domains is continuous. Powerdomains collect sets of possible outcomes, but their synthetic versions had received almost no attention.

The authors build the lower, upper, and convex versions in this setting. They prove the three constructions yield adequate models of nondeterminism. The resulting metalanguage embeds directly into dependent type theory, which then serves as a logic for reasoning about it. Because of adequacy, reasoning through it can be used to study how actual programs behave. The work extends the programme begun by Phoa and Taylor on the convex case.
arxiv-2606-22338:
Rathi introduces RoboMME-Interference in 2026, a cross-session benchmark for memory in vision-language-action robot policies. Deployed robots accumulate experience across many sessions, and a task may require recalling information from several sessions back. Existing robot-memory benchmarks use single episodes or short contexts, so interference from unrelated sessions goes unmeasured.

For each query episode, the benchmark builds a session history around one relevant prior demonstration, followed by unrelated sessions in controlled numbers. The history is given to the policy as memory, and accuracy is measured as distractors accumulate. Running the released memory-augmented policies unmodified, Rathi finds perceptual memory variants help when the history holds no distractors. Their success then decays strongly and steadily as unrelated sessions pile up. Current systems, the benchmark shows, largely fail at long-context recall under interference.
arxiv-2606-22538:
Yu-Xuan Zhang and Jing-Ling Chen present a proof of the quantum Hamming bound in this 2026 paper. The bound is a sphere-packing limit for quantum error correction: code size times the number of correctable error patterns must fit in the Hilbert space. Degenerate codes, where different errors act identically on the code, are the only loophole.

The open question was whether degeneracy could ever break the bound for codes in any local dimension. Zhang and Chen prove the nonbinary part, covering every local dimension of at least three. Any violation reduces to a two-centre ball intersection inequality, which their analysis rules out. Qutrits, the three-level case, sit at the boundary and need machinery including a filtered Lloyd square. Degeneracy can merge error sectors, but never enough to beat the count. Combined with a binary result, the bound holds in arbitrary local dimension.
arxiv-2606-22738:
Saber Zerhoudi builds a simulated user who knows AI text is everywhere in this 2026 paper. Most readers assume some content was written, edited, or selected by AI. Hybrid cases are hardest: model-rewritten human prose, AI-curated lists dressed as editorial, retrieval answers composed on the fly. Existing user simulators model none of this checking behavior.

Zerhoudi's simulator, PA-User, adds three components. A detection-effort budget funds verification and recovers between sessions. A trust component tracks belief about each source class's factuality, defined by domain and provenance, updating it from observed outcomes. A decision rule picks accept, verify, or discard for each result given trust, remaining effort, and stakes. On the HC3 corpus of human and ChatGPT answers, its trust-calibration error was about sixteen hundredths, under half the error without that component. It cut high-stakes regret by twenty-nine percent and verified about a third of results.
arxiv-2606-22938:
Stanley Wei and Juno Kim compare two ways of fine-tuning reasoning models in a 2026 theory paper. Supervised fine-tuning copies worked solutions. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards instead grades only the final answer, letting the model find its own routes. Reward-based tuning often wins in practice, but the reason was unclear. The authors model chain-of-thought reasoning as pathfinding on a graph. A reasoning chain must sometimes backtrack out of dead ends to reach the goal.

Wei and Kim prove that supervised training on golden shortest paths never teaches efficient backtracking, since those paths contain no mistakes to recover from. A reward-trained model can learn to backtrack using outcome signals alone. The gap grows exponentially in inference-time computing. Reward training also teaches where the hard choices sit, so effort goes to the right places. Its traces can even teach a fresh model the same skill.
arxiv-2606-23038:
Hongxin Ding and colleagues let grading rubrics evolve during reinforcement learning in a 2026 paper. Open-ended tasks lack checkable answers, so trainers often score output with rubrics, lists of quality criteria. Fixed rubrics age badly. As the policy improves, old criteria stop separating good output from bad, rewards saturate, and models learn to game the checklist. Earlier dynamic rubrics leaned on outside frontier models or known answers. The proposed framework is called EvoRubrics.

Ding and colleagues pair the policy model with a rubric generator that trains alongside it. Each step, the generator sharpens its criteria to stay discriminating, while the policy improves under the fresh guidance. The contest creates an automatic curriculum of rising difficulty. EvoRubrics beat static and dynamic rubric baselines across benchmarks. Its learned generator also transferred as a reward model elsewhere. A fully self-supervised version gained ground with no outside supervision.
arxiv-2606-23338:
Snehanshu Maiti and Rajaraman Ganesh map how flow statistics and particle transport relate in decaying two-dimensional turbulence in a 2026 fluid dynamics paper. Two viewpoints describe a fluid: the Eulerian view watches fixed points in space, while the Lagrangian view follows moving tracer particles. Earlier work at one high Reynolds number showed the initial vorticity packing fraction strongly governs both views together. This paper sweeps a broad parameter space of packing fraction and Reynolds number, which measures how turbulent the flow is.

Maiti and Ganesh find the Eulerian-Lagrangian relationship largely survives during the early inverse-cascade regime. Transport rises steadily with packing fraction and stays mainly under its control, with only secondary wobbles from the Reynolds number. In the late-time regime of coherent vortices, the Eulerian statistics barely respond to Reynolds number at all. The tracer transport, however, tells a more sensitive story in that regime.
arxiv-2606-23438:
Tareq Jaouni, Roohollah Ghobadi, and Ebrahim Karimi sort optical knots with a full-field device in a 2026 optics paper. Optical knots are light fields whose phase or polarization defects trace linked or knotted paths as the beam travels. They could carry high-dimensional information for communication or quantum protocols. That use needs a reader: a device that tells knots apart with little crosstalk. The team demonstrates a proof-of-principle sorter built from one or two optimized phase-only elements. Each input knot is mapped to its own predefined output region.

Jaouni and colleagues optimize the sorter directly on output intensity patterns, rewarding correct assignment and punishing overlap between distinct knots. Their test alphabet holds three knots: the Hopf link, the trefoil, and the cinquefoil. Two phase planes beat one, giving high distinguishability for the alphabet. The sorter also holds up under common experimental imperfections in their benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-23538:
Arya, Mondal, and Roy compute the energies and information measures of tiny electron systems trapped by a Gaussian potential, in a 2026 theoretical chemistry paper. A Gaussian potential is a smooth, round well that mimics a quantum dot, a nanoscale trap used in electronics and photonics. The systems studied range from hydrogen and helium-like ions to lithium and beryllium atoms, all squeezed inside the well.

Working within density functional theory, a method that tracks electron density rather than every electron separately, the team solves the radial equations with a work function based exchange potential. They test two ways of adding electron correlation, the mutual avoidance of electrons. Narrowing the well raises the energy, and deepening it strengthens every effect seen. Measures such as Shannon entropy and Fisher information show the electron cloud localizing and compressing as the trap tightens, with correlation effects weakening in step.
arxiv-2606-23638:
Lee, Hackner, Agterberg, and Brydon propose a new explanation for superconductivity that returns as a magnetic field grows stronger, in a 2026 paper on condensed matter physics. Magnetic fields usually kill superconductivity, the zero resistance state of some materials. In a few materials the field instead revives it, a puzzle called reentrant superconductivity. The known explanations invoke field compensation or field boosted magnetic fluctuations. Neither seems able to explain the striking phase diagram of the uranium compound UTe2.

The authors show analytically that spin orbit coupling, the link between an electron's spin and its motion, can strongly enhance pairing between opposite spins at high fields. The effect works through the two sublattice sites in each unit cell, with no magnetism required. A pairing state of a specific symmetry then reproduces the directional phase diagram of the reentrant state of UTe2.
arxiv-2606-23738:
Bud'ko and colleagues compare leftover magnetization in a superconductor and in hard ferromagnets, in a 2026 paper on condensed matter physics. When a magnetized sample's field is switched off, some signal remains trapped inside, called remanent magnetization. In superconductors this trapped flux is promoted as strong evidence of the state itself, notably for hydrides in diamond anvil cells. Ferromagnets, however, can mimic similar curves, so the signature is contested.

The authors present data on a known BCS superconductor and several hard ferromagnets under matching test setups. They compare several remanent protocols, including a zigzag temperature sweep variant, setting out where the materials resemble each other and where they differ. The comparison aims to sharpen trapped flux tests as a diagnostic for judging claims about new superconductors.
arxiv-2606-23838:
Makinen and colleagues present a method that automatically finds and untangles degeneracies in scientific models, in a 2026 paper on statistical inference. A degeneracy means different settings of a model's dials produce nearly the same data, so the data cannot tell them apart. That makes both prediction and sampling hard. Yet a degeneracy also reveals which combinations of settings the model truly responds to.
