The method works from pairs of settings and simulated data alone. It estimates the Fisher information matrix, a table of how sensitively the data react to each dial, then flattens it. Flattening yields new coordinates, given as explicit formulas, that act independently on the data. On test problems, these coordinates cut the simulation cost of neural posterior estimation by up to tenfold, while also teaching something physical about the system.
arxiv-2606-24938:
Axel Faes, Stéphanie van den Berg, and Maryam Amir Haeri find shared gene programmes in immune data without pooling patient cells. A tensor decomposition of donor by cell type by gene data can reveal multicellular programmes: patterns of gene activity that span cell types and separate sick donors from healthy ones. Privacy rules increasingly block that pooling. Their federated estimator instead leaves the cells at each hospital.

Each site computes a small local subspace that captures its share of the programme. A central merge then stacks these subspaces and combines them, using a global mean centering done across sites. The authors prove the merged result matches the pooled decomposition, up to truncation. On a 261 donor lupus atlas, the method recovers the known interferon programme. Its scores for gene enrichment and for telling cases from controls nearly match the pooled analysis, and no donor level data ever leaves a site.
arxiv-2606-25438:
Polymer flow can also fail in three dimensions, and Sai Peng pins down exactly what must blow up when it does, in a 2026 companion study. For the Oldroyd-B model without stress diffusion on a periodic box, a strong solution can break down in finite time only two ways. Either the logarithmic size of the polymer configuration escapes all bounds, or a time integral of vorticity in an endpoint norm diverges. The proof leans on endpoint estimates linking velocity and rotation, plus high order control of the log configuration.

A second result prices the defects allowed in relaxed solutions. The cheapest conformation residual that can pay for positive pressure free work is set exactly by an entropy linked lever quantity. That cost shrinks toward zero as the configuration nears the identity, a degeneracy Peng quantifies rather than merely notes.
arxiv-2606-25838:
A blurry photo fed to an expensive vision model is money burned: the answer will be garbage and the bill full price. Duy Tran Thanh builds a gatekeeper in 2026, a small classifier that judges one image as sharp, blurred, or uncertain in about seven milliseconds on one CPU core. A search over forty six configurations in eight sweeps selected the recipe. Input resolution proved the dominant lever; model size paid off only above a few hundred pixels. A confidence aware routing rule, grounded in selective prediction theory, decides what passes.

An extra input channel carrying edge strength, the classical clue for blur, lifted the test score by over a point. The final MobileNet recipe scored near ninety eight percent F1 with a tiny deployable file. The author is candid about limits: one blur distribution, one random seed, and calibration judged by eye rather than measured.
arxiv-2606-26238:
Viola Zixin Zhao, Andrés Franco Valiente, and David Limmer show that odd diffusion can exist in three dimensions after all. Odd diffusion drives currents sideways to density gradients, a signature of chiral active matter. Textbook theory ties it to a coefficient that exists only in two dimensions. Isotropic three-dimensional systems seemed excluded. A nonlinear law breaks the impasse.

Symmetry analysis finds the opening. The three-dimensional Levi-Civita tensor allows an odd current, isotropic at second order in the density gradient. Multi-component systems are required for it. Boundary-driven rotational currents, vorticity, and enstrophy follow, all without external torques or preferred directions. A microscopic model grounds the law: particles interacting through nonreciprocal three-body forces produce it under a Dean-Kawasaki coarse-graining. Minimal ingredients for odd transport in ordinary three-dimensional space are now on the table.
arxiv-2606-26338:
Jack Tregidga and colleagues report a spontaneous odd-parity phase in a family of phosphide semiconductors. The materials pair a lanthanide with cadmium and phosphorus, and they host very few charge carriers. Weak screening lets the scarce carriers interact strongly. Odd-parity order, where the electronic state flips sign under inversion, is one exotic outcome such systems can choose. Optical second harmonic generation catches the transition as it happens.

Symmetry breaks on cue. Bulk inversion and rotational symmetry fall together, and an in-plane polar axis appears. Microscopy shows three domain types, rotated copies of each other by a third of a turn. Ultrafast measurements confirm a sharp electronic reconstruction at the transition. Doping decides everything: lightly self-doped members order, while the insulating samarium member does not. A four-band model shows modest interactions suffice to stabilize the phase. Honeycomb bilayer systems join the platform list.
arxiv-2606-26538:
Huzama Ahmad, Cao Viet Hai Nam, and Se-Young Yun ask why the deepest layers of transformer models add so little. Transformers, the standard architecture behind language models, stack identical blocks. The authors propose Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry as the explanation. In common designs, each layer's training gradient sums the direct path plus all paths through later layers. Early layers therefore receive richer gradients than late ones.

Two efficiency methods follow from that account. CascadeFormer narrows the model with depth, matching the uneven flow of information. It matched a uniform baseline's quality at lower latency and higher throughput. CascadeFlow Pruning removes layers using gradients gathered during training, with no later analysis. It beat standard pruning rules on quality and stability. Experiments on models up to just over a billion parameters supported the theory. Equalising gradient sizes did not restore deep layers, pointing to structure, not size, as the bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-26738:
Tim Küchler, Johann-Friedrich Feiden, Matthias Nießner, and Carsten Rother ask whether image editing models truly understand lighting. Modern editors produce stunning images, but plausibility is not physics. Existing tests use curated internet photos or synthetic scenes. The authors instead captured a real-world data set: one thousand image pairs of indoor scenes where light probes were physically switched on and off.

Specific regions such as cast shadows and metal surfaces were annotated. Models were asked to perform the same light edits, and two new scores measured agreement with reality. The scores allow for photographic side effects like white balance shifts. Model performance differed considerably overall. Differences narrowed slightly for specular highlights, the bright reflections on shiny surfaces. The best models matched real physics remarkably well, though clear room for improvement remains.
arxiv-2606-26838:
Ariane Giesriegl and six colleagues investigate why thin silicon nitride membranes lose energy, limiting sensitive mechanical sensors. Such membranes are prized for sensing, quantum work, and physics tests. As they shrink toward nanoscale thickness, surface effects dominate their losses. The team suspected the surface chemistry, in particular hydroxyl groups, chemical units of oxygen and hydrogen bonded to the surface.

A thin native oxide layer, one to two nanometres thick, was found on the membranes. Acid etching stripped that layer away. A silanisation treatment then attached water-repelling groups to the surface. A battery of surface probes tracked each change. Mechanical quality factors, measures of how long a vibration rings, were measured at each stage. The results support surface hydroxyl groups as a key driver of the loss.
arxiv-2606-27038:
Kozyreff and King question a routine step in perturbation methods, which solve hard equations by treating a small effect as a gentle correction. The multiple-scales method splits time into a fast beat and a slow drift, then treats them as separate variables. The authors test how sound that split is using Van der Pol's equation, a classic oscillator with a Hopf bifurcation. Their 2026 analysis pushes the expansion to very high order.

Carrying the series far out shows it eventually diverges, so the team uses optimal truncation, stopping just before terms grow again. That step reconnects the two scales. A starting shift of the fast beat creates a tiny phase shift that shrinks exponentially with the small parameter. Crucially, that shift depends on the slow drift, so the scales are not truly separate. Computer simulations confirm both the shift and its predicted size.
arxiv-2606-27138:
Hu and colleagues pin down the Go programming language's trickiest corner: generics mixed with structural subtyping. Go interfaces match by structure, not by name, unlike Java-style nominal typing. Runtime values also come in two forms, raw structs and interface values carrying type information. Earlier formal models left out underlying types, unions, and type sets. Their Welterweight Go core model captures those features plus proposed generic methods, in an extended version appearing in 2026.

A second, lower-level language models Go's runtime machinery directly. Type-directed compilation from the core model down to that runtime language shows the features can be implemented faithfully. Separate compilation stays compatible, and no code is generated at runtime. Instead of copying code per type, the strategy uses runtime conversions and adaptor methods. That handles the tangled interplay between structure matching, generics, and runtime type data. Language designers gain a tested blueprint for future Go extensions.
arxiv-2606-27438:
Dai, Bader, and Gysi fold the new breed of time series foundation models into Darts, the open-source forecasting library they help maintain. Foundation models promise zero-shot forecasting: pre-trained once, applied to unseen series without retraining. In practice each arrives as an isolated package with its own interface, blocking joint evaluation and pipeline integration. Their unified FoundationModel class collection standardises several leading models behind one full-cycle interface. Existing Darts pipelines can swap one in by changing little more than a model name in this software paper from 2026.

Zero-shot and fine-tuned forecasting, uncertainty estimation, and backtesting all flow through the same framework. Data processing and evaluation tooling from the library come along for free. External dependencies stay minimal, easing installation pain. The work targets the fragmentation that kept foundation models as demos rather than daily tools.
arxiv-2606-27738:
Text prompts are a weak way to specify a three-dimensional object. They say little about where parts go or how parts relate. Jialin Huang and three colleagues present HandMade in 2026 to give users a spatial channel. HandMade combines virtual-reality sketching with language. Coarse sketches drawn in VR carry part labels. The sketches act as spatial prompts for existing generative models, not as geometry to rebuild directly.

Segmented VR strokes become multi-view part guidance and structured prompts. Users sketch layout and part relations in 3D. Language still names identity, material, style, and local detail. A technical evaluation used twenty varied examples. HandMade preserved user-authored spatial scaffolds better than text-only and sketch-based baselines. A user study with eight participants added detail. People used sketching for layout and language for identity and materials, both when authoring and when revising. The workflow tolerates noisy, incomplete sketches.
arxiv-2606-27938:
Problem-solving competence matters for high school students. Generative AI can support its development. It can also let students offload the mental work that deep learning needs. Lorenzo Betti and ten colleagues study the group-level effects in 2026. A computer model simulates a high school physics classroom. Students work alone, with peers, or with AI support. The peer network takes several forms.

Classrooms with and without AI access are compared across network structures. AI use can slow the growth of competence. It also raises the share of students stuck in lower competence tiers. The effect runs through the classroom as a whole. Looking only at individual outcomes misses it. The authors argue the impact of AI in schools should be judged at group level too. How competence spreads through a class is the right thing to watch. The findings speak to how AI tools should be built into lessons.
arxiv-2606-28038:
Xin Zheng and six colleagues report an on-chip Half Maxwell Fisheye lens in 2026 for silicon photonics. The lens works at telecom wavelengths. It is built as a graded photonic crystal in a non-resonant regime. 3D simulations show excellent broadband focusing. The device was fabricated on a silicon-on-insulator platform, keeping CMOS compatibility.

Two experiments test the lens. Output waveguides probe the focusing first. Scanning near-field microscopy then images the wavefront inside the lens, confirming its curving and the focus. Measured focal width matches simulation closely. The full width at half maximum is about zero point four seven of the wavelength at 1550 nanometres. The lens itself is only about three point two wavelengths thick. Operation across the 1450 to 1590 nanometre range is confirmed. Because the regime is non-resonant, longer wavelengths should also work.
arxiv-2606-28438:
Xinyuan Song, Zekun Cai, and Liang Zhao study what happens when code models train on their own output. Generated code floods real repositories, later becomes training data, and closes a self-training loop. Human review once broke that loop, but artificial intelligence now writes code faster than people can check it, and increasingly reviews it too.

Song and colleagues compare recursive fine-tuning under three regimes: no review, human-style gates using independent checks such as compilation, and self-gates where the model scores its own code. No review collapsed fastest. Independent gates slowed collapse without stopping it. Self-gates looked strong early, then decayed into a rubber-stamp regime where acceptance rose while correctness fell. Their analysis shows self-gating degenerates into ungated self-training, so stable recursion needs outside verification.
arxiv-2606-28538:
Dominik Stammbach and Peter Henderson give a modern language model a legal education. ModernBERT already trained on vastly more text than the original BERT, so it was fair to ask whether old-fashioned domain adaptation still helps. The team further pretrained it on the full corpus of United States court opinions, using the standard masked-word objective.

Adaptation helped clearly: the legal-tuned model beat its vanilla parent significantly on every dataset tied to court opinions, with gains resembling those from the early domain-adaptation literature. Training a model from scratch on legal text alone, by contrast, could not match continuing from the existing checkpoint. The released models handle passages up to eight thousand tokens, embed legal text meaningfully, and can rerank hundreds of passages per query, practical tools the authors publish openly.
arxiv-2606-28638:
T. Luo, C. Sun, J. De Chant, and A. Zabala extend a classic trick for beam position monitors, the pickups that report where a particle beam passes inside an accelerator. Faulty pickup buttons shift the electrical center away from the mechanical one, and the Lambertson method measures that offset indirectly, but only for monitors that mirror both left-right and up-down.

Many modern monitors do not mirror left-right. Luo and colleagues extend the Lambertson construction to that lopsided case. They derive the extension and put it to work on the lopsided monitors of the ALS Upgrade project at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The paper is a compact methods note: classical geometry, one mirror assumption removed, and a direct use on a real machine being rebuilt.
arxiv-2606-28738:
Schwob and Datta tackle a stubborn statistics problem: data that are shares of a whole, such as microbe mixes, where many parts are exactly zero. Such compositional data, meaning values that must sum to one, also hide links between parts and can involve hundreds of parts at once. Older models either force a rigid pattern of links or break down when zeros appear.

Their answer is the ARC framework, which treats a composition as a direction pointing from an unseen abundance vector whose size is unknown. A separate active-set step decides which parts are present, and the present parts are then modelled along positive rays, meaning lines outward from zero. This split keeps exact zeros, allows any pattern of shared response between parts, and stays workable when dimensions grow large.
arxiv-2606-28838:
Roth develops a formal picture in which the cells of a living body act as one coherent classical system, and ageing is what happens when that coherence fades. Coherence here means the cells share a common code that holds the organism's identity together. He writes the whole many-cell system as one state vector in an abstract code space, borrowing quantum theory's bra-ket notation just as compact bookkeeping.

A Biological Hamiltonian, an energy-like rule built from genetic codes and their spread across cells, anchors the identity in DNA sequence space. An operator with code-correcting and code-breaking parts then tracks repair against damage over time. As repair weakens and damage grows, Roth's model has the identity state grow unstable, and death appears as a sudden collapse of coherence. He points to testable signs, such as losing restoration capacity late in life.
arxiv-2606-28938:
Liu, Chen, Wang, Zhang and Zhao build EVLA, a driving assistant that knows the state of the electric car it rides in. Most vision-language driving assistants treat the vehicle as a black box, deciding without any sense of motor torque or battery charge. EVLA fuses camera views, language instructions and live powertrain data into one shared representation. A unified encoder does this, adding a field that models the energy cost of each part of the scene.

A structured reasoning chain then grounds decisions in physical constraints and energy goals. On a driving question benchmark, EVLA beat strong fine-tuned baselines, raising accuracy by 5.6 percent. Removing any component hurt results in ablation tests. The system answered about a third faster than multi-stage pipelines. That supports the claim that vehicle awareness improves driving decisions.
arxiv-2606-29438:
Han and Xu develop fractional stochastic neural networks, whose hidden dynamics follow residual links driven by fractional Brownian motion. That noise process has long memory, meaning distant past values still shape the present, unlike ordinary Brownian motion. Such memory suits some time series and noisy signals. The authors want training rules and guarantees that respect this fractional driver.

They present a discrete-time stochastic maximum principle for the network, which yields a matching adjoint recursion, a backward pass that computes gradients. For fixed parameters, they prove that projected samplewise stochastic gradient descent converges in mean square. Tests cover a closed-form convergence check, noisy regression with uncertainty estimates, and long memory time series generation. Image classification under structured noise is also tested. Results identify settings where the fractional driver improves long memory recovery or robustness over Brownian and plain baselines, rather than helping everywhere.
arxiv-2606-29538:
Fan and colleagues at Microsoft present Resource2Skill, a framework that turns human-made learning materials into executable skills for software agents. Skills package experience as reusable procedural knowledge. Most existing skill libraries are hand-written, text-only, or mined from agent traces. Tutorial videos and other multimodal resources, which mix text, code, and images, stay unused.

Resource2Skill distils videos, repositories, articles, and reference artifacts into a hierarchical Skill Wiki. Each entry packs structured text, code, and visual examples together with metadata and provenance, a record of where it came from. Videos contribute timing and visual effects, code contributes tool patterns, and articles contribute concepts and style. At work time, agents retrieve and compose the skills they need. When coverage falls short, the construction process picks up new skills online. In tests across seven authoring domains, scores rise by about twelve points over agents with no skills.
arxiv-2606-29638:
Cheng and six colleagues tackle noise characterization for multi-qubit gates, a bottleneck for quantum error work. Cycle benchmarking, a standard technique, isolates some Pauli error parts. It cannot resolve coupled error parameters, leaving unlearnable degrees of freedom even in simple gates, and worse in general Clifford gates.

Their generalized cycle benchmarking adds mid-circuit measurements, checks performed partway through a circuit, plus classical analysis. That makes previously hidden Pauli fidelities and non-Markovian noise learnable. Using deferred feed-forward, they show that inserted measurements can undo Pauli cycles induced by a general Clifford gate. A learnability condition for Clifford gates follows. Numerical work shows the method works, and the team runs the protocol on superconducting quantum processors. Results confirm it against standard tomography.
arxiv-2606-29838:
Majumdar and four colleagues model a microscopic heat engine. It is a tiny particle held in a trap, touching an ordinary thermal bath and an active bath. The active bath kicks it with random shot noise, bursts arriving at random times like raindrops.

The system can act as a hybrid machine, working as an engine for one pair of baths and as a refrigerator for the other. Judged naively, its work per unit of heat taken from the cold baths can pass the Carnot efficiency, the classic limit for heat engines. The authors define a proper efficiency that also charges for how distinguishable the engine's statistics are from equilibrium. This proper efficiency respects the Carnot bound. They find shot rates that maximise efficiency and a non-one-to-one link between efficiency and the shape of the particle's position spread.
arxiv-2606-29938:
Guo and four colleagues address a bottleneck in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, training language models on tasks with checkable answers. On the hardest prompts the model almost never samples a correct attempt, so training gets no useful signal, a case the authors call a zero-hit prompt.

Their method, LatentRevise, learns from the failed attempts instead. Given a failed attempt and the gold answer, it adjusts the model's internal representation of the reasoning so far, pushing it away from the failed path and toward the answer. The update stays within the hull of real word embeddings. Continuations from the revised starting point grow longer, show self-reflection, and reach correct answers the original attempts missed. Used as training data, they improve both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning on maths benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-30338:
Ioannis Pitsiorlas, Martha Sourla, and Marios Kountouris give external auditors a statistical method for checking AI fairness while evidence is still arriving. Regulators increasingly demand proof that deployed systems treat groups fairly. Independent auditors usually see only model outputs through queries. Fixed-sample tests fit that setting poorly. Their framework makes auditing sequential and tolerance-aware.

Auditors accumulate evidence from a finite pool of test cases. A sequential generalized likelihood-ratio test tracks the accumulating evidence. Auditing stops once compliance or violation has sufficient support. The method covers decision-based statistical parity and equal opportunity audits. Score and logit based proxy audits extend it when richer outputs exist. Fairness metric choice strongly affects audit efficiency, they find. Richer outputs cut query counts substantially in some regimes. Near decision thresholds, those gains shrink to almost nothing.
arxiv-2606-30438:
Wolf Cukier and five colleagues release a Python tool for simulating clouds in the atmospheres of planets beyond our solar system. Cloud particles shape what telescopes infer about exoplanets. Their sizes and formation rates need first-principles modeling. The code, CARMApy, wraps a battle-tested Fortran predecessor. That lineage stretches back almost half a century. The new package makes the model accessible to Python users.

Microphysical processes include nucleation, growth, evaporation, and coagulation. Vertical transport of particles is modeled as well. Ten condensates come built in for users. Custom condensates can be specified on top of those. The paper documents the theory behind the classic model fully. Benchmarks compare CARMApy against earlier CARMA versions. Results agree with the previous versions' outputs. Speed improves about twofold single-threaded and nearly fourfold multithreaded. Data products the code can generate are described in detail.
arxiv-2606-30538:
Jorge Ibáñez-Marcos, Monika Ludwig, Pedro Tradacete and Ignacio Villanueva classify a family of measurements in convex geometry. A valuation assigns values to shapes so that overlapping pieces combine by a fixed addition rule. Here the shapes are star bodies, forms visible from one centre point, and the values are measures rather than single numbers. Earlier work by Hadwiger and Schneider classified such valuations on convex bodies.

The four authors establish a complete classification for weak-star continuous, measure-valued valuations on star bodies. Two consequences follow from their result. First, they give an integral representation for rotation equivariant valuations, those that rotate along with the shape. Second, they characterise dual area measures, a standard tool in the dual Brunn-Minkowski theory of star bodies. The classification extends the known scalar-valued results for this shape class.
arxiv-2606-30638:
Jameel Hassan, Yasiru Ranasinghe and Vishal Patel give 3D scenes a language interface without heavy feature training. The scenes are built with 3D Gaussian Splatting, which represents a scene as clouds of soft 3D blobs that render fast. Prior language extensions distilled CLIP features, bulky image-text embeddings, into every blob. That limited queries to simple noun phrases and made instance grouping noisy or preset.

GaussDet instead leans on 2D detectors that already answer open-vocabulary and referring queries, such as the red chair by the door. It learns features that split Gaussians into 3D instance groups. Each group is rendered from many views, and 2D detections vote on its label, forming a view-aggregated label distribution per instance. This voting smooths out bad labels from imperfect grouping. In strict zero-shot tests, referring-expression grounding improved by a wide margin over prior methods.
arxiv-2606-31438:
Venanzi and colleagues present a free-space plasmonic modulator that works in the mid-infrared with a single doped semiconductor layer. Modulators in this band matter for sensing and communications, yet simple fast designs are scarce. Their device tunes light just below the semiconductor's plasma frequency, where its mirror behaviour turns sensitive.

A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect structure drives the tuning. Metal grating patches and the doped layer form cavities, the gate oxide spaces them, and gate voltage shifts the free-electron density right where the resonant near-field sits. The team show electric control of linear transmittance and reflectance and of third-harmonic generation, a nonlinear mixing effect. They chart routes to faster, deeper modulation with very simple active material needs.
arxiv-2606-31838:
McAsey and three colleagues ask how to design interactions so addressable self-assembly reaches the highest yield in a given time. Each distinct building block must land in one specific place in a target structure. Yield suffers from monomer depletion: too many partial structures nucleate at once, exhaust the blocks, and trap the system in fragments.

Reaction equations for all intermediate steps, paired with numerical optimization, reveal a sharp pattern. Optimal designs make every bond either very strong or very weak. The strong bonds form a spanning tree of the target, a connected network with no loops. The authors prove depletion cannot occur under a spanning tree, since assembly can always proceed downhill in energy without kinetic traps.
arxiv-2606-32038:
Guo and three others ask when training a language model to explain its own outputs gives genuine introspection rather than polished imitation. Their supervision comes from counterfactual conduct: which input features change the model's output when changed. Standard practice trains on explanations derived from an earlier checkpoint, even though the model's conduct drifts during that very training.

Explanations still track the model's current conduct more closely than the conduct they were trained on, a pattern the authors call introspective coupling. It appears when training explanations stay close enough in line with present conduct while conduct itself shifts. Coupling persists across tasks including sycophancy and refusal, survives label noise, and follows conduct changes induced by concurrent training objectives. Fixed explanation datasets can thus supply scalable signal for introspection.
arxiv-2608-00138: Vibrational spectroscopy identifies the bond asymmetry of hexagonal diamond, arXiv 2608-00138. The diamond bonds. It stands as a research record. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
arxiv-2608-00438: Homogenization of Viscous Sublinear Hamilton-Jacobi Equations, arXiv 2608-00438. The HJ homogenization. The paper endures in the archive. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol4-18:
Volume four of Audubon's Ornithological Biography appeared in 1838. The five volume work forms the written companion to The Birds of America. Audubon presses on with accounts of American birds in their wild homes. His method joins the gun, the sketchbook, and long hours of watching.

Each account gives a bird's looks, voice, food, and breeding habits. Stories from his journeys through forests and along coasts fill the gaps between species. The record reflects decades spent crossing a continent rich in bird life. Volume four nears the end of the set. Its observations still feed the study of American birds. Audubon's firsthand detail is the draw.
becher-physica-subterranea-1738:
Johann Joachim Becher's Physica Subterranea appears here in Georg Ernst Stahl's 1738 edition. Becher, a German physician and adviser on trade, wrote on what lies beneath the earth. Stahl, who edited and praised the work, built his own theory of burning on Becher's ideas.

Becher sorted earths and minerals and argued that one kind of earth, fatty and dry, made bodies able to burn. That idea grew into the phlogiston theory, which ruled chemistry for much of the next century. The book also ranges over mines, metals, and fossils. It is a founding text for a theory that later chemistry would test and then discard.
cia-0000008638:
Two American prisoners of war were observed at a school on Bo Song Street in Hanoi, a CIA item from June 1968 reports. Hanoi held the best-known prisons of the war, yet captives also surfaced at odd, everyday sites in the capital. A school sighting suggests prisoners moved or shown in public view.

Observers' reports from inside the enemy capital were rare and hard to check. Analysts compared each detail with known prisoner lists and earlier sightings. Even a street name could matter when so little was certain. The file adds a precise urban detail to the record of captivity in Hanoi.
cia-0000013238:
Organization and activities of the Viet Cong military and prisoner of war detention system are mapped in a CIA paper from May 1971. The paper traces how the southern enemy was built. It follows the regions, their commands, and their campaigns across the south. It also follows the detention arm that held American and allied prisoners. That arm sat inside the larger machine, and the paper shows exactly where.

Understanding the enemy's organization was the first step toward dismantling it. This paper tried at the level of structure rather than incident. For readers, it is the deep dive: the southern apparatus drawn whole, camps included.
cia-0000015338: Flying Saucers is again the title of a CIA file dated June 2, 1952. The source note says the publication date is unknown. June 1952 stood at the edge of the great summer wave of sightings. A bare title from that month needs no gloss; the whole country was looking up. The Central Intelligence Agency file sits in the Reading Room.
cia-0000022338: Commentary on the Powers trial fills a CIA record dated July 2, 1960. Trial commentary in that summer's press mixed law, politics, and theater in one stream. The agency collected it to track how the Moscow case was playing abroad. A second commentary entry sits near this one in the file, showing how much print the trial drew in a matter of weeks.
cia-0000023238: An American was sighted working with the Viet Cong in Dai Loc District, a CIA record dated in 1972 reports. The district lay in Quang Nam country, south of Da Nang, though the clipped title cuts the province name. Working with could mean many things under duress, and the title does not settle it. The report was kept for checking, not for judgment.
cia-0000044038:
Cristiani condemned the killing of the Jesuits and ordered an investigation, a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog reports. The title ties his words to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Condemnation and an inquiry were the least a president could offer.

Inside, the president's public response to the murders is preserved. His words were weighed for sincerity in every capital that heard them. An order to investigate costs little until it names the guilty. The file holds the promise at its first making, before the long argument over whether the promise was ever honestly kept by his government.
cia-0000045238:
The kidnapping negotiations had become complicated, in a CIA record dated September 6, 1985. Complicated was the word officials used when talks snarled. New demands, new voices, and old hatreds all tangled the case.

Inside, the tangles in the Duarte talks are traced for the record. Each complication cost days, and days cost the captive most of all. They also cost the government credit with an impatient country. A public that hears only of tangles begins to doubt the men untangling them. The file maps that snarled stage of the case, in which the path to a release that had seemed straight kept bending out of sight.
cia-0000046638: An updated status report on the search for American servicemen missing in Southeast Asia reached the files on January 6, 1992. The report belonged to the slow accounting that followed the Vietnam War, case by case and name by name. Items like this one measured what the search had settled, and what it had not.
cia-0000098738: Microelectronics Component Symposium Exhibits New Products is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098738, dated January 3, 1990. The title reports a symposium showing new components. Readers find a short declassified exhibit record from technology watching, companion to the Leipzig Fair item, both tracking displayed electronics rather than testing or policy decisions. Readers meet the record through its catalog heading and date.
cia-0000102938: Soviet Prison Labor Practices, with dates of information 1971 to 1982, are reviewed in declassified CIA document 0000102938, dated October 1, 1982. The title claims the widest span in the cluster, eleven years. The brief file is a practices review in name, the broadest heading among the many single-project labor records around it. Readers meet the record through its catalog heading and date.
cia-0000112338: Take 1 of 2 -- Foreign Press Note--fb Pn 91-003--USSR is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112338, dated January 6, 1991. The title marks the first of two takes of a foreign press note on the USSR. Its code, FB PN 91-003, sits inside the heading itself. The brief record is a press note installment from the Soviet Union's final year.
cia-0000112838: Robert Donald Chisholm - Treason is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112838, dated September 2, 1946. The title pairs a full name and a grave charge: Robert Donald Chisholm, treason. Treason is a heavier word than the espionage labels around it in the files. The brief record is a name and charge file from 1946 as released there.
cia-0000119738: A CIA report gives the Hungarian situation as of 1 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time during the 1956 crisis. The overnight watch ran around the clock that autumn, and this paper preserves the picture filed before sunrise in Washington. The choice of Eastern Daylight Time in the heading places the paper in the war-room rhythm of Washington rather than the local time of Budapest.
cia-0000124338: Dated around July 1952, this CIA document is filed under the heading Military: Biological Warfare, Atomic Weapons. In the early 1950s, such weapons were moving toward the center of war planning on both sides. The paper preserves the file under that label as released. A heading joining germ and atomic weapons in one file shows how new the categories still were, filed together while doctrine for each was still forming.
cia-0000132238: Situation Report 555 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series, dated January 6, 1991, takes up a blunt question: where is Saddam? The Iraqi leader's whereabouts were unknown when the report was filed. Analysts still had to assume that a hidden Saddam remained in command of his country and his forces. The short report follows that open question at the height of the Gulf crisis.
cia-0000132338: Three regions share one CIA briefing for the National Security Council, dated May 2, 1959. The agenda covers the Caribbean, Argentina, and Iraq in a single sitting. Each area carried its own crisis that spring. The short briefing shows the global spread of problems reaching the president's top advisers at once, from Havana to Buenos Aires to Baghdad.
cia-0000132638: Nicaragua cutting its ties with Cuba fills a CIA paper dated May 6, 1960. The freeze-out of Havana was starting, one capital at a time, that spring. The Somoza government was among the first in the region to break with Castro. The short paper records the break and the steps that led up to it.
cia-0000132738: Four fronts share a CIA item on Cuba dated March 4, 1961. The item covers an anti-Castro group, foreign contacts, the economy, and Cuba at the United Nations. It stands beside a three-front roundup from the same month in the file. Four strands of the Cuba story were moving at once that spring. The short item takes each one in turn.
cia-0000135738: Spanish-language papers of the 2506 Brigade fill a CIA record dated February 3, 1961. Its record line misspells estimated as estmated, a slip kept from the original. Of the three brigade text files in the set, this one is the latest by date. The landing in Cuba was about two months away. The record keeps the Spanish text as it was filed.
cia-0000135838: Central American Situation, dated 4 September 1952, is a declassified CIA paper surveying the region as a whole. The early 1950s were tense years in Central America, with reform governments and their opponents drawing close attention from Washington. The catalog title is broad and names no single country or crisis, so the paper is best described as a regional situation report of its date. It was written two years before the 1954 Guatemala coup reshaped the region's politics, and it now reads as a baseline from before that break.
cia-0000136138: The CIA cable of 2 April 1954 is about destroying rail targets, cutting the lines that moved the government's troops and goods, and it survives in declassified form. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136338: Proceed with the present plan, LINCOLN advises in this late June 1954 cable, while admitting it is not optimistic about forthcoming peace talks. The station has no confidence in the enemy junta's sincerity and notes 6,000 tons of arms in enemy hands. Circumstances permitting, it would push back the Beta H-hour to ensure a vessel arrives to serve as floating artillery and communications center, with signal plans prepared for both vessels.
cia-0000136638: Dated 2 February 1961, this Spanish-language document comes from the declassified records of Brigade 2506. The brigade's own paperwork was kept in Spanish, the language of its members. That winter the force was training for the landing in Cuba. The catalog names no subject for this item. It is held in the original Spanish through the CIA Reading Room, a dated piece of the exile archive.
cia-0000136738: Another Spanish text in the 2506 Brigade papers carries an estimated date of 1 January 1961, the estimate noted in the catalog. The brigade was then in winter training for Cuba under CIA direction. The record names no subject for this item. cia-0000136938: Eight fighter planes at about 25,000 dollars each are on offer in this April 1954 cable to LINCOLN, signed under Frank Wisner.
