Their accounts were grouped into themes.

Three themes stood out. First, chronic pain is an invisible disability that firms underestimate. Second, line managers differ widely in how well they support affected staff. Third, control over adjustments is contested between employer and worker. Stakeholders wanted the toolkit. They wanted manager training just as much. The authors say better-equipped managers could cut sickness absence. They could also ease the strain of working while unwell.
plos-pone-0352138:
Chen and colleagues, in a 2026 study, settle an argument about concrete made with steel slag, a waste product of steelmaking, in place of crushed stone. Builders like the idea of recycling slag, but whether the swap makes concrete stronger, and which swap works best, was disputed. The team cast four versions and broke them in the lab.

The four mixes used plain stone, coarse slag with natural sand, stone with fine slag, and slag for both coarse and fine parts. In squeezing, bending, and splitting tests, every slag version beat plain concrete, and the all-slag mix was strongest. Fine slag helped more than coarse slag, and microscope and X-ray checks showed why the inner structure differed. The authors caution that their conditions were specific, yet under them, grinding slag fine and using it widely looks like the best recipe for stronger concrete from waste.
plos-pone-0352238:
Yuxuan Qian and six colleagues report a 2026 plant study on a rice gene moved into lettuce. The gene helps rice absorb nitrate, a key form of nitrogen fertiliser. Lettuce often wastes nitrogen, so the team tested whether the gene helps when nitrogen is scarce. Four high-expressing lettuce lines were grown under normal and low nitrogen.

The engineered lettuce held more chlorophyll and more glutathione, a protective molecule. Its defence enzymes against oxidative damage also worked harder. Inside the leaves, nitrate, ammonium, amino acids, and soluble protein all rose. Enzymes that process nitrogen became more active too. Plant size barely changed, though. The gene mainly improved internal chemistry and nitrogen use, which could help growers cut fertiliser without losing crop quality.
plos-pone-0352438:
Gao and colleagues tested when to move young maize plants into fields in a 2026 study. Growers sometimes raise seedlings first and plant them out to fill gaps, but moving plants can stress them and cut the harvest. Field trials at two sites compared direct seeding with planting out at three young leaf stages.

Moved plants grew smaller roots and leaves than direct-seeded plants and lost yield in the end. Stress showed up in lower leaf efficiency, even though the plants used water more tightly. Moving plants at the middle stage, with three leaves and one heart leaf, came closest to direct seeding. That timing offers the least loss when replanting cannot be avoided.
plos-pone-0352638:
Chen and colleagues studied how to protect glazed parts of ancient Chinese buildings in a 2026 paper. Glazed tiles crown roofs and walls but crack and powder after long exposure to heat, damp, and acid air. The team documented decay forms and reproduced damage processes in the lab.

Two strengthening liquids were tested on weakened tile bodies, applied with an alcohol solvent. The goal is a treatment that firms the tile without changing its look. Heritage repairs fail when coatings peel or gloss clashes with old glaze. Careful material matching, shown here, helps restorers keep historic roofs both sound and authentic.
plos-pone-0352938:
Zarmeen Nasim and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One analysis of dengue fever in Pakistan from 2012 to 2022. They used lab-confirmed cases. They adjusted the counts for how likely people are to seek care and be tested. The team estimated rates by province, district, age, and sex. The aim was to fill gaps left by under-reporting and uneven diagnosis.

Dengue rates climbed over the decade in every age group. Working-age adults carried the highest rates. Men were hit more than women throughout. Sindh province stood out with by far the highest rates in 2022. Baluchistan had the lowest. The authors say the widening, uneven burden demands stronger mosquito control. It also demands better case counting, since official figures miss much of the disease.
plos-pone-0353738:
Christina Due Svendsen and four colleagues test a microbial hunch. Do the microbes in the mouth and lungs differ in people with heart disease? Their study came from Norway. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group had one hundred and twenty-seven patients with chronic lung disease. It also had one hundred and one healthy controls. All had heart scans to grade artery calcium and narrowing. All gave mouth rinses and lung washings for DNA sequencing.

Microbe communities did differ between lung patients and controls. The gap showed in the mouth samples. But people with and without coronary disease looked alike. No meaningful differences appeared in either site. The negative result argues against a simple airway signature of heart disease. At least, none that current methods can find.
plos-pone-0353838:
Lan Zhang led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study linking body-clock disruption to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a long-term lung illness. They merged several public lung data sets, screened clock-related genes that change in the disease, and let machine learning pick the strongest candidates. They then checked the winner in another cohort and in single cells.

One gene, CHRNA1, rose consistently and tracked with inflammatory immune cells, mostly in the lung's B cells. Zhang built a risk model around such signals, while noting the clock-targeting idea still needs testing in patients before clinical use.
plos-pone-0353938:
Mahoukpégo Luc Zinzinhédo and co-authors stress-test crop yield prediction models by feeding them thousands of deliberately flawed datasets. Real farm data arrive with gaps and tangled measures, and advice on cleaning them is scattered. The simulation varied dataset size, predictor count, missing values, and overlap among predictors, crossed with cleaning choices, across seven learning methods, then repeated the checks on five real crop datasets.

Missing data hurt accuracy badly, tangled predictors faked one kind of score while worsening another, and bigger datasets reliably helped. Filling gaps by regression worked best overall, and one forest method stayed steadiest across conditions. Zinzinhédo and colleagues warn that no cleaning recipe wins everywhere, so modelers must match preparation to the dataset in hand.
plos-pone-0354038:
Alina Maryum and seven colleagues build a cheap machine-learning screen for osteoporosis, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study aimed at clinics with few resources. The standard bone scan is costly and often unavailable where patients are poorest. Instead, their model uses records from two Pakistani hospitals and leans on simple inputs: blood group, blood calcium and potassium, weight, and vitamin D levels.

An ensemble of classifiers sorted patients by osteoporosis severity with accuracy around nine in ten. A second model estimated spine bone density moderately well from age, weight, blood group, and vitamin D. If confirmed in larger samples, screening from routine blood tests could flag at-risk patients long before a fracture.
plos-pone-0354138:
Shupeng Wu and three colleagues published this 2026 computer study of bisphenol A, a common plastics chemical, and myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease that weakens muscles. Genes tied to the chemical and to the disease were gathered from public databases, overlapped, and screened with machine learning, then checked with molecular simulations and experiments.

Three genes emerged as plausible links, touching ion transport, nerve-muscle signaling, and immune activation. Wu stresses the evidence shows links, not causes, built mostly in computers, but it sketches how an everyday chemical might nudge a rare disease process.
plos-pone-0354238:
Clément Gouraud and co-authors ask in 2026 whether long COVID patients who also receive a functional somatic disorder diagnosis report worse quality of life. Data came from a specialist programme for people with lasting symptoms after COVID, using a standard health survey that gives physical and mental scores. Most patients in the sample carried the extra diagnosis.

Quality of life was clearly impaired overall, yet scores did not differ by the extra diagnosis once other factors were counted. Lower scores linked instead to depression, anxiety, pain, and low activity, with physical scores also tied to sex, hospital stay, and symptom length. Care should target those drivers, the authors suggest.
plos-pone-0354338:
Hazem Aqel is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE study of a natural wastewater treatment system in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Nature-based systems support water reuse in dry regions, but how well they remove living, disease-capable bacteria was unclear. The team sampled water at five stages of a plant fed with treated wastewater.

Total culturable bacteria fell across the system, and species variety dropped by about half. The fecal indicator E. coli vanished from later stages. Yet Klebsiella pneumoniae, an opportunistic pathogen, survived all five stages, and most of its isolates resisted many drugs. Cloudiness of the water tracked bacterial variety. Indicator tests alone, the authors warn, can miss such lingering risks.
plos-pone-0354738:
Massae and colleagues, writing in 2026, ask why vacuum-assisted birth is so seldom used at a large hospital in Tanzania. A vacuum device can help deliver a baby when the last stage of labor stalls, the mother is worn out, or the baby is in distress. When it is not used, more births end in surgery that might have been avoided.

The team spoke in depth with twelve clinicians who had experience with the method. Two kinds of blocks came up. At the hospital level, gear was scarce, some devices worked poorly, and team choices were not well coordinated. At the personal level, clinicians feared bad outcomes and felt short on skill and hands-on practice. The authors argue that working gear, better training, and stronger team routines could raise use and cut needless surgical births.
plos-pone-0355238:
Parveen Kumari and a large team compared three ways of teaching a computer to hear emotion in speech. Each way was tested under two rules. Under the easy rule, the same actors appear in training and testing. Under the honest rule, test voices are strangers. Their 2026 study used a standard acted emotion corpus. It combined handcrafted sound features with deep network embeddings in a lightweight hybrid.

The hybrid won under both rules. Every method lost ground when voices changed, exposing how inflated easy-split scores are. The team's real contribution is discipline. It used identical preprocessing, repeated runs, and class-by-class error audits. A small web tool lets readers try the model live. Speech emotion systems headed for call centers and tutoring need exactly this kind of honest benchmarking.
plos-pone-0355338:
Jun Tamura and colleagues compare electrodes for body composition testing in dogs in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Multifrequency bioimpedance sends weak currents through the body to estimate fluid spread and cell traits. Reports in dogs are few, so the team tested clip against needle electrodes in seven anesthetized beagles.

Measurements at three frequencies were feasible in every position and path, with low repeat variation within each dog. Clip and needle readings agreed closely on average for most measures. At the lowest frequency, though, two measures correlated weakly and ranged wider, so the types are not fully interchangeable. Body position also shifted some readings. Standardizing setup matters for tracking dogs over time.
plos-pone-0355738:
Gabriel Bertochi and co-authors test in 2026 whether heavy or explosive warm up moves boost a standing jump a few minutes later, and whether men and women differ. Trained adults tried six preparation moves across separate visits, including squats and drop jumps, some with a weighted vest. Jump height was measured before and four minutes after each move.

No preparation clearly raised jump height in that window, for the whole group or for either sex alone. The authors suggest the boost may be tiny after a full warm up already done, and coaches should weigh personal traits rather than expect a set gain. Sex showed no effect on the result.
plos-pone-0355838:
Piyanut Ratphibun Yamashita and co-authors built personal computer models to judge breast cancer risk from gene activity plus cell signalling. Standard risk tools ignore molecular detail, which limits personal prevention advice. Their 2026 framework merged each woman's gene profile with a dynamic simulation of signalling pathways for thirty subjects.

Features drawn from the simulations split the women into four risk clusters with clearly different cancer-free spans. The highest-risk group stayed cancer-free for the shortest time, by a wide margin. Its signature was overactive growth signalling through a well-known pathway chain. Yamashita and colleagues say pathway behaviour adds information beyond static gene readings, and could guide tailored prevention if larger studies confirm it.
plos-pone-0355938:
Hilde EM Augusteijn and three colleagues tested what shapes peer review judgments in psychology, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Reviewers judge manuscripts for quality, but surface features may sway them apart from the science itself. The team studied how a manuscript's own traits shape the quality scores reviewers give scientific work in the field.

Augusteijn's findings expose which features, such as writing flair, formatting, or framing, move judgments. That matters for fairness: if polish beats substance, good work in plain dress gets rejected while weak work in fine dress passes. Journals can respond with reviewer guidance or structured forms. Psychology is a fitting test bed, since it has led debates about research quality and reform in recent years.
plos-pone-0356138:
Ahmad Basil Nasir and colleagues mined American electronic health records for more than one and a half million adults with type 2 diabetes. They asked whether the diabetes drug a person takes tracks with later cognitive decline. Their 2026 retrospective study matched patients across five regimens, with metformin alone as the yardstick. It followed diagnoses of mild cognitive disorder, Alzheimer's disease, and vascular dementia over up to fourteen years.

Adding a GLP-1 drug to metformin was linked to roughly half the risk of vascular dementia and Alzheimer's. It was also linked to a lower rate of mild impairment. Adding an SGLT-2 drug cut vascular dementia only. Insulin alone looked worst on every outcome, likely reflecting more severe disease. The authors stress records show association, not proof.
plos-pone-0356238:
Xiangjun Li, Ruitao Li, Zhui Tu, and Qingting Wei built FusionPHI, a model that predicts which bacteria a given virus can infect. Phage therapy needs that information before it can match a bacteria-killing virus to a patient's strain. Their 2026 paper feeds the model three views of each partner. They are genome letter statistics, protein chemistry, and evolved gene motif embeddings. A two-stage attention mechanism fuses them.

The model scored strongly on its test data. Ablation tests showed each information stream earns its place, and so does the attention fusion. A case check on a textbook E. coli phage behaved as hoped. Faster, trustworthy matching could make phage therapy practical against antibiotic-resistant infections, instead of a laboratory fishing expedition.
plos-pone-0356638:
Lu Dai and coauthors published a 2026 gene study in PLOS ONE on acute liver failure triggered by hepatitis B, hunting for biomarkers where two forces meet: oxidative stress and immune infiltration. Both damage the failing liver, but their combined signature had never been mined. The team sifted a public gene dataset for genes that differed in disease, belonged to oxidative stress lists, and sat in key co-expression modules. Two machine learning methods then voted the list down.

Five candidate genes survived, and checking them in a second dataset trimmed the panel to four: CLU, APOH, AMBP, and GPX8. Each gene alone carried useful diagnostic signal, and enrichment analysis tied all four to metabolic processes. A microRNA network around them was mapped, and candidate drugs predicted. They present the four-gene signature as a starting point for a blood test and for mechanistic work, not yet a clinical tool.
plos-pone-0356838:
Niroshan Chandrajith Lokunarangoda and colleagues publish a plan in 2026 for a systematic review of dengue's long-term effects on the heart. Dengue, a mosquito-borne disease common in tropical regions, is usually seen as a short illness that patients recover from fully. Reports of heart problems weeks or months later, though, have raised doubts about that picture.

Under the registered protocol, the team will gather human studies that report heart or blood-vessel outcomes at least four weeks after dengue infection. They will search seven databases, screen studies in pairs, and weigh the quality of the evidence before combining results. Outcomes range from strokes and rhythm problems to subtle changes picked up on scans and blood tests. The finished review should show whether survivors need heart follow-up and where the evidence is still too thin to judge.
plos-pone-0357038:
Sean P Heffron and colleagues follow patients whose leg arteries were reopened, asking whether gaining everyday activity capacity afterward predicts who fares well. Blocked leg arteries limit walking, and a questionnaire score can capture what patients can actually do. The team scored patients before the procedure and six months later, grouping them as stayed low, stayed higher, or climbed from low to higher, then tracked heart and limb events.

Patients stuck at low capacity faced the highest later risks, including a markedly higher death risk than those who stayed higher. Encouragingly, patients who climbed into the higher group ended with risk much like those who had always been higher. Heffron and colleagues say helping patients gain real activity after the procedure may matter as much as the procedure itself.
plos-pone-0357938:
Ruslana Iskra, Halyna Klymets, and Iryna Oliynyk wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article using rats. It studies lactate dehydrogenase activity, an enzyme tied to energy production, and carbohydrate metabolism in body tissues. The exposure is vanadium citrate, a compound of the metal vanadium, given to the animals.

The effects reported depend on both sex and dose, varying between male and female rats and with how much compound they received. Sex- and dose-dependent results warn against treating one group's response as universal. Toxicologists and researchers studying vanadium, which is also marketed in supplements, are the readers for tissue-level evidence like this.
plos-pone-0358038:
Sandhya Yadav led a team of five authors studying how muscle cells mature, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Muscles grow and repair when precursor cells called myoblasts develop and fuse. The team studied a gene named Tceal7 and the signals that control it during that process.

Yadav's group showed that Tceal7 is switched on through calcineurin signaling, under control of a protein called BRG1, and that it promotes myoblast development. Each defined link like this adds a piece to the puzzle of muscle building. That puzzle matters for diseases that waste muscle and for injuries that heal poorly. Knowing the chain also gives researchers points where they might one day intervene to help muscle grow.
plos-pone-0358338:
Megumi Gonno and Noriyuki Kida published a 2026 questionnaire study in PLOS ONE on when physical contact in sports teaching feels uncomfortable. Coaches often guide movement with a hand on a shoulder or back, but comfort may depend on who touches, where, and how well the two know each other. They asked female university students in Japan to rate dozens of imagined scenarios, varying the toucher's gender, the body region, and whether the toucher was a teacher, close friend, or acquaintance.

Across both sets of scenarios, contact from men caused more discomfort than contact from women, and some body regions were consistently more sensitive than others. For teachers, the toucher's gender and the body region mattered on their own, with no extra combined effect. Among friends and acquaintances, closeness changed how strongly gender mattered. The findings give physical education programs concrete factors to weigh in guidance on instructional touch.
plos-pone-0358538:
Maowen Zhou and three colleagues published a computer vision study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They tackled the task of spotting odd or unsafe events in video when only weak labels are at hand, rather than costly frame-by-frame notes. Their approach leans on how people interact with objects in a scene.

Zhou's system learns from those human-object interactions to judge which clips look normal and which do not. Unusual handling of an object can flag an event that a watcher should review. Using weak labels cuts training cost a great deal. The method suits security and safety settings where staff cannot label hours of video by hand but still need alerts they can trust.
plos-pone-0358738:
Pluemkamon Phuwanatsarunya leads a team of eight cataloguing the chemistry of blow fly larvae in PLOS ONE in 2026. The tropical species Hemipyrellia ligurriens matters in medicine and forensics, yet what its larvae are made of was largely unmapped. Using mass spectrometry, the team profiled proteins in whole body extracts and in the fluids larvae secrete, and listed the fatty acids present, hunting in particular for natural antimicrobial molecules.

The two preparations shared most proteins but each carried thousands of its own, with the secreted fluid especially diverse. Among the small proteins sat several candidates resembling known insect defense molecules, including defensin like and attacin like sequences, plus enzymes that attack bacterial walls. Twenty-six fatty acids were identified. In dishes, the extracts slowed two bacterial species modestly and fungi not at all. The dataset is a foundation for anyone mining fly larvae for drug leads.
plos-pone-0358938: Biello and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a long-term study in New England called RISE-NE. The study will follow people over time as substance use, HIV, hepatitis C, and overdose rise in the region. The plan sets out who will be followed and what will be tracked. A cohort that watches all four harms together can show how they feed each other.
plos-pone-0359538: Bozděch, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on junior girls' tennis over two decades. The study tracks rankings on the ITF World Tennis Tour Juniors from 2004 to 2025. Its theme is a rise in what young players must do, in results and fitness, to keep up. Long ranking records can show coaches and parents how the junior game has grown more demanding.
plos-pone-0359638:
Mohamed Lotfy, Fatema Al Sawai, Dhoha Alyammahi, and Biduth Kundu wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article using fruit flies. The diabetes model is a high-sucrose Drosophila diet, flies fed heavy sugar until they show diabetes-like traits. The drug tested is metformin, the world's most common diabetes medicine, examined for effects on gene expression, on oxidative stress, and on how long the flies survive.

Flies are cheap, fast stand-ins for studying how a drug touches whole-body metabolism. Watching survival and gene activity together shows both the benefit and the molecular footprint of metformin. Diabetes researchers use fly results like these to decide which mechanisms deserve testing in mammals.
plos-pone-0359838:
Birhanemaskal Malkamu and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It compares what female students in Northwest Ethiopia know about human papillomavirus, or HPV, how they feel about it, and what they do to prevent it. The comparison runs between health students and social science students at university.

HPV causes cervical cancer, yet vaccination and screening remain limited in Ethiopia. If even health students show gaps, campus education clearly needs work; if they differ sharply from social science peers, training is doing something. University health educators planning HPV campaigns are the readers for this comparative snapshot.
pmc-11223838:
Letunic and Bork present version six of the Interactive Tree of Life, known as iTOL. Their free online tool helps researchers draw, label, and manage family trees of species and other branching diagrams. Anyone can use it, with no fee or closed access.

Version six brings a modern interface that was rebuilt from the ground up. Users can shape how trees look, add labels and data layers, and adjust displays by hand. Clear tree figures matter because one diagram often carries the main result of an evolution study, so readers need to read it at a glance.
pmc-13128238:
Giovanna Guimaraes Lopes Bergamasco is first author on a 2026 systematic review of nutrition screening tool validation in hospitalized adults. Hospital malnutrition stays common despite decades of study, and many tools exist to screen or assess it. The authors asked how validation studies of these tools were done and whether they reported clinical outcomes.

Searching five databases up to July twenty twenty-two, they included seventy-seven studies covering twenty tools. The Mini Nutritional Assessment was tested most against outcomes. Among full texts checked, over three quarters were excluded for not reporting clinical outcomes at all. In Brazilian studies, two other tools led. Evidence limits, including the hospital-only focus, are frankly discussed.
pmc-13196938:
Haiyan Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 computer vision model called TransitNet. Semantic segmentation means labeling each pixel in an image, such as road, car, or building. Large models are too heavy for car computers, so the team built a light one for traffic scenes.

TransitNet builds on an older model but adds two attention units that weigh which image details matter most. A slim backbone keeps the model small and fast. On standard image test sets, it beat the older model on accuracy scores. It also scored well on aerial land images, a quite different field. The design suits live scene reading for self-driving cars and land mapping.
pmc-13197238:
Robert S Krouse and colleagues recount recruitment lessons from a 2026 telehealth trial for rural cancer survivors. An ostomy is a surgical opening that lets stool or urine leave the body. The trial tested group video lessons to help rural survivors live with an ostomy.

The study ran from 2019 to 2024, first at three sites. Sign-up slowed sharply once the COVID pandemic began. The team added six more sites across the United States. They also widened who counted as rural and lowered the distance from ostomy nursing care that a person needed to qualify. The report shows how flexible design can save a hard-to-fill trial while keeping its core sound.
pmc-13200738:
Jeffery G Klann and colleagues present i2b2-ML, a 2026 module that adds machine learning to a health data platform. Machine learning could transform care, but sloppy methods and privacy risks plague health record research. Their module lets researchers train models inside the platform with no coding and no export of patient-level data.

A proof-of-concept build was tested on a public dataset first. It then trained on records of one hundred thousand patients drawn from a large intensive care database in about seventy-six minutes. Applying the model to classify near twenty-nine thousand patients took under two minutes. The team plans a simpler interface and easier rollout to existing sites.
pmc-13201338:
Hunters and officials who find dead wild boar often cannot draw a clean blood sample, so a 2026 study headed by Denise Meyer tests a simpler option. The research article asks whether blood swabs can detect antibodies to classical swine fever virus during disease surveillance in wild boar.

Meyer and colleagues ran antibody tests and virus neutralization tests on 29 positive and 100 negative samples. Swabs proved suitable for finding the antibodies, though slightly less sensitive than serum early after infection. Because one swab can serve tests for two serious swine diseases, the method could simplify field surveillance programs.
pmc-13201738:
Natural killer cells attack tumors without prior training, and a 2026 study led by Yikun Guo maps their behavior inside lung adenocarcinoma. The research article combines single-cell sequencing with large tumor datasets to characterize these immune cells and build a gene-based risk score for patients.

Guo and colleagues identified five natural killer cell clusters in tumor samples, four of them tied to patient prognosis. From thousands of differing genes they selected a signature of thirteen genes that predicted survival and related to the tumor immune environment. A combined chart pairing the signature with cancer stage predicted outcomes well and may help judge who benefits from immunotherapy.
pmc-13202138:
Health students train under heavy pressure, and a 2026 survey by Katekaew Seangpraw connects their self-care habits with burnout and quality of life. The cross-sectional study questioned 1,426 university students in health-related fields across northern, southern, and northeastern Thailand between January and March 2024.

Most students reported moderate quality of life, and about one in five met the study's burnout criteria on standard inventories. Better psychological self-care tracked with lower exhaustion and cynicism and with higher quality of life across the sample. Factors such as chronic illness, sleep, smoking, and academic performance also mattered, leading the authors to recommend structured mental health support in health programs.
pmc-13203038:
A drug-resistant yeast is spreading through hospitals, and a 2026 genomic study led by Junmin Cao tracks its patterns across China. The research article studies twenty-two ICU patients colonized or infected with Candidozyma auris, sequencing twenty-five isolates and testing their antifungal susceptibility.

Every isolate was immune to fluconazole, and most were immune to amphotericin B too, while the echinocandin drug class remained effective in testing. The gene reads split into two global clades with distinct resistance-gene variants, though single mutations did not predict drug response neatly. Matching 210 genomes traced arrivals from Canada, South Korea, and Pakistan, with Beijing and Guangdong as domestic spread hubs.
pmc-13205138:
A missing complement brake causes severe gut disease in CHAPLE syndrome, and a 2026 study led by Azzeddine Tahiat reports what blocking complement can restore. The research article studies patients who lack the CD55 brake, leaving complement attack unchecked and damaging gut lymph vessels and draining protein from the body.

Beyond the gut disease, The same lack disrupts B cell balance and antibody production in these patients. Blocking it at the C5 step restored normal antibody levels in blood and restored a normal B cell profile in the noted cases. Treated patients also mounted strong protection and answered vaccines as they should, extending the therapy's known benefits to humoral immunity.
pmc-13207938:
Lazy eye can be prevented if screening catches the right focusing errors early, and a 2026 school study headed by Numan Küçük measures those risks in Türkiye. In October 2019, screeners checked 1,126 preschool and first-grade children in the Kozlu district of Zonguldak with a pediatric autorefractometer.

One hundred twenty-five children were referred for full examination, and thirty cases of amblyopia were confirmed among those analyzed. Long-sightedness below the usual referral thresholds still raised risk, as did astigmatism in the statistical models. Unequal focus between the eyes mattered increasingly as the gap in diopters grew, and the authors argue screening cutoffs should be rethought nationally.
pmc-13211538:
Forensic drug laboratories drown in samples, and a 2026 article by Ivan Šoša proposes a two-stage workflow that saves the expensive instrument for last. Writing alone, Šoša argues medium-throughput toxicology labs should predict metabolites on the computer first, screen them cheaply, and confirm only the samples that earn it.

Stage one pairs prediction software with capillary zone electrophoresis, a fast separation well suited to the polar metabolites that chromatography handles badly. Samples that look empty or uninformative stop there, sparing costly mass spectrometry time for the rest. The author presents the sequence as transparent and court-defensible, with effort shifted toward the cheapest steps that still protect evidentiary standards.
pmc-13213138:
Bryan D. Bourland and colleagues compare in 2026 donor cartilage grafts placed on the inner versus outer side of the knee. Surgeons transplant plugs of bone and cartilage into focal defects, yet published work concentrates on the inner side, leaving the outer side less understood.

The cohort held 319 patients, about a third treated on the outer side, followed for roughly nine years on average. Reoperation and graft failure rates matched closely between sides, and ten-year survival sat high for both. Standard knee scores were broadly similar, though inner-side patients reported slightly higher satisfaction and one function subscale favoured them. Outer-side grafting, the authors conclude, performs comparably and should not be overlooked.
pmc-13216338:
Justus Aisu and co-authors present a 2026 taxonomy study confirming the identity of a root-knot nematode found in the Netherlands, well outside the Spanish site where the species was first described. Root-knot nematodes are major crop pests, and telling species apart is notoriously tricky.

Two Dutch populations, found on holly and elm hosts, were examined by body measurements, enzyme profiles, and several DNA markers. Every line of evidence agreed between the populations and matched the original description of Meloidogyne silvestris. The team also produced a nearly complete mitochondrial genome for the species, a first that expands the genomic toolkit for the genus. They argue that combining independent evidence types is the reliable way to fix species boundaries here.
pmc-13218138:
Liming Jiang and co-authors present a 2026 protocol on measuring movement-evoked pain in knee osteoarthritis. Pain that flares during activity, rather than pain at rest, may capture the burden of an arthritic knee, and trialists increasingly treat it as a core outcome. Its usefulness is limited because how reliable and valid the measurements are is not firmly established.

The study has two parts: test-retest sessions about a week apart, and a cross-sectional check of validity. Sixty-two community volunteers with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis will rate movement-evoked pain on an eleven-point scale during five standardized tasks, including a chair stand test, a stair climb, and a six-minute walk. Reliability is quantified with intraclass correlation coefficients. Validity will be judged by how the ratings track the pain subscale of a standard knee outcome score, separately for each task. Ethics approval and public registration are complete.
pmc-13218538:
Richmond Owusu Ateko and co-authors synthesize what is known about abnormal blood lipids among adults in Ghana in a 2026 systematic review. Dyslipidaemia is a major driver of cardiovascular disease, and urbanization, changing diets, and sedentary work are pushing cardiometabolic risk upward across sub-Saharan Africa. Ghana-specific numbers have been scattered across small studies.

Searching six databases for work published between 1980 and late 2025, the reviewers found twenty-four studies from 2003 to 2023 covering roughly 11,400 participants. Reported prevalence swung widely, from 3.0 percent to 72.4 percent, depending on who was studied and which cut-offs were used. Low HDL cholesterol, the protective fraction, was the commonest abnormality, followed by raised total and LDL cholesterol, while high triglycerides were least common. Southern and middle regions, notably Ashanti, Brong-Ahafo, and Greater Accra, reported heavier burdens than the north. Differences in criteria and sampling blocked a pooled estimate, so the authors call for standardized surveillance.
pmc-13220738:
Kevin P. Fiori and Alexander Plum argue United States healthcare should import delivery innovations from poorer countries, in a 2026 paper on global learning and implementation science. American care is rich in technology and poor in equity, while some of the effective models were invented under scarcity in low- and middle-income countries. The obstacle is not admiration but method: transplants fail when nobody manages adaptation.

Two case studies carry the argument. Community health worker practices refined in Togo were adapted to the Bronx to attack disparities, with attention to what changed in translation. A Michigan health center rebuilt its model on principles from women's groups in India, localizing an approach for its patients. In both, implementation science supplied the framework deciding what to keep, what to bend, and how to judge success. The authors propose pairing a global learning network with that discipline as a pathway for closing gaps.
pmc-13222338:
Khlood S. Abdel Zaher and colleagues build epoxy coatings that both decorate surfaces and block gamma radiation, in a 2026 materials study using rice straw waste. Lignin-rich black liquor from straw supplied the base for a manganese nano-hybrid filler. Coatings carried three filler levels and were painted at three thicknesses onto plastic panels.

Structure checks confirmed nanoscale particles with elements spread evenly through the lignin. Darker color deepened as filler content and thickness rose. Radiation tests with cesium and cobalt sources showed shielding power climbing with filler level, gaining roughly eighteen percent across the tested range. A farm waste stream thus becomes a functional coating ingredient with two jobs at once.
pmc-13223638:
Crescensia Baarkoh and co-authors explore what raising a child with autism feels like for parents at a Ghanaian regional hospital, in a 2026 qualitative study. Ten parents of children with autism spoke in depth with the team at Greater Accra Regional Hospital. Their accounts were grouped into themes covering the burdens and coping routes that shape daily care.

Parents told of heavy emotional, social, psychological, and financial strain. Stigma, spiritual charges blaming families, and marital trouble recurred across interviews. Coping leaned on changes in habits and routines, faith and prayer support, and choosing to ignore hostile social attitudes. The authors call for joined-up support, including therapy, marital therapy, and rehabilitation services, to lighten a load parents currently carry nearly alone.
pmc-13224038:
Rachel Knight and a large team report a 2026 randomised trial of a phone-based programme for teenagers at risk of depression. Called One Step Back, the five-week programme trains decentering, the skill of stepping back from unwanted thoughts and feelings. Teenagers were recruited through United Kingdom secondary schools, and 114 took part.

Half received the programme, while the rest did matched physical and cognitive exercises as an active control. The programme group improved more on decentering scores after the course ended. Those teenagers also reported fewer depression symptoms and higher well-being than controls. The findings support brief digital training as a low-intensity option for young people who show early risk signs without severe symptoms.
pmc-13226138:
Jia Li and Yanhong Shi outline a 2026 combined immunotherapy strategy for glioblastoma, the most aggressive primary brain tumour, in a commentary on their recent experimental work. Engineered immune cells alone struggle here: tumour targets vary between cells, targets can vanish under pressure, and the tumour environment quickly exhausts incoming cells. Their platform attacks all three problems at once.

One engineered virus paints two target flags onto tumour cells, so bispecific killer cells built to recognise both flags can find more of the tumour. A second virus releases immune-boosting signals locally to keep those cells active. The components reinforce one another, aiming for broader coverage, less escape, and longer persistence than any single therapy achieves.
pmc-13230938:
Sundar Hengoju and colleagues present in 2026 a droplet system that hunts for new antibiotics in soil microbe communities. Millions of tiny droplets each grow a few bacteria in a space smaller than a raindrop. Two glowing reporter strains, one from each major bacterial group, are added to every droplet to reveal killing activity.

A droplet where a reporter dims signals that its resident microbe made something that stops that reporter. A test with a known antibiotic maker hidden in a mixed sample proved the system can find and recover the right strain. Soil samples then passed through the same screen successfully. Testing both reporters at once sorts finds by which bacteria they can stop.
pmc-13232538:
Arcady A Putilov sorts in 2026 the crowded family of questionnaires that measure whether people are morning or evening types. Fifty years of publishing produced dozens of such forms, and picking the right one for a study has grown hard. Searches of two databases plus past reviews gathered seventy-five questionnaires in total.

Twenty traits of a form, from its length to what it truly measures, anchor the new classification system. Sixty forms measure chronotype alone, while fifteen mix it with other traits such as sleep habits. Any single form can now be told apart from the rest by its trait profile. Researchers can also sketch the traits of a form that does not yet exist.
pmc-13232938:
Ismaila Ajayi Yusuf and colleagues issued a 2026 review comparing a new class of blood pressure drugs called aldosterone synthase inhibitors. These drugs block the making of aldosterone, a hormone that raises blood pressure. No trial has tested the drugs against each other directly, so the team combined seven randomized trials covering 2,828 patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension.

All three drugs lowered systolic pressure more than placebo, with baxdrostat and lorundrostat performing similarly. Benefits looked strongest in resistant hypertension. Risks rose too, including low blood pressure, high potassium, and low sodium. Because no trial pitted the drugs head to head, the authors present the ranking as a guide for doctors, not a final verdict.
pmc-13233638:
Peter Grechenig and colleagues published a 2026 training study on emergency access to the subclavian vessels, the large artery and vein under the collarbone. Bleeding there is rare but life-threatening, and orthopedic trauma surgeons, not chest specialists, may be first on scene. One hundred such surgeons practiced an under-collarbone approach on fifty cadavers over two days at a dissection course.

Confidence and accuracy both climbed steeply with practice. Correct clamping of both vessels improved by roughly a third from day one to day two. The share of successful participants feeling sure of themselves rose from about a quarter to over seventy percent. Prior surgical experience did not predict success. The authors argue that cadaver workshops are essential for keeping rare emergency skills safe and current.
pmc-13234038:
Meltem Ileri and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of body piercing and risky behavior in teenagers. The clinic-based study enrolled 141 adolescents aged twelve to nineteen in Turkey during 2025, seventy-one with at least one piercing and seventy without. Questionnaires covered smoking, alcohol and substance use, self-injury, suicidal thinking, and what the teenagers knew about piercing hygiene and complications.

Pierced adolescents reported far more risk-taking on every measure, including smoking, drinking, and positive suicide risk screening, all by wide margins. Nearly half of the pierced group had suffered local complications like redness, swelling, or pain, and only about half had been pierced in licensed studios. Knowledge scores were middling, weakest on safe settings. The authors frame piercing as one visible thread in a wider pattern of adolescent risk.
pmc-13234338:
Julia Rudert and colleagues described in 2026 a flexible messenger RNA vaccine platform aimed at changing coronavirus variants. As SARS-CoV-2 evolves, older vaccines lose strength against new forms of the spike protein. The team built and compared three optimized candidates in mice during a prime and boost schedule. Each candidate carried instructions for parts of the virus that bind to human cells.

One candidate, called TP2A, covered the original virus plus the Delta and Omicron variants and performed best. It produced an early antibody response dominated by one antibody type and activity across variants. It also raised virus-specific T cells, including killer T cells, in spleen and nearby lymph nodes. Because its parts can be swapped, the platform could be adapted quickly to future variants or other viruses.
pmc-13235338:
Ankita Chakrabarti and colleagues reported in 2026 a case of poisoning from a weekly arthritis drug taken daily by mistake. A 55-year-old woman had taken low-dose methotrexate once a week for rheumatoid arthritis for over a year. Similar-looking packaging after a brand change led her to confuse the drug with another daily medicine. She took the tablets on six straight days before harm appeared.

Severe mouth inflammation and moderate blood changes brought her to hospital for treatment. Fluids, a rescue vitamin, and measures to flush the drug through the kidneys supported her recovery. Measurable drug levels persisted in her blood for ten days after the last dose. A stomach acid medicine she also took may have slowed drug clearance from her body. The authors warn that look-alike packaging endangers patients with limited health education.
pmc-13238238:
Mehdi Loukhnati and colleagues reported in 2026 how a stem cell boost rescued a 55-year-old man whose blood counts never recovered after CAR T-cell therapy for myeloma. Prolonged low counts are a severe complication of this treatment, bringing infection and bleeding risks, and transfusions plus growth factors had failed him. Doctors reinfused his own previously frozen stem cells in an outpatient setting, with no preparatory chemotherapy.

His blood production recovered fully within fourteen days. The authors present the boost as a salvage option when standard support fails after anti-BCMA CAR T-cell therapy. Evidence so far rests on small series and single cases like this one. They call for prospective multicenter studies to settle who should receive a boost, and when.
pmc-13239238:
Brenda Serrão de Freitas and colleagues tested salted dried beef sold in two Central Amazon cities in 2026 and found microplastic contamination in every sample. Six brands from Itacoatiara and Parintins were processed by density separation and digestion, then counted under a stereomicroscope and identified by Raman spectroscopy. In total the team found one hundred forty-one particles.

Elongated blue fibers dominated in both cities, and four polymer types turned up, including PET and polystyrene, pointing mainly to urban sources. Parintins brands carried more particles, though slightly smaller on average. As the first demonstration of microplastics in this food, the study exposes weak points in sanitary control. The authors urge that microplastic checks join food safety surveillance programs in the region.
pmc-13239438:
Susumu Sakamoto and a nationwide Japanese team compare two lung conditions in a 2026 retrospective study. Humidifier lung is a rare form of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, an allergic lung inflammation, while summer-type disease is the better known Japanese variant linked to mould growing in homes.

Records from 214 facilities between 2011 and 2021 yielded hundreds of cases of each type, with humidifier cases rising during the COVID-19 pandemic. Humidifier patients tended to be older men with higher inflammation markers but lower levels of two lung proteins. Scans and tissue samples also differed, including more consolidation and fewer granulomas. The authors argue humidifier lung is a distinct subtype.
pmc-13239938:
Ilyas Atalar and colleagues test hazelnut protein as an egg white substitute in nougat foam in a 2026 food study. Egg white is the benchmark foaming ingredient for aerated sweets, and plant proteins usually foam weakly, so the team chemically linked hazelnut protein with two gums to strengthen it.

Plain hazelnut protein produced denser, weaker foams than egg white at every replacement level. The linked versions performed far better, and the alginate-linked protein at a quarter to half replacement nearly matched the egg control while keeping bubbles evenly spread. Chemical spectra supported stronger water binding in the linked systems. The results open a plant-based route for confectionery foams.
pmc-13240838:
Tingting Hong and co-authors report a 2026 food science study on protecting dough structure under acidic conditions. Acid, as in sourdough, tends to break down the gluten network that gives bread its texture. The additive tested was soluble soybean polysaccharide, a plant-derived fiber.

At a moderate level, the additive improved dough elasticity and water holding, and it shielded gluten from acid damage. Imaging and water-mobility measurements confirmed that more water stayed locked inside the dough. The protein network also gained heat stability and a denser structure. At a higher level, the same additive weakened the network instead. The authors recommend careful dosing for acidic wheat products such as sourdough.
pmc-13241338:
von Groote and colleagues in Münster searched blood proteins for signs that acute kidney injury will turn chronic. Their prospective cohort enrolled two hundred five critically ill postoperative patients with moderate injury. Plasma from one hundred ninety-five patients underwent high-resolution mass spectrometry. The outcome was persistent injury or death within a week.

Just over half the patients progressed to acute kidney disease. Dozens of proteins tracked with progression across depleted and undepleted plasma. Calprotectin stood out strongest, and a targeted assay confirmed higher levels in progressors. The authors propose it as a candidate marker of kidney injury chronification.
pmc-13241838:
Hendrik Dapper and co-authors present a 2026 study of ultrasound elastography for measuring neck scarring after radiotherapy. Radiation can harden soft tissues in the neck, causing problems such as swallowing difficulty and muscle contracture. No accepted standard exists for grading this fibrosis by tissue type.

The paper sets out the problem in detail before turning to shear-wave elastography, a method that maps tissue stiffness directly. Tissue hardening is the core feature of fibrosis, so a stiffness measure suits the task. The authors frame tissue-specific measurement as the missing step between vague symptom labels and targeted care. Their work aims to quantify radiation damage in separate neck tissues rather than treating the neck as one block.
pmc-13242338:
Dhiman in Pune reviews carbon-based light catalysts built to clean polluted water and air. The materials can be made from waste biomass. Carbon frames offer huge surface area, tunable pores, and strong current flow. Routes range from biomass burning to microwave and hot-water methods. Doping with metals, metal oxides, or other atoms tunes light response.

The review walks through how light breaks pollutants down, step by step. Targets include factory dyes, heavy metals, drug waste, and carbon dioxide. Band-gap tuning decides whether a catalyst wakes under sunlight. Dhiman frames nano-carbon as a green option over standard treatment.
pmc-13242438:
Nirmal Gautam and co-authors followed Australian children to see how patterns of early adversity shape health and quality of life. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. They used the kindergarten cohort of a national longitudinal study, covering 3,089 children with repeated measures over time. Statistical grouping sorted children by their mix of adverse experiences, such as family hardship and instability, rather than by a single event count.

Three groups emerged: about two-thirds of children faced low adversity, a quarter faced a moderate level, and under a tenth faced high adversity. Children in the high-adversity group had notably worse mental health and general health than the low group. Their quality of life also ran lower across social, school, physical, and emotional domains. Moderate adversity carried smaller but real risks. Knowing the pattern, the authors argue, helps target prevention where it counts most.
pmc-13243738:
Giyoung Yun and co-authors check a skin sensor that tracks blood hemoglobin without a blood draw in 2026. The setting is major mouth cancer surgery with tissue flap repair, where blood loss can be heavy. Steady hemoglobin readings help doctors decide when to transfuse.

The study covers 55 patients treated between 2023 and 2025 at one center. Sensor readings were matched against bedside blood tests at the start and end of surgery. Agreement was moderate at both points and weaker for tracking change over time. A dopamine drip, used to support blood pressure, widened the sensor's error. The authors see the sensor as a helpful extra, not a swap for blood tests.
pmc-13244138:
Betsabé Hernández-Santos and colleagues baked breakfast flakes from two vividly colored staples, blue corn and purple sweet potato, and measured what each blend delivered. Their study appeared in the International Journal of Food Science in 2026. Five recipes ran from pure corn to pure sweet potato, and the team tested nutrition, water behavior, antioxidant power, crunch, and taste. Each flour covers the other's gaps: corn brings protein and phenolics, sweet potato brings fiber and anthocyanins.

As sweet potato rose in the mix, fiber, pigment, and antioxidant scores climbed steadily, with radical-scavenging near total in the richest tests. Pure sweet potato flakes were the densest and hardest to snap. Corn-rich flakes, by contrast, puffed into lighter structures that soaked up milk faster and carried more protein. The authors conclude the blend ratio is a dial manufacturers can turn between nutrition density and eating quality.
pmc-13244838:
Steven H Ferguson and co-authors sort toothed whales into life strategy groups in a 2026 analysis. Toothed whales vary hugely in how fast they grow, breed, and die. The team asked whether shared habitats or shared ancestry better explains those patterns.

They compared 42 species on six life traits and three habitat measures, correcting for size and kinship. Three clusters emerged: a slow group, a fast group, and a cautious group that hedges its bets. Distant cousins in deep offshore waters converged on like strategies. Whales in icy, seasonal seas instead followed their own lineage paths. The grouping can help tailor protection to each cluster's pace of recovery.
pmc-13245438:
Wenqi Yi and co-authors study how liver tumors grow after heat ablation in a 2026 cohort study. Microwave ablation burns tumor tissue, yet some tumor survives at the edge or sits untreated in multifocal disease. Whether surviving types grow faster after treatment was unknown.

The study covers 103 patients treated between 2013 and 2021 with leftover or untreated tumors. Untreated tumors sped up after ablation of their neighbors, while leftover tumors did not change pace. Poor cell grade and wide ablation zones predicted the fastest growth. After treatment, both tumor types doubled in volume on like timescales. Close watching after ablation matters most for high-grade tumors.
pmc-13245838:
Declerck, Deschepper, and Colpaert documented what gets lost when hospital data are translated into a common research format, in this 2026 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Large multicenter studies rely on the OMOP Common Data Model, which requires mapping each hospital's records into shared concepts. The team mapped lung cancer data from Ghent University Hospital and audited consistency and completeness against the source.

Structured variables mapped consistently and nearly completely. The losses clustered in unstructured information: smoking status, recorded as free text, had to be dropped entirely for lack of a fitting concept. Diagnostic codes differed in granularity between institutions. An evolving reference dictionary added friction throughout. The authors conclude that reliable multicenter datasets require sustained collaboration between clinicians and data engineers, not a one-off technical conversion.
pmc-13245938:
Zhengqiang Luo and co-authors review one gene's split personality across lung diseases in a 2026 synthesis. The gene, FAM13A, sits mostly in lung tissue and helps steer cell growth signals. It has been tied to chronic bronchitis-type disease, scarring, asthma, and lung cancer alike.

Oddly, the gene seems to drive tissue loss in one disease yet soften scarring in another. Many gene variants and species gaps in expression make the picture harder to read. Environment also shifts what the gene does. The review joins genetic, molecular, and functional proof into one framework. It ends by mapping what precision lung medicine still needs to learn about this gene.
pmc-13246838:
Martínez-Cortés and co-authors studied how oxidative stress shapes muscle building in this 2026 Pflügers Archiv paper. Muscle forms when precursor cells fuse into fibers, and the process is sensitive to reactive oxygen species. The team focused on ALDH2, a mitochondrial enzyme that detoxifies a harmful fat-oxidation product, and on aldosterone, a hormone that raises oxidative stress, using mouse muscle cells in culture.

Raising oxidative stress, whether with peroxide, aldosterone, or drugs blocking ALDH2, produced a two-phase effect: fusion was suppressed in the first days, then stimulated later. Drugs that activate ALDH2 prevented both the stress and the odd timing. The authors trace the early and late phases to different signaling helpers, calpain first and a p38 pathway later.
pmc-13247738:
Mehdi Roshdi Maleki reports a diagnostic trap after antibiotic care for a urinary infection in a 2026 case. An 81-year-old woman with diabetes had lasting urinary symptoms and got levofloxacin on a best guess. Her urine held visible bacteria, yet cultures kept coming back empty.

Cultures stayed negative for ten days after the drug stopped, then grew E. coli that resisted the drug family. The author blames a long post-antibiotic effect, where germs stay suppressed well past the last dose. Scans showed only harmless kidney cysts. Clinicians are urged to doubt clean cultures after such drugs in frail patients and to resample when suspicion stays high.
pmc-13248038:
Mishra and Juneja review the metabolic footprint of sepsis in this 2026 World Journal of Critical Care Medicine article. Sepsis is deadly and varied, and standard biomarkers cannot track the deep metabolic upheaval it causes. Metabolomics, the wholesale measurement of small molecules in blood and tissue, can. The authors summarize animal and human studies using magnetic resonance and mass spectrometry platforms.

Patterns recur across studies: disturbed energy production, amino-acid and lipid turnover turned upside down, failing mitochondria, and metabolites made by gut microbes. Such profiles can separate sepsis from sterile inflammation and flag patients headed for organ failure or death. The authors see promise in merging metabolomics with other omics and clinical data for precision critical care, while warning that standardization lags behind the science.
pmc-13248438:
Hlaváčková and co-authors studied a stress-signaling protein in alfalfa, published in Molecular Horticulture in 2026. The protein, called SIMK, belongs to a family that helps plant cells respond to stress. Because SIMK also steers the cell's internal scaffolding, the team bred alfalfa lines making too little or too much of it, with the scaffolding dyed to glow.

Plants with altered SIMK divided along shifted planes in their roots. The low-SIMK line grew smaller, with tangled, poorly bundled scaffolding in leaves and stems. The results tie one stress protein to orderly cell structure and plant size, and the glowing lines offer a test bed for farming chemicals.
pmc-13250838:
Yifei Peng and colleagues build a forecasting model for neck spine surgery in this 2026 preliminary study. Cervical spondylotic myelopathy, spinal cord squeezing in the neck, is common in older adults, and some patients recover poorly after surgery despite it.

The team used a special MRI method that senses cord tissue health, plus clinical factors, in 234 patients at one centre. Three learning models tried to predict who would gain a meaningful recovery. The boosting model led in training and held up moderately in testing, and an explanation tool showed which inputs drove its calls. The authors offer it as a base for sorting patients before surgery.
pmc-13250938:
Paolo Manganotti and colleagues report a 2026 clinical study on Pisa syndrome, a sideways bending of the trunk that affects some people with Parkinson's disease. Treatment options are few and no standard protocol exists. The team tested whether shock wave therapy, applied just before botulinum toxin injections, could ease the abnormal lean and pain.

Fifteen patients entered the study and eleven finished both the real and the sham treatment rounds, separated by a washout of at least three months. Shock waves were aimed at the back muscles on the side of the lean, followed by toxin injections. Right after treatment, the trunk angle shrank more with real shock waves than with the sham version. That gain did not last at one or three months, and pain and quality of life scores did not clearly improve. The treatment caused only mild, brief discomfort.
pmc-13251338:
Jean-Michel Molina and colleagues analyse brief virus rebounds in two large HIV trials in this 2026 paper. Blips are short spikes in virus levels between suppressed readings, and whether they warn of treatment failure matters for people on daily therapy.

The trials tested a doravirine-based regimen against standard rivals over 96 weeks, then extended treatment for 96 more. Blips hit about one in nine participants on doravirine, similar to rivals, and grew rarer later. Lower starting virus levels meant fewer blips. A fuller rebound of the virus was more common in people who had blips during the main trials, at about 14 percent versus six percent without blips.
pmc-13251838:
Giacomo Potente and a large team compare flower supergenes across the primrose family in this 2026 study. Some primroses grow two flower forms with swapped male and female heights, a system Charles Darwin made famous, controlled by a locked cluster of genes.

Studying ten full genomes, seven of them newly built, the team found the cluster arose separately several times within the family. Each time, the same gene had been copied and put to the job, yet the surrounding layouts differed widely. That variety challenges the view that such clusters must sit on only one chromosome copy. Similar flowers, it turns out, can be built by unlike genomic routes.
pmc-13252038:
Weng and co-authors build a prediction chart for stomach cancer returning after surgery, adding a gene signal to standard factors. Their 2026 OncoTargets and Therapy study reviews one hundred fifty-two patients who had radical gastric surgery at one center, followed for eighteen months. Tumor tissue was stained for HOXA9, a development gene.

About thirty-eight percent of patients saw their cancer return during follow-up. Node spread, advanced stage, vessel invasion, and high HOXA9 each independently raised the recurrence risk. Combined into one nomogram, the four factors predicted recurrence far better than any single one alone. The authors offer the chart as a practical tool for sorting patients into closer or lighter follow-up after surgery.
pmc-13252938:
Fan and co-authors link lactate, a sugar-burning byproduct, to bone-eating cell growth in osteoarthritis. Their 2026 International Journal of Molecular Medicine study uses a mouse model made by cutting a knee ligament, plus cell experiments. The team tracked a chemical tag that lactate leaves on histone proteins inside bone-resorbing osteoclasts.

The tag, called H3K18 lactylation, ran high in arthritic joint osteoclasts alongside lower bone density and worse under-cartilage bone damage. Hormone-driven osteoclast formation raised lactate and the tag together, and a lactate blocker curbed both processes. The tag sat on a gene promoter that drives osteoclast activity and switched it on directly. Injecting the blocker into mouse joints cut osteoclast numbers and eased bone loss, marking the pathway as a treatment target.
pmc-13253138:
Capelle and co-authors dissect how young zebrafish flip from swimming toward light to avoiding it as they grow. Their 2026 iScience study combines virtual reality behavior tests with computer modeling of larval and juvenile fish. Big behavior changes during development are common, but the changing mental algorithms behind them are rarely pinned down.

The team separated three parallel computations: sensing overall brightness, comparing light between the two eyes, and tracking brightness change over time. Larvae leaned on the comparison and change streams, while juveniles mostly used overall brightness. Agent-based models built on those streams predicted behavior in richer environments. The authors suggest parallel processing streams are a general way animals retune behavior with age and context.
pmc-13253338:
Shuangling Xie and colleagues build a three-dimensional genome atlas of kiwifruit in a 2026 study. Genes are controlled partly by how DNA folds inside the nucleus, but detailed folding maps existed for few perennial fruit crops. The team used a chromosome capture technique to chart contacts across the kiwifruit genome in leaf and fruit tissue.

They layered the folding maps with data on chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, seven histone marks, and gene activity across tissues and fruit development stages. The combined resource annotates architecture at nested scales, from large active and silent compartments down to small domains and individual loops. The broad layout proved similar between leaf and fruit, while finer features such as domain insulation and loop frequency varied in quantity. The authors offer the atlas as a reference for breeding and functional studies in kiwifruit and other woody perennials.
pmc-13253938:
Arwa Aldeeri and colleagues test guava fruit for holding teeth in place in a 2026 rat study. After braces move teeth, teeth often drift back, called relapse. Twenty-four male Wistar rats had orthodontic treatment, then a 35-day holding phase, with half given guava fruit suspension by mouth at 250 milligrams per kilogram.

Twenty rats finished the study. After retainers came off for a seven-day relapse phase, the guava group drifted back far less, at -0.055 millimeters versus -0.220 millimeters in controls. The authors say guava may improve results, but more work is needed before any human trials.
pmc-13254138:
Bryn Tannar and many co-authors review magnesium in dialysis fluid in a 2026 narrative review. Heart disease causes nearly half of deaths in people on maintenance hemodialysis, a blood-cleaning treatment for kidney failure. The review searched two databases for studies on magnesium levels and heart outcomes.

Twenty studies, including 10 randomized trials, were reviewed. Low magnesium tied to higher heart event and death risk, while higher dialysate magnesium or oral supplements improved vessel markers like calcification and stiffness. Most trials were small and short, so the authors call for a large trial, one of which is now running.
pmc-13254438:
Rafa Ifthikhar, Kellie Schueler, and Sheila Mody explore how patients feel during an uncertain early pregnancy in a 2026 interview study. The diagnosis, called pregnancy of unknown location, means a positive test but no pregnancy seen on a scan yet. Thirty people aged 18 to 45 shared their stories.

Worry and hard feelings from not knowing were common, whatever the person had planned or how things turned out. Support from others, inner strength, and acceptance helped people cope. Kind and quick-to-respond providers made care feel better. Many went to emergency care for lack of clinic slots, facing long waits and little privacy.
pmc-13254538:
Yoshimi Onishi and co-authors describe a single-cut defibrillator swap in a 2026 case report. A 55-year-old man with Brugada syndrome, a heart rhythm disorder, needed his subcutaneous defibrillator replaced with an extravascular model after repeated wrong shocks from oversensing. The old and new device pockets sat in different spots.

X-ray planning showed the two sites were close enough for one pocket incision between them. Dissection both ways let the team remove the old generator and build the new pocket, with layered closure keeping the pockets separate. The approach avoided a large joined pocket and kept standard placement.
pmc-13255438: Matthias Arnold and a large team present a study protocol in a 2026 paper. The plan scales a care and case management system across a German region. It pairs a rollout study of new coordination offices in seven districts with a randomized trial. Adults with complex care needs will get case management or usual care. Outcomes include care experience, hospital use, and quality of life. This entry is a protocol only. It sets out the design and plans and reports no results, so no findings can be summarized here.
pmc-13257338:
Chico and colleagues ran a small open-label pilot trial of a high-dose coenzyme Q10 medical food in primary mitochondrial disease, conditions with few treatment options. Ten patients took the preparation, at two hundred fifty or five hundred milligrams daily, for thirty days after a month on conventional coenzyme Q10. Blood biomarkers, fatigue scores, and a sit-to-stand test were measured before and after.

Every patient kept blood coenzyme Q10 above a target threshold on the new preparation, versus sixty percent before, and dose-normalized exposure rose sharply. One antioxidant capacity measure improved, while disease biomarkers, fatigue, and sit-to-stand performance did not change significantly. The authors call the simplified dosing promising for adherence and seek larger trials.
pmc-13257538:
Yawen Zhou and co-authors study molecular films mixing tangeretin, a citrus compound, with two partner lipids in a 2026 paper. Tangeretin dissolves poorly in water, which limits food and medical use. Single-molecule layers at an air-water surface reveal how it mixes with membrane-like partners before formulation work begins.

With stearic acid, the molecules repelled each other and films stayed unstable. With the phospholipid DPPC, attraction was favorable and films resisted deformation. A tangeretin share of one-fifth gave the strongest attraction and the most stable mixed layer by energy measures. Food and drug formulators gain a pairing rule: phospholipid carriers suit this citrus flavonoid, fatty acid partners do not. Such early screening can save costly failed emulsions later in product development.
pmc-13257938:
Wei Cao and co-authors engineer a metal-organic framework into a strong solid acid in a 2026 catalysis study. Liquid acids corrode equipment and pollute, while many solid acids are weak. Missing-linker defects were deliberately built into MOF-808 so sulfate groups could anchor at the gaps and create acid sites.

More defects meant more numerous and stronger acid centers by direct measurement. The best recipe, with forty percent of one linker swapped, converted nearly all acetic acid into butyl acetate under mild conditions at low loading. Five recovery cycles kept activity steady after simple washing. The open pore network let reactants reach the sites freely. Green chemists gain a design rule: controlled imperfection can outperform perfection. Ester plants making solvents and fragrances are the natural first users.
pmc-13258038:
Maciej Rybicki and colleagues review a rare injury: a torn duodenal diverticulum after blunt trauma. The duodenum can hide a small pouch that bursts when the abdomen is struck, with vague symptoms delaying diagnosis. Their 2026 systematic review gathers every confirmed case reported since nineteen sixty.

Just twenty-one cases qualified, mostly from road crashes and falls from height. Pain was nearly universal, and CT scans caught the perforation in every patient scanned. Surgeons removed the pouch in almost all cases, usually with drainage. Four patients died, underlining why the authors urge early scanning and prompt surgery.
pmc-13258438:
Gege Hu and co-authors map how single-sugar polysaccharide structure drives immune effects in a 2026 review. These long chains, built from one sugar type, act as bioactive nutrients with anti-infection and anti-inflammatory records. Extraction and structure methods are summarized before findings are sorted into a three-level framework.

Primary recognition covers weight, linkage style, branching, and shape, the features immune receptors actually read. Middle levels trace signaling through gut microbes and metabolite networks, including classic inflammatory pathways. Top levels refine outcomes by chemical modification and dose context. Gut and immune researchers gain a shared vocabulary joining carbohydrate chemistry to nutrition science. Fine structure measurement remains the field's bottleneck, and the authors propose modeling that joins structure data across many studies.
pmc-13261638:
Yushan Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 secondary analysis comparing smoking-related low-back pain disability in China and high-income countries. Low-back pain is a leading cause of disability worldwide. The study covered working-age adults, 20 to 54 years, from 1990 to 2023, using Global Burden of Disease 2023 estimates.

In 2023, age-standardized incidence and disability rates were higher in high-income countries than in China. Rates declined in both settings, faster in China, where incidence fell by an average of 0.46 percent each year. Smoking's share of the disability burden moved in opposite directions. In high-income countries, the share fell from 24.05 percent down to 19.60 percent of the total. In China, the share rose slightly, from 16.61 percent up to 18.27 percent of the total. High body-mass index and workplace ergonomic exposures were tracked as context. The authors say these model-based patterns can inform prevention priorities in both settings.
pmc-13262438:
Yakup Bayram and colleagues tested in 2026 whether an egg maturity score predicts fertility treatment success in patients with low ovarian reserve. The Oocyte Maturation Index states the share of eggs that reach maturity. Their records covered 662 patients treated at a Turkish university unit between 2016 and 2024, split into younger and older low-reserve groups.

Egg and embryo counts differed clearly across the score bands in both groups. Among younger patients, the middle band, fifty-one to seventy-five percent, won the best pregnancy and live birth rates. The lowest band fared worst by a wide margin. In older patients the score still shifted early pregnancy rates but not live birth, which age-related egg problems may override. The authors recommend folding the index into routine assessment for personal planning and honest counseling.
pmc-13262838:
Lei Zhang and colleagues study thinking control in a spine disease using brain wave tests in a 2026 journal article. Ankylosing spondylitis is a long-term inflammatory disease of the spine, and thinking problems are increasingly reported in it. Sixteen male patients and 23 healthy controls did a Go and NoGo task, pressing or holding back responses, while brain signals were recorded.

Patients were less accurate and slower on go trials, but tended to be more accurate when holding back. In patients only, holding-back accuracy rose with the size of a late brain signal tied to effortful control. Brain wave power after each cue was also higher in patients in central scalp areas. The authors read this as patients leaning harder on effortful brain control.
pmc-13263038:
Jean-Luc Rolland and colleagues report a starvation-driven hunting behavior by marine bacteria in a 2026 journal article. The bacterium Vibrio atlanticus attacks Alexandrium pacificum, a single-celled alga that can form harmful blooms. Field observation and lab pairing studies let the team watch the interaction step by step and test what triggers it.

First, bacterial products stripped the alga's swimming tails, immobilizing it, they report. Then masses of bacteria briefly surrounded each algal cell without entering it. Finally the algal cells burst and were consumed. The attack depended on nutrient stress and iron supply, tied to the bacterium's iron-carrying system, not on the usual cell-to-cell signaling. The authors suggest this hunting may help control Alexandrium blooms.
pmc-13263138:
Jialin Liu and co-authors present a software tool that locates cell-to-cell signaling in tissue in a 2026 journal article. Cells talk via ligands, messenger molecules that dock onto receptors on other cells. Spatial gene data show where each gene is active, but older tools grouped cells coarsely. Their tool, CytoSignal, scores signaling at single-cell detail for each ligand-receptor pair.

The scores reveal gradients in signal strength and where contact-based versus drifting signals act, the authors report. The tool also flags genes tied to signaling and can predict how a given interaction changes over time at each spot. A lab proximity test confirmed predicted interaction sites in tissue, and the tool located them more accurately than earlier approaches.
pmc-13263638:
İbrahim Korkmaz reports a 2026 journal article grading three AI chatbots as teachers about heart attacks for emergency patients. A heart attack, acute myocardial infarction, is a leading killer. The author gave ChatGPT-4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and Gemini Advanced 2.0 Flash the same case and thirty patient-style questions. Four senior emergency doctors scored the answers.

ChatGPT-4o earned the highest accuracy score and an excellent rating on one quality scale. Claude 3.7 did best on treatment questions and wrote the most readable answers across all measures. All three models were judged good quality with minor shortcomings, and reliability scores did not differ significantly. The author concludes the tools show promise but still need physician oversight.
pmc-13263838:
Wanjun Lu and colleagues argued in 2026 that the amount of fluid around the lung, not just its presence, should guide thinking in small cell lung cancer. Guidelines lump every malignant effusion into the extensive stage, yet patients clearly fare unequally. Their cohort covered 1,026 patients treated in Nanjing between 2008 and 2024.
