Fluid appeared in just over a third of patients. Those with small effusions survived a median near fourteen months, statistically the same as patients with no fluid at all. Moderate or larger effusions cut median survival to about five months. Among 75 patients with proven malignant fluid, poor performance status and a high neuron-specific enolase level predicted early death. Immune therapy stood out in the opposite direction, tied to a large survival advantage. The authors propose effusion volume as a simple bedside stratifier.
pmc-13264038:
Cosimo Damiano Perrone and colleagues describe a 2026 laboratory approach that uses engineered ribozymes to silence the CD93 gene in blood vessel cells. CD93 sits on endothelial cells, which line blood vessels, and blocking it can slow new vessel growth linked to disease. Ribozymes are RNA molecules that cut other RNA, but plain versions break down quickly inside living cells.

The team mapped open regions on CD93 messenger RNA, then built a stabilizing scaffold from histone RNA to protect the ribozyme shape. In primary endothelial cells, the engineered molecules lowered CD93, reduced cell migration and limited tube-like structure formation. The study offers early proof that ribozyme tools might one day treat diseases driven by unwanted vessel growth.
pmc-13264138:
Huanhuan Yang and colleagues review how toxic metals move from soil through crops into people in a 2026 article. Cadmium, lead, mercury, arsenic and chromium enter farmland through industry, city growth and intensive farming. The review follows each metal through soil behavior, plant uptake and human effects that include nerve damage, kidney damage and cancer risk over long exposure periods.

Plant responses such as oxidative stress, enzyme disruption and genetic change are summarized alongside control options. Remedies range from cutting pollution at source and cleaning soils to farm practices and medical measures. New tools include nanomaterials, plant-based cleanup and artificial intelligence monitoring. A whole-chain approach joining source, process, risk and population is urged for food safety.
pmc-13264238:
Youssef Sakhy and colleagues present an imaging teaching case of bowel blockage caused by swallowed cork in a 2026 report. A twenty-five-year-old man with chronic psychosis arrived with pain, vomiting, swelling and no passage of stool or gas. CT showed widened small bowel loops ending at a sharp transition point. A round mottled mass full of tiny air pockets sat in the final section of small intestine. It was first read as trapped fecal material.

Similar masses in the stomach changed the interpretation toward swallowed cork pieces acting as the true blocker. The feces-like pattern is normally a side sign of blockage, not its cause. A discrete mass plus matching stomach material should prompt suspicion of a foreign body before planning treatment.
pmc-13264338:
Burhan Dost and colleagues write a 2026 letter presenting a meta-analysis of two nerve block techniques after breast surgery. Blocking the paravertebral space gives strong pain relief but is technically demanding with some risk. A newer block along the back muscles promises simpler placement. Earlier pooled work suggested similar relief, and a recent large network analysis found no meaningful difference in day-one pain, prompting this focused head-to-head check of randomized trials.

Their registered analysis centers on opioid use in the first day after surgery, judged against a preset threshold for clinical importance. Sequential and regression methods test whether evidence is firm or still fragile. The letter format previews a comparison meant to guide anesthetists choosing between a proven and a simpler block.
pmc-13264438:
Jiang Shu and co-authors report a 2026 study on finding speech-language delay in children from doctors' notes. A delay can be treated early, yet doctors often wait and watch, so the formal code may lag behind written concerns. The team trained a language model to spot the concern in free text.

The model scored near perfect on test data. Among visits where notes voiced concern, only 52 percent carried the matching diagnosis code. Of the rest, 39 percent got a code later, which points to delayed coding in at least 26 percent of such visits. Younger children and those with private cover were less likely to be coded at the time. The authors say note-based tools can close this gap.
pmc-13264638:
Arman Abroumand Gholami, Djalolidin Mansurov, and Tolib Bekmirov wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a nanoparticle therapy for pancreatic cancer. The therapy targets a surface protein called GPC1 and pairs chemo with sound-based treatment and live ultrasound imaging. The letter praises the design but raises three concerns before the work can count as a viable clinical strategy.

First, the study compared its system with a single drug that is not standard care for this cancer, so beating it proves little. Accepted first-line care pairs other drug combinations instead. Second, the mouse model used grows tumors under the skin and lacks the dense, poorly supplied tissue of real pancreatic tumors. That gap weakens claims that targeting drives tumor uptake. The authors urge care in reading the findings.
pmc-13264938:
Dharani Keyan and the team study the rollout of Problem Management Plus in Switzerland, in a 2026 qualitative study. The World Health Organization plan uses trained non-experts to ease common mental disorders. Resettled refugees show rates nearly three times those in the general population. A nationwide scale-up raised practical questions about fit and funding.

Interviews with 30 key players covered policymakers, experts, and peer providers. Enthusiasm for the plan was strong. Barriers included missing quality standards, unclear formal status in the health system, and uncertain long-term funding. Stakeholders favoured professional endorsement, mental health targets in integration plans, and shared financing across sectors.
pmc-13266138:
Bong Joo Kang reviews mammography updates in the 2025 BI-RADS reporting system (2026). The sixth edition was released in December 2025. The review compares its mammography section with the 2013 edition. Density sorting, terms, and write-up rules all changed.

3D mammography is now fully built into the system. One shape term returned while a margin term was removed. Two calcium-spot terms were merged under a broader heading, and one one-sided term retired. Lymph node reporting became a single category. Several linked traits were renamed as extra findings. Radiologists must learn the new language for steady write-ups.
pmc-13267538:
Rahi Gandhi and colleagues present a 2026 case report and literature review on bowel telescoping in an adult. In intussusception, one part of the bowel slides into the next, blocking it. In adults a growth usually leads the slide. Their patient was an 84-year-old man with five days of vomiting, swelling, and weakness, plus Parkinson's disease and kidney problems.

Scans showed a blockage and free air but missed both the hole in the bowel and the cause. Surgery found a telescoped cross-colon led by a five-centimeter mucus-forming cancer, with a perforation. Surgeons removed the segment as comfort-focused care. The man worsened with confusion and sepsis and died twelve days later. The authors stress early team decisions for frail patients.
pmc-13267738:
Esther I Doria and co-authors introduce in 2026 GIGEM, a software suite for measuring how social isolation changes sleep in fruit flies across very large experiments. Sleep loss from isolation is a public health concern, and flies offer a fast genetic model for its roots. The team applied the tool to 38 inbred fly lines plus controls, totaling more than five thousand animals, after short and long isolation.

Short isolation produced mixed responses: some lines lost sleep, some gained, and some barely changed. Long isolation caused clear sleep loss in nearly every line, though amounts varied and a few lines resisted. The software handled batch effects across experiments, making it useful for other large fly sleep studies hunting genetic influences.
pmc-13267838:
Siraç Irmak and colleagues report a 2026 study comparing two allergy treatments in teens. Allergic rhinitis, inflammation of the nose from allergies, can wreck sleep, school days, and daily life. The team followed 80 teens aged 12 to 18 with moderate to severe disease over one school term. Half used steroid nose sprays; half used modern antihistamine pills, as in routine care.

Both groups improved, but the spray group improved more. Their quality of life scores fell further, and 65 percent reached a meaningful gain against 38 percent on pills. Missed school days dropped by two in the spray group and did not drop on pills. Spray users also slept better and reported better classroom output. The authors note the study was not randomized, so results show links, not proof.
pmc-13269038:
Daolin Tang and Rui Kang argue in 2026 that a newborn's risk of E. coli blood infection depends heavily on antibodies received from the mother before birth. Newborn sepsis kills many infants each year, and E. coli is a leading cause, yet only a minority of exposed babies fall ill. The commentary discusses a recent Nature study that shifted attention from the baby's immature defenses to the mother's immune gift.

Antibodies against E. coli cross the placenta late in pregnancy through a specialized receptor, arming the baby to clear bacteria after birth. Babies who receive too little of that protection may fail to control early colonization. Maternal exposure history, even to friendly E. coli strains, could thus shape a newborn's first defense, opening ideas for prevention.
pmc-13270038:
Ravi Shankar, Vahul Sundar, and Karen Sui Geok Chua published a study protocol in 2026 for a planned review of speech-based screening tools for cognitive decline. Such tools analyze speech with language software to flag early dementia and related problems. Adoption in clinics has been slow despite the promise.

No results are reported; the protocol sets out the plan in full. Eleven databases will be searched for qualitative studies on what helps or blocks adoption. Two reviewers will screen studies independently, judge quality with a standard checklist, and rate confidence in the findings. Themes will then be combined. The authors aim to guide better design and rollout of speech screening.
pmc-13270538:
Peng Su, Si-Han Lin, and Fang-Xing Xiao design in 2026 a light-harvesting assembly where the wrapping on metal particles boosts electron tunneling through an insulating film. Classic designs sandwich a plain insulator between a semiconductor and a metal. Here a thin charged polymer coats light-absorbing crystals, and polymer-wrapped gold or palladium particles dock onto it by static attraction.

The wrapping is not passive: it couples with its metal core to form a joint electron trap that pulls charge hard. That pull drives electrons through the insulating layer from the excited crystal, bypassing the usual energy barrier. The assemblies then drove selective chemical conversions and hydrogen peroxide production under visible light more effectively. The authors offer the design as a new handle for programming charge flow in artificial photosynthesis.
pmc-13270738:
Lisa Gittel is lead author of a 2026 journal article on recruiting children and young people with vision impairment into clinical research. The experience came from SeeMyLife, a European multi-centre study of quality of life and participation for these young people, where weak recruitment can undermine a whole trial.

Staff from six countries, 17 in total, answered a survey, and the team also reviewed study emails and meeting notes. Workers used twelve recruitment sources, grouped into health settings, community and school settings, and professional routes. Using the hospital information system was rated most effective and was used by 71 percent of respondents. The article gathers what helped and what hindered enrolment.
pmc-13271138:
Carolyn Kloek wrote a 2026 perspective article arguing that coaching should be a core leadership skill in health care, not an outside service bought for executives. Health systems, she says, face problems that are complex and changing, while leaders still rely mainly on direct, technical fixes, so improvement efforts stall.

Kloek defines coaching here as learnable behaviours any leader can use: taking a coaching stance, listening across the organisation, and asking coaching questions. The proposed framework has three core behaviours and two organisational routines, meant to fit systems of any size. Early use at one academic health system shaped the framework, with outcome reporting promised later.
pmc-13271238:
Rafael Castelli is lead author of a 2026 journal article on compressing nanopore sequencing signals without losing any data. Nanopore machines read DNA by measuring electric current changes as a strand passes through a tiny channel. They produce vast signal files that are costly to store and send.

The authors present PDZ, a lossless compression method that beats the current standard, VBZ, on both squeeze and speed. Across data sets, the squeeze improved by a small margin, under three percent. Compression ran up to about twice as fast, and decompression was also faster. Against a rival with a similar squeeze, PDZ was notably faster both ways. The code is open and built into a standard file format.
pmc-13271438:
Abdulmujeeb Opeyemi Muhammad-Olodo is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on group discussion, of why caregivers in Kwara State, Nigeria, accept or refuse the HPV vaccine for girls. The vaccine prevents over 90 percent of cervical cancers, and Nigeria offered it free to girls aged nine to 14 from October 2023, yet uptake varied amid fertility rumours.

Five focus groups involved 41 caregivers, most of them women, with 35 acceptors and six decliners. Trust emerged at several levels: in government programmes, in health workers, and in religious and traditional leaders. Personal experience of cancer pushed acceptance, while historic medical mistrust, sharpened by COVID-19, fed fertility and population-control fears. Remote communities and language gaps also blocked access.
pmc-13272138:
Mengyu Luan and coauthors analyze in 2026 gene activity in tuberculous meningitis, the deadliest form of tuberculosis, where damage to the blood-brain barrier drives much of the harm. A protein called MARCKS, which helps organize the cell skeleton, appeared alongside the cell-bursting GSDMD pathway. The study blends several omics datasets with lab validation.

Three genes stood out as raised in patients, with MARCKS concentrated in microglia in a mouse model and also raised in patients' blood cells. Its levels moved together with key members of the inflammatory cell-death pathway. The authors position MARCKS as a hub linking inflammation and barrier breakdown, pending checks in human brain tissue.
pmc-13272238:
Wattanachai Ratanapornsompong is lead author of a 2026 case series on a robotic operation for ureteropelvic junction obstruction, a blockage where the kidney meets the ureter, the tube draining urine. The standard repair cuts the ureter, risking its blood supply, while this single-port robotic approach reshapes the junction with a Y-V flap without cutting it through.

Reviewing 21 patients treated between December 2020 and December 2024, median operating time was 109 minutes and median follow-up 73 weeks. Overall surgical success was 95 percent, with no complications during surgery, median blood loss of only 15 millilitres, and most patients discharged the same day. One patient re-blocked after stent removal and was fixed with a secondary scope procedure.
pmc-13273038:
Ni Wang and co-authors tested salvianolic acid B, a compound from a medicinal plant, against depression like behavior in a 2026 study. Depression involves brain inflammation, neuron damage, and poor growth of new neurons in the hippocampus. The team asked whether the compound protects the brain through one signaling pathway.

In lab cells injured by a stress hormone, the compound cut inflammation, oxidative stress, and cell death. In mice put through chronic mild stress, it improved behavior, calmed overactive immune cells in the brain, and reduced neuron death. New neuron growth and synaptic proteins also rose. The compound quieted the JAK-STAT pathway, and a drug that switches that pathway back on erased the benefit.
pmc-13273438:
Olivia Gilbert leads a 2026 illustrative case of a rare neuronal tumor in the sellar region of the skull base, where the pituitary gland sits. Such tumors mimic far more common pituitary growths, making diagnosis before surgery hard. The patient was a 40-year-old man with worsening vision loss in both outer fields, headaches, and partial pituitary failure.

MRI showed a mixed cystic and solid mass reaching into the cavernous sinus. Surgery through the nose removed as much as safely possible and relieved pressure on the optic nerves. After surgery, vision, headaches, and thyroid function improved. Tissue tests confirmed a neurocytoma with low growth activity, and the authors advise long surveillance and possible radiation if tumor remains.
pmc-13273538:
Lansaol Yang and a very large team reviewed sovereign AI supercomputers for biomedical research in a 2026 article. Governments now fund national AI systems on a scale the authors compare with Apollo and the Manhattan Project. Publicly owned machines promise secure computing for sensitive health data.

The review maps where these systems sit, what they can do, and how medicine uses them. Heavy tasks that gain most include cancer imaging, tailored treatment, genome and single cell analysis, and drug discovery. The authors describe their own United Kingdom project, which builds AI foundation models to speed cancer vaccine work. Governance sections weigh privacy, intellectual property, and cross border collaboration. The authors argue such infrastructure can deliver broad public benefit if rules keep pace.
pmc-13274138:
Carmen Correale and a large team report a 2026 journal article on protecting the gut during chemotherapy. The chemo drug 5-fluorouracil often injures the intestinal lining, causing pain and diarrhea that can force treatment cuts. The team tested rifaximin, an antibiotic that stays in the gut, and asked how it shields the lining.

In mice, rifaximin given before chemo reduced inflammation and tissue damage and kept the gut barrier sealed, without weakening the drug's anti-tumor effect. pmc-13275738:
Paul Gehret and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on rebuilding narrowed airways in young children. Severe subglottic stenosis, a tight narrowing just below the voice box, affects many infants each year. Surgeons now widen the airway with cartilage taken from a rib, but small children may not have enough to spare.

Ear cartilage starter cells filled it within three days and matured in three weeks. In rabbits, the grafts widened the airway, grew new cartilage, and healed without the problems seen in any of the animals studied. They beat rib cartilage on every measure the team checked.
pmc-13276038:
Xin Yan and co-authors wrote a 2026 letter reporting a study of survival prediction in a rare blood cancer. The disease, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, varies greatly between patients. Doctors use scoring systems to spot high-risk patients who may need a stem cell transplant early.

The team compared four scoring tools in one hundred twenty-seven Chinese patients treated at four hospitals. Two newer tools, named BLAST and BLAST-mol, use simple clinical measures like blast counts, white cell counts, and anemia. An older standard tool is called CPSS. As the title states, BLAST predicted survival more accurately than CPSS in this group. The older tool struggled to separate its two middle risk groups here. The newer tools had so far been tested only in Western patients.
pmc-13276338:
Moustafa Mansour and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on how traumatic brain injury scrambles the brain's networks. They treat the brain as a connectome, a web of regions and their connections. Injury is thus not just a local wound but a whole-network disorder, which helps explain why outcomes vary so much.

It covers cell-level and system-level flexibility, the brain scans used to measure network change, and the key split between helpful and harmful rewiring. pmc-13276938:
Chisato Matsuoka leads a 2026 laboratory study of plant compounds that may block a chemical from causing mutations, meaning harmful DNA changes. Earlier work showed two compounds from licorice blocked mutation by a nitrosamine chemical in bacteria. The team asked whether the compounds work by binding to DNA itself.

pmc-13277138:
Zubaida Bibi and Kausar Ali wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study on light-based testing for breast cancer. The study they discuss used diffuse reflectance spectroscopy, a method that reads how tissue reflects light, during biopsy of removed breast tissue. Bibi and Ali praise the optical design and the care taken to match results with tissue exams.

Labels from flat tissue slices may not match the three-dimensional volume the light probes. Outside testing on new patients is still missing.
pmc-13278738:
Yi-Huan Ou-Yang and co-authors slim down a brain signal algorithm for implantable stimulators in a 2026 paper. Adaptive deep brain stimulation for Parkinson disease reacts to bursts of beta rhythm in brain signals. Existing burst detectors are too heavy for small implanted chips to run.

Their redesign slices the search for peak frequency and shares information with a live-updating model. Tests on rat brain-surface recordings matched the standard method closely in output. Computing effort for the frequency search fell by more than half. The authors argue the savings make real-time biomarker tracking feasible inside future implants, a step toward stimulation that adjusts itself moment by moment.
pmc-13278938:
Jingxian Zhao and co-authors test a simple blood ratio for diagnosing overactive parathyroid glands in a 2026 study. Primary hyperparathyroidism comes in high-calcium and normal-calcium forms that can be hard to separate. Data came from 135 surgically confirmed patients and matched healthy controls at one Chinese centre.

A combined index of calcium, chloride, and phosphorus, read alongside the enzyme ALP, performed strongly. Together they separated patients from controls with accuracy close to the standard hormone test. The pair also distinguished the high-calcium form from the normal-calcium form better than rival measures. Telling gland overgrowth from a single adenoma worked less well, though still best among the options. The authors present the cheap panel as clinically practical.
pmc-13280338:
Yuming Huang and colleagues published a 2026 study of hybrid membrane nanovesicles built to calm the self-feeding inflammation behind intervertebral disc degeneration, a leading source of back pain. Failing discs lack blood vessels, so drugs reach them poorly. Activated macrophages plus oxidative stress keep damaging the tissue matrix. The team fused macrophage membranes with those of the disc's own nucleus pulposus cells into vesicles carrying two drugs, daphnetin and pioglitazone.

Gene tests showed inflammatory and matrix-destroying programs dialed down, while matrix building returned and fibrotic change was suppressed. In a rat model, treatment preserved disc structure and tissue quality and eased pain signs. The authors present this microenvironment-level reprogramming as a strategy worth developing for a condition current drugs barely touch.
pmc-13280638:
Bruno Azevedo Randi and colleagues published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of what happens when quinolone antibiotics are stopped in stem-cell transplant patients before the graft takes hold. Bloodstream infections are a danger in that window. Quinolones prevent many but breed resistant bacteria. Stopping the drugs did not raise infection-related death, and the resistance burden did not fall after stopping. pmc-13281438:
Lei Li and colleagues probed fungus enzymes that tailor natural poisons in a 2026 study. The poisons, called cytochalasans, freeze a cell's inner scaffold and affect many living things. Fungi build them with help from enzymes that add oxygen at set spots. Those enzymes are picky at home yet can accept near kin of their usual targets. The team mined gene maps of six fungi for hidden build plans. They then placed seven enzymes into a test fungus.

The work shows why some enzymes sat idle on the targets at hand. The authors say the mix-and-match method can scout enzymes as tools for green chemistry. It also helps read what new poisons a fungus might make.
pmc-13282238:
Nicola Luigi Bragazzi and co-authors wrote a 2026 systematic review on how to choose sample size before starting metabolomics studies. Metabolomics measures many small chemicals in the body at once. Picking too few samples weakens findings, while too many wastes resources. The field's data are complex and highly variable, making that choice hard.

They mapped the methods now used for sample size and power checks in metabolic profiling and combined multi-layer studies. Gaps and limits in those methods are set out plainly. The review aims to give researchers a practical frame for planning stronger studies. It also points to where better tools are still needed, so future work can rest on firmer ground from the start.
pmc-13282338:
Lenka Hapakova and co-authors report a 2026 study linking reflexive eye movements to hidden impulsive-compulsive behaviours in Parkinson's disease. Parkinson's harms movement control and can also bring urges such as gambling or overeating, often tied to its dopamine drugs. Subclinical forms, below clear diagnosis, are common and missed. The team tested twenty-nine patients and twenty healthy peers on tasks where they had to look toward or away from a target.

Patients made more very fast eye movements toward targets and were slower on the look-away task, a sign of weak inhibition. Within the patient group, fast movements tracked the severity of hidden impulsive behaviours and drug dose. They also tracked lower quality of life. Statistical modelling suggested drug dose acted partly through those behaviours. The authors say eye tracking offers an objective window on this vulnerability.
pmc-13282738:
Qinyi Yu and colleagues reported in 2026 that a protein called WDR82 acts against breast cancer growth. Levels of the protein run low in human breast tumours, and low levels track with worse outlook. The study asked how this protein shapes the immune setting around a tumour.

With that signal off, tumour cells make less of two chemokines, CXCL2 and CXCL7, which draw neutrophils toward the tumour. Delivering WDR82 into tumours in mice slowed tumour growth. The findings point to this pathway as a possible route for new breast cancer treatments.
pmc-13282938:
David M Anderson, Dylan Nagy, and Coleman Drake examined in 2026 whether wider access to bare-bones health plans changed sign-ups in the United States insurance Marketplaces. In late 2025, federal guidance let many more people buy catastrophic plans, which carry low monthly costs but very high deductibles and no premium subsidies. Before, such plans were mostly limited to people under thirty or with hardship status.

The study design compares counties where catastrophic plans were on sale with counties where they never were, before and after the change. That design separates the policy effect from wider trends in sign-ups. The question matters because subsidy holders already had cheap standard options, so the wider access may have moved sign-ups only a little.
pmc-13283138:
Takeshi Murata and colleagues asked in 2026 whether tiny lymph node deposits change outlook in a high-risk form of early breast cancer. The cancer type feeds on hormones and lacks the HER2 marker. A past trial, monarchE, set high-risk rules that let in both large node deposits, called macrometastases, and tiny ones, called micrometastases, yet it never reported how the tiny-deposit group fared.

The team reviewed 844 patients and sorted them by deposit size, tumour grade, and tumour size. Five-year results for the tiny-deposit high-risk group closely matched the large-deposit group on both disease-free and distant relapse measures. Tumour size, not deposit type, was the factor tied to outcomes. The findings support treating both groups as truly high risk.
pmc-13284438:
Wing Fai Yeung and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial in Hong Kong on self-administered acupressure for depression. Adults with moderate depression were split between acupressure training and mental health education, with the same contact time in each arm. The acupressure group had two training sessions, then daily practice for 12 weeks.

A total of 250 adults took part. The acupressure group showed a larger drop in PHQ-9 depression scores at weeks 4, 8, and 12 than the education group, though the gains were small in size. No serious harmful events were reported. The authors present the low-cost self-help program as a possible added option for moderate depression in community settings.
pmc-13285438:
Young people who use opioids speak for themselves in a 2026 commentary by Atika Juristia and co-authors, members of an international Youth RISE cohort formed in 2023. The group spans Canada, Indonesia, Kenya, Mexico, Uganda, and the United States. Weekly online talks over two months traded views on needs, hurdles, and fixes in each home country.

Their shared call moves past punishment toward care built for young people: drug checking, supervised use spaces, naloxone access, prescribed safer options, and honest drug teaching. They also urge real youth voice in policy and action against stigma and watchful, abstinence-only systems.
pmc-13285538:
Star-shaped support cells do far more than prop up neurons, Lihui Qian and co-authors stress in a 2026 review on the aging brain. Astrocytes run much of the brain fuel trade, handing neurons building blocks and clearing spent signals. The review maps how astrocyte shape and genes vary by brain zone, then tracks their fuel swaps with neurons.

Glucose, fats, and glutamate handling, lactate shuttling, and signals from cell power plants all get covered. Animal work ties breaks in this buddy system to age-linked brain ills. Restoring a sound fuel partnership, the authors argue, could form a fresh therapy lane for aging brains, since neurons fail when their support cells falter.
pmc-13285638:
Neutron bursts wound many organs at once, with harm that shifts by dose and time, Tracy Gasperetti and co-authors chart in a 2026 rat study. Such exposure threatens people after nuclear accidents and even on deep-space trips. Male and female rats took whole-body fast neutron doses with slight bone marrow shielding, then faced a year of checks.

Weight, blood counts, breathing, kidney tests, and urine profiles all drifted with dose and time. Altered urine proteins pointed to oxidative stress and kidney strain.
pmc-13285738:

pmc-13285938:
Alexis Ferré and co-authors study repeat intensive care stays for severe COPD flare-ups in a 2026 French cohort study. The team compared patients with one intensive care stay against those who came back again and again between 2015 and 2022.

Repeat patients were younger, had better daily function at first, and showed higher counts of one white cell type in blood. Death within a year struck both groups at much the same rate. pmc-13287038:

pmc-13287138:

pmc-13287838:

pmc-13288038: Zhi Yang and co-authors issued this 2026 correction for their study of Epstein-Barr viral load and hospital stay length in children with infectious mononucleosis. The notice is a correction only, fixing author unit lines and adding no new findings. One unit name was fixed from nephrology to pediatric nephrology, and the Department of Pediatric Infectious Disease was restored for three authors. pmc-13288538:

pmc-13289138:

pmc-13289238:

pmc-13289338:

pmc-13289438:
Wenchuan Zhou, Xuanyi Chen, Jiagen Li, and Jincan He report a 2026 mouse and cell study on nanoplastic harm to the retina. Tiny polystyrene particles can now reach body tissues, yet eye effects were little known. pmc-13289638:

Four reviewers screened and graded the material, with two sleep doctors pulling out the core advice. A total of 31 recommendations fell into five domains, from guiding principles and lifestyle steps to talk therapy for insomnia, medicines, and added options. Family support and stress care run throughout.
pmc-13289838:

Each vertebra got the authors' refined Modified Slide method on one side and a standard method on the other side at random. Screws then faced repeated up-down loading until loosening or a top load cap. The refined method outlasted the Slide and Funnel methods by wide margins in cycles. It fell slightly short of the Conventional method instead.
pmc-13289938:

Both steps were seen in mouse and cell tests.
pmc-13290438:

The cohort held 722 emergency trauma patients admitted between January 2021 and November 2023, and 33.1% of them developed sepsis during care. After adjustment, each rise in CONUT score came with higher sepsis odds, while each rise in PNI came with lower odds, and both links bent rather than running straight. pmc-13290638:
A pregnancy hormone test said no, yet a chronic ectopic pregnancy was there, Shushu Yu and colleagues warn in a 2026 case report. Their patient carried an adnexal mass with ongoing abdominal pain, a picture that pointed the team first toward a tumor.

The woman's serum β-HCG was negative nearly three months after a curettage, which is exactly why the diagnosis slipped. They urge clinicians to keep the condition in mind for women with adnexal masses and persistent pain, test or no test.
pmc-13290738:
Replacing a neck disc instead of fusing it looks just as safe in women with osteoporosis, Kikelola Afolabi-Brown and colleagues report in a matched cohort study from 2026. Comparative data in this fragile group have been scarce even though both operations are standard for cervical disease.

From the PearlDiver national database, the team identified 678 women aged 55 and over with osteoporosis who had single-level disc replacement (170) or fusion (508) between 2010 and 2022. Ninety-day medical and surgical complication rates matched between the groups, as did every measure of later health care use at 30 days, 90 days, and two years. The authors conclude replacement can be offered safely with an administrative osteoporosis diagnosis, while calling for studies that sort patients by measured bone density.
pmc-13290938:
A young woman kept her uterus after a rare womb cancer and later delivered a healthy baby, E. Ziegler and colleagues describe in a case report from 2026. The 29-year-old's bleeding led to removal of a polyp that proved to be uterine adenosarcoma, an uncommon tumor usually treated by hysterectomy.

pmc-13291238:

pmc-13291338:

pmc-13291738: Zhibing Gong and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of quality of life in patients with bruising after total knee replacement surgery. The notice fixes two numbers in the Results text: the osteoarthritis count becomes 122 cases, and left-knee cases become 63, matching the total of 138 patients. Table 1 was already correct, and the authors state that the errors do not change the findings or conclusions. Only the correction notice itself is available here, so the original study's methods and results cannot be described from it.
pmc-13291938:

pmc-13292038:

pmc-13292338:
Muhammad Alaa Eldeen and a large team profile a 2026 pan-cancer suspect, LSM12, a protein involved in RNA processing that had never been mapped across tumor types. pmc-13292438:

pmc-13292538:

Self-management, living with illness as an adult, and keeping healthy dominated, often anchored to the bodily changes of adolescence. Doctors sounded dialogic and supportive, yet the script stayed prescriptive about responsibility and adult health behavior. The authors say transition programs quietly produce ideas of autonomy and adulthood, and that naming that process could improve practice.
pmc-13292638:
Yanhua Li's team compares a 2026 pair of gut scores for predicting short-term fate in intensive care: the newer gastrointestinal dysfunction score, GIDS, against the established acute gastrointestinal injury grade. Their secondary analysis drew on two prospective cohorts, a single-center group of 1,091 patients and the multicentre NEED trial with 904, all with organ failure on admission.

Death by day 28 struck 20.2 percent of the first cohort and 13.4 percent of the second in the data. Each extra point on either score raised mortality risk by a similar hazard, about 1.45 to 1.49 per point in the main cohort. Overall discrimination tied, but GIDS separated outcomes better in the sickest patients and tracked ICU-free days more consistently. Validation in the second cohort held. The authors give GIDS an edge where illness runs deepest.
pmc-13293738:
Akira Kimura links, in a 2026 ecological study, car-bound daily life in Japan to deaths from stroke, diabetes, and care needs across all 47 prefectures from 2013 to 2022. Built environments that block walking may carry a population death cost that town planning has not priced.

Prefectures where more people could only commute by car had higher stroke and diabetes deaths and heavier long-term care loads. Stroke links held through all adjustment rounds. In 2020, when COVID-19 cut movement, the most car-bound third of prefectures saw excess stroke deaths of 8.3%, a rise the author reports, while other areas saw near none. Walkable design gains a health case.
pmc-13293838:
A 2026 review by Zheng Tai Kuai and colleagues centers on CHCHD3, also called MIC19, a core part of the MICOS system that shapes folds inside mitochondria. Those folds, called cristae, support energy production. The authors pull together what is known about the protein structure, its chemical modifications, and its links to cell metabolism and death.

Both too little and too much CHCHD3 can disturb balance, a pattern the authors call a Goldilocks effect. Faulty function is tied to brain disorders, heart disease, metabolic problems, and cancers. The review weighs early drug ideas, notes their limits, and flags open questions that block clinical use.
pmc-13294638:
Ali Devebacak, Müge Yılmaz, and Gül Arıkan compare four formulas for choosing artificial lens power during cataract surgery, in a 2026 study of eyes that also received a capsular tension ring. The ring steadies the lens capsule in eyes with weak supports, but it may shift where the lens sits and bend formula accuracy. Ninety-eight eyes from ninety-two patients were measured before surgery with swept-source optical scanning, then checked against the glasses prescription they actually needed.

Two formulas, Barrett Universal II and Holladay II, predicted the outcome most closely, with clearly smaller average errors than the Haigis and SRK/T formulas. Barrett placed just over half of eyes within a quarter diopter of target. Every formula leaned slightly toward farsightedness after surgery. Surgeons choosing target refractions for ring cases, the authors note, should factor in that gentle shift.
pmc-13294838:
Jonathan Shaw and co-authors present a 2026 case report on severe self-injury in a young man with schizophrenia. Non-suicidal self-injury is common in schizophrenia spectrum illness and can suddenly escalate into major self-mutilation. The authors suspect a copycat influence, known as social contagion, played a part here.

The 25-year-old patient arrived after tying ligatures around several fingers on both hands. A closely similar case in nearby Los Angeles county raised concern that one event may have prompted the other. The report argues for ongoing screening for self-harm in psychotic illness and for watching how severe presentations can spread between patients.
pmc-13294938:
Banpot Klinpratoom and a team of analysts build a faster, greener way to pull toxic metals out of tricky samples, in a 2026 methods study. Lead, cadmium, and arsenic hide inside herbs, cosmetics, drinks, and wastewater, and labs must extract them before measuring. The method uses ultrasound, whose tiny collapsing bubbles shake metals loose from the sample in dilute acid, cutting both time and reagent use. Galangal root served as the test plant.

A statistical design varied acid strength, soaking time, and acid volume to find the sweet spot, landing on moderate acid, about eleven minutes of ultrasound, and a mid-sized volume. Recoveries at those settings landed close to one hundred percent for all three metals, with low interference from the sample matrix. Checks against reference materials scored well, and the method held up across seven galangal varieties and several product types. The authors offer it for routine safety surveillance.
pmc-13295738:
Guolin Yang and colleagues study moisture handling in alfalfa silage in a 2026 article. Water level decides how well cut alfalfa ferments in storage, yet spraying water back after wilting is poorly understood. Four treatments compared plain wilting with wilt-then-spray at two target moisture levels over 90 days.

Sprayed batches ended with lower acidity and fewer spoilage signs than plain wilted batches at the same moisture. Milk-acid bacteria dominated every batch, above 97 percent of the microbe community, led by Lactobacillus. Yeast counts ran lower in sprayed silage, and chemical profiles shifted toward phenolic acids and fats, explaining the cleaner fermentation.
pmc-13295838:
Junaid Abdul Razzak and colleagues report a cluster-randomised pilot trial from 2026 on ambulance telemedicine for sick children in Karachi, Pakistan. Ten ambulances were split between live video support from child specialists and usual care, after practice runs with simulated cases.

Of 166 parents approached, 151 agreed to take part, and calls were completed for nearly all children. Sound and picture quality scored well, no contact was judged unsafe, and early warning scores were recorded for every child in the ambulance. The authors conclude that remote support during transport can work safely where resources are limited, and they call for larger trials of its effect on care.
pmc-13296038:
Lisine Tuyisenge and colleagues describe, in 2026, a six-year programme to improve newborn care in Rwanda. Deaths among newborns had stopped falling fast, with most now occurring inside facilities from prematurity, birth asphyxia and infection.

Working across 21 hospitals, Rwandan and British paediatric bodies paired bedside training and mentoring with hospital-run quality projects. In twelve hospitals with full data, deaths among admitted newborns fell by nearly half between 2017 and 2023, and core care measures improved. The team also name system strains, from staff rotation to patchy supplies, that shape whether gains last.
pmc-13296338:
Antonio Sarria-Santamera and co-authors examine how health policy shapes use of first-choice antibiotics in Kazakhstan in a 2026 nationwide study. The focus is the Access group in the World Health Organization system, the antibiotics meant for routine first use. Consumption data from 2017 to 2024 were analysed alongside the policies governing availability and prescribing.

Access antibiotic use fell through 2023, then rebounded in 2024, still missing the recommended sixty percent share of total use. Fifty Access products were unavailable in the country, including nine on the essential medicines list. National care standards often favoured Watch antibiotics or antibiotics where none were indicated. The authors call for coordinated reform of registration rules, standards, and stewardship.
pmc-13296938:
Xena C. Montoya and colleagues test, in 2026, whether realistic cloudy water harms fish gills and stamina across species. Suspended solids rise with land use and climate shifts, and most prior work used one species, so five kinds, from trout to minnows, were exposed for four days.

A mid-level dose damaged gills in every species tested. Trout and minnows also lost metabolic capacity and swam worse. The authors warn that sediment-laden water leaves fish short of energy for fleeing predators or handling stress. Their results argue for tighter control of solids entering streams.
pmc-13297238:
London P. McGill and colleagues test CRISPR guides that knock out a drug-resistance gene in pancreatic cancer cells in a 2026 feasibility study. The gene, NRF2, acts as a master switch for cellular defences. Guides aimed at different parts of the gene were delivered into tumour cells and scored by genetic and functional tests.

Editing rates ranged widely between guides, with heavy random insertions and deletions at cut sites. Guides hitting three middle exons produced the strongest combined effects. Disrupting two of them cut cell survival and restored sensitivity to the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine. The authors identify the sweet spots for a deeper study of this resistance-breaking strategy.
pmc-13297538:
A sugar-binding protein in zebrafish blocks a fish virus at more than one point of attack, Kelsey Abernathy and her team show in a 2026 study. They asked how the galectin Drgal1-L2 stops infectious hematopoietic necrosis virus from latching onto the cells that line the fish.

Past work showed the protein grips the virus coat and slows it down. The new tests add targets on the host side. The galectin binds fibronectin, the cell protein the virus uses as its dock. It also binds β1 integrin, which the virus stuck to in tests and may use as a back door. A coat of the galectin on either side cut how much virus could attach, and binding to mucus sugars added one more shield.
pmc-13298038:
Dan Cristian Luca and colleagues issued a 2026 correction clarifying the methods behind their review of progress toward cervical cancer elimination under the World Health Organization strategy. The core evidence base came from a structured search with set inclusion rules, which yielded the studies used for the main analysis. A larger table also drew on reviews, guidelines, reports, and datasets for context.

Because that mix differs from a conventional systematic review, the article type and title change to signal a literature review with narrative synthesis. Secondary sources support interpretation only, not scoring against the elimination targets. The authors state the data and overall conclusions remain unchanged.
pmc-13298538:
Pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma is rare enough that its behavior is still being charted, and Yoon Suk Lee with colleagues assembled 37 South Korean cases in a 2026 multicenter study. They reviewed how these tumors look on imaging, who gets them, and how patients fare.

About a fifth of patients were diagnosed before age 50, a broader spread than typical pancreatic cancer. Scans usually showed large, weakly enhancing solid masses, though some lit up brightly or mixed solid and cystic parts. Despite their size, the tumors tended to be well circumscribed and often removable, giving surgery a real chance at long survival, a contrast with the usual pancreatic cancer outlook.
pmc-13299138:
Eva Charlotte Rogasch and Marie Bergner scan YouTube videos for consumer risks from epoxy resin craft projects, in a 2026 public health study. Epoxy can sensitise skin and cause contact allergy, historically an occupational problem now appearing among consumers. Roughly two hundred popular videos showing do-it-yourself resin work received analysis.

Projects covered decorative objects, jewellery, lamps, tabletops, counters, and floors, with uploads growing in recent years. In a large share of videos, makers wore no gloves while handling resin. Because popular videos double as tutorials, the authors warn that missing protective measures may spread unsafe habits and raise allergy risk among home users.
pmc-13299238:
A ginseng compound slowed colon cancer in mice by reshaping gut bacteria and their chemistry, report Linqian Lu and co-authors in a 2026 study. Mice given cancer-inducing chemicals received ginsenoside Rh1 at 100 mg per kilogram daily for six weeks.

Treated mice showed lower disease activity, longer colons, and fewer tumors. Their gut communities grew more diverse, with more Lactobacillus, and produced more indole compounds from tryptophan, which strengthened the gut barrier and calmed inflammatory cytokines. The treatment also cut an immune-suppressing enzyme, IDO1, lifting brakes on killer T cells. The authors connect the benefit to a chain running from microbes to metabolism to immunity.
pmc-13299938:
Jia Yin Ruan leads a team developing a Traditional Chinese Medicine lifestyle programme for depression through a stepwise multi-method process, in a 2026 study set in Hong Kong. Evidence review, a Delphi expert survey, context analysis, and programme theory building shaped the final design. Few earlier studies had documented such development transparently, the authors note.

The finished programme runs six weekly two-hour sessions under three themes covering heart nourishment, living by seasonal timing, and energy nourishment. Content spans sleep, diet, stress management, self-acupressure, and traditional exercise, with teaching materials prepared. A mixed-methods clinical study will now test feasibility, acceptability, and early effects on depression.
pmc-13300538:
M S Shehada and colleagues ask whether pulsed field ablation changes resting heart rate, in a 2026 single-center study. Heat based ablation often damages nerve clusters near the pulmonary veins and speeds the resting heart, while the newer non-thermal energy is thought to spare them. The analysis covered fifty-three patients with mixed forms of atrial fibrillation treated with a pentaspline catheter, comparing resting rates before ablation and within a day afterward.

Mean resting rate barely moved, from about seventy-one beats per minute before the procedure to about seventy afterward, a non-significant shift. Individual patients rose and fell in near equal numbers. One nuance emerged after adjustment: delivering more lesions was tied to a slightly lower post-procedure rate, roughly two beats per minute per ten extra lesions. The authors read the overall picture as autonomic preservation, sparing patients unwanted speeding of the heart.
pmc-13300838:
Abdulelah F Alshehri and co-authors review randomized trials of antibiotic stewardship for children with chest and airway infections in a 2026 paper. Most such infections are viral, yet antibiotics flow freely in outpatient care for children. So the team grouped trial interventions by how they work. Groups covered education, shared decision making, diagnostic guidance, and digital support. They then checked how well each style curbed prescribing.

Eight trials met criteria, and their results were mixed, so pooled statistics were not possible. Interventions built on accountability pushed use down, or toward better fit, most reliably. Such designs used audit with performance feedback, or asked for a reason when prescribing. Communication training, shared decision tools, diagnostic-led approaches, and stand-alone digital aids showed inconsistent or neutral effects. Where safety data existed, leaner use did not raise return visits or hospital stays. The authors back stewardship designs with several parts at once.
pmc-13301238:
Pengfei Wang and co-authors build a reinforced gel foam meant to shield wood and vegetation from forest fire in a 2026 materials study. Their recipe folds a plant derived cellulose polymer and nanosilica sol into a water glass base, forming a hybrid network held by hydrogen bonds, chain tangles, and nanoscale filling. The team benchmarked the foam against the plain gel and a version with the cellulose alone.

The full composite kept about twenty percent of its mass after five hours at one hundred degrees, several times the plain gel's retention. Under direct flame it survived about 164 seconds before carbonizing, against one hundred for the base gel, and it left seventy-six percent residue at eight hundred degrees in testing. Microscopy tied the gains to a dense silica rich crust that slows heat reaching the wood. The authors present the foam as a barrier material under laboratory screening conditions.
pmc-13301638:
Ayyad Zartasht Khan and co-authors gather scar hiding tricks in direct brow lift surgery in a 2026 review. The operation lifts brows through a cut above the brow. It is unmatched for control of height and shape, but the scar sits in plain sight. The authors searched a decade of studies and distilled ten publications covering nine hundred patients into a summary of what keeps it hidden.

Four habits recur: beveling the cut so hairs regrow through the scar, lifting the skin over a centimeter or two while sparing fat. Two more habits: anchoring the flap to the bone lining so skin closes without tension, and closing in layers with everting stitches. Added measures split: silicone gel evidence stayed unclear, while laser treatment and relaxing injections around surgery improved appearance. Across studies, over eighty-five percent of scars ended unnoticed, with high satisfaction, supporting the operation's refined survival.
pmc-13302038:
V Leitermann and co-authors examine exercise testing safety in a 2026 study of a rare inherited rhythm disorder tied to the CACNA1C gene. This form of long QT syndrome stretches the heart's electrical recovery and can cause cardiac arrest, sometimes in early childhood. Families face hard questions about safe physical activity.

Fitness levels averaged modestly below predicted values, and a few patients showed stray extra beats during testing. One patient showed frequent extra beats with short runs of fast rhythm, yet nobody fainted or arrested across all tests. The authors conclude that supervised testing on treatment appears safe and that exercise should be encouraged.
pmc-13302438:
K Krieger and A Wutzler published a 2026 comparison of two bedside devices that measure activated clotting time during heart ablation procedures. Thirty patients on continued oral anticoagulants contributed 55 paired measurements taken at the same moments. The mechanical and optical system read higher by an average of 61.5 seconds, a gap the paired test found highly consistent. At a 250 second safety threshold, the two devices judged very different shares of patients adequately treated, 90 percent against 46.6 percent in the comparison. The authors warn that a single cutoff applied across devices risks too little or too much anticoagulation.
pmc-13303338:
A dental mouthpiece eased both sleep apnea and depression in a 2026 case report by Angela Mirea Bellocchio and colleagues. Their patient, a fifty-eight-year-old woman with moderate obstructive sleep apnea and major depressive disorder, refused CPAP because of psychological discomfort with the mask. Apneic events fell, oxygen saturation rose, and her mood improved noticeably, all while her psychiatric medication stayed unchanged. The authors credit the better sleep and highlight interdisciplinary teamwork for patients whose mental health blocks first-line therapy. One case cannot set policy, but it widens the option set for CPAP-intolerant patients.
pmc-13304338:

Methanol is toxic and hard to spot by eye, yet conventional sensors need very hot working surfaces that waste power and age quickly. A one-pot water-based synthesis set the zinc content at zero, two, and four percent.

All sensors peaked at a reduced working temperature, well below the usual range for such devices. Response to a standard methanol dose climbed steeply with zinc content, nearly tripling at the highest doping. The sensors stayed selective against similar vapours and could detect methanol down to a few parts per million. The authors credit engineered defects and better charge movement inside the doped material.
pmc-13304938:
Jiakai Wang and co-authors review plant chemicals in pulses, the dry seeds of legume crops, and their gut benefits in a 2026 synthesis. Beans, lentils, and peas carry rich phenolic compounds whose effects depend on gut microbes.

These compounds calm oxidation and inflammation, support the gut barrier, and act like prebiotics that feed helpful microbes. Such actions may ease bowel problems linked to chronic disease. Farming and processing tricks including sprouting, fermenting, and physical treatments can raise compound levels before eating. Better grasp of these pathways could guide new functional foods built on everyday pulses.
pmc-13305338:
Luan Prado, Ryan Musich, and co-authors profile, in a 2026 study, urine proteins at hospital admission in alcohol-associated liver disease, hunting markers in the complement system. pmc-13305638:

pmc-13306038: Thorsten Rudroff published a fix in 2026 to his 2024 review of AI as a stand-in for animal tests in neurology. The notice is a correction only: Table 1 carried wrong sources, and cite changes follow through several sections. The first source list held faulty cites from a layout slip in drafting. Rudroff states the findings stand as before, the journal editor signed off, and the first article has been updated.
pmc-13306738:

In the featured case, combined imaging plus spinal fluid findings pointed toward demyelination rather than cancer, guiding care away from needless invasive steps. pmc-13307438:

pmc-13308338:

pmc-13308538:

Adults were spotted more often than young snakes on the path itself in these staged runs. Most tourists showed calm interest, with few showing strong fear or hostile acts. pmc-13309138:

The family freed the bat and sought no care, since no bite mark showed and the bat seemed calm at the time. pmc-13309438:

The authors suggest self-rated standing deserves a place in cancer care research.
pmc-13309538: Hai Wang is first named among the authors of a 2015 article on a hybrid nanoplatform for delivery of theranostic agents, retracted by a 2026 note in Nature Communications. pmc-13309738:
Jian-mei Gong and colleagues describe a man whose lupus first appeared as pancreas and spleen damage in a 2026 case report. The 50-year-old patient arrived with belly pain as an early symptom, and kidney failure joined the picture. Fast diagnosis and immune-suppressing treatment reversed organ damage in this case. Male patients sit outside the usual pattern, which adds to the risk of late recognition. The authors urge clinicians to keep lupus in mind when several organs fail at once without a clear cause.
pmc-13309938:

Scans showed swollen kidneys and then a kidney abscess, while standard cultures stayed negative and fever persisted. Only prolonged culture and targeted testing on day five named the germ. The authors stress directed testing when fragile patients fail to improve.
pmc-13310638:

All pregnancies were unplanned singletons, all patients used injected semaglutide into part of the first trimester, and all were overweight or obese at baseline in the series. No major fetal anomalies were found, and no patient lost weight during pregnancy. The authors add the series to counseling evidence.
pmc-13310838:

All marker ratios fell sharply over the month, while white cell mixes shifted back toward calm. Ranges given here may help staff spot abnormal paths early.
pmc-13310938:

pmc-13311138:

pmc-13311638:

Two blood samples are drawn from each new line, one from the first backflow and one after flushing. Lab tests based on clot firmness and plasma assays will compare how much each brand stirs clotting. The results could steer catheter choice for safer care.
pmc-13311938:
Holly Morgan and co-authors survey postmortem checking of implanted heart devices across the United Kingdom in a 2026 study. Device data can explain sudden death, yet practice after death is unclear.

Each mortuary handled about 2400 deaths a year, with an estimated 5 percent having a device in place. Only 15 of 75 sites with heart physiology on site checked devices routinely after death. Findings rarely reached records or care teams. The authors see a missed source of answers for families and coroners.
pmc-13312538:

Obesity care, it says, should be judged by a wider set of patient-centred outcomes.
pmc-13312738:
Maria Regina Torloni and co-authors write a 2026 commentary challenging the trustworthiness judgments behind the 2025 Cochrane review of calcium supplements in pregnancy. The update concluded the supplement may do little or nothing, a reversal driven mainly by dropping trials judged untrustworthy.

The same trials passed as trustworthy in a sister Cochrane review updated in 2024, and sensitivity checks show that restoring the two examples would shift the pooled preeclampsia estimate significantly. They urge a reassessment of every excluded trial and warn that unvalidated trustworthiness tools can bend guidelines.
pmc-13312838:
