pmc-13313038:
Marie-Francoise Van Bressem and co-authors describe, in a 2026 study, a rare skull deformity in a northern bottlenose whale that stranded on the Rhode Island coast in 1867. Pathology in this deep-diving beaked whale is almost unreported, so the team examined the museum specimen's skull and fourteen cranial measurements against two normal adult females of the species.

Her right pterygoid bone was misshapen, its far end curving outward. A large bulbous bony growth swelled from its base and partly blocked the right nasal passage, with pitted resorption craters at the growth's rear. The left pterygoid sat thin and displaced. Without tissue samples no firm diagnosis was possible, but the growth resembled an osteoma, a benign tumor familiar from the jaws of horses and cattle. Since the female was lactating when she died, the authors judge her general fitness held despite the obstruction.
pmc-13313238:
Vinita Jagannath leads a phase 3 trial report, published in 2026, on a pneumococcal vaccine for children at higher risk. Pneumococcal disease brings much illness and death, above all in young children, older adults, and people with lasting health problems, so at-risk children are often urged to get extra doses.

The STRIDE-13 study tested V116, a vaccine covering 21 types of the bacterium, against the older PPSV23 vaccine. Children aged 2 to under 18 years with set health problems, such as diabetes or lasting lung or heart disease, took part after finishing their first vaccine series. The trial weighed safety, tolerance, and the strength of immune response in this group. Its results can guide which vaccine at-risk children should get for the best guard.
pmc-13313738:
Kiran Paudel and a multinational team survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, cannabis use among men who have sex with men in Nepal's Kathmandu Valley. This population faces elevated cannabis-related risks, yet Nepali data were absent. Using respondent-driven sampling between October and December 2022, the researchers recruited 250 participants. They modeled which characteristics accompanied cannabis use in the past six months.

About 27.3 percent had ever used cannabis and 15.6 percent had used it recently. Odds of recent use fell with age. They rose sharply among single participants and those detained by police at least once, and daily tobacco smokers also showed higher odds. Two healthcare factors protected. Seeing a doctor in the last six months and having a trusted provider both came with much lower odds of use. The authors direct prevention attention toward young, single, daily-smoking men. Regular, trusted healthcare contact, they argue, may be a lever against use.
pmc-13314538:
Yunyi Wang and co-authors dissect, in a 2026 study, how a stress master-switch helps colorectal cancer spread. Tumors must survive low oxygen and oxidative attack to metastasize. Across cohorts and cell lines the team found the switch protein HIF-1 alpha raised with two metabolic workers: a glucose importer and the fat-building enzyme FASN, strongly in metastatic deposits. Tumor cell subpopulations with the highest switch activity cloned and invaded, and seeded more lung tumors in animals.

Signals through insulin pathways fed the program, letting cells run fat production, sugar burning, and antioxidant defense. Dividing the labor, FASN bought resistance to oxidative injury while the glucose importer bought tolerance of low oxygen. A nanoparticle-wrapped drug that blocks the switch shut three programs down, stalled tumor growth, and eliminated lung metastasis in models. The authors nominate this stress state as a drug target in metastatic colorectal cancer.
pmc-13314738:
Di Zhang and co-workers ask whether MRI traits of a worn knee match its pain pattern, in one 2026 study. Knee osteoarthritis pain comes in flavors: steady, on-and-off, both, or none, and which joint changes drive each kind was unclear.

The team used a big American cohort visit with 6631 knees from 3494 people, as counted in the report. Pain was classed by a set score into no pain, constant pain, intermittent pain, or both. Scans from a 3T machine were graded by a standard atlas, and deep learning gave odds for bone, cartilage, inflammation, and growth patterns in each knee. Those patterns, plus cartilage measures, differed clearly across the pain groups and rose in steps from no pain upward, as reported. The link may help match scan findings to the pain a patient feels.
pmc-13315138:
Jiawei Zhao and a team examine, in a 2026 study, how often stents placed during heart attack treatment end up deployed suboptimally under the eye of optical coherence tomography. That imaging method sees stent expansion and tissue protrusion in fine detail. Between January 2018 and December 2020 the researchers enrolled 881 heart attack patients, covering 906 lesions. All were stented and imaged, then tracked for device events over a median of four years.

Three imaging findings predicted failure: a minimum stent area under 4.5 square millimeters, tissue protrusion, and narrowing of the vessel's distal reference segment. Patients whose stents met the study's suboptimal definition suffered more of the composite endpoint, driven by cardiac death and repeat procedures on that lesion. In a subgroup imaged before treatment, ruptured plaque, cholesterol crystals, and a smaller reference lumen predicted who would end up suboptimal. The authors argue earlier imaging can flag lesions needing care at deployment.
pmc-13315438:
Masuho Saburi and co-authors report a single case in 2026 of leukemia returning without its target marker after targeted therapy. A 69-year-old woman with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cleared standard chemotherapy but still had measurable leftover disease, then reached negativity after one cycle of blinatumomab, a T-cell engaging drug aimed at CD19.

Treatment stopped early at her request, and relapse came three months later. The returning blasts had lost CD19 but kept inner CD22, and chromosome tests looked normal instead of the earlier extra-chromosome pattern. A CD22-directed drug gave a second remission, though control did not last. The case warns about marker loss.
pmc-13315638:
Akash Kumar Sinha and Prasad Garimella report in 2026 a case of fast, severe septic shock from pneumococcal blood infection with no pneumonia on early scans. A 48-year-old woman with a healthy immune system arrived with very low blood pressure, high lactate, low platelets, kidney injury, and breathing failure.

Blood cultures grew Streptococcus pneumoniae, a germ usually tied to lung infection, yet chest X-ray and CT scans showed no focal pneumonia at first. Later scans did show patchy changes at both lung bases. Checks ruled out heart valve and brain membrane infection. Strong resuscitation and targeted antibiotics brought rapid recovery, stressing early suspicion.
pmc-13316238:
Peiyan Sun and colleagues updated in 2026 a network comparison of treatments for small liver cancer, following PRISMA 2020 rules. Searches of three databases from 2021 to March 2026 gathered randomized trials of surgery, heat ablation methods, arterial chemo infusion, radiotherapy, and their combinations.

Forty-one trials with 5,804 patients entered the component network analysis. Outcomes were overall survival, recurrence-free survival, and complication rates, with subgroup and regression checks probing weak spots. Splitting combinations into parts helps show which element drives benefit, guiding choices among many options for early liver tumors. Safety was weighed beside survival in each match-up. The update builds on two earlier published analyses of the same clinical question.
pmc-13316738:
Rachel Gottlieb-Smith leads a 2026 education study that used health record data to map what child neurology residents actually see during training. New doctors often feel unready for solo practice, yet the spread of cases behind that feeling was poorly measured.

Records for 11 residents over eleven months yielded 3,109 meaningful outpatient and 4,469 inpatient encounters, sorted by an algorithm for teaching value. Diagnosis codes were matched to the national board exam blueprint across 385 categories, capturing 90.0 percent of clinic codes in the mapping. Epilepsy and migraine led clinic work, while stroke and convulsions led ward work. Over half the exam areas appeared less in real care than on the test, a gap programs can now target.
pmc-13316838:
Begüm Turan Maviş and Ahmet Yasin Aktaş compared, in a 2026 dental study, jaw joint knob shapes on the two sides of patients with one upper canine tooth stuck in the gum. Missing canine guidance might reshape the joint unevenly, and panoramic X-rays offered a cheap look.

The records covered 364 patients, classed by whether the stuck tooth sat right or left. Knob shapes were sorted into round, angled, flat, and pointed, then compared side to side within each person and by age band. No side difference reached significance in any group. Older patients showed fewer round knobs and more angled or pointed ones on both sides alike. A stuck canine alone, they conclude, does not bend joint shape.
pmc-13317038:
Thea Laurentius and a German team studied, in a 2026 two-cohort analysis, how common drugs shift blood potassium in older patients taking many medicines at once. Both low and high potassium are risky, and kidney health changes each drug's push.

The combined data held 1,097 cases aged seventy or more on at least three drugs; low potassium appeared in 28.4 percent and high potassium in 20.3 percent of them. Modeling by kidney stage showed water pills pulling potassium down hardest in early and middle stages, while a hormone-blocking class pushed it up most, especially in late kidney disease. Effects differ by class and kidney stage, so monitoring must be personal, not generic.
pmc-13317538:
Abdirahman Mohamed Jimale and co-authors review, in a 2026 narrative article, drug resistance in Somalia, where war-damaged systems leave surveillance thin and drug use loosely controlled. They gathered studies and policy sources from 2010 to March 2026.

What evidence exists clusters in city hospitals, above all Mogadishu, and shows worrying resistance in major germs. National tracking, lab capacity, quality checks, stewardship teams, and drug regulation all remain underbuilt, and animal, food, and environment data are scarcer still. Their prescription is phased: sentinel surveillance sites, stronger labs, stewardship programs, infection control, clean water work, and cross-sector coordination. Resistance control, they stress, rides on rebuilding the whole health system.
pmc-13318038:
Nicolas Legrand and colleagues introduce pyhgf in a 2026 software paper, a Python library for predictive coding, the theory that brains learn by constantly predicting sensory input and updating on errors. Standard neural network tools force these models into shapes that fight their biology.

Built on JAX and Rust, the package keeps network parts transparent and changeable during message passing, so belief updates can reorganize the network itself. That openness lets one framework express structure learning, meta-learning, and causal discovery as natural growth from surprise. Core functions stay differentiable for sampling and optimization workflows. Ready examples include general Bayesian filtering and the hierarchical Gaussian filter used in brain research, easing adoption by labs.
pmc-13318538:
Francisca Teixeira da Costa Maia and Gabriel José Morgado Santos report a 2026 eye case. Travoprost drops appear to have caused fluid build-up behind the iris. The drops are widely used to lower pressure in glaucoma. Their patient was an 84-year-old woman with open-angle glaucoma and an implanted lens.

She had used the drops for three years. Then she noticed two weeks of worsening sight in her left eye. Her vision shifted toward short-sightedness, and the front chamber grew shallower. Pressure reached 22 mmHg in that eye during assessment. Scans suggested ciliary body swelling pushing the iris and lens forward. Within a week of stopping travoprost, the problem largely cleared. That response makes the drug's role likely.
pmc-13319038:
Xiancheng Zeng, Wei He, and Zhigang Guo present a 2026 network analysis of what keeps primary school children playing football. The sample held 287 students aged 8 to 13, with a mean age of about 9.7 years. Parental support, peer support, self-efficacy, and participation were mapped as one network. Gender differences were tested formally.

Self-efficacy emerged as the most central node in the network. It was also the main bridge linking social support to actual participation. The overall network structure did not differ significantly between boys and girls. Descriptive patterns hinted that persistence items mattered more for boys. Participation and relationship items looked more central for girls. The authors suggest support programmes should build children's confidence first, with some gender-sensitive touches.
pmc-13319538:
Zakieh Amiraslanzadeh and Elnaz Javanshir write, in a 2026 letter, for wider use of focused bedside heart ultrasound when heart failure suddenly worsens. Acute decompensated heart failure fills hospitals worldwide, and early decisions often rest on examination and blood markers, which estimate pressures and fluid status imperfectly. Full echocardiography may not be available quickly.

A focused scan can estimate pumping strength of the left ventricle and check right ventricle size and function. It can also spot fluid around the heart or severe valve problems, and gauge a large vein as a guide to congestion. Each finding maps to a treatment choice, from adjusting diuretics to urgent specialist referral. The authors propose an algorithm that ties scan results directly to management steps in the first hours.
pmc-13319638:
Franck Lamontagne and co-authors draw lessons from a child breathing project in a 2025 article on finger oxygen sensors. The AIRE project brought the small clip on sensors into front line care for young children in parts of Africa. Teamwork among aid groups, research centers, and health ministries helped build real world proof and place the tool in national child care rules.

Sensors alone did not save lives where referral paths were weak, oxygen was scarce, or staff lacked training and support. Fees for care also blocked some families. Lasting gains need the sensor to sit inside a full care chain, with funded training, steady oversight, and oxygen on hand when low readings are found.
pmc-13320038:
M Bendszus argues, in a 2026 commentary, that new European guidelines on bleeding from a burst brain aneurysm undervalue modern catheter-based treatments. The guidelines aim to standardise neurovascular care. Yet the author contends that newer techniques face stricter evidence demands than older surgical traditions that still shape recommendations.

Balloon-assisted coiling is one example, where two small early single-centre reports receive heavy emphasis despite first-generation devices and selection bias. A larger, more rigorous modern study is treated more cautiously. Intrasaccular flow devices offer another example: the guideline says studies lacked independent review, while the author notes named trials did include core laboratory checks. Mid-term results for these devices look favourable. The piece calls for evidence weighting that reflects current practice.
pmc-13320638:
Hao Yu and co-authors review brain scan studies of working memory in bipolar disorder in a 2026 article. Holding and using information in mind is often impaired in the condition, but whether type I and type II differ in brain terms was unclear. The review gathered task based scan studies that reported the two types apart.

Searches of three databases for work from 2011 to 2025 yielded 22 studies for joint reading. Type I studies more often showed strained control networks and weak quieting of resting networks under load. Type II proof was very thin, with only three studies, and hinted at more preserved function when mood was stable. The authors stress that firm type contrasts await more type II research.
pmc-13321038:
Mehdi Akbari, Mohammad Seydavi, and Sonay Sheikhi explore motives behind problematic pornography use in a 2026 survey study. The work uses self-determination theory and covers 613 adults, mostly male, with a mean age near 25 years. Problematic use means use that feels out of control and causes distress.

Such use was tied to motives such as stress relief, emotional distraction, and fantasy, and also to impulsivity, loneliness, distress, and sexual problems. It went with lower relationship satisfaction and sexual self-esteem. Mediation checks found fantasy, low sexual satisfaction, and emotional distraction as the steadiest pathways, though most effects were small. The authors judge those pathways too weak to guide treatment on their own.
pmc-13322938:
Kristin Vassbotn Guldhav and a large Norwegian team report caregiver outcomes from the PALLiON trial, in a 2026 secondary analysis. That cluster-randomised trial tested earlier, systematic palliative care built into oncology across 12 Norwegian hospitals, since such care often starts late.

The intervention paired a doctor education programme with a patient-centred care path and routine symptom checks. Adults with advanced cancer and their caregivers joined the trial, and caregiver satisfaction was tracked over time with the FAMCARE-20 scale. Patient quality of life was scored with a short palliative questionnaire. Statistical models tested whether the intervention changed caregiver satisfaction, and whether patient quality of life at entry shaped that satisfaction over time.
pmc-13323738:
Xiao Wang and co-authors test moral disengagement as the bridge between violence exposure and cyberbullying, in a 2026 survey of 936 middle school students in urban Hunan, China. Pupils in grades 7 to 12 completed standard scales for violence exposure, moral disengagement and cyberbullying behaviour.

Violence exposure predicted cyberbullying directly, and moral disengagement carried part of that link in their structural model. Boys scored higher on moral disengagement than girls, non-only children reported more violence exposure than only children, and older pupils bullied online more. The authors suggest that teaching which challenges moral excuses, rather than only punishing acts, could cut cyberbullying among exposed teens.
pmc-13324638:
Jia Sun and team checked whether self-chosen vitamin use around pregnancy relates to premature birth. Their 2026 secondary analysis drew on a nested case-control study within a large prospective cohort in Wuhan, China, covering 6,656 births from 2011 to 2013. Intake was checked both before conception and while pregnant, with models that allowed for social, lifestyle, and medical factors.

Vitamin use in both periods was linked with higher odds of doctor-ordered early birth, with an adjusted odds ratio of 1.54. The authors stress that causality cannot be confirmed: exposure assessment was limited, residual confounding remains, and reverse causation is possible, since complications may prompt supplement use. While vitamins matter for maternal health, they cannot replace medical prevention of early birth, and the authors call for monitoring vitamin levels and clearer provider guidance.
pmc-13324838:
Duanwu Liu and co-authors test heat treatment of micellar casein as a carrier for the red pigment betanin in a 2026 food study. Betanin colors foods well but breaks down fast under heat, alkali, and oxygen.

Casein bound betanin mainly through hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces at mild heat, shifting toward charge-based binding at 65 °C. Pre-heating at 55 °C gave the strongest binding and the most ordered protein shape. That version also held up best across heat and pH swings and boosted antioxidant action. In lab digestion it slowed release in stomach fluid yet reached 89.33 percent release by three hours in intestinal fluid, well above free betanin.
pmc-13325138:
Matteo Piscitelli and colleagues chart how antibody layers reshape themselves on gold in a 2026 surface study. Antibodies stuck to sensors and chips form the working face of many tests, yet their layout is hard to predict.

Anti-IgM antibodies were laid from solutions spanning 0.5 to 1000 micrograms per mL for times from 1 to 330 minutes. Infrared spectra read the protein structure at each stage. At low coverage the antibodies sprawled in loose, partly disordered shapes. Crowding and time pushed them into compact, beta-sheet-rich packs. A single surface-density score merged dose and time into one axis that maps the contest between spreading and packing.
pmc-13325938:
Ping Wang and co-authors show how the protein PLIN5 shields kidney podocytes from fat-driven injury in a 2026 study. Angiotensin II lowers PLIN5 in these filter cells, and the loss feeds chronic kidney disease.

Mice lacking PLIN5 only in podocytes suffered worse fat buildup, mitochondrial failure, and cell death under angiotensin II. Adding PLIN5 back eased each harm. Protein screening found PLIN5 gripping FKBP8, a protein on the mitochondrial surface, and the grip weakened under stress. Knocking down FKBP8 broke the contact between fat droplets and mitochondria and worsened injury. A stretch of FKBP8 spanning residues 70 to 200 proved required for the bond.
pmc-13326638:
Aurélie Guyet and team showed that the Bacillus subtilis motor loader DnaB acts as a hub for starting DNA replication. Their 2026 study tackles an unclear step. The master starter DnaA unwinds the origin, letting two copying motors load onto each DNA strand. How loading is managed at the origin was still unknown. The team mapped DnaB parts key for the start, using single-particle cryo-imaging, AlphaFold3 predictions, and two-hybrid interaction analyses.

Three necessary protein-protein interactions emerged, linking DnaB to the start proteins DnaA, DnaD, and DnaI. The data suggest DnaB runs dual motor loading at the origin through these contacts. The authors propose a model for replication start in Bacillus subtilis and related Firmicutes pathogens that use DnaB-type loaders. It clarifies a conserved mechanism that could inform understanding of bacterial growth and its vulnerabilities.
pmc-13327538:
Peter R Cook offers a cluster-based view of gene activity in a 2026 review on how DNA sequence shapes cell fate. Genes are usually treated as lone units, yet much RNA seems to be made in shared clusters of copying machinery, also called factories, condensates, or hubs. Cook asks what that grouping changes.

New artificial intelligence tools predict gene output with striking skill, but they strain against too many dimensions, sparse data, and hard-to-read reasoning. Contacts between DNA stretches inside clusters carry rich, underused information, Cook argues, and feeding those contacts into such tools could sharpen forecasts of development. The piece maps routes toward equations that give the odds of an egg cell becoming each cell type.
pmc-13329538:
Hiroki Hori, Tomokatsu Hori, and Takaomi Taira report staged two-side pallidothalamic tractotomy with MR-guided focused ultrasound for advanced Parkinson's disease. Their 2026 case paper notes that tractotomy burning is a choice for drug-resistant disease, but the target sits among key structures, so exact aiming is vital to curb nerve harm. Diffusion tensor imaging fiber tractography may lift accuracy by showing the tract directly.

The case was a 45-year-old woman with advanced Parkinson's disease. In the first round, tractography showed the tract and set the target. In the second, other-side aiming used mirrored points from the first to stay consistent. Movement signs got better after both rounds, with the movement score falling from 24 to 11 after the first and from 52 to 11 after the second. No nerve harms showed during follow-up. The team hints tractography-led aiming may sharpen showing, while noting the one-case limit.
pmc-13330838:
Juan He and team present a cubane-like heterometallic molybdenum-iron-sulfur cluster. Their 2026 structure paper covers [(Tp*)MoFe3S3(μ3-Cl)(PMe3)3](BPh4), with distinct site shapes for the metal sites. Mo-Fe-S clusters have received steady focus for likeness to nitrogenase's iron-molybdenum cofactor, which turns dinitrogen into ammonia in mild settings. Cubane-type clusters act as vital mimics of that cofactor.

The title cluster is a typical example in the Mo-Fe-S cluster family, with uses for making FeMo-co mimics. In the crystal, the cluster shows layered stacking along the b-axis, with charged cluster units and tetraphenylborate anions in rows throughout. Charge links dominate the packing, held by weak links between units, including a C-H···π contact between a phosphine methyl group and a borate benzene ring. Cubane-type M-Fe-S-Cl clusters remain rare, making this example a useful find.
pmc-13331238:
Zoha Faheem and a large team study how type I interferon shapes B cells in lupus in a 2026 report. Blood cells came from 18 healthy controls, 25 patients in quiet phases, and 41 patients in recent flares. A mass cytometry panel tracked B cell types, activation marks, and interferon-stimulated proteins as a proxy for interferon exposure.

All B cell types carried higher interferon marks in flares than in quiet disease in the reported data. A harmful subset, DN2 cells, grew more common in flares and tracked with the interferon score. Lab tests showed both interferon forms pushed healthy B cells toward that subset. Blocking interferon signals in treated patients lowered both marks and subset share.
pmc-13332338:
Pranitha Vadigireddy Gari and colleagues study 2026 how general dentists treat early childhood tooth decay. Decay in young children remains a major challenge in child dental care, given its high frequency and complex treatment needs. The team compared treatment choices and asked whether dentist experience, child age, and decay severity shaped those choices. The cross-sectional study watched 150 general dentists from October 2021 through March 2022, with five consecutive visits per dentist in children aged two to five.

That yielded 750 observed cases, sorted into fluoride varnish or remineralization, atraumatic restorative care, standard fillings, preformed metal crowns, and extraction. A standard checklist captured dentist experience, child age, and a decay index for each case. The study gives a grounded picture of everyday choices in child decay care. It also points to where training or guidance could steer dentists toward less invasive options where they fit.
pmc-13332438:
Cornel Nesseler and colleagues ran a large field experiment in 2026 to test whether German amateur sports clubs treat hopeful members differently based on the name in an inquiry email. Clubs are meant to build health and social mixing, yet participation gaps for immigrants and minorities persist.

The team emailed more than 8,900 clubs across seven popular sports, varying whether the sender's name sounded native German, Syrian, or Turkish. Native-sounding names drew positive replies more often. The gap was about 6 percentage points, roughly a 12 percent lower chance of a warm answer for foreign-sounding names, with Syrian and Turkish names hit hardest. The pattern held across sports and showed no regional split, and asking openly about membership fees changed nothing. The authors argue small individual biases stack into institutional barriers and call for targeted action by governing bodies.
pmc-13332738:
Iga Stukan and a large team evaluated albumin nanoparticles built to carry two nerve growth proteins into the eye, in a 2026 study spanning chemistry, rabbits, and stressed human cells. The proteins BDNF and NT3 protect nerve cells but break down quickly and clear fast, blocking medical use.

Coating human serum albumin particles with PEG let them self-assemble into stable spheres of 5.9 to 54.2 nm that held together for 28 days, in two strengths carrying 5 or 10 µg/mL of the proteins. Injected into rabbit eyes, BDNF remained detectable in eye tissues for up to 72 hours without triggering a joined-up cell death gene response. In cell models of oxidative damage, the particles raised internal protein levels, improved survival, cut cell death, and lowered lipid damage, most strongly at the higher strength. The authors support further development of albumin carriers for protein medicines.
pmc-13333138:
Mohammed Uddin and colleagues report a 2026 case of widespread muscle mineralization after severe trauma and prolonged critical illness. Soft tissue mineral buildup is an uncommon complication of severe trauma and critical illness, linked to metabolic disturbance, tissue injury, and long immobility. The patient was a 26-year-old man who developed extensive skeletal muscle calcium deposits after multiple stab wounds, hypovolemic shock, and surgeries including limb amputation and bowel resections.

Early imaging showed no calcification, yet CT six weeks after injury showed extensive amorphous calcium deposits in the abdominal wall, chest, iliopsoas, and gluteus maximus. The cause may involve a breakdown state and disuse, driving bone breakdown, mineral loss, and high blood calcium with later soft tissue deposition. The case urges recognition of muscle mineral buildup in critically ill trauma patients, with multi-mode imaging for early diagnosis and care.
pmc-13333238:
Sewon Mun and colleagues review how T cells age in a 2026 synthesis on immune decline. As the body ages, the immune system weakens, and T cells change most deeply of all, leaving older people open to infection, cancer, and poor vaccine responses.

Both helper CD4 and killer CD8 T cells eventually stop dividing. The review stresses that they get there by different roads, with distinct triggers, fuel use, and outcomes shaped by whether DNA damage is involved or not. The shrinking thymus cuts the supply of fresh cells while worn-out cells pile up and pour out inflammatory signals. These subset differences help explain how the aging immune system remodels itself. The authors close by weighing treatments that target the metabolic and signaling pathways behind T cell aging, aiming to restore defense without unleashing the worn cells' inflammatory side effects.
pmc-13333338:
Manana Melikishvili and colleagues measure 2026 how DNA methylation, nucleic acid structure, and Rett mutations tune MeCP2 binding. MeCP2 is a chromatin-linked factor whose dysfunction causes Rett syndrome. Although it favors methylated DNA, its pull toward methylated targets is only about three times stronger than toward unmethylated DNA, which raises the question of how it picks targets with care. The team quantified binding of full-length normal MeCP2 and Rett variants R106W, T158M, R270X, and R306C to varied nucleic acid substrates.

Normal and mutant MeCP2 favor double-stranded DNA but also latch onto single-stranded and double-stranded DNA and RNA with nanomolar strength. Latching onto single-stranded targets rests largely on local duplex formation, while 5-methylcytosine adds stabilizing contacts and boosts affinity when canonical duplex shape is absent. Rett mutations fall into mechanistic classes detailed in the full paper.
pmc-13333438:
Jia Chen and colleagues report a diagnostic near-miss in a 2026 case report: sky-high eosinophil counts blamed on a hidden whipworm infection that routine stool tests kept missing. Such severe eosinophil rises usually point doctors toward blood disorders, while parasites slip down the list outside the tropics.

A 24-year-old man arrived with two months of chronic diarrhea and an eosinophil count of 11.56 × 109/L. Repeated stool checks and a first colonoscopy found nothing, and treatment for a vague gut disorder helped only briefly. On readmission, a second colonoscopy spotted two Trichuris trichiura worms in his cecum and ascending colon and removed them; tissue study showed dense eosinophil infiltration. A three-day course of albendazole at 400 mg daily then cleared his symptoms completely and his eosinophil count normalized fast, with no return of trouble at follow-up. The authors urge repeat scoping when the picture stays unexplained.
pmc-13333538:
Yujun Jiang and co-authors interview liver cancer patients in a 2026 qualitative study about what helps and what blocks behavior after chemoembolization. Through the health belief model, recovery after TACE depends on patients weighing benefits against barriers. The team wanted those scales described in patients' words.

Fifteen patients treated at a Chongqing hospital between June and September 2025 gave semistructured interviews. Colaizzi's seven-step method sorted them into five themes and thirteen subthemes. Barriers dominated the physical side: symptom burden, gut dysfunction, exercise tolerance. They dominated the mental side: helplessness, feeling a burden, emotional overflow. Support gaps, caregivers and money strain, completed the barrier set. So did knowledge gaps: wrong ideas about what the treatment achieved and hard-to-reach health education. Against them sat benefits: function, support received, and confidence from experience. The authors urge nurses to aim programs at each patient's perception profile in the days after the procedure.
pmc-13333738:
Omer Mohammed and co-authors weighed treatments that target mitochondrial dysfunction in heart failure in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Faulty mitochondria drain heart muscle energy and drive oxidative stress and cell death, making them an attractive treatment target.

Searches across five sources through May 2025 gathered 31 studies, including 24 randomized trials and 7 crossover trials. Pooled results showed treated patients gained in left ventricular ejection fraction compared with both their starting point and control groups. Functional class improved, and risks of hospital admission for heart failure and death from any cause fell. The authors caution that real-world benefit remains uncertain, but the combined evidence supports continued clinical testing of mitochondria-directed drugs.
pmc-13336538:
Jia Shen Sio and co-authors present SKALE 2.0 in a 2026 research article on protein clumping linked to brain disease. Their computer method sorts the building of harmful protein clumps into two stages. The first stage is nucleation, when clumps start. The second is elongation, when fibers grow longer.

Working with the proteins SOD1, TDP-43, MAPT, and PRNP, the team found distinct change patterns for each stage. Hidden, water-avoiding parts of a protein drove the first stage, while exposed surfaces shaped the second. Tests with lab-made SOD1 confirmed predicted changes that could block, boost, or switch clumping. Such stage-specific control could guide new drugs that stop harmful clumps early.
pmc-13336838:
Yanze Liu and co-authors craft wing-shaped molecules that remember in a 2026 electronics study. Organic memory devices could ease the bottleneck between processing and storage in standard computers. The team built four azobenzene molecules that differ only in their end groups, from nitroimidazole to triphenylamine.

Swapping end groups tuned the memory style, from write-once storage to switchable forms, all with high on-off ratios, low voltages, and good stability. Charge transfer that twists the molecules explains the different behaviors. One version also mimicked synapse responses and ran logic gates plus adder circuits inside memory itself. It even handled image edge detection in a neural network demo, pointing toward brain-like organic computing.
pmc-13336938:
Huaiyuan Zhao and co-workers used quantum calculations to study a layered magnet called FePd2Te2, in work published in 2026. The material holds its layers together with sparse palladium-tellurium bridges that carry some covalent bonding, yet it still peels apart almost as easily as a van der Waals crystal. The team traced how its magnetism changes as the crystal thins from bulk down to a single layer.

Thinning raised the local iron moments and the within-layer coupling slightly, while the ordering temperature fell from 173 kelvin in bulk to 27 kelvin in one layer. The drop traces mainly to the loss of coupling between layers, with added push from a competing antiferromagnetic term. Near the Fermi level, a reshaped orbital pattern keeps a strong easy-axis preference, which matters for thin magnetic devices.
pmc-13337438:

pmc-13387138:

pmc-13387738:

pmc-13390738:

pmc-13391738:

pmc-13392438:

pmc-13393838:

pmc-13393938:

pmc-13394838:

pmc-13396038:

pmc-13396238:

pmc-13396338:

pmc-13396438:

pmc-13396738:

pmc-13397538:

pmc-13399838:

pmc-13402838:

pmc-13405738:

Searches to February 2026 found fourteen sources, but only three were peer-reviewed comparative studies. The rest were grey literature such as guidelines and hospital documents. Most of those permitted or recommended the push method for preventive doses. Evidence is charted across safety, drug behaviour, infection outcomes and cost, exposing how thin the formal research base remains.
pmc-13407938:
Anindini Winda Amalia and co-authors review, in 2026, a Javanese long pepper as a power-plant-protecting prospect against high blood pressure. Hypertension damages vessels through oxygen-radical stress, failing cell power plants, and chronic inflammation. Piper retrofractum's compounds, including piperine and piplartine, show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects that converge on those mechanisms.

The review assembles pathways by which the plant's chemistry might cut power-plant reactive oxygen, recouple the vessel-relaxing enzyme, activate energy-sensing and defence master switches, and tune power-plant shape-shifting and recycling. Together these would be expected to improve vessel lining function and restrain wall remodelling. The evidence remains preclinical, with thin clinical data, poor bioavailability, and standardisation problems acknowledged. Modern omics and network pharmacology are proposed to firm up the multitarget picture.
pmc-13408038:
Nicolas Vatiliotis and co-authors model, in 2026, ring-shaped defence peptides borrowed from baboons. Theta-defensins are cyclic antimicrobial peptides prized for toughness and broad germ-killing reach. How solvents and small sequence changes bend them was poorly understood. The team therefore ran all-atom molecular dynamics on baboon theta-defensin-2, chosen for its extra arginine content and ensuing potency.

Three starting shapes of the same peptide were followed under different solvent conditions, tracking flexibility, residue-level wobbling, and heat strength. Despite sharing a sequence, the conformations behaved distinctly over time, each with its own temporal signature. The analysis feeds the rational design of peptide antibiotics and antivirals, where knowing which shape survives which environment can decide whether a would-be drug holds together.
pmc-13408338:
Katarína Karl’ová and Jozef Strečka use an exactly solvable physics model in 2026 to ask how the ends of a tiny magnet chain change its behaviour. They study a chain of spin-half particles with antiferromagnetic coupling, comparing chains left open at the ends with chains looped into rings, using the transfer-matrix method.

Open chains showed distinctive magnetic features at any size, largely because the end spins behave differently. Rings depended on whether the spin count was odd or even, since odd rings frustrate the alternating pattern and produce an extra plateau in the magnetisation curve. Curiously, odd open chains showed the same plateau, linking two effects with different origins. Basic response constants, by contrast, stayed the same under either boundary choice, a useful check for theory and teaching.
pmc-13408438:
Mahas, Ferreira, Riedmayr, and Church build, in 2026, SONAR, a platform that lets human cells sense a DNA or RNA sequence and switch on a payload. It aims at diagnostics and cell therapies that react to molecular signatures like viral genomes or cancer mutations. The sensor is a single-stranded DNA that can be tied into a circle by the cell's ligase enzymes only when it has latched onto its target. For RNA targets, antisense primers first copy the RNA into DNA.

Circle formation drives expression of the loaded payload, from fluorescent reporters to recombinases and genome editors. The team demonstrated sensing DNA, foreign RNA, and the cell's endogenous RNA targets, with sensor activation jumping several-fold for integrated targets in comparisons. They used the system to enrich and clonally recover target-positive cells from populations. They argue the circle-based mechanism, unexplored for sensing, makes the platform modular and predictable.
pmc-13408838:
Guofang Xia and colleagues identify in 2026 a macrophage enzyme that limits the damage when blood flow returns to a starved heart. Reopening a blocked artery saves muscle, yet the returning flow itself injures tissue, and heart macrophages steer that second wave. Spatial gene mapping and cell sorting singled out adenylyl cyclase 7 as a macrophage-specific player, a finding confirmed in patient tissue.

In male mice, macrophages lacking the enzyme let injury and inflammation run worse, while extra enzyme protected the heart. The mechanism runs through a calming chemical messenger pathway that keeps a master inflammatory switch out of the cell nucleus. The team even built a light-activated version of the cyclase that eased inflammation and injury on demand. They propose the enzyme as a drug target for reperfusion damage.
pmc-13409038:
The EFSA Panel on Additives and Products or Substances used in Animal Feed assesses in 2026 an amino acid made by fermentation for use in feed for every animal species. The product is l-leucine, produced by a genetically modified strain of Corynebacterium glutamicum, and requested both as a nutritional supplement and as a flavouring. The applicant is CJ Europe.

The panel found no safety concern from the genetic modification itself, and neither living production cells nor their DNA were detectable in the finished additive. Used in feed at levels matching animals' nutritional needs, or as a flavouring, the leucine was judged safe for the target species. One reservation stands out in the opinion: delivering the amino acid through drinking water raised concerns, a distinction feed formulators will need to respect.
pmc-13409338:
Christopher Moran and co-authors report in 2026 a tumour so rare that only about a hundred cases like it exist in print: an adult granulosa cell tumour growing in a man's testicle. These tumours are the male counterpart of an ovarian cancer. Their patient, a fifty-year-old man, came in with pain and swelling, and ultrasound found a two-centimetre mixed mass with its own blood supply in the upper testicle.

Under the microscope the cells matched the ovarian pattern, long grooved nuclei in sheets and cords, and staining confirmed the identity. Gene sequencing found no mutations or fusions but did find low-level extra copies of four cancer-relevant genes, a profile not previously documented for this tumour. The testicle was removed radically, and the patient remained alive and disease free forty-two months later. The case adds molecular detail to a tumour most pathologists never meet.
pmc-13410438:
Souto-Trinei and co-authors create, in 2026, cationic lipopeptides, molecules fusing fat-loving lipid tails with plus-charged peptides, that assemble themselves into hollow vesicles able to ferry genes into cells without viruses. Viral carriers work well but are immunogenic and hard to make; these synthetic compartments mimic cell membranes while staying body-friendly and programmable.

The assemblies grabbed nucleic acids eagerly. The best performer, LP2, reached about 90 percent complexation at 20 micrograms per milliliter and stayed efficient across a broad range, while LP1 managed roughly 85 percent binding in assays. Transfection of the easy HEK 293T cell line was strong, and performance extended to mesenchymal stem cells, a harder target. Cells survived at above 75 percent at all tested concentrations, beating the 62 percent survival of the positive control in their comparisons. The authors envision programmable cells delivering varied nucleic acids into hard-to-transfect cells.
pmc-13410538:
Prapassara Sirikarn and colleagues trace in 2026 what kills people in Thailand long after an ischemic stroke. Stroke ranks among the top causes of death and disability worldwide, yet long-term data from poorer countries are scarce. Their study follows patients for up to 18 years.

National hospital records from 2004 to 2022 covered 888,003 patients, and nearly half died during follow-up. Death rates climbed steeply with age, passing 80 percent past age 85. Stroke itself caused most deaths in hospital and in the first month after discharge. Later deaths came mainly from complications such as pneumonia and sepsis, plus other illnesses like heart disease and dementia. Care after discharge clearly needs the same weight as acute care.
pmc-13411038:
Gayaneh Petrossian and co-workers introduce in 2026 soft conductive foams built from coated microspheres that can be printed and recycled. Wearable electronics need materials that bend like tissue, carry current, and avoid the landfill. Ordinary conductive foams rarely offer all three traits at once.

Tiny polymer spheres coated with a conductive polymer set the foam's pores and stiffness. The foams stayed as soft as body tissue while keeping steady conductivity across wide ranges of air content. Heat could reshape them, and dissolving the matrix freed the coated spheres for reuse. Worn as electrodes, the foams cleanly picked up heart, muscle, and even in-ear brain signals, including clear shifts in brain rhythm bands.
pmc-13411238:
Marius Werner, Truc Lam Pham, and Franziska Thomas review in 2026 methods for decorating finished peptides while they still sit on their synthesis resin. Peptide drugs often need unusual building blocks added late to tune their action. Working on the resin saves time and money and suits mass screening.

Reactions covered range from simple swaps and carbonyl chemistry to metal-driven and light-driven couplings developed over the past decade. Most handle both short and long peptides, and several demonstrably change biological activity. Libraries built this way in high-throughput formats show the method's reach. The authors expect on-resin tailoring to speed the design of peptide medicines, especially where many variants must be tried quickly.
pmc-13411438:
Elske Ammenwerth, Iiris Hörhammer, and Michelle Bindel map in 2026 how logic models and theories of change have been used for health technology projects. Such tools lay out the assumed chain from action to outcome. Digital health projects are complex and context-bound, yet their designers often skip that step.

Five databases were scoured under scoping review rules across health and social care settings. Sixty-nine publications from 2012 to 2025 qualified, with use climbing sharply after 2020. Work spanned informatics, public health, and implementation science. Models varied in structure and stated purpose, which limits shared learning. The authors press medical informatics to theorize its interventions as carefully as it builds them.
pmc-13411738:
Mai Mohamed, Asmaa Sayed, and Dalia Hegazy compare in 2026 two nanoparticle boosters for hydrogel sponges that strip blue dye from wastewater. Textile dye pollution is a stubborn water problem. Gels built from common polymers were set with gamma rays, then loaded with either titanium dioxide or graphene oxide flakes.

Microscopy and heat tests confirmed both fillers took hold and changed gel structure. Filled gels gelled almost completely, versus about two thirds for the plain gel, and swelled most in alkaline water. Dye removal climbed from about 64 percent for the plain gel to near total for the graphene version. Surface area and dye-grabbing chemistry explain the winner's edge, the authors argue.
pmc-13412138:
Manan Shukla and colleagues test in 2026 whether machine learning can predict which surgery patients will need critical support afterwards. Complications after operations drive much illness and death, and simple risk scores give only rough, group-level estimates. Using the public INSPIRE perioperative database of about 131,000 surgical cases, the team trained neural networks and random forests on lab results, medicines, surgery type, and vital signs recorded during operations.

Models forecast four supports: breathing machines, ECMO, balloon pumps, and continuous kidney therapy. Accuracy on a held-out set of nearly 39,000 patients ranged from about 95 to 99 percent depending on the outcome. The authors present the work as proof of concept for earlier, targeted intervention.
pmc-13412538:
Shahla Shahbazi and co-authors compare in 2026 the infections patients caught in Iranian intensive care units before and in the first COVID-19 year. Such infections drive illness, death, and cost. The pandemic forced much tighter infection control, which may have changed the pattern. Records from Taleghani Hospital in Kermanshah covered 1,778 ICU stays across 2019 and 2020.

The team logged 301 caught infections, a rate of 16.9 percent across both years. The rate eased from 18.2 percent in 2019 to 16.0 percent in 2020, even as stays rose. Gram-negative germs caused nearly all cases in both years. Ventilator-linked events stayed the top type. Urine and blood infections rose, while lung ones fell.
pmc-13414038:
Li Zhang and co-authors teach a generative network the physics of antenna arrays in 2026 so it can design unevenly spaced arrays that account for elements interfering with each other. Nonuniform arrays focus beams with fewer elements, yet mutual coupling makes design a thorny search usually run by slow full-wave simulation. Their physics-informed GAN generates layouts and excitations, judges them against target patterns, and swaps the simulator for a fast learned stand-in for each element's behaviour.

Trials on a sixteen-element line and a three-hundred-element plane reached lower peak sidelobes than the comparison designs reported. A built sixteen-element prototype measured close to simulation, confirming the pipeline works off the page. The authors pitch the approach for next-generation wireless and radar hardware design.
pmc-13415138:
Gregory D. Hawley and co-authors present three traveler cases of probable leptospirosis in a 2026 narrative review. All three patients had rafted whitewater in rural Ecuador after heavy rain and flooding. Two arrived with acute fever soon after travel, during a confirmed regional outbreak.

The third sought care four weeks after a feverish illness with jaundice abroad. Confirmatory laboratory tests for this waterborne bacterial infection return slowly, so treatment often starts on clinical suspicion alone. The review covers symptoms, diagnosis, therapy, and outlook in depth. Fever after freshwater adventure travel should put leptospirosis on the list early, the authors argue.
pmc-13415238:
Jong-Min Kim and colleagues validate a faster blood test for the diabetes and obesity drug semaglutide in 2026. Measuring this GLP-1 mimic in plasma supports drug level studies, yet older methods took about eighteen minutes per run. Their liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry assay finishes within nine minutes.

Only fifty microliters of rat plasma are needed, cleaned by precipitation and solid phase extraction. The assay measured reliably from 1 to 500 nanograms per milliliter, with accuracy near 95 to 104 percent. Stability held under every tested condition. A rat dosing study at fifty micrograms showed the method works in practice.
pmc-13415338:
Sabasadat Seyednikkhoo, Mirko Weide, and Markus Egert profile bacteria inside home washing machines that users call smelly or fresh, in 2026. Eight machines of each type were swabbed at the detergent drawer, door seal, and sump. Full length gene reads named the species, and a count test weighed bacterial DNA.

The reads found 1,492 distinct species across the machines. Moraxella osloensis, a known odor producer, was most abundant in door seals. Overall community makeup barely differed between smelly and fresh machines. Smelly machines held somewhat more bacterial DNA, yet the gap stayed small and not firm. What germs do, or how noses sense smell, may drive the odor people notice.
pmc-13415538:
Anatoli Ulmer and a large team show that ultra short X-ray flashes can partly undo their own excitation damage, in 2026. Intense X-rays ionize atoms fast, blurring diffraction images of tiny structures. Pulses shorter than a femtosecond end before the usual Auger decay, the process that normally locks in damage.

The team compared thousands of diffraction patterns and ion readings from neon nanoparticles between sub-femtosecond and fifteen femtosecond pulses. Shorter pulses gave stronger diffraction with less absorbed energy. Modeling points to stimulated emission near atomic resonances, akin to Rabi flopping, which stretches the life of excited states. Active control of X-ray damage could sharpen nanoscale imaging.
pmc-13415638:
Miranda P. Walker and Jack M. Parent review human brain organoids as models for epilepsy, in 2026. Organoids are miniature brain like tissues grown from human stem cells, including cells donated by patients or edited with CRISPR. Animal models miss some human cortex development details and rarely seize spontaneously like patients do.

Organoid work now probes faulty neuron production, wandering interneurons, and abnormal network firing tied to seizure disorders. Both genetic and acquired epilepsies are covered in the review. Remaining hurdles include tissue maturity and variability between batches. Combined with animal studies, organoids may sharpen mechanism hunting and guide more precise therapies.
pmc-13415838:
Krisztina Kőhalmy, Ayaan Borthakur, and Pálma Porrogi model how inflammation and drug clashes can override a patient's genes in antipsychotic metabolism, in 2026. Their focus is people with two nonworking copies of CYP3A5, an enzyme variant written as star three over star three. A mathematical model adds drug interactions, inflammation marker CRP, and kidney function to the genetic baseline.

One patient pattern showed quetiapine levels near 1,850 nanograms per milliliter, almost four times the accepted ceiling, when a blocking drug was present. Strong inflammation alone mimicked a poor metabolizer state. Inducer drugs pushed others toward ultra rapid clearance and likely treatment failure.
pmc-13417738:
Mikaeli Carmichael and colleagues test a menstrual health education programme for female athletes, in a 2026 intervention study. Fifty one athletes in three cohorts attended two workshops and received handouts, answering surveys before, right after, and three months later. Topics covered cycle knowledge, talking with support staff, and the value of cycle tracking.

Knowledge, both real and perceived, rose after the workshops and held at three months. Willingness to talk with teammates and performance staff also rose, while talks with coaches and medical staff did not shift. Perceived value of tracking grew by follow up. Age, schooling, and contraceptive use shaped some outcomes.
pmc-13417938:
Daniel Habib and colleagues mined the FDA's adverse-event database in 2026 for cochlear implant problems reported from 2016 to 2024. As implants spread, complication patterns matter for patients and makers, yet few studies had charted national trends across both patient harms and device faults.

Reports counted 34426 patient complications and 33487 device complications, rising through 2020 then leveling, while skin healing, infection, fit problems, hospital stays, and life-threatening outcomes grew as shares of the total. The paper gives implant teams a watch list for the problems that keep rising even as overall reports stabilize.
pmc-13418138:
Xiaoyu Hu and co-authors identify a sugar pathway enzyme lost early in Alzheimer disease, in a 2026 study. Brain cells favour a glucose route called the pentose phosphate pathway, whose flow drops in this disease. Protein profiling of synaptic endings from patient cortex pointed to that pathway as the most disturbed network, with the enzyme transaldolase 1 sharply reduced.

Lowering the enzyme in cells and mice collapsed energy output, drained antioxidant stores, and damaged synapses and cognition. Restoring it in a mouse model improved glucose uptake, calmed oxidative stress, and rescued memory related function. The enzyme is proposed as a treatment target for restoring brain metabolism.
pmc-13418238:
Rachelle Austin and co-authors pair two light based methods to watch chloride vapours and iodine in hot nuclear systems, in a 2026 study. Fast chemical checks can help salt based reactors and fuel reuse stay safe. A custom hot cell let the team read two kinds of spectra at once. One method names the molecules present. The other names the elements.

Four target compounds were read alone and mixed: iodine and the chlorides of three metals. Each one was found and measured with success. The pairing gives both form and element counts in real time. That could aid safeguards and stock checks in new reactor types.
pmc-13418538:
Andrea Gottinger and a large team reveal how two chaperone proteins shepherd coenzyme Q building blocks inside mitochondria, in a 2026 study. Coenzyme Q carries electrons for cell energy, and its greasy intermediates cannot travel alone through watery compartments. The COQ8 proteins burn ATP to open and close a pocket that recognises intermediate head groups.

Crystal structures show ATP driven gating controls pocket access. Finished coenzyme Q blocks early intermediates from binding, creating feedback that throttles production when supply is ample. Disease linked mutations helped map the pocket. The model explains how the assembly line stays supplied without overproducing.
pmc-13418738:
Giuseppe Pelosi and colleagues ask whether lung neuroendocrine tumors and carcinomas sit on one shared path of change. Their 2026 computer-based study pooled gene activity data for 205 tumors drawn from four public collections. The set spanned the full range of these lung growths, from slow carcinoids to fast, high-grade carcinomas.

The team grouped the tumors with a curated set of 20 genes tied to hormone-like cell identity, growth pathways, and cell lineage. Two large clusters emerged, and the split did not follow the standard tissue-based classes. One cluster had lost much of its neuroendocrine character and switched on programs of other lung cell types. That same group showed an inflamed yet worn-down immune setting and linked to worse outcomes in part of the cases. The pattern hints at a shared route of change across the whole family.
pmc-13420138:
Emily Frankel and colleagues map how community engagement cores across a national research network build local capacity for health studies. These cores belong to a program serving states with historically low research funding, and they help communities partner with investigators as equals. A 2022 landscape analysis catalogued what each core actually does.

Common threads ran through the sites: sharing knowledge, learning together, and building lasting local infrastructure. Beside the shared core, each site shaped its work to its own communities and needs. A standing interest group spreads the lessons between sites as a community of practice. The map shows funders and centers where engagement work is strong and where it is thin.
pmc-13420338:
Yao Qi and co-authors test whether pretreating lymphoma cells with BTK inhibitor drugs makes them easier for CAR-T cells to kill. The authors conclude BTK inhibitor pretreatment can reverse macrophage-driven resistance in this system.
pmc-13421238:
Andreas Krause and Géraldine Cellière set out, in a 2026 methods paper, formal strategies for choosing children's drug doses from adult population pharmacokinetic models before paediatric trial data exist. Regulators require rigorous dose justification, and model-based exposure matching offers a reproducible route: children should reach drug exposure similar to adults.

Their procedure first derives ideal doses across a fine grid of body sizes, then selects practical doses from the strengths actually manufactured. Three rules are compared on peak, trough and total exposure. One seeks the best fit to adult exposure. One is conservative and never lets child exposure pass the adult level. One is progressive and never lets it fall below. Simulations show the spread between children, and an implementation in R and Monolix accompanies the paper.
pmc-13421338:
Éanna Fennell leads a twenty-author team mapping, in a 2026 study, the immune landscape of Epstein-Barr virus-positive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. This aggressive lymphoma has poor outcomes and is often blamed on ageing immunity, yet it strikes younger people too, so the authors looked for other mechanisms.

Patients showed broadly weakened antiviral T-cell responses, worst in the virus-positive group. Spatial protein mapping revealed tumours short of killer T cells and crowded with suppressive macrophages gathered around tumour cells expressing the viral protein LMP1. Among related conditions, this lymphoma carried the strongest suppressive signature. Lab modelling backed the picture. The authors describe a double failure: weakened body-wide antiviral immunity plus a locally suppressive tumour niche.
pmc-13421538:
Maximilian Bleilöb and five colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether directly 3D-printed teeth aligners are safe against gum tissue at thicknesses well beyond the standard. Printed aligners let orthodontists make appliances in-office and vary thickness by region, yet thicker parts might cure less completely under the standard twenty-minute ultraviolet post-cure.

Discs from half a millimetre to six millimetres thick were printed in a dental resin through the manufacturer's closed workflow. Dimensions matched their targets closely. In a standard cell-viability test on human gum fibroblasts, every thickness stayed above the seventy percent threshold that defines non-cytotoxic material, with no meaningful difference from the standard thickness. The authors conclude the standard cure suffices up to six millimetres.
pmc-13422038:
Tomas Lindmark, David Hallman, Gunnar Bergström and Annika Strömberg interview eldercare managers in Sweden, in a 2026 study, about life built on temporary staff. Municipal care leans on short-term workers to cover shortages, yet the practice can erode continuity for residents and pile pressure on permanent teams.

The second was leading with tied hands, since recruitment and planning sit beyond their control. The third was a wish list moving from rigidity to flexibility. Managers across residential and home care told a consistent story. The authors argue reform must hand managers real workforce levers.
pmc-13422238:
Joon Sin Ser and Siew Kwaon Lui describe, in a 2026 case report, a woman in her early sixties left unable to walk by Guillain-Barré syndrome. A robotic exoskeleton helped her learn to walk again. The illness paralysed all four limbs and her breathing needed support; after antibody treatment stabilised her, weakness and poor trunk control stalled standard gait training.

Ten sessions with the Hybrid Assistive Limb exoskeleton were added over fifteen days of inpatient rehabilitation, without adverse events. Walking distance and independence climbed steadily, and by the end she covered fifty metres with a stick and minimal help. Continued ordinary therapy brought independent walking by discharge. The authors call for studies on who benefits and when to start.
pmc-13422338:
Jing Shi leads an eight-author team studying, in a 2026 paper, why diabetes stalls the natural drift of teeth after a neighbour is lost. Seventy diabetic and seventy control mice carried unopposed lower molars. The diabetic animals remodelled periapical bone abnormally: fewer bone-building cells, more bone-eating cells, and lower levels of three growth signals in both message and protein. One transcription factor tied to bone formation rose on the message side instead. Measurements of eruption distance and bone volume complete the comparison. The authors map a remodelling imbalance behind the diabetic stall.
pmc-13422638:
Pongsatorn Gunun leads an eight-author team feeding rubber seed kernels to beef cattle, in a 2026 study of a plantation byproduct as a supplement. Rubber seeds are rich in protein and fat yet usually wasted, and pellets made from their kernels might lift growth cheaply if cattle thrive on them.

Twelve crossbred bulls were assigned for sixty days to no supplement or to daily pellets at two levels. Feed intake stayed level across groups, while fat intake and the digestibility of protein and fat rose with supplementation. Blood chemistry barely moved, apart from cholesterol. Daily weight gain improved with pellets, peaking at the lower level, and feed conversion sharpened. The authors nominate the lower dose as the practical optimum.
pmc-13422838:
Fei Ma, Enhong Han and Jianjun Gao examine, in a 2026 study, whether a blood marker of heart muscle injury predicts death in people with chronic kidney disease. Troponin leaks when heart cells are damaged, and kidney patients often carry raised levels whose long-term meaning was unclear.

Drawing on national survey records representing over twenty-two million adults, the team found injury — at least one high troponin reading — in about a quarter of the cohort. Those patients were older and sicker, with worse kidney function. Across a median follow-up approaching twelve years, their survival was significantly worse at every horizon checked. The association held in adjusted models and when patients with known heart disease were excluded. The authors propose troponin as a risk flag in kidney care.
pmc-13422938:
Ulrich Reininghaus leads a twenty-one-author team launching, in a 2026 protocol, a two-arm population study of mental health in Mannheim, Germany. Public mental-health monitoring needs the whole spectrum, from wellbeing to severe disorder. German population research on that full range has been quiet for twenty years. The MAKO study is built to close the conceptual gaps that leaves.

One arm hunts every new case arising in the catchment during 2024 and 2025 through structured clinical interviews and case records. The other recruits a characterised population cohort — spanning people without symptoms, those at risk and those already ill — and follows them forward. The authors present the design as a test of an integrated model of population mental health.
pmc-13423038:
Pilar Ficapal-Cusí and six co-authors survey doctors in Catalonia, Spain, about technostress, the strain that digital tools can place on clinicians at work. Their 2026 survey drew online answers from 423 doctors in March and April 2024. It scored overall strain plus overload, invasion, complexity, insecurity, and uncertainty.

Overall technostress sat at 2.91 out of 5, a middling level, with overload and uncertainty rated highest and insecurity lowest. More years in practice predicted more strain. So did a mix of being a woman, working in hospital care, and practising outside city areas. Frequent technical faults also mattered, while skilled use of tools softened the burden. The authors treat the links as exploratory, given the non-random sample.
pmc-13423438:
Atsushi Hirata leads a ten-author prospective pilot study testing Doppler ultrasound with superb microvascular imaging to judge bowel blood flow during colorectal cancer surgery. The standard dye-based fluorescence method works, but it depends on contrast timing and cannot be repeated freely, so a probe-based alternative could help surgeons pick a safe join line.

Eight patients were enrolled, seven analysed. The ultrasound boundary sat a median of 4 mm closer to the tumour side than the dye boundary. That boundary is where fine vessels crossing the bowel wall vanish. One case differed by 60 mm. Two observers agreed closely on the ultrasound line, within a median of 2 mm. No procedure-related harm appeared within thirty days.
pmc-13424038:

Their carrier-free particles co-assemble a STING activator with a light-absorbing dye, so near-infrared light both heats tumour cells into an immune-visible death and trips the alarm. A coating borrowed from PD-1-bearing cell membranes steered particles to tumours about five times more strongly and delivered checkpoint blockade on site. In models the approach converted quiet, cold tumours into active ones and left immune memory against spread.
pmc-13424138:
Lesley H Thorne leads a 25-author account of a year-long pulse of unusually fresh water in the New York Bight and its ripple through the whole marine food web. Monitoring caught water turning corrosive for shell-building creatures, with aragonite saturation below 1. Tiny copepods boomed through spring and summer. Fish and invertebrates, meanwhile, shifted toward the equator, reversing recent poleward moves. Humpback whales stayed longer and looked fatter than usual, and endangered right and sei whales appeared at unusually high rates. The study shows how one climate jolt can reorganise an ecosystem.
pmc-13424638:

Sequencing 41 resistant mutants showed changes in just two polymerase subunits. The changes sat at a few hotspots. Rifampicin resistance spreads more widely by contrast. Corallopyronin resistance also cost the bacteria 12 to 15 percent of fitness in head-to-head growth contests. The authors argue the narrower escape routes make the new drug harder to beat.
pmc-13424938:
Ming-Hui Hung and Shu-Yueh Cheng write a letter questioning the comparison group in a trial of day-case breast-conserving surgery. That trial found regional anaesthesia with dexmedetomidine sedation beating general anaesthesia for early recovery. The letter's point targets the general anaesthesia arm, which used both a starting dose of sufentanil and a running infusion of remifentanil, hardly an opioid-sparing design.

Remifentanil, they note, can rebound into extra pain and nausea once stopped. The item-level recovery scores fit that suspicion. The biggest gaps at two hours sat in function items, sleep actually favoured general anaesthesia, and sickness was commoner there. By twenty-four hours the groups nearly met. Future trials, the authors urge, should compare against gentler general anaesthesia.
pmc-13425538:
Gabrielle M. Salvatore and coauthors present the Project PACE protocol in 2026, a study of daily activity and menstrual experiences in women who move too little. Sixty women aged 18 to 50 with at least one cardiovascular risk marker will report symptoms, activity, motivation, and sleep twice daily for 45 days. Each participant also wears a Fitbit Inspire device for continuous activity and sleep recording.

Multilevel models will test whether worse-than-usual symptom days bring lower motivation, intentions, and confidence for activity within the same person. Findings should guide activity programs that adapt to daily menstrual changes instead of assuming steady behavior.
pmc-13427338: Gao and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their article on serious games and adolescents' internet adaptability. One error was fixed: equal contribution had been wrongly credited to Shihao Ma instead of Shijie Gao. The author list now marks Gao and Min Jia as equal contributors, with Ma no longer carrying that mark. The corrected article was resubmitted to PubMed, PubMed Central, and other repositories, and the fix appears in the online version.
pmc-13427538:
Audrey Dumont leads a large French team that set out in 2026 to test the safety of rotigotine in polycystic kidney disease. The inherited condition fills the kidneys with cysts and often raises blood pressure early in life. Rotigotine is a skin patch drug that stimulates dopamine receptors. Early work hinted that it might repair faulty sensing in kidney cells and blood vessel walls.

The plan enrolls 120 adults aged 18 to 60 at four university hospitals in France over two years. Participants are assigned by chance to receive the patch or not, while usual care continues. Safety comes first, with kidney and heart measures as early clues for a later, larger trial. Readers see how a repurposed drug moves from lab promise to careful human testing.
pmc-13427738:
Aydogan and colleagues built a new refractory alloy in 2026 by laser-based 3D printing and tested whether it can survive the radiation inside future nuclear reactors. The alloy mixes chromium, molybdenum, tantalum, titanium, and vanadium. Its printed structure forms a branched main phase plus a second oxygen-rich phase, and printing gave it both higher strength and better ductility than cast versions.

Even at one thousand degrees Celsius the alloy kept a yield strength of about nine hundred fifty megapascals while still deforming without cracking. Under radiation doses up to eighteen displacements per atom, at room temperature and at six hundred fifty degrees, both phases stayed stable with no voids or phase changes. Damage loops formed but stayed controlled, helped by slow atom movement in the mixed matrix. The authors see promise for fission and fusion reactor parts.
pmc-13427838:
Khanh Nguyen and colleagues hunted for blood markers that predict whether a heart drug will work in premature babies. The babies had a patent ductus arteriosus, a blood vessel that stays open after birth and strains the heart and lungs.
