Before treatment, four fat-like signals called oxylipins ran higher in the blood of babies who went on to respond. Those signals fell after treatment in responders but stayed flat in non-responders, hinting at a future test to guide dosing.
pmc-13427938:
Mehmet E. Akyuz and colleagues map the brain's superior longitudinal fibre system against branches of the middle cerebral artery, a pairing surgeons need in three dimensions. The fibre bundle links temporal and frontal lobes through the parietal lobe, yet its blood supply was unreported.

Ten donated hemispheres were dissected for fibres, ten more were dissected in place with arteries kept, and scans from ten healthy people were rebuilt in 3D. The work names the superior longitudinal complex and its second and third parts plus the arcuate bundle. Neurosurgeons get a spatial guide for cutting near language pathways without harming their supply.
pmc-13428038:
Tang and colleagues develop a gene silencing injection that lowers uric acid for months after one dose. High uric acid, the driver of gout, comes largely from the liver enzyme xanthine dehydrogenase. Their 2026 preclinical study builds a small interfering RNA, a molecule that switches off one chosen gene. A sugar tag steers it into liver cells. It is tested in human liver cells, mice, and cynomolgus monkeys.

The RNA strongly cut the enzyme's message and protein in liver cells. One under skin dose in mice lowered blood uric acid and liver enzyme levels for more than six weeks. In monkeys, one dose held uric acid down for up to half a year, with enzyme suppression lasting about four months. The drug piled up in liver, thousands fold over blood, and lingered for weeks. Full safety checks, including off target gene scans, found no harm.
pmc-13428438:
Ahmed Awad and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, how war damaged the mouths and dental care of people in Gaza. Conflict wrecks clinics and daily routines, yet oral health rarely gets measured in humanitarian research. An online questionnaire reached 599 residents, who rated their oral state and habits both before October 2023 and during the 2023 to 2024 war. All twelve areas checked grew significantly worse.

Severe oral pain jumped from about 7 percent of respondents before the war to about 74 percent during it. Twice-daily brushing collapsed from about 78 percent to under 10 percent, and unmet dental needs soared above 90 percent. Canned food dependence and stress habits rose sharply. Nearly everyone felt their oral health had worsened. The authors press for dental care inside emergency health responses, not after them.
pmc-13428538:
Shatha Alaoufi and Raghad M. Alhomaid survey, in a 2026 study, what adults in Saudi Arabia know and believe about protein supplements. Gym culture has pushed powders and shakes into the mainstream, yet safety knowledge may lag behind use. An online questionnaire ran through most of 2024 and drew 358 completed replies from adults across the country. Questions covered knowledge, attitudes, personal use, health beliefs, and safety habits, split by gender.

About 68 percent knew of the supplements, with men ahead of women on awareness. Nearly two thirds did not know the risks tied to them. About 36 percent had used supplements at some point, and roughly one in nine users reported side effects. Half of users did not know whether powders can hide banned doping substances. Fewer than half of users checked for a respected safety certification mark, a gap the authors flag.
pmc-13429138:
Miranda A. Farage and colleagues propose, in a 2026 conceptual paper, a framework that treats skin as the meeting point of body and world. Health research often splits inner biology from outer environment, missing how they trade signals over a lifetime. Their Integrated Human System Framework stacks inner systems, such as hormones, immunity, metabolism, and nerves, against outer influences like behavior, surroundings, and social context. Skin sits between them as a living, measurable interface.

Life stage, sex, and social setting cut across the whole model as shaping forces. The authors position the framework beside, not above, existing whole-person models in medicine. Its promised uses are practical: sharper hypotheses, new biomarkers read from skin, and study designs that join clinic and environment. Empirical testing across disciplines is the work the paper calls for next.
pmc-13429538:
Francesco Saverio Papadia reappraises hypoabsorptive weight-loss surgery, operations that cut nutrient uptake and stay underused despite strong durable weight loss and metabolic gains. Registry data, head-to-head studies, and cohorts followed up to 30 years feed the review.

After adjusting for starting differences, 30-day harm was no higher than for gastric bypass. At five years, total weight loss reached 40.6 percent versus 33.8 percent for bypass, with diabetes remission at 92.8 percent. Yet long-term nutrition costs touched over 80 percent of patients in some cohorts, and repeat operations hit 37 percent at ten years. The review weighs unmatched power against heavy lifelong trade-offs.
pmc-13430738:
Kexin Xu and colleagues studied how hard life events link to thoughts of suicide among teens treated for depression in a 2026 survey across five hospitals in China. The group enrolled 341 patients aged ten to nineteen, each with a clinical diagnosis. Teens filled out forms on hard events, inner strength, mood signs, and thoughts of suicide.

Hard events went with weaker inner strength. Weaker strength then went with worse mood signs, which in turn went with stronger thoughts of suicide. Age shaped the last link, since mood signs predicted such thoughts more sharply in younger teens than in older ones. The authors frame inner strength and mood care as prime targets for prevention work. They also urge plans tuned to each age band.
pmc-13431438:
Jiejun He and co-authors profiled helper T cells in the blood of people with hay fever in 2026, hunting for shifts in the cell groups that steer antibody output. Hay fever grows from an immune overreaction tied to a class of antibodies. Helper cells of one lean are known to back that class, yet the full spread of groups had stayed murky.

The study drew blood from 39 patients and 17 healthy peers. Cell counts showed the antibody-linked group ran higher in patients, and its share grew with worse illness. Armed helper cells ran higher too. A deep gene read on a small side group split helper cells into six clusters and found a further group loaded with cell-killing genes, also richer in patients. The authors say blood helper profiles may help map body-wide immune change in this allergy.
pmc-13431738:
Rhett T Bryant and co-authors made twin-iron complexes in 2026 that hold a nitrogen pair between two iron atoms. Heat then tore all four bonds of a silicon gas at once. Nitrogen-bridged twin-metal hosts are rare for iron in its lowest charge state. The team formed them by stripping electrons from iron chloride starters with one or two reduction steps.

Full checks with sound-based, crystal, and iron-probe tools confirmed the new hosts and their calm spin state. Warming them with silane gas split each of its four hydrogen bonds, which left a silicon atom pinned between the two irons, each iron also holding two hydrogens. The iron-to-silicon bonds rank as the shortest yet seen, and the three atoms sit near a straight line. The work extends a trick first shown with cobalt to iron.
pmc-13431838:
Guz-Mark and colleagues assessed the mouths and teeth of 22 children with intestinal failure. In that condition the gut cannot sustain nutrition, and intravenous feeding is required. The checks ran at a tertiary pediatric clinic in 2024. Causes in the group were short bowel syndrome in 50 percent of cases. Congenital gut disorders made up 27.3 percent, and motility disorders 22.7 percent.

Most of the children, 72.7 percent, needed daily intravenous support for a median of 10.5 hours a day. Half had restricted oral intake. Brushing habits were poor: only 18.2 percent brushed twice daily. More than half, 54.5 percent, had no regular daily brushing routine at all. Dental calculus coated the teeth of 63.6 percent of the children. Plaque and gum scores ran meaningfully above normal reference values. Cavities were found in 18.2 percent of the children. Enamel defects appeared in two-thirds of children examined. The findings prompt calls to embed dental care in multidisciplinary follow-up.
pmc-13434538:
Bräuner and colleagues ran a simulation study in 2026 on how machine learning tools affect team decisions in colorectal cancer care. Care teams from several specialties meet to plan each patient's treatment, but proof that these meetings improve outcomes is thin. Four cancer centres each ran four simulated meetings, testing the standard setup, a risk prediction model, a structured data display tool, and both aids together.

Bräuner found that clinicians and the model sorted patients into risk groups in similar shares, yet they disagreed on specific patients, above all those at higher risk. Staff saw the main gain as more standard care, less swayed by personal views of single doctors. They also insisted that clinicians must stay free to overrule the tools when a case holds details the model misses. Overall views of the aids were positive across the centres.
pmc-13434638:
Tommaso Croese and a large team trace a brain to spleen line that slows Alzheimer type decline in mice in 2026. Tracing shows the link thins as amyloid disease advances. Cutting the spleen nerve early, before signs show, tests what the line does.

Cut mice lost thinking skills sooner and made fewer fresh blood cells. Fewer guard cells reached the brain, and brain immune cells stalled in a calm state. Boosting the spleen signal reversed each trend and delayed decline. An eye injury test gave the same verdict. Spleen cells, the work argues, help set the pace of disease.
pmc-13434738:
Michael Shamash and Corinne F Maurice pool twelve infant gut virus studies from eight countries in 2026. Bacteria in the baby gut are well charted, yet their viruses were not. The pooled data track virus change across the first three years of life.

Virus variety rose fast in the first eight months, while evenness fell. Change between visits slowed with age, and babies grew more alike in virus mix. Mild viruses that hide in bacteria thinned out, and virus carried helper genes shifted. The shared path gives clinics a baseline. Illness linked shifts can now be spotted against that norm.
pmc-13435238:
Smith and Kolopenuk examine the colonial roots of research ethics in biological anthropology in this 2026 article. Modern science grew alongside European colonization, and Indigenous Peoples have long resisted research that extracts their knowledge, bodies, and genetic material. Ethics rules claim to guard against such harms, and the authors analyze how those rules actually operate in anthropological and genetic research affecting Indigenous communities.

Ethics frameworks run on a language of goodness, inclusion, and reconciliation, they argue. That language can hide the power relations at work. Those relations shape who produces knowledge about Indigenous Peoples. Following institutional ethics can make research look virtuous while leaving colonial control untouched, they contend. Ethics alone, however well intentioned, cannot dismantle that structure, because the coloniality of research operates precisely through benevolence and good intentions.
pmc-13435438:
Yuxin Xie's team mined safety reports in 2026 for a first-line HIV regimen combining bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide. Long-term real-world safety data were thin. The team analyzed 5,815 adverse event reports in the FAERS database from 2018 to 2025, validated key signals in EudraVigilance, and probed one surprise signal, pancreatitis, with added models and lab data.

Known effects like weight gain, headache, and immune reconstitution syndrome appeared as expected, while pancreatitis emerged as an unexpected signal worth watching. Sex, timing, and sensitivity checks were run to test how firm the signals were. HIV clinicians get a large post-market safety map, with pancreatitis flagged for vigilance rather than proven as caused by the drugs.
pmc-13435938:
Jin Ho Choi's team attacked drug resistance in pancreatic cancer in 2026 by triggering iron-driven cell death, an iron-driven cell death marked by fat damage. Resistance to the drug limits treatment, and iron-driven death offers a separate kill route. The team built forty-two patient-derived tumor organoids, profiled their genes and drug responses, and tested the ferroptosis inducer artesunate alongside oxaliplatin.

Drug-resistant lab tumors showed weak iron-death defenses, and artesunate plus the drug synergized in cells and lab tumors, raising iron, fat damage, and energy failure, and shrinking grafted tumors in mice. Iron transport proteins rose with treatment, and blocking a key defense gene mattered. Oncologists get a combination lead for resistant pancreatic cancer, still preclinical but grounded in patient-derived models.
pmc-13436338:
Chao Zhang and coauthors test an AI slide reader for tuberculosis at Beijing Chest Hospital in 2026. Spit slides from suspected patients were stained two ways and scanned across set fields. Manual reading, culture, and a gene test serve as yardsticks.

Among 352 confirmed cases the reader with glow stain caught about one third. Culture caught slightly fewer cases, while manual reading caught under one fifth. Wider scanning fields lifted catch rates for both stains. False alarms stayed under one percent in non TB lung patients. The reader gives busy clinics culture grade speed at smear cost.
pmc-13436638:
Angela G Campbell and coauthors check how often pregnancy goes unrecorded during Indiana emergency visits in 2026. Records cover 4,597 visits by pregnant patients who later had live births in 2022 to 2023. Visits sat between six weeks and about forty weeks of pregnancy.

Documentation was missing in 273 visits, or 5.9 percent. Misses fell harder on Black patients than on White patients. Imaging of chest, belly, or spine hit 11.0 percent of undocumented visits versus 3.4 percent of documented ones. Matched math doubles the imaging odds when pregnancy is missed. Record prompts may shield both fetus and staff.
pmc-13437238:
Manisha Goel and a large Dresden team paired gene readings with receptor sequencing to study T cells in gut graft-versus-host disease. Donated immune cells can attack the gut after transplant, and about a third of patients stop responding to steroids for reasons that stay unclear. Their 2026 study took matched gut tissue and blood from nineteen patients checked for suspected gut disease, twelve of whom truly had it.

Blood told a weak story: only nine genes differed between the groups, with no clear pattern. That split supports the idea that the fight is local, driven by T cells settled in tissue rather than those passing through blood. The authors frame the paired method as a hunt for tissue-bound drivers of stubborn disease, which blood tests alone may miss.
pmc-13438138:
Soroush Toutounchian's team compared deep learning models in 2026 for diagnosing apple leaf disease, a threat to yields and food security. Eight convolutional networks and two vision transformers were tuned with DropBlock regularization on a 2021 plant pathology image set covering five diseases plus healthy leaves, with thresholds later tuned by swarm optimization. A moderate DropBlock and dropout setting worked best.

Swin transformer variants led, reaching about ninety-one percent accuracy and the top F1 score, edging newer convolutional rivals. Orchard managers and plant pathologists get a ranked model comparison for fast, image-based diagnosis. Field photos with varied light and background will test whether lab accuracy survives the orchard.
pmc-13439338:
Altay Aitmagambetov's team integrated a flat GSM antenna in 2026 into the case of a cargo tracking seal. Seals that track cargo need reliable mobile links, yet housing material, tight layout, and nearby electronics can detune antennas. Twenty-eight commercial flat antennas plus a home-built Zmeyka design on thin FR-4 board were compared in an anechoic chamber and in field tests. Runs came first in ABS plastic, then in a reinforced polyamide case.

Zmeyka achieved excellent matching in the reference case while several commercial antennas matched poorly, but reinforced polyamide shifted resonance down about fifty megahertz, worsened matching, and cut main-lobe transmission. Logistics engineers get a housing-aware antenna comparison and a caution: seal material choice can make or break tracking links.
pmc-13439838:
Shevchuk and colleagues survey the thick shelled river mussel Unio crassus, an endangered freshwater species, in the rivers of right bank Ukraine. Mussels filter water and signal river health, and this species has lost half its Central European range. Their 2026 study checks 191 sites across four river basins. In the Prypiat basin, finds fell between survey periods, though small samples urge caution. The data feed plans for protected Emerald Network sites and species management in Ukraine.
pmc-13441038:

Its docking grip on CETP nearly matched curcumin and approached the old reference drug, while simulations showed the bound pair staying as steady as the reference complex. pmc-13441138:
Huayuan Liang's team studied switch-to-surgery in 2026 for stomach cancer with belly spread or found belly cell test, where immune therapy plus chemo may shrink disease enough for surgery. In a single-center cohort of 144 patients treated from 2019 to 2024, those who responded underwent second-look scope check. Thirty-six patients reached surgery, three quarters with complete removal, and median life stretched to about thirty-three months versus twelve months with comfort care, with progression-free life also far longer. Low belly cancer index predicted the best life. Oncologists get a strong look-back case for active restaging after immune-chemo, pending trial proof.
pmc-13441938:
Dzmitry Matsiukevich and David M Ornitz separate two kinds of heart stress in mice, pressure overload versus the hormone angiotensin II, to see which remodels coronary vessels. The authors call the two patterns distinct vascular phenotypes.
pmc-13442638:
Kenan Kaya and Ziyaettin Erdem review cyber grooming of children and teens in a 2026 scoping paper. Risk ran higher for teens with heavy online time, low digital skill, raw feelings, or thin social support. Offender playbooks leaned on emotional tricks, secrecy, and chat tools to hold control. Guard plans that worked best mixed digital skill lessons for youth with family and school steps. Laws alone lagged behind the tech shifts. The authors call for joined plans across homes, schools, and platforms, since no single shield stops a patient offender.
pmc-13443338:
Kristina Rosqvist follows 107 people in late-stage Parkinson disease for a decade in a 2026 study. Late stage meant high Hoehn and Yahr marks or low daily-life independence at entry. Death records and clinic files gave causes and risk marks across the span.

After three years, 52 people, a 54 percent share of the cohort, still lived. Shares fell to 31 percent at five years and 15 percent at seven years. Choking pneumonia led causes at 34 percent of deaths, then sepsis at 16 percent of deaths. Poor motor scores, poor cognition, and low mood each raised death risk in joint models. The author urges swallow care as front-line work, since choking drives the top killer.
pmc-13443738:

Local phase shifts bend local group speed, so spin density reshapes itself into stable multi-lobe ranks. Total spin charge stays fixed while the inner pattern blooms. The team then used the pattern's beat rate to send data through open air, with clean encode and decode runs. The work turns passive swirls into coded carriers. Uses span dense light links and fast light tools in their outlook.
pmc-13444638:

The survey ran alongside a test-and-treat plan meant to find cases early and clear them. Pinworm spreads with ease in daycare rooms, so child care settings were the focus of the work.

Staff collected tape swabs from 12,608 children aged up to six years in daycare and kindergarten across eight cities and counties. Only 28 children tested positive, and the yearly rate fell across the survey years. Rates ran higher in children aged four to six, and the authors urge steady checks, since small local clusters can still appear without warning.
pmc-13446138:

pmc-13446338:

pmc-13446738:

pmc-13446838:
Yodsapat Paemanukornruk and colleagues follow a Bangkok school sealant program for five years, asking which children gain from sealing first molars, in a 2026 study. Sealants coat the chewing pits where decay starts, yet proof of who gains most has run thin. Records joined a 2019 first-grade round to a 2024 sixth-grade check.

Six hundred ninety-five students with 2,198 sound first molars entered the analysis, split by how many untreated decayed teeth they began with. Sealed teeth showed no clear edge in the low and middle risk groups. In the high-risk group, children with at least one sealed tooth faced about half the decay risk of unsealed peers. pmc-13447238:
Reyila Abasi and colleagues report kidney transplant outcomes in children with disease linked to the WT1 gene in a 2026 single-centre cohort. pmc-13447438:

pmc-13447738:
Soyoung Jung, Hae Jin Kang, and Yoo Kyoung Park reviewed studies of digital tools that tailor diet advice to older adults. Their 2026 scoping review maps what these tools do, how well they work, and what users think of them.

Gains were steadiest for eating habits and day-to-day diet control, while proof for strength, memory, and heart health stayed thin. Familiar screens and human support helped older users stay engaged, while hard navigation and weak food databases put them off.
pmc-13448038:
Svensson and colleagues used the Swedish Spine Registry in 2026 to learn what predicts neck disability, headache, and pain two years after neck decompression surgery. Demographic, lifestyle, surgical, and general health factors added smaller effects. Together the models explained between thirteen and thirty-five percent of outcome variation. pmc-13448138:
Manaloto and co-authors explore what nursing students learn by leading undergraduate thesis groups in this 2026 qualitative study. Eight themes emerged, covering the leaders' responsibilities, the emotional ups and downs of the role, and academic and research-related difficulties along the way. Group dynamics and interpersonal friction featured prominently, as did the support, or absence, of faculty mentorship. Participants described evolving leadership styles. They also reported growth in communication, accountability, resilience, and collaboration. Their recommendations could help programs prepare students for professional roles, the authors say.
pmc-13448438:

Arrived late, at a median of about thirty months after the first cancer diagnosis and well after bone spread. Nearly half of primary tumors carried gene changes that existing drugs can target, and those patients tended to live longer. supports spinal fluid gene testing and full-spine imaging rather than scanning one segment alone.
pmc-13449038:

In other groups it goes only into serotonin cells or only into other cells. The team then records brain waves over time in males and females.

Those shifts came with changes in delta wave power, the slow waves that mark deep sleep. pmc-13449338:

Eiichiro Nakagawa and four colleagues tell in 2026 of a man whose hidden Brugada syndrome, a genetic rhythm disorder that can kill suddenly, only declared itself after he received a new liver. He had lived eighteen years with liver disease before a living donor transplant restored his organ function. Nobody had previously linked liver failure to masking this syndrome.

From then on his electrocardiogram showed the diagnostic Brugada pattern consistently for more than three years. Hormones are known to shape this tracing, and the syndrome's strong male skew hints at testosterone's role. The authors propose that normalized hormones unmasked a phenotype his illness had kept quiet.
pmc-13492838:
Yaztappeh and colleagues ran a 2026 randomized trial of the Unified Protocol, a therapy that treats shared roots of emotional disorders rather than each diagnosis separately. They enrolled 30 university students with below-threshold depression and anxiety symptoms and split them into treatment and control groups of fifteen.

The treatment group received fourteen 90-minute sessions. Depression, anxiety, and stress scores fell sharply by the end of therapy, and the gains held at a six-month follow-up. Emotion regulation, meaning control over emotional responses, and cognitive flexibility also improved more in the treated group than in controls. The authors present the protocol as a strong option for catching emotional disorders early, before symptoms reach full clinical levels in students.
pmc-13493638:
David Saceda-Corralo leads a nine-author team reviewing in 2026 their results using botulinum toxin injections for trichodynia, the burning scalp pain that accompanies several hair loss disorders and resists standard treatment. Charts covered twenty-one patients who had quit or refused whole-body medicines. The toxin was placed shallowly across the scalp with a multiple-puncture technique, and pain and disease activity were scored over six months.

Patients with scarring hair loss, where inflammation hugs the follicles, improved most, and their disease activity scores fell significantly. Side effects stayed minor. The authors credit the toxin's calming of pain-signaling chemicals and want a controlled trial.
pmc-13493738:
Hasnaki and co-authors report a 2026 computer simulation study of antimony-119, a radioactive element proposed for targeted cancer therapy. Its dose values ran up to five times higher than lutetium-177 and four times higher than iodine-125 in some setups. The advantage held even when the nucleus sat off-centre in the cell. The authors caution that producing antimony-119 remains difficult, which may slow clinical use.
pmc-13494038:
Ainhoa Osa-Sanchez leads a five-author team detecting in 2026 a stubborn class of food allergens with light and learning algorithms instead of laboratory chemistry. Adding purified protein examples to training lifted performance sharply, and the convolutional model reached about ninety-six percent accuracy with the best overall balance. Explanation tools pinpointed which spectral regions carried the allergen signature, keeping the verdict interpretable. pmc-13494638:
Ma and colleagues presented a 2026 method for drawing trustworthy maps from single-cell data, where each cell is described by thousands of gene readings. Popular neighbour embedding tools such as t-SNE and UMAP flatten such data into maps, but they can distort shapes and mislead readers. The team worked within a framework stressing predictability, computability, and stability.

The team then built NESS, a method that uses algorithmic stability to clean up neighbour embedding maps. Applied to stem cells changing type, organoid growth, and tissue lineage data sets, NESS produced smoother structures that matched known biology. The authors present it as a more reliable route to reading cell state transitions.
pmc-13495738:
Tim S Veth and Nicholas M Riley present, in a 2026 paper, GlycoDiveR, a free software framework for exploring glycoproteomics data. The results form tangled, high-dimensional tables that defy the plain charts used for simpler protein marks. Existing tools often demand expert coding and fit one study only.

Users can zoom between whole-proteome patterns and single-site detail with little code, and can still pull the data out for custom work. Its modular build invites new charts and analyses over time. pmc-13498538:
Jing Ding, Xuefeng Huang, Wenxiu Yao, and Tongyu Lin explore in 2026 whether a newly described form of cell death can split pleural mesothelioma into useful subtypes. The low group showed distinct fuel use and more natural killer cells. An 11-gene score predicted survival well in this dataset, though the authors note outside validation is still required.
pmc-13499038:
Disha Gupta, Akash Bhatnagar, and Zoya Chowdhary report in 2026 two cases where orthodontic hardware became buried under the soft tissue of the mouth. Surgeons removed each device under local anaesthetic, and healing was complete within about two weeks in both cases. The authors stress routine monitoring of braces hardware and a team approach when complications arise.
pmc-13499338:
Yushan Yuan, Yang Su, Minjin Wang, and Yong He look back in 2026 at patients in western China whose seizures had no clear cause. Thyroid and general autoimmune antibodies ran higher in the firm autoimmune group, and spinal fluid white cell counts were also raised there. Certain infection antibodies differed between groups as well. Combined testing, the authors argue, helps sort causes sooner and spot patients who may benefit from early immune treatment.
pmc-13499838:
Joseph K Han and co-authors compare in 2026 tezepelumab with rival antibody drugs and with sinus surgery for severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. It consistently outperformed two other antibodies and placebo, and beat a fourth antibody on most shorter-term outcomes. Surgery ranked highest for shrinking polyps in sensitivity checks, while tezepelumab led on the remaining endpoints, a pattern the authors offer for treatment planning.
pmc-13500138:
Phongthorn Kongmun and colleagues test in 2026 whether an emulsifier blend, dosed differently across growth phases, can offset cheaper low-energy feed for meat chickens. Dietary energy is the priciest part of broiler feed, and emulsifiers help birds digest fat, which might rescue performance on reduced-energy diets. Options compared standard energy, reduced energy, and reduced energy plus the blend at two steady doses or a phase-specific schedule.

In the starter phase the blend improved weight and feed efficiency against the reduced-energy control, and phase-specific birds matched the standard-energy group. Grower-phase gains appeared at both steady doses, yet overall performance did not differ significantly among diets in the reported analysis. Gut transit sped up with the blend, energy values trended higher without reaching significance, and carcass yield tended to improve.
pmc-13500538:
Nosheen Naseer and co-authors formulate in 2026 a gel carrying ferulic acid in nanoemulsion droplets for treating psoriasis-like skin inflammation, testing it in rats. Ferulic acid, a plant antioxidant, dissolves poorly in water, which limits skin delivery, so the team built tiny oil droplets with ultrasound and set them into a hydrogel. Disease was triggered on shaved backs with imiquimod cream for seven days in four of five small groups of male Wistar rats, then the gel was applied to the treatment group.

Droplet size sat in the colloidal range with even distribution and stable charge, and the gel spread and acidity suited skin use in their characterisation. Treated rats showed sharply lower inflammatory and oxidative markers than untreated diseased rats, and spleen swelling eased. Tissue sections showed psoriatic changes greatly reduced, with docking simulations supporting a direct interaction with a key inflammatory cytokine.
pmc-13500838:
Saito Sakaguchi and colleagues report a 2026 study of touch sensitivity in identical twins, designed to separate inherited influences from health and lifestyle. The team studied 25 pairs of monozygotic twins, who share essentially the same genes. Touch thresholds were measured with gentle suction stimuli applied to the cheek, and the results were compared with questionnaire answers and objective measures of physical and mental state.

In 18 pairs the twins had similar thresholds, pointing to a genetic influence on how sensitive skin is to touch. In the seven pairs whose thresholds differed, the twin with reduced sensitivity tended to report more physical and mental complaints, such as fatigue and anxiety. The authors suggest that dulled touch may act as a marker of wider health strain shaped by lifestyle, and could one day guide preventive care.
pmc-13501638:
Seval Ceylan Şen leads a six-author team reporting a 2026 questionnaire study of how much pulmonologists know about the link between gum disease and lung disease. Periodontitis and conditions such as COPD and asthma share inflammatory pathways, and evidence for a two-way relationship is growing. The cross-sectional survey reached 111 pulmonologists and asked about training, knowledge of the periodontal-pulmonary connection, and habits around asking patients about oral health or referring them to dentists.

A wide desire-knowledge gap appeared: 91.9 percent had no formal education on the link, yet 68.5 percent wanted structured training on the topic. While 61.3 percent said their patients did get referred to dentists, 54.1 percent never asked about oral symptoms at all. Awareness was solid for local inhaler side effects but shaky on shared inflammation, with 66.7 percent unsure whether treating gums affects COPD flare-ups. Women and university-based doctors scored higher and asked more.
pmc-13501838:
Lesly Yanira Xajil-Ramos leads a twelve-author team reporting a 2026 pharmacokinetic model of tacrolimus in children with kidney transplants. The drug prevents rejection but has a narrow safe window, and children clear it at wildly different rates. The study analysed 165 whole-blood drug measurements from 51 recipients, all at least six months past transplant, using nonlinear mixed-effects modelling in Monolix. Genetic testing covered CYP3A5, the liver enzyme variant that speeds the drug's breakdown, alongside clinical measures.

A two-compartment model with first-order absorption fitted the data well. The CYP3A5 genotype shifted clearance, kidney function estimates influenced both clearance and the central distribution volume, and older age sped absorption. The authors present the model as groundwork for dose individualization. A child's genes, kidney function, and age could one day set the starting dose instead of trial and error, with blood tests fine-tuning it afterward.
pmc-13503438:
Uta Hofmann and others develop a rapid mass weighing method to measure drugs in city sewage under new EU rules. In 2026, the method extracts two tiny samples and at once tests twelve marker drugs, nine listed in the Urban Sewage Treatment Rule plus three stand-ins. The tests use ultra-high speed liquid sorting with Orbitrap high-detail mass weighing.

Measured limits mostly fell between fifteen and thirty billionths of a gram per litre, with higher limits for three drugs, and lab testing showed steady results and rightness. Applied to plants in the Saxon-Czech border region, the method checks removal rate for fourth-stage treatment boosts. Rule-keepers and plant runners gain a fast tool for compliance tracking.
pmc-13503738:
Wenjun Li presents a vision training method meant to hold up in messy real scenes, in this 2026 paper. Models trained on clean sets often fail in fog, rain, low light, or when objects are partly blocked. The method needs no data from the new scene and little to no labeling.

One part makes paired views of a scene by faking fog, rain, light shifts, and blocks, then weights hard cases more in training. A second part aligns traits across several depths of the network so meaning does not drift between layers. Tests on two benchmark sets beat a range of rival methods, with gains of about four points. Gains grew largest when scenes were hit hardest.
pmc-13504338:
Simon Schnaiter leads a consortium study asking whether a tumor's DNA repair score can help judge if a BRCA gene variant is harmful, in a 2026 paper. Ovarian tumors that cannot fix DNA by one repair route carry a scar score from a commercial test. That score already guides drug choice; its use for variant calls was untested.

Four past cohorts gave data on nearly five thousand tumors with both variant and score results. Nine in ten tumors with a harmful variant scored high, against three in ten without one. The math turned those rates into evidence weights under the standard variant rules: a high score adds support for harm, and a low score adds fair support for safety. The authors say scores can sharpen calls on variants of unclear meaning.
pmc-13505138:
Xu Zhang and co-authors present a computer method for outlining diseased regions in pathology images when only rough labels are available. Their network, called MPGR-Net, treats the patches as nodes in a graph and links neighbours at several scales, so local detail and wider context can inform each other. A light attention step then ties global features back to local ones through channel adjustment. Tests on pathology benchmarks showed better accuracy and steadiness than earlier weakly supervised methods. Removing the graph module weakened the results, which supports its central role in the design.
pmc-13505738:
Dalel El Marrouki and colleagues designed glowing polymer nanoparticles whose inner layout can be tuned to balance brightness against energy transfer for sensing. Their one-pot water-based process locks light-emitting BODIPY dyes into chosen zones: the core, the shell, or both.

Dyes kept in the core shone brightest because water, which dims them, was kept away. Dyes placed in the shell passed energy onward most efficiently, reaching about seventy-five percent transfer, because donor and acceptor sat closer together. Extra surface attachment points amplified the transfer further. In a test assay built on biotin and streptavidin binding, brightness mattered most for sensitivity, and the best design detected targets at a few nanomoles per litre. Readings worked even on a cheap LED device, pointing toward bedside tests without heavy metals.
pmc-13507138:
Babak Emami and colleagues test, in 2026 work, a photonic entropy computer on the hard puzzle of protein design with a fixed backbone. Designers must pick amino acids and side-chain poses that minimize energy, and options explode as proteins grow. Benchmark proteins held from about five hundred to about nine hundred variables, with exact classical answers known for fair scoring. Best Dirac-3 samples landed within a few percent of the ideal energies across cases. The classical solver stayed faster here, while Dirac-3 run time grew gently with size. The study sets a careful benchmark for this new optimizer class.
pmc-13507238:
Xueyuan Wei, Hai Huang, and Yujie Wang propose, in 2026 work, a scheduling framework for medical edge computing that fuses fuzzy logic with reinforcement learning. Hospital devices generate urgent tasks that nearby edge servers must place quickly, balancing delay, energy, and battery limits. A learning agent then refines placement choices from feedback, with the two parts mathematically coupled rather than loosely joined. Simulations in medical internet-of-things settings cut average latency by up to two fifths against benchmarks and lifted energy efficiency notably. pmc-13508238:
Jee-Eun Hwang and four co-authors review how drug-carrying nanoparticles could be designed around the unique surroundings of each tumor, in 2026 work. Tumors sit in a messy local habitat of stiff fibers, leaky vessels, low oxygen, acid buildup, and immune cells held at bay. Their aim is precision engineering driven by biology, replacing one-size designs that ignore how varied tumors really are.
pmc-13508438:
Maxwell Hogshead and six co-authors show that long-term smoke exposure reshapes how a nicotine receptor gene is spliced, in 2026 work. Long smoke exposure, not short, shifted the mix of forms in the cell tests. The authors argue smoking rewires its own receptor, a feedback that could deepen dependence and cancer risk beside the inherited effect.
pmc-13508638:
Liangbo Linus Shen and seven co-authors build a pixel-level map predicting where dry macular degeneration will eat into the retina next, in 2026 work. Closer to the border meant higher risk, while distance from the center also mattered. The pixel model predicted growth far better than a whole-eye model. pmc-13510338:
Dilek Altun Varmış and eight co-authors compare routine blood and chemistry markers in children with specific learning disorder against healthy peers, in 2026 work. The disorder covers lasting trouble with reading, writing, or math despite normal teaching. After strict correction for many comparisons, the disorder group showed a distinct pattern centered on lower average platelet size and higher counts of one white cell type tied to allergy responses. pmc-13514138:
Rasmy and colleagues proposed a hybrid method for aligning satellite images of the same place taken at different times, in a 2026 study. The method reaches accuracy finer than a single pixel. pmc-13517538:

pmc-13518938:

pmc-13519038:
Kalman and colleagues compared the breaking strength of zirconia dental crowns and veneers made by 3D printing against the standard milling method, in a 2026 laboratory study. pmc-13520138:

A longitudinal cohort adds twice-yearly follow-up on behavior paths and social drivers. Measures cover prevalence, new products, attitudes, and campaign exposure using adapted national instruments. Timely local evidence should feed cessation programs, policy checks, and harm reduction.
pmc-13520238:

pmc-13521938:

With only fifty training cases, validation accuracy still held near 91 percent.
pmc-13522538:

pmc-13523038:

pmc-13523238:
Keralem Anteneh Bishaw, Bewket Yeserah Aynalem, and Demewoze Kefale pool evidence on labor pain care in Ethiopia in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Working in facilities with adequate supplies or a written protocol, and perceiving labor pain as moderate to severe, also raised use substantially. The authors conclude that both individual preparation and institutional support must improve for labor pain care to become routine.
pmc-13525738:
Goto and co-authors explain a baby's back lump that turned out to be a split rib. Their 2026 case report describes a ten-month-old boy with a palpable mass on his left back. Such lumps in infants range from harmless congenital variants to tumours, so imaging had to settle the question.

MRI confirmed no associated soft tissue mass. Because the eleventh rib is a floating rib pointing backwards, its forked end presented as the palpable lump. The child was managed without surgery. pmc-13528138:
Jenni Hirvikallio, Ari Haaranen, and Tarja Kvist survey leadership and wellbeing among Finnish paramedics in a 2026 study. An online survey reached 322 ambulance staff at basic and advanced levels. It scored transformational leadership, work engagement, and job wellbeing. Transformational leaders inspire, coach, and model values. Ethics earned the highest marks. Feedback and rewards scored lowest.

When engagement entered the model, the direct leadership tie shrank but stayed firm. That pattern fits a path where good leaders raise engagement, which lifts wellbeing. The authors note a one-time survey cannot prove cause. Still, they back leadership training as a lever for staff health.
pmc-13528738:

pmc-13528838:

Final survival medians were about twenty-three months against about seventeen. That gap also missed significance. Serious side effects were somewhat more common with the added drug. The authors conclude the combo did not prove a benefit. The search for partners to PD-L1 blockers continues.
pmc-13529838:
Palser and colleagues asked in 2026 whether toddlers who were late to speak carry lasting language weaknesses into later childhood when they also have dyslexia. pmc-13530838:
Scheiderer and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 190, a cohort comparison of the two commonest graft choices for elbow ligament reconstruction in baseball players. The choices are the palmaris longus tendon from the forearm and the gracilis tendon from the thigh. Biomechanics says they are equally strong; clinical proof was thin.

Seventy-one players with at least two years of follow-up, fifty with gracilis and twenty-one with palmaris grafts, completed outcome surveys. The groups matched on age, body mass, playing level, position, and every preoperative measure, and surgery details and complication rates did not differ either. After surgery, elbow scores, satisfaction classifications, and return classifications were all statistically similar between the grafts at two years. The one difference favored the forearm graft: elbow flexion reached 148 degrees against 144 with the thigh graft.
pmc-13531738:
Jiayi Ren and colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial of a bundled recovery package after keyhole bowel cancer surgery. The bundle mixed electrical acupuncture, belly massage, breathing training, and supervised walking adjusted to symptoms. A total of 105 patients were assigned to the bundle plus standard care or standard care alone.

Ninety patients completed the analysis. Recovery quality scores ran alike at days three and seven, then separated clearly by day 30 in favor of the bundle. Pain and effort ratings also favored the bundle later on. No serious harms appeared, suggesting a medium-term comfort gain rather than faster early recovery.
pmc-13531838:
Simon Rio and co-authors release in 2026 a software package that untangles mixed ancestry in plants with many chromosome copies, then apply it to sugarcane. Standard ancestry tools assume two copies and break on cane, which carries about twelve. Simulations checked the new method against leading rivals for accuracy and speed.

Modern cane genomes proved mostly descended from the sweet domesticated species, with one to four chromosome copies from distinct wild subgroups. A mystery wild contribution from the Pacific appeared in most cultivars. The conserved pattern dates those crossings to early breeding about a century ago.
pmc-13532138:
Guanfei Shen and colleagues designed star-shaped and branched polyesters inspired by natural tannins. Published in 2026, the chemistry paper mimicked gallotannins, whose galloyl ester chains radiate from a sugar core, using glucose-derived cores and phenolic acid building blocks. Branched polymers offer useful flow, solubility, and function, yet biobased aromatic versions remain rare.

A stepwise joining strategy yielded core-arm shapes, checked with model compounds. Direct joining gave partly grafted analogues, while one protocatechuic acid polymer formed stable water mixes of particles near four hundred nanometers. Those particles loaded a water-shy dye, Nile red, showing promise as nature-inspired carriers. The authors open a path to useful polyesters from renewable phenolics. Readers get a modular build with a delivery demo attached.
pmc-13532238:
Catharine R Carlin and colleagues propose in 2026 a housekeeping fix for naming a harmless Listeria species found in North Carolina forest soil. Formal species status needs a representative type strain stored in collections, yet the originally named type breaks naming rules and lacks a typical enzyme trait. A replacement strain from the same survey fits the rules.

Genome comparisons place the replacement squarely inside the species cluster and far from any known species. The species carries no disease genes and shows no blood-breaking behavior, supporting a nonpathogenic profile. Correct naming prevents costly false alarms in food safety testing.
pmc-13536738:
Chris Fleming and colleagues refine measures of low-value care that primary care doctors can actually influence in a 2026 Medicare study. Low-value services offer little benefit yet cost money and may cause harm. Starting from 31 services found in claims, the team checked which ones primary care doctors commonly perform, order, or refer. Data covered millions of patients in a large primary care payment program in 2018.

Two smaller sets were built, holding 4 and 11 services most tied to primary care choices. Both sets distinguished high and low users of low-value care more reliably than the full 31-item set, with the 4-item set performing best. The authors note that claims can mislabel some fitting care, and they call for further work on best use in quality efforts.
pmc-13538538:
Tian-long Gao and colleagues map immune cell genes tied to Alzheimer risk in a 2026 multi-layer genetic study. Immune dysfunction outside the brain increasingly looks involved, yet which cell types and genes matter stays unclear. Single-cell genetic effect data from a large cohort were joined with genome-wide Alzheimer results through causal inference and shared-signal tests. Blood cell profiles, trait-wide scans, drug databases, and docking models then weighed targets.

Twenty-four genes passed both causal and shared-signal bars, each tied to one immune cell type such as monocytes or B cells. Most showed few off-target trait links, hinting at safe intervention room. Three candidate compounds emerged, two predicted to cross into the brain with stable docking poses. The authors pitch the gene list as a base for targeted immune therapy.
pmc-13538638:
Julius S Missanga, Patrick A Ndakidemi, and Pavithravani B Venkataramana map gene differences among lablab bean lines with opposed drought responses in a 2026 marker study. Lablab is a hardy many-use legume still lacking bred types in many regions. Twenty seed lines, ten drought tolerant and ten sensitive from earlier seedling screening, were tested with sixteen gene-based repeat markers after DNA was drawn out and run on gels.

Overall differences between the tolerant and sensitive groups ran low, hinting the markers told them apart weakly. Plots, grouping, and spread checks still singled out three tolerant and three sensitive lines as standing strongly apart. Seven tolerant lines were put forward for breeding use. The authors call for sharper markers and genome tools to pin down drought genes.
pmc-13540838:
Jiahao Xiangli and four colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review, studies of diaphragmatic pacing for people with spinal cord injury who cannot breathe unaided. An implanted system stimulates the breathing muscle directly, offering an escape from mechanical ventilation with its own complications.

Searches of four databases through March 2025 yielded six within-cohort studies reporting weaning rates. Pooling gave a seventy-five percent weaning success rate with little statistical variation between studies. Certainty, however, was graded very low, reflecting non-randomised designs, small samples, and mixed patient groups. The authors ask for large randomised trials before pacing can be recommended with confidence.
pmc-13541638:
Tao Huang and colleagues opened a special issue on computer tools for infectious disease research. Published in 2026, the issue gathers ten papers spanning gene-level analysis to crowd-level tracking. Infectious diseases remain a top global health threat, and the flood of gene, protein, case, and clinic data demands tools that turn bulk data into usable insight.

The papers show language models reading gene and protein strings for clues on immune flags and viral genomes. An RNA model traces SARS-CoV-2 ties to host messages, and a deep-learning tool maps human-virus protein links. Other papers add knowledge graphs, open-box AI, and half-rule-based models to foresee outbreaks. All told, they show computing changing how threats are spotted, read, and answered. Readers get a tour of the field's sharpest tools, with gaps like scarce data on new germs flagged.
pmc-13542038:
Benyao Zhang and nine colleagues chart, in a 2026 multi-omics study, what changes inside human kidney 293 cells as they learn to live floating in suspension instead of stuck to a surface. Industry grows these cells in suspension to manufacture viral vectors, yet the adaptation journey was poorly described.

Adapted cells grew more slowly, drank less glucose, made more lactate, and gripped surfaces more weakly. Gene, protein, and metabolite profiling together found thousands of shifted genes and hundreds of altered metabolites. The pattern resolved into three survival moves: rebuilding internal structure, rewiring energy metabolism, and hardening stress defences. The resulting line outproduced an internal reference for adenoviral vector work.
pmc-13542138:
Bekalu Mekonen Belay and colleagues survey diabetic patients in 2026. The city is Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia. The topic is preventing chronic kidney disease. That disease is a costly complication of diabetes. It can end in kidney failure if it is left unchecked. Interviews at public hospitals reached 386 adults. Sampling was systematic throughout. The team asked what each patient knew and how each felt about prevention.

Only about a third had adequate knowledge of prevention. Roughly half held a favourable attitude toward it. Higher schooling multiplied the odds of both. Having heard of kidney disease was the strongest single correlate. Longer diabetes duration also predicted knowledge. Younger age predicted it too. A family history of kidney disease predicted attitude. The authors urge targeted teaching inside diabetes clinics.
pmc-13543438:
Qiaoran Ma and colleagues published a 2026 field study on how light levels shape American ginseng grown under forest canopy, a prized medicinal root often farmed in agroforestry systems. Forest light is patchy, so the team evened out its spatial variation and compared four light transmission levels, from under one percent to nearly twenty percent of full light. They tracked plant physiology, root growth, soil chemistry and enzymes, and the community of soil microbes.

At 13.1 percent transmission the plants coordinated their best response: photosynthesis and chlorophyll rose, a stress chemical fell, and root dry weight beat every other treatment, dramatically exceeding the darkest plot. Soil nitrogen availability and enzyme activity also improved, and particular pH-linked and nitrogen-cycling microbes became more abundant. Path modelling showed light helped roots both directly, through plant physiology, and indirectly, through soil conditions. Moderate shade, evenly spread, is the recipe this study supports.
pmc-13543638:
Igor Adamski and Anna Wardowska published a 2026 review of how lupus attacks the nervous system, producing neuropsychiatric symptoms from mood change to seizures and stroke-like events. This manifestation is among the disease's most severe and least understood. The review organises evidence around two overlapping routes: an autoimmune-inflammatory route, where immune attack inflames the brain directly, and a clotting-ischaemic route, where vessels are injured and blocked.

Both routes converge on a leaky blood-brain barrier, immune cells entering brain tissue, and overactivated microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. The authors weigh the case for neutrophil traps, complement, interferon signalling, and self-reactive lymphocytes, separating what human studies show from what animal and cell models merely suggest. Better biomarkers and mechanism-matched treatments are the field's pressing needs, they conclude.
pmc-13545338:
Po-Fang Tsai and colleagues traced how meeting donors' kin reshapes medical students' bond with their silent mentor. Published in 2026, the interview-based study tracked 12 third-year students, interviewing them before family interviews and after course end. Cutting work often stirs dark emotions, yet how students' views of donors evolve across the course was little explored.

Early on, students swung between seeing the mentor as person and as object, swayed by time edges and sense clashes. The family interview then flipped the bond, turning the mentor into teacher, bridge, or companion, and thoughts spilled into ties with living people. The authors call the interview far more than a human touch: a teaching move that builds a doctor's selfhood and compassion. Readers get a two-phase map of how a doctor's care takes root.
pmc-13547238:
Yuling Chen and colleagues built a country-wide map of China's tallest-tree heights for 2020. Published in 2026, the dataset leans on 1,117 square kilometers of drone laser scans spread across eight plant zones. Top height tracks site quality and growth promise, yet steady country-wide height data were scarce.

Thirty map inputs from weather, soil, terrain, plant cover, and radar feeds fed a two-stage hybrid model that kept local detail while smoothing zone edges. The map gives a shared baseline for site ranking, yield planning, biomass and carbon counts, layered structure study, and space laser mission checks. Readers get a fine-grained tool for forest care and carbon tracking across China.
pmc-13548638:
Esmaeil Asadi Khameneh and colleagues review whether a harmless-looking eye finding can flag a hereditary colon condition, in a 2026 systematic review. Congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium, a flat dark spot layer in the eye, often appears in familial adenomatous polyposis, where hundreds of colon growths precede cancer. Finding the eye sign could prompt genetic testing before bowel disease declares itself. The team gathered forty-three studies of patients and at-risk relatives.

The eye finding proved highly specific: when defined strictly, it rarely appeared in people without the gene fault. Sensitivity swung widely between studies, from forty percent upward, depending on how lesions were counted. Demanding multiple lesions in both eyes sharpened accuracy but missed more carriers. The authors conclude the sign helps as part of an assessment, not as a stand-alone screen, and they call for shared definitions plus modern genetic confirmation.
pmc-13550538:
Xiao Zhang and colleagues tailor mouth care for chemotherapy patients by watching the acidity of their saliva day by day, in a 2026 two-stage clinical study. Painful mouth ulcers plague people receiving high-dose cytarabine for blood diseases. In stage one, a hundred patients got standard oral care while saliva acidity and ulcer grades were logged daily for a month. In stage two, those whose mouths stayed stubbornly acidic entered a small randomized comparison of standard care versus alkalizing care steered by the readings.

A single starting acidity reading did not predict who would ulcerate. Among the persistently acidic subgroup, guided alkalizing care healed ulcers in under seven days. Routine care took more than eleven. Mouths also returned toward neutral faster, with less pain reported along the way. The authors conclude the trend matters more than any one reading.
pmc-13551238:
Ling-Yi Guo, leading seven colleagues, published a 2026 scoping review of emergency department care for people with bleeding disorders. Guidelines call for clotting treatment within 30 to 60 minutes, yet delays are common. The team searched five databases to March 2025 under a pre-registered protocol, screening studies on barriers and improvement efforts.

Seventeen of 3,541 studies qualified. Barriers included weak electronic record tools, missing standard protocols, limited staff education, and poor communication with haematology teams. Reported treatment delays ran from well over an hour to more than five hours in some studies. Combined record changes plus education improved times in every intervention study, while patient and caregiver voices were rarely included, a gap the authors highlight.
pmc-13554038:
Caroline Raymundo leads a six-author team checking a life-quality survey built for a rare skin lymphoma in a 2026 study. The disease, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, puts cancer cells in the skin and can burden daily life. Their survey was made for this disease, yet no one had tested whether its questions truly fit patients. Twelve patients and eight experts gave feedback through careful one-to-one interviews.

Nearly every question struck both groups as apt, and most were clear to all patients. Instructions and answer choices were easy for everyone to follow. Both groups judged the survey complete, with no big topic missing. The team backs wider use of the survey, while urging tests in larger and more mixed groups of patients.
pmc-13554238:
Candela Fernández-Naval leads a nineteen-author team measuring how many people in Barcelona and Catalonia carried COVID antibodies in 2020, before vaccines existed. Leftover blood from routine hospital draws supplied the samples. Two rounds, in April and July 2020, tested for the full family of antibodies. Rates in Barcelona held steady at about one person in ten across both rounds.

Across Catalonia the July rate sat slightly lower, with women testing higher than men. People aged fifty to sixty-four showed the highest rates in both settings. Barcelona province outpaced the region's other provinces. The authors urge study of why age, sex, and place shaped exposure so unevenly during the pandemic's first months in Spain.
pmc-13554438:
Eojin Kim and three colleagues test Korean red ginseng saponins against fatty, inflamed liver disease in a 2026 mouse study. The condition, shortened to MASH, blends fat buildup, inflammation, and scarring. Mice fed a diet lacking two nutrients developed the disease and received the saponin mix for eight weeks. Liver cells and immune cells were also tested in dishes.

Treated mice stored less liver fat, with fat-building genes turned down. Liver injury markers in blood fell, and immune invasion and scarring eased. The mix blocked two inflammation switches and a protein that bursts inflamed cells open. In dishes it likewise cut fat storage and inflammatory output. The authors nominate the saponins as a candidate therapy worth further study.
pmc-13555938:
Zahra Ghaeli, Rosa Aghdam, and Changiz Eslahchi benchmark six methods that infer microbe interaction networks in a 2026 study. Such networks reveal how gut and soil microbes affect each other, yet no proven answer key exists to grade guesses. The team tested the methods on four real microbiome datasets plus shuffled, noisy, and resampled variants. Reproducibility under small disturbances became the yardstick.

Mild noise and resampling kept real data's key traits, making them fair test beds. Fully synthetic data from a popular generator strayed far from real patterns, though. Some algorithms could not even tell structured networks from random ones. The authors propose grading by real-data disturbance tests, with strict statistical checks before any synthetic set is trusted.
pmc-13556338:
Wenying Gao and ten colleagues showed in 2026 that the coronavirus behind COVID-19 borrows a host enzyme to protect a key part of its copying machine. The protein NSP8 helps the virus replicate, and host defences normally tag such proteins for destruction with ubiquitin labels. A host enzyme called OTUB2 removes those labels, and the team traced its effects in infected cells and in a hamster model.

OTUB2 strips labels from NSP8 directly, keeping it stable. The same enzyme also protects the virus's own label-removing protease, which shields NSP8 a second way. Preserved NSP8 helps the virus mute the cell's interferon alarm, aiding spread. Blocking OTUB2 broke the protection, sharply cutting viral replication and disease severity in the animal model. The authors nominate OTUB2 as a target for host-directed antiviral drugs.
pmc-13558438:
Steffen T. Ubl and seven colleagues measured in 2026 how the antibiotic cefazolin binds to proteins inside human joint fluid after a standard surgical dose. Only the unbound share of the drug kills bacteria, and binding can saturate at high levels, which would change dosing logic. Their prospective study collected joint fluid from 201 adults having knee or shoulder surgery who had received the usual preventive dose, then measured total and free drug by mass spectrometry.

About a quarter of the drug in joint fluid was free, at the median. The free share rose steadily as free concentration climbed, with no sign of levelling off across the observed range. Binding is therefore concentration dependent yet unsaturated at preventive doses. Surgeons and pharmacologists gain a firm number for how much active drug actually reaches the joint during an operation.
pmc-13558638:
Jantien W. Wieringa and eleven colleagues study infant immunity after womb exposure to maternal IBD drugs. Guidelines advise continuing immunomodulating drugs in pregnancy, yet infant immune effects stay uncertain. Their 2026 observational study follows infants of mothers with IBD, vaccinated on the Dutch schedule. It measures vaccine antibodies at 6 and 12 months and immune cells, antibodies, and infections at 2, 6, and 12 months.

Vaccine responses on a 3-plus-1 schedule matched or beat controls on a 2-plus-1 schedule for all components except filamentous haemagglutinin and pneumococcal serotype 19F. Neutropenia ran more often than reference values suggest, but resolved on its own in all cases. T- and B-cell low counts matched healthy controls. Mildly low total IgG appeared in about 10 percent at 6 months, and low IgA in about 28, 41, and 15 percent at 2, 6, and 12 months.
pmc-13560138:
Emmanuel Alote Allotey and colleagues map the cytokine and chemokine profile of Ghanaian children with sickle cell disease during steady state, the calm periods between crises. Their 2026 cross-sectional study compared 63 affected children with 66 healthy controls, all aged two to seventeen. Twenty-three signaling molecules were tested with multiplex assays next to blood counts.

Most pro-inflammatory signals ran higher in the sickle cell group, showing that steady state is not truly quiet. Two interleukins bucked the trend and sat lower, while two other molecules showed no group difference. Ratios showed a skewed mix favoring inflammation, tempered by regulatory counterweights. Cytokine plus blood data split the two groups cleanly in discriminant analysis. The authors offer the signatures as reference points for spotting when a child tips toward acute complications, above all in African groups where the disease burden is heaviest.
pmc-13560438:
Xiao Zhang and colleagues map how adverse childhood experiences connect to eating disorder symptoms in Chinese clinic patients, and which inner traits carry the effect. Their 2026 cross-sectional study assesses 970 patients treated between 2008 and 2015, nearly all women. Standard forms gauged childhood adversity, clinical behaviors, and traits such as perfectionism and feelings of failing.

Adversity tracked with most clinical behaviors after adjustment, most strongly with binge eating, laxative use, and age of onset. Emotional abuse in childhood hit psychological traits hardest of any adversity type. More bad experiences meant more severe traits and a higher chance of disordered behaviors. Path checks showed traits carrying much of the link: a sense of ineffectiveness alone conveyed over half the path from certain abuse patterns to binge eating in the reported proportions. The authors urge routine adversity screening and trauma-informed care.
pmc-13560638:
Matias Garcia-Mendoza and colleagues report the complete genome of a Cytobacillus strain scooped from a microbial soil crust on a high-Andean salt flat in Chile's Atacama Desert. Their 2026 genome announcement describes strain C11.1, taken twenty centimeters down in a green-layered evaporitic crust at about 3,320 meters elevation. The site, Salar de Aguilar, had never been explored for such organisms.

Nanopore sequencing on a portable MinION device fed a de novo assembly that closed into one circular chromosome. The genome spans 4.99 million bases, a size supporting its placement in the genus Cytobacillus, whose members tolerate salt, drying, and ultraviolet stress. The authors offer the sequence as a resource for work on adaptation to hypersaline, high-altitude life. Desert crust microbes remain barely sampled compared with their flowering-plant counterparts.
pmc-13561738:
Cao and colleagues build a survival model for bladder cancer from genes tied to protein acetylation, a chemical tagging process that helps cells keep internal balance, in 2026 oncology research. Combining gene activity data with machine learning, they distilled the signal into a five-gene model. The model split patients into risk groups and was tested as a stand-alone predictor of overall survival alongside standard clinical factors.

High-risk patients showed much poorer survival, distinct immune cell mixtures inside their tumors, and different sensitivity to drugs. One gene, CES1, stood out: it was highly active in bladder cancer and tracked with worse outlook. Silencing CES1 in lab cells markedly suppressed their growth, invasion, and migration, and lowered levels of coenzyme A, a molecule central to acetylation chemistry. Cao suggests CES1 as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target, pending deeper work.
pmc-13562738:
Qian Liang and five colleagues recalibrate the earthquake load curves that Chinese building design relies on, using records from genuinely destructive shaking. The design response spectrum tells engineers how hard a quake of a given strength can push a structure, and its three shaping values matter enormously. Their 2026 calibration drew on strong-motion records at intensity 7 and above on the Chinese scale. An improved differential evolution algorithm, with a hybrid mutation step, fitted the curve values faster and more tightly the longer it ran.

Comparisons with the current building code surfaced systematic gaps. The average site period for rock and hard-soil classes ran longer than the code allows, and it grew with shaking intensity, peaking above intensity 10. The platform value converged toward the code's number as intensity rose, while the decay index consistently exceeded the code's. The authors argue the code's spectrum deserves updating where their data disagrees.
pmc-13562938:
Liam M. Crowley and a Darwin Tree of Life consortium present the genome of the 16-spot ladybird, a tiny mildew-eating beetle. The sequenced animal was a single male, Tytthaspis sedecimpunctata, a three-millimetre beige ladybird whose fused spots draw a wiggly line across its wing cases. Unlike its famous aphid-hunting cousins, this species grazes on mildew in grasslands, scrub, and dunes. The 2026 assembly totals 355.68 million bases.

Most of the sequence, 88.7 percent, is scaffolded into ten chromosome-scale pieces, including the X sex chromosome. The mitochondrial genome was completed too, at 18.38 thousand bases. Adults of this species sometimes gather in spectacular crowds inside fence-post cracks, a habit the background notes record. The genome joins the Darwin Tree of Life catalogue of British and Irish species. It gives evolutionary researchers a reference for a ladybird lineage that abandoned predation for fungus, useful for tracing how diets reshape genomes.
pmc-13563738:
Abdirahman Ibrahim Abdi and three colleagues test how training quality becomes employability for medical laboratory graduates in post-conflict Mogadishu, Somalia. Labs underpin diagnosis and disease tracking, yet fragile systems struggle to staff them. The 2026 study surveyed 291 final-year students and recent graduates, modelled the pathways with structural equations. Three teaching inputs were tracked: how relevant the curriculum feels, how much hands-on practice students get, and how competent their instructors are. Confidence and job readiness sat between teaching and employment.

All three inputs built student confidence, and confidence predicted both readiness and getting hired. Readiness did not predict employment. The model explained 68.3 percent of confidence and 58.2 percent of readiness, yet only 2.3 percent of employment, a gap the authors own. In a thin job market, they argue, reform should strengthen practical training and faculty skill, since belief in one's ability is the bridge that carries teaching into work.
pmc-13563838:
Jakkrit Juhong and three colleagues report the first human use of an injectable gel made from processed amniotic membrane to close a large macular hole. Holes wider than 400 micrometres defeat standard surgery about forty percent of the time, and biological plugs are fiddly to place. The patient was a 62-year-old man with a stage 4 hole measuring 572 micrometres and vision of 20/200. After cataract and vitreous surgery with membrane peeling, the team injected the heat-sensitive gel through a soft cannula and sealed the eye with gas.

Bench tests had already cleared the gel's safety. Scans at one month showed the hole fully closed in the best pattern, with vision at 20/80. By four months vision reached 20/40, distortion had vanished, and the sensing layer was rebuilding on scans. Electrical testing confirmed working foveal responses. No eye complications appeared. A registered trial is running to test the method against standard care.
pmc-13564238:
Anne Chenuil and co-authors compare, in a 2026 field study across ten northwestern Mediterranean sites, ways of monitoring sea life that settles on standardized reef structures left in the water. Photographs of each structure face were matched against DNA barcoding of organisms collected face by face, instead of pooling everything together.

DNA testing found roughly fifteen times more species per site than photographs and tracked distance and environmental patterns more sharply, thanks to finer identification. Photographs still added information on large organisms and surface cover. Keeping faces separate raised richness further. Marine monitoring teams get practical guidance on combining both methods instead of choosing one.
pmc-13569438:
Anu Korukonda and David Weinshenker review, in a 2026 article, the locus coeruleus as a driver of the psychiatric symptoms that often open Alzheimer's disease. The locus coeruleus is a small brainstem nucleus that supplies the chemical messenger norepinephrine. Anxiety, agitation, depression, sleep trouble, and appetite change can precede memory loss, and overactivity of this system is implicated by human and animal evidence.

Circuits linking the nucleus to emotion, arousal, and stress regions are mapped symptom by symptom. New imaging and body measures can track the nucleus in living patients, opening the door to targeted drugs or stimulation that restore its balance early. The authors frame this system as a hopeful early treatment point.
pmc-13570138:
Ioanna Saougou's team charted immune profiles and outcomes across childhood autoimmune neutropenia subtypes over twenty years, in a 2026 cohort study. This condition covers varied entities, and how each subtype's immune picture relates to infection risk was incompletely defined. The team reviewed 112 antibody-confirmed children at one tertiary centre, sorting them into primary, long-lasting, and late-onset groups.

Late-onset disease stood out with multi-lineage lymphocyte drops, frequent antinuclear antibodies, and linked autoimmune disease, yet paradoxically no infection-related hospital stays, likely reflecting intact antibody levels. Resolution took a median 19 months for primary disease versus 67 and 59 months for the other two groups. The authors argue subtype-based monitoring can guide follow-up and treatment choices.
pmc-13570338:
Abdel-Wareth and colleagues report a 2026 feeding trial that replaced part of the soybean meal in hen diets with brown mushroom stem powder. The team fed 120 Lohmann LSL Lite laying hens for six weeks, swapping in the powder for 10 or 20 percent of the soybean meal.

Hens on the 20 percent diet laid more eggs and produced greater egg mass in the later weeks of the trial. Yolk color rose in a steady dose-dependent way, while feed conversion stayed unchanged. Blood tests stayed within normal ranges, with shifts in two liver enzymes read as adaptation rather than harm. The authors conclude the powder can replace up to one fifth of soybean meal safely.
pmc-13570838:
Veera Nurmela and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 retrospective study at a Finnish university hospital, the long tail of side effects from immune checkpoint inhibitor cancer drugs. Records covered 230 patients treated between 2015 and 2024. Up to half of such patients develop immune-related side effects, and this study asked how many become chronic and how much clinic work they create.

About sixty-one percent of patients with side effects had chronic ones lasting beyond twelve weeks, with thyroid inflammation the commonest. Steroid treatment beyond three months sharply raised steroid-related harm. Managing one side effect took about five oncologist contacts on average, most for liver and bowel inflammation. The figures help clinics plan staffing and warn patients honestly.
pmc-13571038:
Laurel Ovrom and colleagues present, in a 2026 clinical case, a 51-year-old woman who arrived at a headache clinic with three weeks of a new, constant, worsening headache. A week of vision loss in her right eye followed. Her past history included menstrual migraine and endometriosis treated by surgery, with estrogen replacement afterward.

The headache differed from her old pattern in length and severity and came without the usual warning signs. She found a dark blind spot with an irregular edge in the lower inner field of the right eye while applying makeup, with no eye pain or color change. Temple and scalp tenderness appeared on examination. The case sets up a diagnostic puzzle where giant cell arteritis and optic nerve ischemia sit high on the list.
pmc-13572338:
Fatoş Uncu and colleagues survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, 871 older adults surveyed in 2025 about successful aging. Their question is how spiritual transcendence and kinesiophobia shape it. Transcendence means a sense of connection beyond the self, and kinesiophobia means fear of movement. Standard scales were analyzed with layered regression and machine learning.

Spiritual transcendence alone accounted for over half the variation in successful aging scores. Adding fear of movement raised the explained share to about two thirds, with more transcendence and less fear each tied to better aging. Machine learning ranked fear of movement as the single strongest predictor. Programs for older adults, the authors argue, should build spiritual resources while directly treating fear that keeps people still.
pmc-13573438:
Clarissa Tania and Aaron Tigor Sihombing report a 2026 study of peritonitis in Indonesian children on home dialysis. Peritonitis, infection of the belly lining, is the worst common complication of this dialysis form, which cleans blood through the belly. In low-resource settings, home and care factors can drive the risk.

The single-centre study sorts risk through the classic epidemiologic triad: the host child, the germ, and the environment. Host and home factors were weighed for links to infection, while the germs found were described in plain counts. That split shows which risks a clinic can change, such as training and hygiene at home, and which germs local teams must expect. The authors aim to cut infection rates in a group with few spare options if dialysis fails.
pmc-13575138:
Nailya Kozhekenova leads a 2026 study of COVID-19 death rates in three Central Asian countries and how they relate to response measures. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Mongolia each acted against the pandemic, yet death patterns differed. The team used monthly death and population data from January 2020 to December 2021.

Age-standardised death rates ran higher in men than women in every country and year. Kyrgyzstan peaked early, Kazakhstan rose later, and Mongolia saw no deaths in 2020 before a late climb.
