Deaths rose sharply from age 60, most steeply in men. A few deaths appeared in infants and young children. The authors call for fast, coordinated responses that protect older people and account for sex differences.
pmc-13575238:
Mathilde Phillips-Houlbracq leads a 2026 French study on the timing of breathing tube placement in severe COVID-19 lung failure. Non-invasive supports such as high-flow nasal oxygen can delay intubation, yet waiting too long might harm patients. The team used records from the OUTCOMEREA intensive care network.

Of 1,206 patients with severe COVID pneumonia, 288 were still in intensive care on day seven. Those intubated late had a 60-day death rate of 78.5 percent. A trial-style analysis of 234 patients linked late intubation with nearly triple the adjusted risk of death against staying on non-invasive support. The authors read the pattern as a marker of worsening disease rather than proof that timing itself caused the deaths.
pmc-13578838:
Robert M Heirene and Philip Newall test where to set the spending line that triggers a money check for online gamblers in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 study. Rules now call for checks when net deposits pass a set line in thirty days. The team reused bank data and survey risk scores from 424 people who gambled in the past year.

Over twelve months two thirds of at risk gamblers crossed the proposed line, yet so did nearly half of low risk gamblers. That mix leans toward catching harm at the cost of bothering safe users. A slightly higher line balanced the trade a touch better, while pure harm hunting argued for a far lower line and pure freedom for a far higher one. Lines counted across all betting firms sorted risk better than per firm lines.
pmc-13579738:
Juan Zhang, Hao Chang, Shixue Liu, Xin Huang, and Qing Chang compare eye surgery with and without an air bubble for a stretched, split retina layer, in a 2026 study. The condition strikes highly shortsighted eyes, where the center layer splits and lifts. Forty seven patients had the inner gel removed with a peeling step that spares the center, then split into air filled and no air groups.

The air group thinned toward normal faster in the first month and reattached sooner. By three months and at one year the two groups matched on thickness, layer repair, and sharpness of vision, which improved clearly in both. Starting width of the lifted zone predicted final vision. Complication rates, including new holes in the center, did not differ. The authors frame air as a speed aid, not a final outcome changer.
pmc-13584438:
Qian Zhang and colleagues review how gene-control marks shape kidney injury during sepsis in this 2026 paper. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection, and the kidney is its most often hit organ. The marks at issue are epigenetic, meaning chemical tags on DNA and its packing proteins that turn genes up or down without changing the code itself.

The review follows those tags cell by cell, in immune cells, vessel-lining cells, and kidney tube cells. Mis-set tags keep inflammation burning, disturb small blood vessels, and rewire how cells make energy. Because such tags can be undone, the authors see them as both early warning signs and drug targets. They argue that reading and resetting these marks could open a more precise way to treat this deadly condition.
pmc-13586638:
A. Ashokan and colleagues ask how a widespread orchid manages to live on poisoned mine land in Italy. Orchids are famed as fussy plants that need the right fungi in their roots and the right pollinators, so bare, metal-laced soil should defeat them. Yet the broad-leaved helleborine thrives at old mining sites in Sardinia and Tuscany where most plants fail. The team compared root fungi and plant genes at paired mine and woodland sites.

The fungi living inside roots differed sharply between the two settings. Woodland plants leaned on fungal partners that were scarce in mines, while mine plants took up tougher, more opportunistic kinds. Plant genes, though, barely differed between settings, which points to fresh colonization and steady gene flow. The orchid's trick seems to be flexibility in choosing fungal partners, not a special mine-born breed.
pmc-13587438:
Lai Wei and colleagues measure the fat wrapped around the heart in patients recovering from a major heart attack. This epicardial fat hugs the heart muscle and, when swollen, leaks inflammatory signals that may worsen artery disease. Their 2026 study used heart MRI scans from a registry of 540 patients whose blocked artery had been reopened, then followed them for a median of four and a half years.

About one patient in eight suffered a major bad event in that time. Those patients carried clearly more epicardial fat at the first scan, and the fat volume predicted events even after standard risks and scan measures were counted. Fat volume also tracked with the size of the heart injury itself. Six months on, the fat had barely changed. The authors offer the scan measure as a steady extra marker for sorting risk after a heart attack.
pmc-13592638:
Kantika Yadav and six colleagues lay out a study protocol for healthy aging among tribal communities in Jharkhand, India. Tribal elders age early under hard physical labor and poor nutrition, yet adapted care models barely exist. The two phase plan covers 25 villages and 520 adults aged forty five and up. Phase one mixes health and function measures with interviews of residents, healers, and health workers. Phase two builds a care model with the community.

Standard scales will chart daily living ability and quality of life, while talks surface cultural views and access barriers. The model is then tried in one chosen village to test whether it works and whether people accept it. Yadav and the team expect baseline data on tribal aging and a care model ready to scale.
pmc-13592738:
Javad Sarvestan and six colleagues set out a protocol for spotting rheumatoid arthritis flares remotely while drug doses taper. Clinic visits with joint counts and blood tests catch flares, yet they strain services and patients alike. Their Newcastle study will follow up to 100 adults in remission who are cutting disease modifying drugs. Wrist sensors will log activity, gait, mobility, and sleep around the clock, while patients file a weekly flare questionnaire.

Clinic checks every three months for a year anchor the stream of home data. Dynamic models will estimate flare risk over set horizons, and their accuracy, timing, and warning lead will be judged against confirmed flares. Sixteen people had joined by July 2026. Sarvestan and the team frame the work as pilot groundwork for larger trials.
pmc-13593538:
Ratika Parkash and Amir Abdelwahab report a difficult removal of an Aveir atrial leadless pacemaker in a 79-year-old man on dialysis, published in 2026. The device, a small self-contained pacemaker fixed to the heart wall by a corkscrew-like helix, had reached its planned replacement time when the helix broke during retrieval.

Their account shows these devices can still come out after sitting in the heart for several years. A fractured helix, though, is a real risk of the procedure. Parkash and Abdelwahab argue doctors need a better shared understanding of retrieval. They suggest prospective registries collecting cases worldwide would help teams prepare for such complications.
pmc-13598138:
Junwei Du and colleagues asked whether the chemotherapy drug oxaliplatin causes wasting by itself, apart from the cancer it treats. Giving tumor-free mice a human-equivalent dose in their 2026 study produced the cachexia picture seen in patients: severe weight loss driven by fat depletion and skeletal muscle wasting.

The mice ate less, moved less, ran cooler, and breathed differently, while their muscle fibers shrank and immune cells moved in. Gene activity profiling across fat, muscle, and the hypothalamus showed metabolic rewiring as the dominant response. Fat-signaling genes were disturbed in both fat and brain. Inflammatory pathways were switched on in muscle. The authors conclude the drug drives wasting through its own metabolic and central nervous pathways, a distinction that matters for designing protective treatments that do not blunt chemotherapy.
pmc-13599238:
Jiaojiao Zhou and four co-authors write a letter to the editor questioning a study of vancomycin dosing in very ill patients on kidney replacement therapy. Vancomycin is an antibiotic used against hard-to-treat infections, and the dose must stay high enough to work yet low enough to spare the kidneys. The letter praises the original team's large study, then raises two safety concerns about how its dosing charts were built.

First, the simulations treated drug exposure up to a level of 700 as safe, while the guideline they cite sets the top at 600. Second, a validation group of 27 patients showed large prediction errors that the summary did not stress, hinting the model may overestimate drug levels in patients still passing urine. Zhou's group asks for the simulations to be rerun at the lower limit and for the dosing charts to carry a clear warning.
pmc-13600638:
Nicola Gaibazzi and five colleagues describe a 2026 case where non-invasive imaging pinned down a hidden cause of chest pain. The patient, a middle-aged man being cleared for competitive sport, developed chest discomfort and strong ECG changes on a treadmill test, yet CT showed clean coronary arteries. That pattern points to coronary microvascular dysfunction, a fault in the heart's tiny vessels that usually needs invasive testing to confirm, so it often goes missed.

Stress ultrasound with a vasodilator drug showed a normal flow reserve of 3.2 in the main artery: the vessels could still widen when driven directly. Contrast perfusion imaging, though, revealed patchy areas where blood refilled slowly, a sign the vessel lining's own control pathway was failing. The ECG changes also repeated under stress. Gaibazzi's team argues this combination identifies the endothelium-dependent form without catheters, opening the way to earlier treatment.
pmc-13602438:
Frank Bevacqua, Emma Choong, and Nelson Low test smart glasses as a surgeon's-eye camera in plastic surgery in 2026. Operative video aids teaching and review, but capturing the surgeon's viewpoint has been awkward. The team recorded de-identified segments with Meta AI Glasses. Curated clips and stills then went to 35 viewers, medical students, junior doctors, and consultants, who rated the footage anonymously.

Every respondent rated video quality and clarity as good or excellent. Field of view and audio scored slightly lower, and documentation quality impressed 94.3 percent. Nearly all, 97.1 percent, agreed the recordings teach and review technique effectively. Consultants were the skeptics: half rated field of view and audio only middling, and most opposed routine documentation use. Free-text answers asked for zoom, better light and sound, and firm consent and privacy rules. The authors back the glasses for education now, with medicolegal use waiting on those fixes.
pmc-13610938:
Dan Ioan Avasiloaiei leads a seven-author team arguing that the common bean deserves breeding goals far wider than yield. Common bean is a staple grain legume and a pillar of organic farming, famous for fixing nitrogen. The review reframes the plant as a holobiont, a host plus its microbes, whose root-zone engineering and nutrient cycling are themselves selectable traits. The authors synthesize work on the plant's biology and field constraints.

Weed pressure, pests, disease, food scarcity, and a shortage of low-input varieties all limit what the bean can express. Against those limits, the review weighs farming practices and measurement tools, then the accelerants: precision farming, phenomics, molecular breeding, and genome editing. Priority targets include nitrogen-fixation efficiency, root shape, recruiting helpful microbes, nutrient-use efficiency, and stress resilience. The authors position ecosystem-minded bean breeding as a strategic lever toward regenerative organic farming.
pmc-13612338:
Cuimeng Tian leads a six-author team telling how a 90-year-old man was cured of lung cancer most doctors would only palliate. His squamous tumor of the left upper lung was staged IIIC, invading vertebrae and pressing on the spinal cord, which ruled out surgery. Trials exclude patients his age, so no guideline covered him. The team chose definitive concurrent chemoradiation anyway: 60 gray in thirty fractions, with image-guided planning.

During treatment his back pain eased and the tumor shrank, letting planners adapt around the cord. He finished with mild esophagitis and one episode of severe neutropenic fever, and skipped maintenance immunotherapy. Nearly six years later he remains progression-free with excellent function. The tumor kept shrinking for three years after radiation ended, and destroyed bone regrew. The authors offer the case as proof that extreme age alone should not bar curative intent.
pmc-13612938:
Richard Kahalu, Joy Notter, and Chris Carter survey critical care in Ministry of Health hospitals across Zambia, covering all ten provinces. Critical care treats the sickest patients, yet in many lower-income countries little is recorded about staff, beds, and equipment. Zambia has grown these services over fifteen years, so the authors set out to measure what public hospitals now provide.

All 14 hospitals with critical care units replied, reporting 131 beds in total. Every unit had trained critical care nurses and access to ventilators and monitors, but only 28.6 percent had a critical care doctor on site around the clock. Equipment levels varied widely between hospitals. The survey gives planners a national baseline for closing gaps in staffing and gear, rather than guessing where the weakest points lie.
pmc-13614138:
Jobe and colleagues review how adding dopant ions switches on light emission in zero-dimensional cesium zinc halide phosphors, in 2026 optoelectronics research. Phosphors are materials that absorb energy and re-emit it as light. These compounds are called zero-dimensional because their light-emitting metal-halide units sit isolated from one another in the crystal. That isolation leaves room to insert foreign ions, dopants, which can tune the emitted color for displays and lighting.

Zinc halides attract interest for simple synthesis, a wide bandgap, and chemical stability compared with lead-based alternatives that raise toxicity concerns. The review surveys which dopants, from copper and manganese to rare earths, produce which emission wavelengths and efficiencies in cesium zinc hosts. It also examines how the host's structure shapes absorption strength and the Stokes shift, the gap between absorbed and emitted light. Jobe maps the design rules for engineering these phosphors.
pmc-13616838:
Grace A. Whitaker and colleagues run a drug experiment on inhibition of return, the attention effect that makes people slower to look back at a spot they just attended, which helps search stay fresh. Brain dopamine is thought to tune this effect, since both too much and too little signalling shrink it in disorders. Healthy volunteers took, in turn, a dopamine-2 stimulator, a dopamine-2 blocker, and a placebo, while their attention shifts and brain waves were measured.

Both the stimulator and the blocker shrank the effect compared with placebo, backing a curved relationship: the middle range of dopamine works best, and pushing either way harms. Wave recordings showed which mental steps each drug moved. Same-person comparison of raising and lowering one chemical gives clinics a cleaner map for disorders where dopamine runs off balance.
pmc-13617438:
Nuo Xu and seven colleagues feed crucian carp a probiotic bacterium, Weissella cibaria strain XN-2a, which makes a natural bacteria-killing substance and was isolated from fish intestines. Crowded fish farming raises disease risk and antibiotic use, so the team tested whether the strain could protect a freshwater species. Carp received the supplemented diet for thirty days and were then challenged with the pathogen Aeromonas hydrophila.

Fed fish gained about twice as much weight as controls, roughly twenty-eight percent against fourteen percent, and converted feed more efficiently. After the pathogen challenge, half of the supplemented fish survived while no control fish did. Their intestines showed healthier folding, stronger immune markers, and lower inflammation after challenge. Gene surveys of gut microbes showed a shift away from pathogen-style virulence traits toward commensal communities with greater butyrate-making potential, without raising the overall antibiotic resistance burden.
pmc-13619638:
Elisa Gatta and six colleagues reviewed whether thyroid hormone changes during severe illness predict death. Two patterns were compared: a broader syndrome where several hormone levels shift, and an isolated low level of triiodothyronine, the active thyroid hormone. The team searched three databases for studies from 2014 onward covering critically ill and heart patients.

Twenty-two studies entered the pooled analysis. Both patterns linked clearly to higher mortality, and statistical comparison found no firm difference in strength between the two definitions. Results varied a good deal from study to study, which tempers the pooled numbers. The authors suggest the broader syndrome may still give a fuller biological picture of thyroid disruption in acute illness. Either way, a low active hormone reading in a very ill patient marks higher risk.
pmc-13623638:
David Mendive-Tapia and colleagues published a 2026 theoretical chemistry study of the hydrated proton, the charged particle that makes acids acidic and carries charge through water and fuel cells. Two classic pictures compete: one where the extra proton sits shared between two water molecules, and one where it anchors a small cluster. Real spectra suggest a blend of both.

The team ran quantum dynamics simulations, which follow every atom's quantum behaviour, on a six-water cluster that can wear either shape. Removing one water molecule from the outer shell, step by step, tilted the cluster from the shared-proton shape toward the anchored shape. The simulated infrared spectrum shifted with it in ways matching recent laser experiments. The results tie the lopsided water surroundings to the spectrum and to how protons move. The authors offer the map as a base for understanding proton flow in energy devices.
pmc-13624038:
Roope Mustasilta and colleagues search for risk groups among facial fracture patients who also carry injuries elsewhere in the body. Those extra injuries, called concomitant injuries, range from bruises to life-threatening brain or chest damage, and missing them can be fatal. The study used data-driven grouping on patients treated at major trauma centres between January 2013 and October 2020.

The cohort held 4,170 patients, about seventy percent men, with an average age near forty-six. Just under a third had at least one injury beyond the face. Women showed a slightly higher share than men. Risk climbed steadily with age and passed half in the oldest group, patients in their early nineties. The types of extra injury shifted across age groups as well, so a single screening habit will not fit everyone. The authors urge routine checks for hidden injuries alongside facial imaging, with extra care for the high-risk groups.
pmc-13624238:
Taylor T Schwartz leads a 2026 Medicare study comparing how long rheumatoid arthritis patients stay on their first advanced drug, a real-world sign of whether a treatment works and is tolerated. The patients studied all carried two antibody markers linked to harder disease, and earlier trials hinted that one drug, abatacept, might suit them especially well.

Using full Medicare claims linked to lab results from 2012 to 2019, the team followed 3,105 patients. They started abatacept, a tumour necrosis factor blocker, or a JAK inhibitor as their first advanced therapy. Twelve months later, about forty-eight percent of the abatacept group were still on their drug, against a third of the blocker group and just under forty percent of the JAK group. Statistical modelling confirmed the gap. The authors suggest antibody results deserve a place in choosing a first drug for these patients.
pmc-13628638:
Mia A. Brantley and five colleagues injured the sensory dendrites of fruit fly larvae with a pinch rather than the usual laser cut, to learn how damage to surrounding tissue affects nerve regrowth. Their modified technique wounded only half of a neuron's branching dendrites, leaving the other half intact for comparison.

Both fast-changing and stable dendrites regrew, mainly by adding branches on the uninjured half, a compensatory pattern. New growth steered into intact tissue and avoided the pinched zone. Examining the scene showed torn skin and matrix layers around the wound, though not the glial support cells, plus a strong immune response. The authors conclude that collateral tissue damage and lingering inflammation make the wound bed unwelcoming for regeneration.
pmc-13628838:
Tido von Schoen-Angerer and six colleagues surveyed a representative sample of 4,065 adults in Germany about traditional, complementary, and integrative medicine, from homeopathy to natural healing methods. The study asked which illnesses drive people to these treatments and how much benefit users feel they get.

Seven in ten respondents had used such medicine at some point, and about a third had used it within the last year. Use ran highest for respiratory and digestive complaints, and reported benefit stayed high across fifteen illness categories, even among people in poorer overall health. Comparing use with research activity showed no matching pattern. The authors call on the German health system to evaluate these therapies rigorously and consider fairer insurance coverage.
pmc-13629538:
Karen E. Hauer and nine colleagues apply systems thinking to a stubborn problem in health training. Competency-based programmes run in split stages. They fail to form one smooth path from student to practising clinician. Learners and teachers thus travel broken paths that miss single needs.

The authors use a classic framework of leverage points. Those are places where small pushes trigger large change. They locate where the system can truly move. Their five proposals include joint control across training stages. They also urge accepting progress at varied speed as normal. Learner data tracked over time matters too. So do rewards for proven skill, and steady data feedback. The deepest lever, they argue, is a mental shift. Move from time served to skill shown.
pmc-13631238:
Nicolas M Viart and twenty-one colleagues trained a deep learning model to read breast tumour slides. It flags women whose cancer likely stems from an inherited ATM gene variant. Their study appeared in 2026. Carriers face sharply raised breast cancer risk. Their relatives gain from testing. Yet many carriers are found only through genetic screening programmes.

On a first set of 187 tumour slides the model split carriers from noncarriers with strong accuracy. It held up respectably on a separate second set. Reviewing what the model used, the team found telling patterns. Carrier tumours often showed loosely joined cancer cells like lobular cancers. Dense immune cell infiltrates appeared too. They propose slide reading as a cheap first-pass triage at diagnosis.
pmc-13631338:
Andreísa Teixeira de Castro and six colleagues tuned a yeast to turn biodiesel waste into two saleable products at once. Their study appeared in 2026. The yeast Cystofilobasidium ferigula feeds on crude glycerol, the cheap leftover of biodiesel making. It stockpiles both oils and orange carotenoid pigments inside its cells. Yet it had barely been studied for biotechnology.

The team used a structured design to vary yeast extract, temperature, and aeration. They hunted for the sweet spot. The resulting oils mirrored vegetable oil makeup. Oleic, stearic, and palmitic acids dominated. The pigment extract scored well on three antioxidant tests. At the optimum the biomass reached over half lipid by weight. The authors present the strain as a sustainable production platform.
pmc-13632938:
Betony Adams and colleagues explore a speculative link between quantum physics and evolution in a 2026 theoretical paper on magnetic sensitivity in living things. Organisms evolved under Earth's magnetic field, and mounting evidence says they can sense weak fields, possibly through radical pairs, short-lived molecule pairs whose chemistry depends on electron spin. The open puzzle is how natural selection could act on such quantum details at all. The authors inspect the spin mathematics at the heart of the radical pair account.

They show that hyperfine coupling values, set by the protein environment and thus by gene sequence, can shift reactive oxygen species outcomes, giving selection a handle on quantum parameters. A simple qualitative model illustrates how changes in nuclear spin, coupling strength, and direction dependence might alter reactive oxygen levels under different fields.
pmc-13633238:
Ramojus Balevicius and nine colleagues report long-term follow-up of two siblings with a rare inherited brain disease. The condition, tied to a gene called CSF1R, damages the brain's white matter by weakening its resident immune cells, the microglia. Both siblings carried the same gene variant. Between 2014 and 2017, each received four infusions of rituximab, a drug that removes a class of immune cells blamed for feeding inflammation in this disease.

Over five years after treatment, their disability scores held steady at high levels, though other function and thinking measures moved in mixed directions. Brain scans across more than two decades showed shrinking tissue, yet no new focal lesions appeared after treatment. A marker of nerve damage in spinal fluid returned to normal levels. The authors stay cautious, since one sibling had always progressed slowly. Still, the stability makes a case for controlled trials.
pmc-13635038:
Silvia Pignatto and five colleagues published this 2026 family study of a rare inherited eye disease. The syndrome distorts the retina's light-sensing cells, flooding it with one cone type and eroding night vision. Three siblings carried the same fault in the gene NR2E3. The team examined them from early childhood, tracking vision, prescriptions, and retinal images.

The eldest brother's first sign was a sudden eye turn from abnormal new retinal blood vessels. A vessel-blocking drug settled that complication in two doses. Night blindness arrived between ages eleven and fourteen for the older two siblings, followed by cystic changes in the central retina. Drops meant to drain such cysts did not help. Despite the changes, all three kept stable vision sharpness across twelve years. The authors say this record, the longest of its kind, shows how uneven the disease can be.
pmc-13635238:
Wei Lv and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of a cleaner way to win nickel from low-grade rock. Nickel feeds stainless steel and the batteries behind clean energy, while rich sulfide deposits grow scarce. Vast ultramafic deposits hold tens of millions of tonnes of nickel that current methods cannot use kindly. The team's process heats ore with cheap metallic iron at moderate temperatures. The iron acts as a magnet for nickel, pulling it into a separate alloy.

The whole treatment takes three hours and avoids sulfur dioxide emissions, since sulfur stays locked in solid form. The product is a ferronickel alloy that standard refining can upgrade to battery grade. Careful tuning of heat, atmosphere, and iron dose makes alloy grains separate cleanly from waste rock. Trials at mini-plant scale verified the route. The authors frame it as a path to a fairer, sturdier nickel supply.
pmc-13638038:
Muluneh Assefa and eight colleagues pool Ethiopian data on the most drug-resistant forms of tuberculosis. Multidrug-resistant TB already demands long, harsh treatment. Pre-extensively and extensively resistant cases resist even the backup drugs, and Ethiopia lacked a national estimate. The team gathered studies of multidrug-resistant patients, applying standard meta-analysis methods with adjustments suited to rare events. Eight studies covering about fifteen hundred patients made the cut.

Fifty-two pre-extensive and thirteen extensive cases surfaced in the pool. The combined prevalence landed near three percent for the pre-extensive form and one percent for the extensive form among multidrug-resistant patients. Rates varied by region, with multi-region studies higher and one region's single study showing a strikingly high extensive share. A stats test flagged possible publication bias in the extensive estimates. The authors press for stronger surveillance and wider drug testing across all regions.
pmc-13638138:
Olga Fedorova and Fuad AlSaraj published this 2026 case report of a single patient, a 60-year-old man with melanoma and autoimmune disease. He picked up a cascade of hormone disorders during immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy. These drugs unleash the immune system, which can attack endocrine glands. His course unfolded: insulin-requiring diabetes appeared after six weeks, eosinophilic asthma after ten weeks, and at twenty-eight weeks he was admitted with secondary adrenal insufficiency.

Doctors traced the adrenal failure to isolated ACTH deficiency, a pituitary failure linked to the immunotherapy, and his pituitary MRI was normal, showing that imaging cannot rule the condition out. He carried underactive thyroid and giant-cell arteritis. After operations for melanoma and basal cell carcinoma, he is maintained on hydrocortisone, levothyroxine and insulin. The authors stress team care, and note that side effects like his call for hormone replacement but rarely justify stopping cancer therapy.
pmc-13641338:
Ultrasound clues that warn of a twisted fibroid on a stalk are gathered by Paoli and colleagues. Torsion of a pedunculated subserosal leiomyoma, a benign womb tumour hanging from the uterus surface, is rare but can demand emergency surgery. Early recognition before the operation is difficult. The team reviewed thirty-eight reports covering forty-two cases and added a case of their own, a pregnant patient at twenty-one weeks.

The most common findings were a large mass averaging about ten centimetres, growth since earlier scans, uneven internal texture, and smooth borders. Shadowing behind the mass, free pelvic fluid, and patchy cystic areas were also frequent. Blood flow inside the mass was absent or reduced in every case, though a twisted stalk itself was seen in only a minority. Paoli and colleagues conclude that ultrasound, read against these patterns, can support earlier preoperative diagnosis and future diagnostic standards.
pmc-13641838:
Andrea Moreira Candido led a 2026 prospective cohort study that built a clinical tool to predict problems within thirty days of total hip replacement. Hip replacement is among the most successful elective operations, yet early problems still affect roughly five to twenty percent of patients, and risk scoring before surgery could guide preparation and shared decisions. The team followed 122 patients having first, planned hip replacement at a public referral hospital between November 2021 and April 2022, recording clinical, social, and functional measures.

Problems within thirty days struck 13.1 percent, most often wound infection and anemia. Abnormal blood fats, inactivity, higher anesthesia risk class, and low fitness for surgery each raised risk roughly fourfold. The model was built into an online tool for clinical use. Surgeons get a practical checklist with good accuracy in this single-center sample, while the authors call for validation in larger, independent groups before wider adoption.
pmc-13642938:
Siyuan Chen and seven colleagues present a 2026 benchmark study of how accurately large language models answer vaccine questions in three languages. Clinicians and the public increasingly ask chatbots about vaccines, yet accuracy outside English was barely measured.

Their VaxEval test holds 1,886 multiple-choice questions covering fourteen vaccines in English, Spanish, and Chinese. Thirteen models averaged about eighty-six percent correct in English, with lower scores in Spanish and Chinese. Newer flagship models beat older ones, a few example answers helped, and step-by-step reasoning prompts actually hurt. The authors urge guardrails before chatbots speak on vaccines.
pmc-13643638:
Charles N. J. McGhee and three colleagues present a 2026 review of biopsy techniques for tumors of the iris and the eye's front chamber. Many growths there are harmless, but telling a growing benign spot from a melanoma by sight alone can be impossible.

The guide covers fluid sampling, fine needle aspiration, cutter and forceps methods, small-device excision, and full surgical removal. Diagnostic yield for cell, tissue, and genetic results is typically high, serious complications are uncommon, and no external tumor spread has been reported with clear-corneal approaches. The authors aim to ease reluctance among patients and doctors about sampling these delicate structures.
pmc-13645538:
Zhenyu Wang and two colleagues present a survey of how sport mindfulness links to flow in Chinese college athletes. Flow is the deep, lost-in-the-game state that athletes prize. The team asked whether two inner skills carry the effect of mindfulness on flow.

A total of 583 athletes from four provinces filled out the forms. Mindfulness went with more calm rethinking of events, more sport confidence, and more flow. In the path model, calm rethinking carried the largest share of the link. Confidence carried a smaller share. A chain through rethinking and then confidence added a small share more. A direct link also stayed. Coaching in rethinking may help athletes reach flow more often, they say.
pmc-13645738:
Jhelum Chakravorty, Nicolò Ripamonti, and Tor Laneryd present a 2026 paper on finding hidden models of electrical machines from data, a task called system discovery. Power engineers need such models to manage equipment, yet real data are often sparse and noisy. The trio use a method that blends machine learning with known physics. Their test case is the heat behavior of electrical induction machines.

Their end-to-end approach beat nearly all rival methods, cutting validation error by wide margins in most comparisons. One rival Bayesian method scored slightly better but took far longer to run, while their method cut computing time sharply. A sampling trick made the predictions hold up when data were thin. The authors frame the work as a balance of accuracy and cost that could suit real asset management in power systems.
pmc-13648138:
Tae Jin Ahn and five colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether longer commutes relate to working while sick and to sickness absence among Korean wage workers. Korea has some of the longest commutes among wealthy countries, so the question carries practical weight for employers and policy makers.

The analysis covered 28,349 workers from the sixth Korean Working Conditions Survey, with commute time split into three daily bands. Workers commuting over an hour showed higher odds of working while sick for both sexes, and those beyond two hours also showed higher odds of absence. Women with the longest commutes showed especially high presenteeism, and the authors urge that commute time be treated as a modifiable health factor.
pmc-13648938:
Lucy Carleton and four colleagues report what they describe as the first case of repeated clot-busting treatment with tenecteplase for early recurrent ischaemic stroke. Giving such drugs again soon after a stroke is normally considered contraindicated, although repeated use of the older drug alteplase has been reported with good outcomes.

Their patient was a sixty-nine-year-old man who deteriorated after initial thrombolysis and was treated a second time with tenecteplase, a longer-acting variant with easier administration. The report sets out the case to explore the safety and possible benefits of the repeated approach. The authors place it against a background of guidelines that accept either drug for acute stroke.
pmc-13649438:
Chenggong Xie and five colleagues pooled studies of heart disease risk models that blend Chinese medicine signs with Western measures. The hope is that tongue, pulse, and symptom patterns add facts that standard checks miss. Sixteen studies were found in their search.

On average, the blended models sorted future cases from non-cases fairly well. Yet the studies differed wildly from each other, most carried a high or unclear risk of bias, and few were tested on fresh patients. Group splits did not explain the spread. The authors call the results a lead for more work, not proof of benefit, and they ask for large shared studies with clear rules before clinic use.
pmc-13650438:
Hyekyung Seo and two colleagues, publishing in 2026, validate a Korean fit test panel for respirators, the standardized set of face shapes used to judge whether protective masks seal properly. Korea lacked a panel reflecting its own population's faces, even though international rules urge each country to build one.

The panel was drawn from face measurements of more than eleven thousand Korean adults, sorted into size categories. Fifty people representing those categories wore various respirator models for quantitative fit testing, and matching rigid headforms were tested the same way. Human pass rates beat the American reference benchmark, supporting the panel's use, and full-face masks passed more often than half-face ones. Headforms, though, scored lower than people and agreed poorly with them, especially for small sizes. The authors back the panel while calling for more realistic headforms.
pmc-13650538:
Maroof Arshadul Hoque and eleven co-authors make water-cleaning crystals whose fluorinated pore walls grab PFAS, the long-lived industrial chemicals that contaminate drinking water and resist breakdown. Their materials are covalent organic frameworks, stable sponge-like lattices, and the team produced them by mechanochemistry, grinding ingredients jointly as a greener route to scale.

Three versions differed only in pore-wall chemistry: plain, methylated, and fluorinated. The fluorinated version crystallized best, offered the most surface area, and tolerated the most heat. In batch tests it captured the most of two notorious PFAS compounds and their short-chain relatives, removing one compound almost completely within minutes and keeping its edge at high contamination levels. Methylated and plain versions trailed. The authors conclude that decorating pore walls, paired with the grinding-based synthesis, is a hands-on way to tune these sponges for PFAS cleanup.
pmc-13652538:
Anna Green and five colleagues test whether the three-dimensional shape of a protein can predict which mutations will make tuberculosis bacteria resist antibiotics. Resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis grows mainly through small changes in proteins, and standard analysis reads only the letter sequence of those proteins. The team built structural notes for the bacterium's whole protein set from crystal data and AlphaFold predictions, then mapped mutations from tens of thousands of clinical isolates onto those shapes.

Mutations known to cause resistance clustered together in physical space, even inside proteins where damaging changes are scattered along the sequence. That clustering means location within the folded protein carries information the sequence alone misses. Adding structural context to prediction tools could sharpen drug-resistance forecasts from genome data. Helping doctors choose effective treatment faster for a pathogen that still kills large numbers of people each year.
pmc-3069738:
Winn, Ballard, Cowtan, and co-authors give an overview of the CCP4 suite and its current developments. CCP4 is a long-running collection of programs for macromolecular crystallography, the method that reveals protein shapes from crystal diffraction. The suite joins tools for each stage, from raw data to finished structure.

Their overview describes what the suite contains and where development was heading in 2011. A shared, maintained suite keeps methods consistent across hundreds of labs. It also lowers the barrier for new groups, who gain a tested pipeline instead of assembling software alone.
pmc-6086938:
Yury Goltsev, Nikolay Samusik, Julia Kennedy-Darling, and coauthors profiled mouse spleen tissue with CODEX imaging in 2018. CODEX tags antibodies with DNA barcodes and reads them out in repeated rounds. One tissue slice can thus show dozens of proteins at once.

The team built detailed maps of healthy spleens and of spleens from a lupus mouse model. The maps reveal how immune cells arrange into neighborhoods and how disease reshapes them. Seeing arrangement, not just cell counts, exposes contacts that drive immune behavior. The method points toward richer tissue maps in human disease studies.
pmc-6351938:
Emanuele Rinninella, Pauline Raoul, Marco Cintoni, and coauthors asked what a healthy gut microbiota looks like in 2019. Each person carries a unique gut community that aids digestion, guards the gut wall, and trains immunity. Its makeup shifts with age, place, and diet.

The review describes the main bacterial groups in a healthy gut and what they do. It then shows how antibiotics, birth mode, and illness disturb that balance. No single perfect profile exists, which the authors stress. The paper gives clinicians a grounded picture of normal before judging what counts as disturbed.
pmc-7088738:
Xin Zou, Ke Chen, Jiawei Zou, and coauthors analyzed ACE2 expression at single-cell level early in the COVID-19 outbreak in 2020. The new virus enters cells through the ACE2 receptor, as the earlier SARS virus did. Lung cells carrying ACE2 were thought to be its main targets.

Scanning public single-cell data, the team found ACE2 in a small set of lung cells that also make mucus-related proteins. They flag higher expression patterns that might mark greater risk. The quick analysis, done from open data, helped focus early thinking on which tissues the virus could reach.
pmc-7250738:
Jing Yang and many co-authors set out shared guidelines in 2020 for research on epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a process often shortened to EMT. During this process, cells that normally sit in ordered sheets loosen their grip, change shape, and gain the ability to move and invade nearby tissue. It shows up in normal development, in wound healing, and in diseases such as cancer and scarring disorders.

The problem the guidelines tackle is disagreement, since labs were using the same terms for different cell states and drawing clashing conclusions. The authors lay out agreed definitions and describe which traits should be measured before a change counts as this transition. For a fast moving field, a shared language lets results from different labs be compared with confidence.
pmc-7486838:
John Donnelly and colleagues issued in 2019 a revised set of shared definitions for invasive fungal disease. Two research groups stand behind the update, one European and one international consortium devoted to fungal disease study. Earlier versions of these definitions had become a common language that let hospitals and researchers describe the same illnesses in the same way.

The revision spells out what counts as proven, probable, or possible infection, and which lab tests and scans support each level. It also folds in newer diagnostic tools that had appeared since the previous edition. Clear case definitions sound dry, but trials of new antifungal drugs and comparisons between hospitals stand or fall on exactly this kind of agreement.
pmc-7755038:
Gregory Roth and a global team of collaborators charted in 2020 the worldwide burden of cardiovascular diseases and their risk factors across three decades. Heart and blood vessel diseases, above all ischemic heart disease and stroke, are the leading cause of death on the planet. They also account for a large share of the years people live with disability.

The study reviews the total burden from 1990 to 2019, covering more than a dozen underlying causes of cardiovascular death and a set of major risk factors. It shows where the burden is rising, where it is falling, and which risks drive it in each region. Health systems use this accounting to decide where screening and prevention will save the most lives.
pmc-8446938:
The NCD Risk Factor Collaboration pooled data in 2021 on high blood pressure, covering two hundred countries and three decades. Hypertension is easy to detect in primary care, and cheap treatments control it well, yet control remains poor in much of the world. The analysis combined more than twelve hundred representative studies with well over one hundred million participants.

The authors measure how common hypertension was from 1990 to 2019, and how far each country got with detecting it, treating it, and bringing it under control. The results expose a stark divide, with some health systems controlling most cases and others very few. The study is a scorecard for one of the most fixable major health risks.
pmc-8728138:
David Wishart and colleagues presented HMDB 5.0 in 2021, the 2022 edition of the Human Metabolome Database. The database has provided reference information on human metabolites, the small molecules produced by the body, since 2007. It records their biological roles, the diseases they connect to, and their chemical properties.

The authors describe how the resource grew and changed over fifteen years, with far more metabolites and richer detail on each. They also explain the tools for searching and comparing entries. Doctors and researchers use the HMDB when a blood or tissue measurement turns up an unfamiliar molecule, making it a standard desk reference for the study of metabolism.
podcast-tuckercarlson-mXO-EvCtY38:
Quarterback Aaron Rodgers joins Tucker Carlson's podcast for a long, unfiltered talk. Rodgers, one of the NFL's great passers, became a public lightning rod over his vaccine stance. With Carlson he ranges far past football, into the stories that made him a culture-war figure.

He talks about Jeffrey Epstein's death, his psychedelic experiences, and fake vaccine cards in the NFL. He also discusses Pat Tillman, who left football for the Army and was killed in Afghanistan. Carlson lets him run on each. The segment is a star athlete off the leash, kept as a record of views his league would rather he kept quiet.
poe-narrative-arthur-gordon-pym-1838:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote his sole long tale, the Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym, in 1838. Pym stows away on a brig bound for the south seas. Mutiny, wreck, and thirst drive the crew to the edge of death. Poe tells the tale as a true log found in print.

A rescue ship turns out to be a death ship full of corpses. Pym sails on south past ice to a warm sea and a black isle. White birds, strange signs, and a vast white form close the tale in mist. The book is the root text of the polar tale of dread.
solenopedie-ou-revelation-d-un-nouveau-s: A garbled title page is all that can be read here. It names a French work printed at Paris in 1838 by the Librairie Médicale de Labé: Solénopédie, ou révélation d'un nouveau système d'éducation phrénologique pour l'homme et les animaux. The rest of the opening is OCR noise, mixed with a fragment on diseases of the eye that does not belong to this book. Nothing of the system's teaching can be described from it.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5038:
Franklin D. Roosevelt gives twelve yearly addresses, from January 3, 1934, to January 6, 1945, parted by three stars. The first comes at the opening of the regular session of the 73d Congress. Roosevelt says he comes not to ask for special or detailed bills. He comes to take counsel with Congress, chosen like him to carry out the mandate of the whole people, so that both may work as one.

The shared aim is to carry on the mending of the nation's well-being. Just as weighty is the task of building on the ruins of the past a new frame better fit for the problems of modern life. That frame takes in how trade, farming, and finance bear on each other, and how all three bear on each citizen and on the whole people. Now that the climb back is well begun, Roosevelt draws lines between its friends and its foes.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated July 29, 1897, this is number 38 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here: a masthead and the paper's book premium offer, the same offer printed in number 36. A reader who brings in one new subscription may pick one book from the list. The books are bound in red buckram with gilt tops. Titles range from Andersen's Fairy Tales and Black Beauty to Baron Munchausen.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
Part 38 of Don Quixote, Miguel de Cervantes' novel, appears in John Ormsby's translation. Chapter sixty-two deals with the adventure of the enchanted head, with other trivial matters that cannot be left untold. Don Quixote's host in Barcelona is Don Antonio Moreno, a gentleman of wealth and intelligence.

Moreno loves fair, good-natured diversion, and with the knight in his house he sets about devising ways to draw out his mad points in harmless fashion. Jests that give pain, the narrator notes, are no jests. A talking head and a printing house await, in a city episode that tests the knight among wits rather than giants.
the-life-of-samuel-taylor-coleridge-1838:
James Gillman published his life of Samuel Taylor Coleridge in 1838, written by a friend who had housed the poet in his last years. His preface praises Izaak Walton lives of eminent men for sweetness and simplicity. Walton angling book fame, Gillman notes, hides biographies that flow like a gentle stream.

Gillman borrows a long passage from Walton preface to Donne sermons as a fit frame for Coleridge. The dedication honors Joseph Henry Green, Coleridge faithful friend and medical adviser. Readers get a memoir shaped by personal care, talk, and opium era sorrow at Highgate.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, October 11, 1828, No. 335, illustrates Lavenham Church in Suffolk. Lavenham was once eminent for manufactures, with eight or nine cloth halls and rich clothiers. The De Veres, earls of Oxford, held the manor from Henry I's reign to Elizabeth's, and one earl won his tenants toll-free passage throughout England. Manufacture has since dwindled to woollen yarn, calimancoes, and hempen cloth.

The church, though, is accounted the most beautiful fabric of its kind in Suffolk. Freestone and curious flintwork build its 150 feet of length and 68 of breadth. The De Veres and the Springs, wealthy clothiers, built it together, their arms quartered on the fabric. Its porch is enriched with shields and garters of noble families, and the letters I.O. probably mark John, fourteenth Earl of Oxford. Readers see a cloth town's profits frozen into one splendid parish church.

A supplementary number of the Mirror, No. 373, reviews Sir Walter Scott's new novel Anne of Geierstein, or The Maiden of the Mist. Scott's fertility, the reviewer says, leaves the rhetoric of admiration and the vocabulary of criticism nearly exhausted. The Waverley incognito is removed, the piece notes, but none of the genuine fame with it. Their popularity, it predicts, will outlive hundreds of matter-of-fact works.

The novels are praised as more than pictures in which fact and fancy meet under a masterly hand. They abound, the reviewer argues, in knowledge of the human heart and mastery of its passions. Scott strikes at once at feeling and common sense rather than appealing tediously to judgment. Chapter endings work like good stage exits, ensuring curiosity for the next page. Having overrun Scotland, England, France, Palestine, and Germany, the author is followed into Switzerland in this notice.

Pontefract Castle as it looked in 1648 illustrates volume 19, No. 531, dated January 28, 1832. Pontefract in Yorkshire lies near Ferrybridge, east of Wakefield and north-west of Doncaster. Even the town's name is disputed in the opening account.

One legend derives Pontefract from a broken bridge and a fall into the River Aire, after which St. William of York saved the victims. The writers note, though, that the town bore the name in charters decades before that supposed miracle. In Saxon times it was called Kirkby. After the Norman Conquest, William gave the manor to Ilbert de Lacy, who built the castle over twelve years, finishing in 1080.
the-principles-of-phrenology-1838: Sidney Smith's Principles of Phrenology was printed at Edinburgh in 1838, as the title page's Roman numerals read. A long Bonnet quotation imagines a being who could read the brain's organs as we read print. The opening leaves also carry a Boston Medical Library stamp and the Internet Archive's 2010 digitization note, with funding from the Open Knowledge Commons and Harvard Medical School. Nothing beyond the title pages is present in the leaves provided.
the-tale-of-peter-rabbit-pg14838:
Frederick Warne first published Beatrix Potter's Peter Rabbit in 1902, the book that began her famous series of small animal tales. Four young rabbits, Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter, live with their mother beneath a huge fir-tree's roots. One morning she sends them into the fields or down the lane. She forbids Mr. McGregor's garden, where their father had an accident and was put in a pie.

Then she goes out herself, trusting the little rabbits to keep out of mischief. Peter, of course, is the one least likely to obey. Potter's calm warning and the pie detail give the garden adventure its quiet danger, and generations of children have followed Peter through the gate ever since.
tob-0038:
Senator Frank Church led the Senate committee that pried open the secrets of United States intelligence in 1975. Its interim report on alleged assassination plots examined claims that the CIA had plotted to kill foreign leaders, among them Fidel Castro of Cuba and Patrice Lumumba of the Congo.

Rafael Trujillo and Ngo Dinh Diem also figure in the charges and evidence. The committee traced orders, memos, and denials through layers of official fog. Its findings shocked the country and led in time to a standing ban on political assassination by United States agents. Modern oversight of the spy agencies starts here.
tob-0138:
A second catalog copy of John Robison's 1797 Proofs of a Conspiracy presents the famous exposé of an alleged Illuminati plot. Secret societies and Masonic lodges, in Robison's telling, concealed a hidden hand behind the French Revolution and a campaign against all religions and governments of Europe. The duplicate record mirrors the book's own wide, repeated circulation.

Robison's charges taught the English-speaking world to fear the secret society as a political weapon. Presidents and pamphleteers answered him, and the template he set, suppressed order, infiltrated lodges, revolution as engineered plot, still structures conspiracy writing. Readers can consult either copy; the text is the founding document in duplicate.
tob-13138:
E. A. Wallis Budge, the great Victorian Egyptologist, gave English readers the Egyptian Book of the Dead in his pioneering translation. Spells, hymns, and underworld maps were buried with pharaohs and scribes to secure safe passage after death. Budge drew on papyri held in the British Museum, where he worked.

The weighing of the heart against a feather, the forty-two judges before whom the dead declare innocence, and the Field of Reeds promised to the justified all appear. Budge's renderings have been corrected by later Egyptology, yet his edition carried these texts to a wide public for the first time and still reads powerfully.
tob-13338:
Paramahansa Yogananda published his Autobiography of a Yogi in 1946, and the memoir did more than any other single book to bring yoga to America. Yogananda tells of his Bengali childhood, his search for a master, and his meeting with his guru, Sri Yukteswar. Training, travel, and teaching in India fill the first half.

Encounters with saints, reports of miracles, and conversations with figures such as Mahatma Gandhi give the narrative its wonder-tale quality. Yogananda then crosses to the United States, where he founded the Self-Realization Fellowship. Part spiritual autobiography and part introduction to Kriya Yoga, the book has guided millions of Western readers onto the path ever since.
tob-4138:
Paracelsus, the fiery Swiss physician born Theophrastus von Hohenheim, gets his English dress in Waite's translation of his hermetic and alchemical writings. Volume one covers the elements, the arcana of nature, and his attacks on the medicine of the schools. Paracelsus called himself the Luther of healing, and he wrote like it.

Disease, for him, has seeds and signatures that the wise physician reads in nature herself. Alchemy serves medicine, not gold-making greed. The prose erupts with scorn, prayer, and sudden insight. Verified from the 1919 edition, Waite's first volume gives the Renaissance rebel at full voice, in Victorian English.
treatises-on-physiology-and-phrenology-1:
P. M. Roget's treatises on physiology and phrenology were reprinted at Edinburgh in 1838 by Adam and Charles Black. They come from the seventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica. Roget was secretary of the Royal Society and professor of physiology at the Royal Institution.

His preface explains why the physiology article had to be written fresh. The science had improved so greatly since the former edition that patching the old text would not do. Roget took the commission at the editor's request. Readers get a leading doctor's survey of the body's functions, paired with the era's popular science of phrenology.
un-ga-res-38:
Panama came to the young United Nations with a draft Declaration on the Rights and Duties of States. It was a bid to write down the basic rules of how states must treat each other. Resolution 38, passed on 11 December 1946, sets the draft on a long road of review. The Secretary-General must send the text at once to all member states and to bodies that work on world law.

Comments were due back by 1 June 1947. The draft then goes to a new Assembly team charged with the study of how world law should be codified. That team must report to the second regular session, and the question earns a place on that session's agenda.
un-ga-res-58-238:
Guatemala asked for one more year of the UN watch, and Resolution 58/238, passed in 2003, weighs the plea. The Verification Mission in Guatemala had its term stretched through 2003 by a vote of the year before. The state restated its pledge to put the peace deals into full force. The follow-up team's timetable for the work now ran through 2004.

The text takes note of the state's wish to keep the mission through the end of 2004. A new state team would take office in January 2004, and the mission's watch in that first year counts for much. Civic groups in the land, and the world at large, had voiced worry at parts of the peace that still lagged. The plea is taken up in that light.
un-ga-res-a-69-38:
Trust between states can be built in space as on earth, argues Resolution A/69/38, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls a chain of texts since 2005 on trust-building steps in outer space. It also recalls a 1993 report of the Secretary-General, which held a study by state experts on how such steps could work above the earth.

All states hold the right to study and use space under world law, the text affirms. To bar an arms race in space serves peace for all, and it is a must for joint work in the peaceful use of space. Open word on space plans, shared by all, is the path the vote commends.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 38 was adopted on 11 December 1946, at the fifty-fifth plenary meeting. It set the draft Declaration on the Rights and Duties of States in motion. The Assembly told the Secretary-General to send the draft, put forward by Panama, at once to all member states. He was to send it also to bodies working on international law. He was to ask for their comments and views before 1 June 1947. He was to pass what came back to its new committee on writing down international law.

Resolution 58/238 of 23 December 2003 is the General Assembly's final Guatemala verification decision. It renews the United Nations Verification Mission in Guatemala for 2004. That was the last year of the agreed peace implementation timetable. The text reviews the mission's reports and the Secretary-General's account of the peace process.

For its closing phase the mission is told to concentrate on human rights. It is told to concentrate on demilitarization and strengthening civilian power. The Assembly voices concern at intimidation aimed at justice officials, human rights defenders, and journalists. It also welcomes an agreement for a United Nations human rights office to open in Guatemala in 2004. That way monitoring would continue after the mission itself wound down. The decision thus planned an orderly handover rather than an abrupt end to a decade of verification.

Resolution 69/38 of the General Assembly backs transparency and confidence-building measures in outer space work. The Assembly urges member states to review and apply the measures put forward by its Group of Governmental Experts in its 2013 report. They should do so by choice, through national mechanisms. It sends recommendations to the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space, the Disarmament Commission, and the Conference on Disarmament. It decides to convene a meeting of its First and Fourth Committees. The meeting is on challenges to space security and sustainability.
un-sc-res-1038: One of the Council's formal texts, Resolution 1038 is carried in this catalog under 1992. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1338:
East Timor's road to independence shaped a mandate renewal on 31 January 2001. The Secretary-General had reported on 16 January, and the goal was independence by the end of 2001. The United Nations Transitional Administration, UNTAET, was handing more power to East Timorese hands. Large numbers of refugees still sat in camps in West Timor, where militia activity threatened them.

The Council extended UNTAET's mandate to 31 January 2002. The special representative was told to keep delegating authority to the East Timorese people as a core part of the transition. Donors and financial bodies were called to fund the territory's needs, including the creation of an East Timor defence force. UNTAET had to answer the militia threat with robust action under resolution 1272 (1999). The Council also backed fixes to the justice system and a full solution to the refugee problem across the border.
un-sc-res-138:
Resolution 138, adopted on 23 June 1960, examines Argentina's complaint about Adolf Eichmann. Israeli agents had seized Eichmann, a former Nazi officer accused of mass crimes against the Jews, and taken him from Argentina to Israel to stand trial. Argentina said the transfer violated its sovereignty.

The Council agrees that violating a member state's sovereignty clashes with the Charter, and warns that repeats of such acts would breed insecurity and distrust. At the same time, it notes the worldwide condemnation of Nazi persecution and the wish that Eichmann face proper justice. It states plainly that the resolution must not be read as excusing the crimes he was accused of.
un-sc-res-1438: The catalog's entries for 2002 include Resolution 1438 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1538:
Claims of corruption in Iraq's oil-for-food program reached the Council in 2004. News reports had questioned how the program was run. On 21 April 2004 the Council welcomed an independent high-level inquiry. The probe would study efforts by Iraq's former government to evade sanctions. Bribery, kickbacks, and surcharges on oil sales were named. So were illicit payments tied to humanitarian goods.

The Council calls on all states to cooperate fully with the inquiry. The Coalition Provisional Authority in Iraq had the same duty. National regulators were singled out as holders of key records. The Council said it looked forward to the final report. The inquiry's findings later confirmed large-scale abuse of the program.
un-sc-res-1638:
Liberia's former president faced arrest if he came home, under a 2005 ruling. Charles Taylor had left power in 2003 and taken shelter in Nigeria. He stood indicted by the Special Court for Sierra Leone. That court charged him over his role in Sierra Leone's civil war. On 11 November 2005 the Security Council added a task to its Liberia mission. The Council thanked Nigeria for helping to calm the region.

UNMIL troops gained the power to seize Taylor if he returned to Liberia. They would hold him and send him to Sierra Leone for trial. He did try to flee Nigeria months later and was caught. He was then sent to face the court. The mandate is a rare case of peacekeepers ordered to arrest a named man.
un-sc-res-1738:
War reporting gained formal protection in Resolution 1738, adopted in December 2006. Journalists were being killed and kidnapped in growing numbers in Iraq and other conflicts. The Council stated clearly that media workers in war zones count as civilians under the law of war.

The text condemns deliberate attacks on reporters, demands their release when seized, and reminds fighters that news equipment is not a military target. It also asks the Secretary-General to track the issue in his reporting. For readers, the resolution is the Security Council's clearest statement that silencing witnesses is itself a crime of war.
un-sc-res-1938:
Liberia's mission gained a further year by a decision of 15 September 2010. The Secretary-General's report of 11 August 2010 advised the renewal. Liberia's Truth and Reconciliation Commission had sent its final report. Progress on the drawdown benchmarks, above all the national police, was mixed, and violent crime stayed a real problem.

The Council let UNMIL help the Liberian government, as asked, with its 2011 polls for president and parliament. Help would cover transport, secure conditions, and joint work with the poll commission. Free, fair, and peaceful elections were made a core benchmark for the mission's drawdown. UNMIL and the government were told to press on with plans for handing security duties to Liberian authorities. The Secretary-General would send a technical team after the elections to set timelines for further troop cuts.
un-sc-res-2338: Kept under number 2338, a Security Council resolution survives in official-record form through English Wikisource. The number jumps ahead in the sequence preserved by this collection, into the Council's later output. The text at that address is complete: stated grounds, recalled precedents, and numbered decisions, kept together as the members issued them.
un-sc-res-238: Adopted by the Security Council and numbered 238, this formal text is catalogued under the year 1967. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-338:
The October war of 1973 had run for two weeks when the Council set its terms on 22 October. Israel was fighting Egypt and Syria. Resolution 338 is short, with only three points, but it became one of the Council's best-known texts. It was adopted that day, in the middle of the fighting.

All parties to the fighting had to cease all firing at once. All military activity had to end no later than twelve hours after the decision was adopted. The forces would stop in the positions they then held. Right after the cease-fire, the parties had to start carrying out Resolution 242 of 1967, in all its parts. Talks also had to start at the same time, under suitable auspices. Their aim was a just and lasting peace in the Middle East.
un-sc-res-38:
India and Pakistan faced the Council together for the first time in January 1948. The subject was Kashmir, disputed since the partition of British India. On 17 January 1948 the Council heard both governments. It noted the urgency of the situation. Days earlier its president had urged restraint on both sides, and both had pledged to honor the Charter.

The resolution calls on India and Pakistan to calm the situation at once. They should use every means they have, including appeals to their own people. They must avoid statements or acts that could make matters worse. Each government also had to tell the Council at once of any material change. The vote was nine to none, with two abstentions.
un-sc-res-738:
Security Council Resolution 738, adopted on January 29, 1992, recommended Tajikistan for membership in the United Nations. Tajikistan had declared independence from the Soviet Union in September 1991, weeks before the union itself came apart. The poorest of the new central Asian republics, it moved at once to claim a place in the world body.

The Assembly admitted Tajikistan on March 2, in the same wave as its neighbors. Within months the country slid into a civil war that lasted five years, which makes this calm formal vote read like the quiet before a storm. The short text still marks the legal start of Tajikistan's life as a sovereign state.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1038, adopted on 15 January 1996, authorizes United Nations military observers to keep monitoring the demilitarization of the Prevlaka peninsula for a further three months. One more three-month extension is possible, if the Secretary-General reports it would continue to lower tension. Prevlaka, disputed between Croatia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had been demilitarized under a 1992 joint declaration. The Council also asks for a report by 15 March 1996. The report is on progress toward a peaceful settlement, and on whether another organization might take over the monitoring.

Resolution 1338, adopted unanimously on 31 January 2001, steers East Timor through its last year before independence. The UN transitional administration, UNTAET, was governing the territory after the violence of 1999. The Secretary-General's January report backed giving East Timorese a growing share in running their own affairs, with independence aimed for the end of 2001.

The Council extended UNTAET's mandate for another year, to January 2002. It urged further steps to hand authority to the East Timorese as an essential part of the transition, and backed plans for free and fair elections run with them. It also repeated a warning from its own visiting mission: strong international support would still be needed after independence day.

Argentina's complaint over the capture of Adolf Eichmann is the business of this text from 23 June 1960. Eichmann, accused of mass crimes against Jews under Nazi rule, had been taken from Argentina to Israel to face trial. Argentina argued the transfer violated its sovereignty as a member state.

The Council declared that acts harming a member state's sovereignty could endanger world peace if repeated. It asked Israel to make proper reparation under the Charter and the rules of international law. At the same time, it stressed that nothing in the text excused the crimes Eichmann was accused of, which the world condemned.

Bomb attacks in Bali, Indonesia, two days earlier are condemned on 14 October 2002. The blasts of 12 October killed and injured large numbers of people. Other recent terrorist attacks in various countries are cited in the same breath.

Deepest sympathy goes to Indonesia's government and people and to the victims and their families. All states are urged, under their duties in resolution 1373, to work urgently with the Indonesian authorities. The aim is to find and bring to justice those who carried out, organized, and sponsored the attacks. The Council also restates its resolve to fight terrorism in all its forms.

Serious corruption claims hung over the Iraq oil-for-food programme in 2004. Reports alleged bribes, kickbacks, and surcharges on oil deals. Saddam Hussein's government had gamed the system for years. Resolution 1538, adopted unanimously on 21 April 2004, backed a full investigation. The Secretary-General had already decided to launch one.

The Council welcomed the independent high-level inquiry. It called on Iraq, the Coalition Provisional Authority, and all states to cooperate fully. Regulators everywhere were asked to help. The text brands illegal acts by UN staff or contractors unacceptable. The inquiry, later led by Paul Volcker, became a landmark UN scandal probe. Its final report was awaited eagerly.

The label on this file names Iraq's war. The text is pure Liberia. Charles Taylor, the past Liberian strongman, sat in exile in Nigeria. A war crimes court in Sierra Leone had charged him. His crimes were said to span both lands' wars. Word spread that he might slip home. Resolution 1638 passed on 11 November 2005.

A new task was glued to the UN force in Liberia. If Taylor set foot in the land, UN troops had to seize and hold him. They would hand him to Sierra Leone for trial. The Liberian and Sierra Leonean states, and the Council, had to be kept in the loop. Praise went to Nigeria for sheltering him for a time, with world backing. His homecoming was ruled a threat to peace in the whole area.

Attacks on journalists and other media workers in armed conflict are condemned on 23 December 2006. Reporters were being killed, wounded, and kidnapped in war zones in rising numbers. Journalists on dangerous professional missions count as civilians under the Geneva Conventions, the Council recalls, and must be protected as such.

All parties to armed conflicts are demanded to stop deliberate attacks on journalists, media staff, and their equipment, and to end the culture of impunity for such acts. States are reminded of their duty to prosecute those responsible for grave breaches of humanitarian law against civilians, including media workers. The safety of journalists will also be addressed when peacekeeping mandates are set up and renewed.

Resolution 1938, passed on 15 September 2010, keeps the UN force in Liberia for one more year. A UN report of August 2010 urged the move. The Council cheered Liberia's work on mending its wounds and on growth. It praised steps against graft and for state grip on mines, farms, and woods. It also noted the truth panel's final report. That report gave Liberians a chance to talk through the roots of their war.

The force, UNMIL, won a new term to September 2011. Its drawdown was to be judged by set marks, most of all the growth of Liberia's own police. Some marks had been met. Others lagged. A UN team was to help plan the next cuts.

Resolution 2038, adopted on 29 February 2012, staffs the court that will inherit the Rwanda tribunal's unfinished business. The International Residual Mechanism was created in 2010 to take over from the war crimes tribunals for Rwanda and Yugoslavia as they closed. Its Rwanda branch was due to start work on 1 July 2012, and it needed a prosecutor.

The Council appointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the job, effective 1 March 2012, for a four-year term. Jallow was already prosecutor of the Rwanda tribunal, and the rules allowed him to hold both posts at once. The appointment kept one hand on the tiller as fugitive cases and archives passed to the successor court.

Cyprus is the subject of Resolution 2338, adopted on 26 January 2017. Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot leaders were negotiating a full settlement to reunite the divided island. Cyprus's government agreed that UNFICYP, the United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, should stay beyond the end of January.

The Council extended UNFICYP's mandate until 31 July 2017. It welcomed the progress in the talks between the two leaders. Both sides were urged to seize the moment and secure a complete settlement. The text pressed for steps that build trust. More crossing points on the Green Line and renewed mine clearing in the buffer zone were named. The Committee on Missing Persons was also to get fuller access to its work.

Cyprus's peacekeeping force received another extension on 19 June 1967, when the Council adopted Resolution 238 unanimously. A report from the Secretary-General said the force was still needed to keep the peace on the island. The government of Cyprus agreed that it should stay beyond 26 June.

The Council reaffirmed its line of Cyprus resolutions reaching back to Resolution 186 of 1964. It urged the parties to show the utmost restraint. They were also asked to keep working together toward the Council's aims. The force's stay was extended for six months, ending on 26 December 1967. The Council expected that enough progress toward a solution would be made by then. That progress might let the force withdraw or shrink.

In the middle of the Yom Kippur War, the Council ordered the guns to stop. On 22 October 1973, it adopted Resolution 338. Egypt and Syria had attacked Israel just over two weeks before. Fighting still raged on two fronts when the Council met.

The text calls on all parties to cease fire at once. All military action must end within twelve hours. The sides must hold the ground they then stood on. Next, they must carry out Resolution 242, the land-for-peace formula of 1967. Talks toward a just and lasting peace must start at the same time. Those paired demands framed Middle East diplomacy for decades.

Kashmir's first winter of war drew the Council's opening plea in 1948. On 17 January, it adopted Resolution 38. Nine members voted yes and none voted no. The Ukrainian and Soviet republics held back. India and Pakistan had been free states for five months. Both were fighting over the princely state of Kashmir. Both had told the Council they meant to honor the UN Charter.

The text calls on both governments to act at once. All steps in their power must be used to calm the crisis. Public appeals to their own peoples are named as one such step. No words or acts may make things worse. Any big change must be reported to the Council straight away.

Tajikistan took its seat on the edge of civil war in 1992. On 29 January, the Council adopted Resolution 738 without a vote. The same round of meetings handled Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The Republic of Tajikistan had claimed freedom the September before. The Soviet Union was then in its last weeks. Tajikistan was the poorest of the Central Asian republics.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Tajikistan. Admission followed in March 1992. War broke out at home within months of the vote. The new state's first UN years were spent asking for aid. The seat it won here became its lifeline to the world.
